'What part of the changes feels the hardest?'
'Tell me more about what is wearing you out.'
qs.e: 'You would feel better if you just tried harder' judges the client's effort, which is the assigned nontherapeutic barrier. Reflecting burden and asking for more detail are therapeutic.

qs.q: Which roles are assigned in each group for this therapeutic and nontherapeutic role-play? Select all that apply.
c: Patient
Therapeutic nurse
Nontherapeutic nurse
Narrator
Observer/feedback coach
Unit secretary
qs.e: Every group assigns a patient, therapeutic nurse, nontherapeutic nurse, and narrator. The observer/feedback coach is added only to the single group of 5, and a unit secretary is not one of the activity roles.

qs.q: Which expectations apply when students build their skit? Select all that apply.
c: Create your own dialogue; the scenario is a starting point
Keep the interaction realistic and respectful
Use course materials to support your choices
End by explaining why one response is therapeutic and the other is not
Memorize the scenario dialogue word for word
Make the scene as dramatic as possible
qs.e: Students write their own dialogue, keep it realistic and respectful, support choices with course materials, and close by explaining the difference. Word-for-word memorization and over-dramatizing contradict the instructions.

qs.q: Which timing suggestions are given for the activity? Select all that apply.
c: Group preparation: 8–10 minutes
Skits: 2–3 minutes each
Debrief: 1 minute per skit
Group preparation: 30 minutes
Skits: 10 minutes each
Debrief: 5 minutes per skit
qs.e: The slide recommends 8–10 minutes to prepare, 2–3 minutes per skit, and a 1-minute debrief per skit. The longer times would make the activity unmanageable with 21 groups.

qs.q: Which fields appear in the Role Assignments section of the Student Dialogue Planner? Select all that apply.
c: Narrator
Patient
Therapeutic nurse
Nontherapeutic nurse
Observer/feedback coach
Charge nurse
qs.e: The planner's role assignments list narrator, patient, therapeutic nurse, and nontherapeutic nurse. Observer/feedback coach belongs to the group-of-5 structure, not the planner's role lines.

qs.q: Which narrator responsibilities are described in the Student Dialogue Planner? Select all that apply.
c: Introduce the setting and the patient's concern
Briefly explain that two different nursing responses will be demonstrated
Explain why the therapeutic response worked
Explain why the nontherapeutic response was ineffective
Deliver the nurse's therapeutic dialogue
Demonstrate the communication barrier
qs.e: The narrator sets the scene and then explains and wraps up why one response worked and the other did not. The nurse lines belong to the therapeutic and nontherapeutic nurses.

qs.q: Which elements should the patient include in a follow-up response during rehearsal? Select all that apply.
c: Words
Tone
Facial expression
Body language
Vital signs
Laboratory results
qs.e: The patient's follow-up response includes words, tone, facial expression, and body language. Vital signs and lab results are not part of the acting cues for this activity.

qs.q: Which items are on the rehearsal Final Check? Select all that apply.
c: Both nurses responded to the same patient concern
The assigned techniques are clear
The scene is realistic and respectful
The narrator explains why the responses differ
The skit is at least 5 minutes long
A full reference list is submitted
qs.e: The four check boxes confirm the same patient concern, clear assigned techniques, a realistic and respectful scene, and the narrator's explanation. Skit length and references are not check box items.

qs.q: Which patient acting cues belong to Scenario 1 (the angry ED waiting-area patient)? Select all that apply.
c: Speak sharply
Glance toward the desk
Interrupt once
The patient is upset but not threatening
Cry uncontrollably
Refuse all contact
qs.e: The cues are speaking sharply, glancing toward the desk, and interrupting once — upset but not threatening. Uncontrolled crying or refusing contact would change the scenario the group is assigned.

qs.q: Which instructions apply when using humor as the therapeutic technique in Scenario 2? Select all that apply.
c: Keep the humor gentle
Let the humor be patient-led
Pair the humor with a real answer to the concern
Stop and use another supportive approach if the patient does not respond positively
Use sarcasm to lighten the mood
Continue the humor even if the patient withdraws
qs.e: Humor must be gentle, patient-led, and paired with a real answer, and it stops if the patient does not respond positively. Sarcasm or pushing through a negative reaction is not therapeutic.

qs.q: Which behaviors demonstrate the nontherapeutic barrier of failure to listen in Scenario 3? Select all that apply.
c: Looking distracted
Changing the subject
Responding without attending to the concern
Pausing before answering
Speaking quietly
Avoiding eye contact
qs.e: Looking distracted, changing the subject, and responding without attending are the failure-to-listen behaviors. Pausing, quiet speech, and avoiding eye contact are the patient's acting cues, not the nurse's barrier.

qs.q: Which nurse actions belong to the therapeutic response in Scenario 5 (preoperative anxiety)? Select all that apply.
c: Acknowledge the fear
Explain what the team can do
Offer to find answers to specific questions
Do not promise an outcome
Guarantee that nothing bad will happen
Refer procedure-specific questions to the appropriate surgical team member
qs.e: The nurse acknowledges the fear, explains the team's role, offers to find answers, avoids promising outcomes, and refers procedure questions to the surgical team. Guaranteeing nothing bad will happen is the nontherapeutic barrier.

qs.q: Which patient acting cues belong to Scenario 6 (the frustrated hypertension client)? Select all that apply.
c: Fold your arms
Sound frustrated rather than indifferent
Speak sharply and interrupt once
Pull your arm close to your body
Pause before answering
Fidget with the blanket
qs.e: Scenario 6 cues are folding the arms and sounding frustrated rather than indifferent. The sharp interruptions, arm pulling, pausing, and blanket fidgeting are cues from other scenarios.

qs.q: Which are the therapeutic techniques assigned across the six scenarios? Select all that apply.
c: Reflective question or comment
Using appropriate, gentle humor
Exploring statement
Open-ended questions
Offering realistic reassurance and support
Active listening
qs.e: Each scenario pairs one therapeutic technique: reflection (1), gentle humor (2), exploring (3), open-ended questions (4), realistic reassurance (5), and active listening (6).

qs.q: Which are the nontherapeutic barriers assigned across the six scenarios? Select all that apply.
c: Aggressive behavior
Arguing
Failure to listen
Accusatory 'why' questions
False reassurance or promises
Judgmental comments
qs.e: The six barriers map one-to-one to scenarios 1–6. None of these match the therapeutic technique paired with the same scenario.

qs.q: How many distinct scenarios does this communication activity include?
qs.e: Slide 1 lists 20 distinct scenarios covering patient-centered communication and clinical judgment.

qs.q: The recommended grouping for 82 students totals how many students in groups of 4?
qs.e: 20 groups of 4 = 80 students, with the remaining 2 students placed in one group of 5.

qs.q: How many minutes are suggested for group preparation?
qs.e: Group preparation is timed at 8–10 minutes, long enough to write dialogue but short enough for 21 groups.

qs.q: Each skit should run approximately how many minutes?
qs.e: Skits run 2–3 minutes each; longer skits would crowd out other groups and the debrief.

qs.q: How many minutes of debrief are suggested per skit?
qs.e: Debrief is 1 minute per skit — just enough for the narrator to explain the difference between the two responses.

qs.q: In which setting does Scenario 1 take place?
qs.e: Scenario 1 is the angry patient in the emergency department waiting area, a long-wait complaint setting.

qs.q: What nontherapeutic barrier is assigned to Scenario 1?
qs.e: Scenario 1 pairs the reflective question or comment with the nontherapeutic barrier of aggressive behavior.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 2 (the IV start)?
qs.e: Scenario 2 uses appropriate, gentle humor, which must still be paired with a real answer to the patient's fear.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 3 (the client expressing hopelessness)?
qs.e: Scenario 3 uses an exploring statement to find out what 'no point' means to this patient.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 4 (the client who does not understand the plan)?
qs.e: Scenario 4 uses open-ended questions; the nontherapeutic counterpart is accusatory 'why' questions.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 5 (the anxious preoperative client)?
qs.e: Scenario 5 uses realistic reassurance and support, never a promise about the outcome.

qs.q: What chronic condition is the focus of the Scenario 6 follow-up visit?
qs.e: Scenario 6 is a hypertension follow-up visit where the client is worn out by pills and diet changes.

qs.q: At what point must the Student Dialogue Planner be completed?
qs.e: The Dialogue Planner is to be completed before rehearsal so the group can build and refine its dialogue (Slide 4 footer: COMPLETE BEFORE REHEARSAL).

qs.q: A client says, “I know my blood pressure is high, but I’m worn out from pills and changing everything I eat.” Which response best demonstrates active listening?
c: “You need to be more responsible.”
“Taking pills and changing your eating habits have become exhausting for you.”
“Let me explain your options before you say more.”
“You are choosing to be noncompliant.”
qs.e: Reflecting the burden and listening without interrupting demonstrate active listening. Labeling the client or moving to options before hearing the concern does not.

qs.q: Which nurse statements are judgmental responses to the client who is tired of managing high blood pressure? Select all that apply.
c: “You are being lazy.”
“You are irresponsible about your health.”
“You are just noncompliant.”
“What makes taking your pills difficult?”
“Changing your eating habits sounds burdensome.”
qs.e: Lazy, irresponsible, and noncompliant are the labels identified as nontherapeutic. Exploring difficulty and reflecting burden avoid those judgments.

qs.q: Before discussing options with the care team, which barriers should the nurse explore with this client? Select all that apply.
c: Medication cost
Side effects
Daily routines
Food access
Whether the client deserves a label of noncompliance
qs.e: The clinical note specifically identifies cost, side effects, routines, and food access as barriers to explore. Assigning a judgmental label is not barrier assessment.

qs.q: A student portrays the client who feels worn out by blood pressure management. Which performance follows the acting cues?
c: Fold the arms and sound frustrated.
Remain indifferent and unconcerned.
Become tearful and silently hold a tissue.
Brace the abdomen before standing.
qs.e: This role calls for folded arms and frustration rather than indifference. The other physical cues belong to different scenarios.

qs.q: The designated therapeutic technique for the client exhausted by blood pressure management is ______.
qs.e: Active listening includes hearing the client without interruption and reflecting the burden. Immediately discussing options skips the exploration emphasized in this scenario.

qs.q: After her mother's death, a family member says, “I don’t know how I’m supposed to go home without her.” Which response is most appropriate?
c: “Everything happens for a reason.”
“What kind of support would feel helpful right now?”
“Let me tell you about my own loss.”
“You need to feel better before going home.”
qs.e: Asking what support would help offers emotional support without assumptions. A stock phrase such as “Everything happens for a reason” is a cliché.

qs.q: Which actions support therapeutic communication with the grieving family member? Select all that apply.
c: Ask what support would feel helpful.
When appropriate, ask about spiritual practices that matter to the family.
When appropriate, ask about cultural practices that matter to the family.
Assume the family's beliefs from their appearance.
Try to make the grief feel better immediately.
qs.e: Support should be guided by the family's expressed needs and relevant spiritual or cultural practices. The slide warns against assuming beliefs or trying to resolve grief immediately.

qs.q: Which response to a grieving family member requires follow-up?
c: “What support would help you?”
“Are there cultural practices that matter to your family?”
“Everything happens for a reason.”
“Would you like to tell me what matters to you right now?”
qs.e: “Everything happens for a reason” is the slide's example of a nontherapeutic cliché. Individualized questions about support do not impose a stock explanation for the loss.

qs.q: Which acting cues belong to the grieving family member role? Select all that apply.
c: Become tearful.
Pause.
Hold a tissue without speaking for a moment.
Check a phone and shrug.
Attempt to stand while looking frightened.
qs.e: Tearfulness, pauses, and silently holding a tissue portray this grieving family member. Looking frightened while attempting to stand belongs to the newly confused client scenario.

qs.q: Complete the designated technique: Offering emotional or ______ support.
qs.e: The technique is offering emotional or spiritual support. Spiritual support should not be based on assumptions about the family's beliefs.

qs.q: A client is newly confused after a procedure and asks, “Where am I?” Which response follows the demonstrated reorientation sequence?
c: Offer a next step, then leave without explanation.
Introduce yourself, calmly explain where the client is and why, and offer a simple next step.
Tell the client not to worry and discuss options later.
Ask the client to stop being silly before introducing yourself.
qs.e: The demonstrated sequence is introduction, calm explanation of place and reason, then a simple next step. Minimizing the concern does not reorient the client.

qs.q: A client develops new confusion after a procedure. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: Assess the new confusion.
Report it promptly.
Protect the client from falls.
Assume it is a normal part of aging.
Tell the client the concern is silly.
qs.e: New confusion requires assessment, prompt reporting, and fall protection. It must not be dismissed as normal aging.

qs.q: Which statement minimizes the concerns of a frightened, confused client?
c: “I am your nurse.”
“You are in the hospital after your procedure.”
“Let me explain a simple next step.”
“You are being silly; there is nothing to worry about.”
qs.e: Calling the client silly or saying there is nothing to worry about minimizes the concern. Calmly explaining the situation presents reality instead.

qs.q: Which cues are specified for the newly confused older client? Select all that apply.
c: Look around the room.
Attempt to stand.
Appear frightened.
Pull sleeves over the hands.
Present an already-final decision about treatment.
qs.e: The role includes looking around, attempting to stand, and appearing frightened. Pulling sleeves over the hands belongs to the body image scenario.

qs.q: Complete the technique for the newly confused client: Presenting reality and ______.
qs.e: Presenting reality and reorientation address the client's uncertainty about the situation. Reassuring the client that nothing is wrong does not replace assessment of new confusion.

qs.q: A hospitalized adolescent says, “My friends barely text me anymore. I think they’ve forgotten about me.” Which response best uses mirroring?
c: “It sounds like you feel forgotten by your friends.”
“This is just teen drama.”
“You should stop checking your phone.”
“Your concern is not important right now.”
qs.e: Mirroring reflects the central feeling or meaning and allows the adolescent to respond. Dismissing the concern as teen drama is specifically discouraged.

qs.q: Which nurse behaviors demonstrate nonverbal boredom in the isolated adolescent scenario? Select all that apply.
c: Sighing
Checking a phone
Looking at the clock
Appearing uninterested
Reflecting the adolescent's central feeling
Allowing the adolescent to respond
qs.e: The slide lists sighing, checking a phone, looking at the clock, and appearing uninterested as nontherapeutic cues. Reflecting meaning and allowing a response are therapeutic.

qs.q: Which action is most appropriate when discussing the adolescent's isolation from friends?
c: Dismiss it as teen drama.
Maintain privacy and speak respectfully.
Reflect the feeling but do not allow a response.
Check the time repeatedly while listening.
qs.e: The clinical note emphasizes privacy and respectful communication. Reflecting a feeling without allowing the adolescent to respond is incomplete mirroring.

qs.q: Which acting sequence is specified for the isolated adolescent?
c: Look at the phone, place it face down, and shrug.
Reach toward the nurse, then hesitate.
Brace the abdomen and hesitate before standing.
Fold the arms and sound frustrated about pills.
qs.e: Looking at the phone, putting it face down, and shrugging are the assigned cues. Reaching toward the nurse belongs to the client afraid of dying.

qs.q: The isolated adolescent scenario pairs restating with the equivalent technique of ______.
qs.e: Restating or mirroring reflects the central feeling or meaning. It is not an opportunity to replace the adolescent's concern with advice.

qs.q: After difficult chemotherapy cycles, a client says, “I’m not sure it’s worth it.” Which response is most appropriate?
c: “You cannot give up now.”
“What does ‘not worth it’ mean to you, and what matters most right now?”
“I will consider your decision final.”
“You should be ashamed of stopping.”
qs.e: Clarification explores the client's meaning and current priorities. The scenario does not present the decision as already final.

qs.q: Which responses are disapproving communication toward the client questioning chemotherapy? Select all that apply.
c: Scolding the client
Shaming the client
Implying that the client is giving up
Asking what matters most now
Clarifying what “not worth it” means
qs.e: Scolding, shaming, and implying that the client is giving up are the specified nontherapeutic behaviors. Clarifying values and meaning supports understanding instead.

qs.q: Which actions follow the clinical note for a client considering whether to continue chemotherapy? Select all that apply.
c: Support informed decision-making.
Avoid pressuring the client.
Communicate concerns and questions to the oncology team.
Treat uncertainty as a final refusal.
Shame the client into continuing.
qs.e: The nurse supports informed decisions without pressure and shares concerns and questions with the oncology team. Uncertainty should not be converted into a final decision.

qs.q: Which portrayal follows the acting cues for the client questioning chemotherapy?
c: Speak slowly, appear tired, and remain uncertain about the decision.
Speak forcefully and present the decision as final.
Act indifferent to the side effects.
Focus only on friends not sending messages.
qs.e: The client should speak slowly and appear tired without presenting a final decision. Portraying a settled refusal changes the scenario's intended uncertainty.

qs.q: The designated therapeutic technique for exploring what a client means by chemotherapy being “not worth it” is a ______.
qs.e: A clarifying statement explores meaning and what matters most to the client. A disapproving comment instead scolds or shames.

qs.q: A new parent says, “I barely sleep, and I’m scared I won’t know what to do at home.” Which response best validates the feeling?
c: “This transition sounds difficult, and you are feeling scared.”
“You should follow my advice before discussing your worries.”
“Your fear means you are not a good parent.”
“There is nothing difficult about this transition.”
qs.e: Validation recognizes the difficulty and the feeling without judging parenting ability. Immediately directing the parent without listening is the nontherapeutic approach in this scenario.

qs.q: Which nurse action demonstrates the nontherapeutic use of advice in the overwhelmed-parent scenario?
c: Listening to the parent's concerns first
Recognizing the difficulty of the transition
Immediately telling the parent what to do without listening
Acknowledging fear without judging ability
qs.e: The specified problem is immediately telling the parent what to do before listening. Recognizing the difficult transition is validation, not premature advice.

qs.q: Which reports from the new parent require a serious response and appropriate assessment and escalation? Select all that apply.
c: Feeling unsafe
Being unable to care for themselves
Being unable to care for the baby
Having thoughts of harm
Asking for help without knowing exactly what to request
qs.e: The clinical note identifies feeling unsafe, inability to care for self or baby, and thoughts of harm as escalation concerns. An unclear request for help is an acting cue, not one of those specifically listed triggers.

qs.q: Which performance follows the overwhelmed new parent's acting cues?
c: Look tired, speak softly, and ask for help without knowing exactly what to request.
Speak loudly and claim no help is needed.
Look at a phone, place it face down, and shrug.
Insist pain is zero while guarding an incision.
qs.e: The cues emphasize fatigue, soft speech, and an uncertain request for help. Guarding an incision despite denying pain belongs to another scenario.

qs.q: Recognizing a new parent's difficult transition and feelings without judging ability demonstrates a ______.
qs.e: A validating statement acknowledges the parent's experience. It does not judge parenting ability or replace listening with immediate advice.

qs.q: A postoperative client says pain limits getting out of bed. Which question is neutral and focused?
c: “It’s not that bad, is it?”
“You can move without much pain, correct?”
“Where does it hurt when you try to get out of bed?”
“You are exaggerating, aren't you?”
qs.e: Asking where the pain occurs neutrally explores its location. Questions that suggest an expected answer are leading rather than focused assessment.

qs.q: Which pain dimensions are specifically suggested for neutral questions in this scenario? Select all that apply.
c: Location
Severity
Timing
Effect on movement
Whether the client agrees the pain is not bad
qs.e: The slide names location, severity, timing, and effect on movement. Seeking agreement that pain is not bad embeds an expected answer.

qs.q: Which actions follow the clinical note for unexpected postoperative pain? Select all that apply.
c: Assess pain.
Assess associated symptoms.
Follow the care plan.
Report concerning changes.
Assume pain is an expected complication.
qs.e: Pain and associated symptoms require assessment, with care-plan follow-through and reporting of concerning changes. The slide explicitly warns against assuming pain is an expected complication.

qs.q: Which acting cues portray the postoperative client whose pain limits movement?
c: Brace the abdomen when shifting and hesitate before standing.
Hold a tissue silently after becoming tearful.
Watch the nurse's reaction while answering cautiously.
Avoid eye contact and cover the hands with sleeves.
qs.e: Abdominal bracing during shifting and hesitation before standing are the assigned cues. The other behaviors portray different communication scenarios.

qs.q: “It’s not that bad, is it?” is an example of a ______ question.
qs.e: A leading question suggests the answer the nurse expects. A neutral question instead asks about the client's pain without supplying the answer.

qs.q: A teen reports hurtful body comments at school, disliking the mirror, and skipping lunch. Which response is most appropriate?
c: “Those comments sound hurtful and embarrassing.”
“You look fine, so there is no reason to worry.”
“Let me quickly ask every personal question before we talk.”
“Your appearance is the real issue.”
qs.e: An empathetic statement acknowledges hurt and embarrassment without judging appearance. Appearance-based reassurance is specifically discouraged.

qs.q: Which approaches are appropriate for the teen with eating changes and intense body dissatisfaction? Select all that apply.
c: Provide sensitive follow-up.
Arrange appropriate assessment.
Acknowledge hurt without judging appearance.
Offer appearance-based reassurance.
Reinforce weight stigma.
qs.e: Eating changes and intense body dissatisfaction warrant sensitive follow-up and assessment. Reassurance based on appearance and weight stigma are not appropriate substitutes.

qs.q: Which nursing behavior demonstrates intrusive or premature probing?
c: Acknowledging the teen's embarrassment
Establishing trust before exploring personal concerns
Rapidly asking prying personal questions before establishing trust
Responding sensitively to reported eating changes
qs.e: Rapid personal questioning that feels prying before trust is established is the specified nontherapeutic behavior. Appropriate assessment is still needed, but it should be sensitive.

qs.q: Which acting cues are specified for the teen with body image concerns?
c: Avoid eye contact and pull sleeves over the hands.
Fold the arms and express frustration about pills.
Reach toward the nurse, then hesitate.
Look around and attempt to stand in fear.
qs.e: Avoiding eye contact and pulling sleeves over the hands are this teen's cues. Reaching toward the nurse belongs to the client afraid of dying.

qs.q: The designated therapeutic response that acknowledges the teen's hurt and embarrassment is an ______.
qs.e: An empathetic statement acknowledges the emotional experience without judging appearance. Saying the teen looks fine is appearance-based reassurance rather than the requested response.

qs.q: A client with advanced illness says, “I’m scared of dying,” and reaches toward the nurse, then hesitates. What is the most appropriate action?
c: Take the client's hand without asking.
Ask permission before offering a hand and respect the response.
Tell a lengthy story about the nurse's own experience.
Assume touch will comfort every client.
qs.e: Therapeutic touch requires permission and respect for the client's response. Reaching and then hesitating does not replace asking.

qs.q: Which considerations should guide the nurse's use of touch with the client afraid of dying? Select all that apply.
c: Consent
Culture
Trauma history
The client's cues
The assumption that touch is universally comforting
qs.e: The slide identifies consent, culture, trauma history, and client cues as considerations. Touch is not universally comforting.

qs.q: A nurse responds to a client's fear of dying by telling a personal story that shifts attention to the nurse. How should this response be evaluated?
c: It is the designated therapeutic technique.
It is nontherapeutic talking about yourself.
It demonstrates permission for touch.
It presents reality and reorientation.
qs.e: The problem is shifting attention away from the client through the nurse's own story. The scenario calls for remaining present with the client's experience.

qs.q: A client does not want touch while discussing fear of dying. Which actions remain appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: Respect the client's response.
Remain present.
Listen.
Insist that touch will help.
Withdraw support because touch was declined.
qs.e: Presence and listening are alternatives to touch, and the client's response must be respected. Declining touch is not a reason to withdraw support.

qs.q: In the afraid-of-dying role-play, the client speaks ______ and reaches toward the nurse before hesitating.
qs.e: Quiet speech, reaching toward the nurse, and hesitation are the assigned cues. These cues do not remove the need to obtain permission before touch.

qs.q: A postoperative client reports pain of zero while grimacing and guarding the incision. Which response best demonstrates making observations?
c: “You are not being honest about your pain.”
“I noticed you grimaced and guarded your incision when moving. Can you tell me about that?”
“Your pain must be severe because of your appearance.”
“You said zero, so no further assessment is needed.”
qs.e: Making observations describes specific behaviors without accusation and invites explanation. Neither dismissing the behaviors nor assigning pain solely from appearance follows the slide.

qs.q: Which behaviors accompany the client's report of zero pain in this scenario? Select all that apply.
c: Grimacing
Guarding the incision
Grunting when moving
Holding a tissue while grieving
Looking at a phone and shrugging
qs.e: Grimacing, guarding the incision, and grunting with movement are the specified behaviors. They invite further assessment rather than automatic rejection of the client's self-report.

qs.q: Which nursing action requires follow-up when the client reports zero pain but shows discomfort while changing position?
c: Respecting the self-report while assessing further
Inviting the client to explain the observed behavior
Accepting the number without further assessment
Using an open, culturally responsive approach
qs.e: Accepting the number without further assessment ignores the nonverbal cues. Respecting self-report is compatible with exploring the discrepancy.

qs.q: Which statement indicates understanding of the clinical note about mismatched pain reports and behavior?
c: “Appearance alone determines the client's pain.”
“Everyone should express pain in the same way.”
“I should respect self-report and assess further without stereotyping pain expression.”
“A zero rating means I should ignore guarding.”
qs.e: The slide directs an open, culturally responsive assessment that respects self-report. It prohibits inferring pain solely from appearance or stereotyping how pain should be expressed.

qs.q: Describing a client's specific behavior without accusation and inviting an explanation is the technique of ______.
qs.e: Making observations focuses on what the nurse notices and invites the client's meaning. It does not label the client dishonest or assign pain from appearance alone.

qs.q: During admission, a transgender client worries that staff will use the wrong name or pronouns. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Ask what name and pronouns the client uses, use them consistently, and acknowledge the concern.
Explain that identity is irrelevant to respectful care.
Argue about the requested name.
Tell the client to educate every staff member.
qs.e: These actions demonstrate affirmation and validation of identity. Dismissing or arguing about the request is dehumanizing or dismissive communication.

qs.q: Which actions follow the clinical note for respectful care of the transgender client? Select all that apply.
c: Protect privacy.
Follow applicable documentation policies.
Follow applicable care policies.
Avoid making the client responsible for educating the entire team.
Treat the client's identity as irrelevant to respectful care.
qs.e: The note emphasizes privacy, applicable documentation and care policies, and not placing team education on the client. Treating identity as irrelevant dismisses the expressed concern.

qs.q: Which portrayal follows the acting cues for the transgender client concerned about respect?
c: Answer cautiously and watch the nurse's reaction.
Speak slowly about a final chemotherapy decision.
Brace the abdomen before standing.
Become tearful and hold a tissue after a death.
qs.e: Cautious answers and watching the nurse's reaction are the assigned cues. They accompany concern about repeated experiences with the wrong name or pronouns.

qs.q: Which nurse response demonstrates dehumanizing or dismissive communication toward the transgender client?
c: “What pronouns do you use?”
“I hear your concern about having to explain repeatedly.”
“Your identity is irrelevant to respectful care.”
“What name do you use?”
qs.e: Treating identity as irrelevant to respectful care is explicitly identified as nontherapeutic. Asking about the client's name and pronouns supports affirmation and validation.

qs.q: Which context is provided for Scenario 17, “The Parent of a Chronically Ill Child”?
c: A clinic visit after another hospitalization for the child
An admission interview about names and pronouns
A family room immediately after a loved one's death
A postpartum stay involving a new parent's worries
qs.e: The available scenario places the parent in a clinic after another hospitalization for the child. The source cuts off during the parent's statement and does not provide this scenario's communication technique.

qs.q: Scenario 17: A parent comes to a clinic visit after another hospitalization and says, 'It's not fair that my child has to go through all this. I wish I could take it all away,' while becoming tearful and looking at the child's belongings. Which therapeutic technique does the nurse use?
c: Therapeutic use of silence
Relying only on a yes-or-no question
Collaborative problem-solving
Offering self and support
qs.e: Scenario 17 pairs the parent's grief with the therapeutic use of silence. Relying only on a yes-or-no question is the listed nontherapeutic response that cuts off the emotion.

qs.q: Scenario 17: Which response by the nurse is nontherapeutic when the parent of a chronically ill child becomes tearful?
c: Allowing a brief, attentive silence
Asking only a yes-or-no question
Following the parent's lead
Staying attentive and offering support
qs.e: Relying only on a yes-or-no question is the named nontherapeutic response because it limits expression. The other choices are what the therapeutic nurse demonstrates.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a parent who says, 'I wish I could take it all away,' and then cries quietly. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
c: Sit attentively through a brief silence, then follow the parent's lead
Ask, 'Are you okay?' so the parent can answer quickly
Change the subject to the discharge paperwork
Leave the room so the parent can cry alone
qs.e: The slide directs the nurse to allow a brief, attentive silence without rushing to fill it, then follow the parent's lead. Asking 'Are you okay?' is the closed question that cuts off the emotion, and leaving the room turns silence into withdrawal.

qs.q: Which statement by a student nurse indicates a need for further teaching about therapeutic silence in Scenario 17?
c: Silence should communicate presence, not withdrawal.
I will stay attentive and offer support when the parent is ready.
I will step out so the parent does not have to cry in front of me.
I will allow a brief silence without rushing to fill it.
qs.e: The clinical note states that silence communicates presence, not withdrawal, so the nurse stays attentive. Stepping out is withdrawal, not therapeutic silence.

qs.q: Which actions demonstrate therapeutic use of silence with the parent of a chronically ill child? (Select all that apply.)
c: Allow a brief, attentive silence without rushing to fill it
Follow the parent's lead
Stay attentive during the silence
Offer support when the parent is ready
Cut off the emotion with a closed question
Fill the silence immediately with a yes-or-no question
qs.e: All four behaviors show attentive presence during silence. Cutting off emotion with a closed question or filling silence quickly are the nontherapeutic responses described on the slide.

qs.q: Which responses are nontherapeutic in Scenario 17? (Select all that apply.)
c: Relying only on a yes-or-no question
Cutting off the emotion with a closed question that limits expression
Rushing to fill the silence
Withdrawing so the parent is left alone
Following the parent's lead after a brief silence
Offering support when the parent is ready
qs.e: The slide identifies the yes-or-no/closed question as nontherapeutic and tells the nurse not to rush to fill silence or withdraw. Following the parent's lead and offering support are therapeutic.

qs.q: In Scenario 17, the clinical note states that silence should communicate ______, not withdrawal.
qs.e: Silence is used to show presence and support; withdrawal removes the nurse's support entirely.

qs.q: The therapeutic technique for the parent of a chronically ill child (Scenario 17) is ______.
qs.e: Scenario 17 is paired with therapeutic use of silence; the nontherapeutic counterpart is relying only on a yes-or-no question.

qs.q: In Scenario 17, the parent becomes tearful while looking at the child's ______.
qs.e: The patient acting cue is to look at the child's belongings and become tearful, which prompts the nurse's attentive silence.

qs.q: Scenario 18: A student speaks privately with a clinical instructor after missing a deadline and says, 'I feel like I can't keep up, and I'm afraid I'm going to fail.' Which therapeutic technique does the instructor use?
c: Collaborative problem-solving
Gossip or rumors
Therapeutic use of silence
Relying only on a yes-or-no question
qs.e: Scenario 18 is paired with collaborative problem-solving to identify the immediate concern and next steps. Gossip or rumors is the listed nontherapeutic response.

qs.q: Scenario 18: Which response by the clinical instructor is nontherapeutic?
c: Collaborative problem-solving
Gossip or rumors
Offering self and support
Using a qualified medical interpreter
qs.e: Gossip or rumors is the named nontherapeutic response for the student nearing burnout. The other choices are therapeutic techniques from other scenarios.

qs.q: Which actions demonstrate collaborative problem-solving with the student in Scenario 18? (Select all that apply.)
c: Work with the student to identify the immediate concern
Identify realistic next steps together
Take over the problem so the student does not have to decide
Blame the student for missing the deadline
Involve the student in deciding what to do next
Spread assumptions about the student's situation
qs.e: The slide directs the nurse to work together to identify the immediate concern and realistic next steps. Taking over or blaming replaces collaboration, and spreading assumptions is the nontherapeutic gossip response.

qs.q: Which responses are nontherapeutic in Scenario 18? (Select all that apply.)
c: Gossip or rumors
Discussing the student's situation with others unnecessarily
Spreading assumptions
Taking over or blaming the student
Respecting confidentiality
Clarifying when information must be shared for safety or academic support
qs.e: Gossip/rumors, unnecessary discussion with others, spreading assumptions, and taking over or blaming all undermine the therapeutic response. Respecting confidentiality and clarifying required sharing are correct behaviors.

qs.q: The instructor is worried about a student's burnout but the situation may affect clinical safety. Which statement about information sharing is correct?
c: Respect confidentiality and clarify when information must be shared for safety or academic support.
Share the student's situation with the whole clinical group to get advice.
Confidentiality does not apply to nursing students.
Make the student explain the situation to every staff member.
qs.e: The clinical note requires confidentiality and clarifies when sharing is needed for safety or academic support. Unnecessary sharing with others is exactly the nontherapeutic gossip response.

qs.q: In Scenario 18, the instructor must respect ______ when the student shares personal information.
qs.e: The clinical note names confidentiality as the duty when a student speaks privately about a personal struggle.

qs.q: The student looks exhausted and embarrassed, wants help, but fears being judged. Which response by the instructor is best?
c: Work together to identify the immediate concern and realistic next steps
Discuss the student's situation with other faculty unnecessarily
Tell the student to withdraw from the program
Assume what the student needs and decide for them
qs.e: Collaborative problem-solving means working together on the immediate concern and realistic next steps. Unnecessary discussion of the student's situation is the nontherapeutic gossip response.

qs.q: Which statement about Scenario 18 is accurate?
c: The scenario is a communication practice exercise, not a substitute for formal support.
The scenario replaces formal support services for students.
The scenario means the instructor should spread rumors to get help.
The scenario removes the need for confidentiality.
qs.e: The clinical note states the practice exercise is not a substitute for formal support. It does not remove confidentiality or justify gossip.

qs.q: Scenario 19: A parent at discharge teaching says, 'I'm scared I'll make a mistake with my daughter's insulin.' Which therapeutic technique does the nurse use?
c: Offering self and support
Poor professional presentation of self
Therapeutic use of silence
Becoming frustrated or dismissive
qs.e: Scenario 19 is paired with offering self and support. Poor professional presentation of self is the listed nontherapeutic counterpart.

qs.q: The nontherapeutic response in Scenario 19 (parent learning a child's diabetes care) is ______ of self.
qs.e: The slide names poor professional presentation of self as the nontherapeutic behavior, such as appearing rushed or unprepared.

qs.q: Which behaviors reflect poor professional presentation of self when teaching a parent about a child's insulin? (Select all that apply.)
c: Appearing rushed
Appearing distracted
Appearing dismissive
Appearing unprepared
Offering time to practice
Reviewing the steps together
qs.e: The slide lists rushed, distracted, dismissive, and unprepared as the nontherapeutic presentation. Offering practice time and reviewing steps together are the therapeutic demonstrations.

qs.q: Which actions does the therapeutic nurse demonstrate with the parent learning a child's diabetes care? (Select all that apply.)
c: Offer time to practice
Review the steps together
Identify what the parent wants to work on first
Use teach-back and supervised return demonstration as appropriate
Tell the parent to give the insulin tonight without instruction
Hand over the written instructions and leave
qs.e: The slide directs the nurse to offer practice time, review steps together, and identify the parent's first priority, with teach-back and return demonstration. Implying the parent can medicate without instruction is explicitly prohibited.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a parent who is scared to give a new insulin injection. Which action best confirms the parent's understanding?
c: Use teach-back and supervised return demonstration as appropriate
Ask 'Any questions?' and accept a nod
Ask the parent to read the instructions aloud
Hand over the written instructions and end the visit
qs.e: The clinical note directs use of teach-back and supervised return demonstration. Accepting a nod or just reading instructions does not demonstrate understanding.

qs.q: The clinical note for Scenario 19 directs the nurse to use teach-back and supervised return ______ as appropriate.
qs.e: Supervised return demonstration shows the parent can safely perform the skill before doing it at home.

qs.q: A parent at discharge asks to give the insulin dose at home right away. Which statement by the nurse requires follow-up?
c: We will practice the steps together first.
Let's use teach-back to confirm the steps.
You can give the insulin tonight; the instructions are in the bag.
I will supervise a return demonstration before you do this at home.
qs.e: The slide states never to imply the parent should administer medication without adequate instruction and demonstrated understanding. Practicing, teach-back, and supervised return demonstration all meet that standard.

qs.q: Before a parent administers a child's medication at home, the nurse must provide adequate instruction and confirm demonstrated ______.
qs.e: The slide requires both adequate instruction and demonstrated understanding before the parent gives medication.

qs.q: Scenario 20: A patient with limited English proficiency nods politely but cannot explain when or how to take a new medication. Which therapeutic technique does the nurse use?
c: Using a qualified medical interpreter
Asking the patient's child to interpret
Becoming frustrated or dismissive
Relying on gestures alone
qs.e: Scenario 20 pairs with using a qualified medical interpreter. Frustration, dismissal, gestures alone, and using a child are all identified as nontherapeutic or inappropriate.

qs.q: Which actions does the therapeutic nurse take when explaining a new medication to a patient with limited English proficiency? (Select all that apply.)
c: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter
Speak directly to the patient
Speak in short segments
Pause for interpretation
Raise the voice so the patient hears better
Treat polite nodding as proof of understanding
qs.e: The slide directs the nurse to arrange a qualified interpreter, speak directly to the patient in short segments, and pause for interpretation. Raising the voice and trusting nods are listed as nontherapeutic.

qs.q: Which responses are nontherapeutic when caring for a patient with limited English proficiency? (Select all that apply.)
c: Becoming frustrated or dismissive
Raising the voice
Relying on gestures alone for complex information
Treating nodding as proof of understanding
Speaking directly to the patient
Pausing for interpretation
qs.e: Frustration or dismissal, raising the voice, gestures alone for complex information, and trusting nodding are all named as nontherapeutic. Speaking directly to the patient and pausing for interpretation are therapeutic.

qs.q: The patient speaks limited English and nods politely but cannot state when or how to take the medication. What does the nurse conclude?
c: Nodding is not proof of understanding; arrange a qualified medical interpreter.
The patient understands the instructions.
The discharge instructions are complete.
The patient is refusing the medication.
qs.e: The slide states the nurse must not treat nodding as proof of understanding. A polite nod indicates uncertainty or politeness, not comprehension.

qs.q: A nurse must explain a new medication to a patient with limited English proficiency; the patient's English-speaking 10-year-old is present. Which action is appropriate?
c: Use a qualified medical interpreter and follow organizational policy.
Ask the child to interpret the medication instructions.
Rely on gestures alone for the complex information.
Show the patient the medication label and end the conversation.
qs.e: The clinical note says not to rely on a child or unqualified bystander to interpret important clinical information when qualified interpretation is available. Gestures alone are also listed as nontherapeutic for complex information.

qs.q: When qualified interpretation is available, the nurse must not rely on a child or unqualified ______ to interpret important clinical information.
qs.e: The clinical note names the child and unqualified bystander as inappropriate interpreters for important clinical information.

qs.q: When arranging interpretation, the nurse should follow organizational ______.
qs.e: The clinical note directs the nurse to follow organizational policy for interpretation services.

qs.q: Which patient acting cues belong to the patient with limited English proficiency (Scenario 20)? (Select all that apply.)
c: Use short phrases in your language
Look uncertain
Point to the medication label
Do not pretend to understand
Nod and claim to understand everything
Explain the medication back in fluent English
qs.e: The slide lists short phrases, looking uncertain, pointing to the label, and not pretending to understand as the acting cues. Claiming understanding contradicts the scenario.

qs.q: The nurse should speak directly to the patient in short segments and pause for ______ when an interpreter is used.
qs.e: Short segments with pauses allow the qualified medical interpreter to interpret accurately.

qs.q: A parent looks between the written instructions and the nurse and asks the same question twice. Which response is most appropriate?
c: Offer time to practice and identify what the parent wants to work on first
Tell the parent the answer is already in the written instructions
Rush to finish the discharge paperwork
Ask the parent to stop repeating the question
qs.e: These cues signal fear of making a mistake, so the nurse offers self and support with practice time. Rushing or pointing to the paper reflects poor professional presentation of self.

qs.q: A parent says, 'It's not fair that my child has to go through all this,' and becomes tearful. Which nonverbal cue does the parent show in Scenario 17?
c: Looking at the child's belongings
Pointing to the medication label
Looking between written instructions and the nurse
Looking exhausted and embarrassed
qs.e: Scenario 17's acting cue is looking at the child's belongings and becoming tearful. The other cues belong to Scenarios 20, 19, and 18 respectively.

qs.q: When a nurse identifies a clinical or safety concern, the nurse should ______ the concern appropriately.
qs.e: The debrief 'Remember' list tells nurses to escalate clinical or safety concerns appropriately rather than ignoring them.

qs.q: A patient asks a question about a new treatment and seems unsure. Which action reflects the debrief 'Remember' guidance?
c: Use plain language and listen before advising.
Use clinical terminology to show expertise.
Advise before listening to the patient's concerns.
Speak mostly in medical abbreviations.
qs.e: The slide reminds nurses to use plain language and listen before advising. Advising first or using jargon works against understanding.

qs.q: Which points are included in the debrief 'Remember' list? (Select all that apply.)
c: Respect the patient's dignity and choices
Use plain language and listen before advising
Notice verbal and nonverbal cues without making assumptions
Escalate clinical or safety concerns appropriately
Make the patient responsible for educating the entire team
Treat nodding as proof of understanding
qs.e: The 'Remember' list contains dignity/choices, plain language with listening first, noticing cues without assumptions, and escalation. Making the patient educate the team and trusting nods contradict the slides.

qs.q: Which prompts are used to discuss each skit during the debrief? (Select all that apply.)
c: What did the therapeutic nurse do or say?
How did the patient respond?
What made the nontherapeutic response ineffective?
What could the nurse try next?
How many medications was the patient taking?
What was the patient's diagnosis?
qs.e: The debrief prompts focus on the nurse's behavior, the patient's response, why the nontherapeutic response failed, and the next step. Medication counts and diagnoses are not part of the debrief prompts.

qs.q: A nurse is caring for a client with a complex new care plan and multiple staff coming on shift. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Follow applicable documentation and care policies and share needed information through proper channels.
Ask the client to explain the plan to each new staff member.
Leave it to the client to update the care team.
Skip documentation if the client knows the plan.
qs.e: The slides direct nurses to follow applicable documentation and care policies and not make the patient responsible for educating the entire team. Documentation is the nurse's responsibility, not the client's.

qs.q: Nurses must follow applicable documentation and care ______ rather than making the patient educate the team.
qs.e: The slide states to follow applicable documentation and care policies and not make the patient responsible for educating the entire team.

qs.q: Which scenario-to-technique pairings from the role-play slides are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: Scenario 17: therapeutic use of silence
Scenario 18: gossip or rumors
Scenario 19: offering self and support
Scenario 20: using a qualified medical interpreter
Scenario 17: collaborative problem-solving
Scenario 20: relying on gestures alone
qs.e: Scenario 17 uses silence, Scenario 19 uses offering self and support, and Scenario 20 uses a qualified medical interpreter. Gossip/rumors and gestures alone are the nontherapeutic responses.

qs.q: The nurse must explain discharge instructions to a patient with limited English proficiency. How should the nurse speak to the patient?
c: Speak directly to the patient in short segments and pause for interpretation.
Speak to the interpreter only and ignore the patient.
Raise the voice and use gestures alone.
Speak in long, detailed paragraphs without pausing.
qs.e: The slide directs the nurse to speak directly to the patient in short segments and pause for interpretation. Raising the voice and gestures alone for complex information are nontherapeutic.

qs.q: A student nurse wants to show support to a fearful parent learning insulin administration. Which action demonstrates offering self and support?
c: Stay with the parent, offer time to practice, and review the steps together.
Hand the parent the printed instructions and rush to the next client.
Tell the parent that other parents manage fine.
Avoid the topic so the parent does not become upset.
qs.e: Offering self and support means being present with practice time and reviewing steps together. Rushing or appearing dismissive is the nontherapeutic poor professional presentation of self.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly lists the elements of the communication process as described by Berlo (1960)?
c: Source (encoder) → message → channel → receiver (decoder)
Receiver (decoder) → channel → message → source (encoder)
Source (encoder) → noise → feedback → receiver (decoder)
Channel → source (encoder) → feedback → message
qs.e: Berlo's classic model runs source (encoder), message, channel, receiver (decoder). Noise and feedback are real parts of the exchange, but they are not the four core elements listed in that order.

qs.q: In the communication process, which person or group initiates or begins the communication?
c: The sender or source (encoder)
The receiver (decoder)
The channel of communication
The feedback provider
qs.e: The source (encoder) is the person or group who initiates or begins the process. The receiver (decoder) instead translates and interprets the message that is sent.

qs.q: A nurse holds the hand of a frightened client before surgery. In the communication process this is an example of which channel?
c: Kinesthetic
Auditory
Visual
Feedback
qs.e: Kinesthetic is the channel of touch. Auditory targets hearing (spoken words and cues) and visual targets sight, observation, and perception, so those do not fit a touch.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching wound care to a client while the television plays loudly and the client reports pain. How should the nurse interpret these factors?
c: They are noise that can distort the quality of the message
They are feedback confirming the client understood the message
They are channels used to transmit the message
They are stimuli that initiate the communication process
qs.e: Noise includes distractors such as a television and the pain or discomfort the client experiences. Feedback is the receiver's evidence of understanding, which is the opposite function.

qs.q: At which point in the communication process can noise interfere?
c: At any point in the process
Only when the source sends the message
Only when the receiver decodes the message
Only during feedback
qs.e: Noise can interfere at any point in the process, because communication is reciprocal and simultaneous. Limiting noise to one stage is a common misconception.

qs.q: To be an effective communicator, the nurse selects a message that appeals to the client's interests and that:
c: Requires minimal effort and time to decode
Contains as many technical terms as possible
Is sent through a single sensory channel
Is chosen without regard for the receiver
qs.e: The nurse must be considerate of the receiver and choose a message that appeals to the client's interests and takes minimal effort and time to decode. Extra technical terms increase decoding effort and work against understanding.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who has been comatose for several weeks. Which communication approach is most appropriate?
c: Send messages that are simple, clear, and easy to understand
Speak in long, detailed explanations to stimulate arousal
Avoid speaking to the client because no response is possible
Communicate only with family members in the room
qs.e: The client's altered mental status mandates simple, clear, easy-to-understand messages. Stopping all interaction ignores the client as a person, and complex wording only makes decoding harder.

qs.q: Which statement reflects the AACN standard for healthy work environments cited in this chapter?
c: Nurses must be as proficient in communication skills as they are in clinical skills
Communication skill is secondary to technical skill in acute care
Only nurse managers need skilled communication
Communication proficiency has no effect on patient care outcomes
qs.e: AACN's skilled communication standard requires nurses to be as proficient in communication as in clinical skills. Technical skill cannot substitute for communication when the work environment affects outcomes.

qs.q: On a unit where nurses freely exchange ideas, solve problems together rather than assign blame, compliment one another, and use humor creatively, which result does the chapter associate with this environment?
c: High staff morale and a higher level of attainment of patient outcomes
Increased disruptive behaviors and staff turnover
Good morale but poorer patient outcomes
More blame assigning and lower patient safety
qs.e: These behaviors produce high staff morale and better attainment of patient outcomes. Harassment and disruptive communication produce the opposite consequences.

qs.q: The nurse documents care by writing a nursing note in the client's chart. In Berlo's communication process, the nursing note is the:
c: Message
Channel
Source (encoder)
Feedback
qs.e: The message is the actual communication product—speech, interview, conversation, chart, gesture, memorandum, or nursing note. Touch is a channel, not a message.

qs.q: Many experienced nurses identify which single most significant element in determining their helper effectiveness?
c: The quality of their interpersonal relationships
The number of electronic monitoring devices they manage
Their ability to complete documentation quickly
The length of their daily shift assignment
qs.e: The chapter names the quality of interpersonal relationships as the most significant element in helper effectiveness. Communication skills are the building blocks of those professional relationships.

qs.q: Which of the following are channels nurses use to send a message to clients and other health care providers? Select all that apply.
c: Auditory
Visual
Kinesthetic
Feedback
Noise
Semantics
qs.e: Nurses use auditory (spoken words and cues), visual (sight, observation, perception), and kinesthetic (touch) channels. Feedback and noise are other parts of the process, not channels.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to teach a client about discharge medications. Which of the following does the chapter identify as noise (distractors) that can distort the message? Select all that apply.
c: A television playing in the room
Pain experienced by the client
Discomfort experienced by the client
A chart or memorandum
A touch on the client's hand
Spoken words and cues
qs.e: The text names the television and pain or discomfort as noise. A chart is an example of a message and touch is a kinesthetic channel, so neither distorts the message.

qs.q: Which of the following are consequences of harassment or disruptive communication and behaviors between health care professionals? Select all that apply.
c: Effects on the emotional and physical well-being of those involved
Effects on the functioning of the organization
Effects on the safety of patient care
Improved staff morale
A higher level of attainment of patient outcomes
Greater mutual respect among team members
qs.e: Disruptive communication harms well-being, organizational functioning, and patient safety. Improved morale, better outcomes, and mutual respect come from open communication and collaboration instead.

qs.q: A student nurse hears a colleague discussing an unresponsive client's appearance and odor at the bedside, in the client's presence. Which actions demonstrate professionalism and respect for the client's human dignity? Select all that apply.
c: Acknowledge the client through words or touch
Calmly ask the nurse and residents to step out of the room before discussing the client's condition
Set an example by speaking to the client and touching the client's hand
Continue the bedside discussion because an unresponsive client cannot hear
Focus only on the technology and monitoring equipment
Avoid all interaction with the client because no response is possible
qs.e: The desired outcome is a team that acts professionally and respects human dignity, with regard for the whole patient. Talking about the client at the bedside and ignoring the person in the bed fail those criteria.

qs.q: Which of the following are described as parts of the communication process? Select all that apply.
c: Source (encoder)
Message
Channel
Feedback
Language
Semantics
qs.e: The process includes the source (encoder), message, channel, and receiver (decoder), with feedback confirming understanding. Language and semantics are only listed as key terms here and are not described as process elements.

qs.q: Which statements about communication are correct? Select all that apply.
c: It is the process of exchanging information and generating and transmitting meanings between two or more people
It is the foundation of society and the most primary aspect of a nurse–patient interaction
It assists in meeting psychosocial needs of love, belonging, and self-esteem
It is a one-way process in which only the sender participates
Human needs are best met in isolation from other people
Only spoken words can carry a message
qs.e: The chapter defines communication as exchanging information and meaning between people and notes it supports psychosocial needs. Communication is reciprocal rather than one-way, and messages may also be charts or gestures.

qs.q: In the communication process, the process is initiated based on a __________ (for example, a patient need for comfort or information) that must be addressed.
qs.e: The stimulus—often a patient need such as discomfort or desire for information—starts the communication process. The message is the product created after the stimulus.

qs.q: Confirmation of the message that provides evidence the receiver has understood the intended message is called __________.
qs.e: Feedback confirms that the receiver understood the intended message. Noise does the opposite by distorting the message.

qs.q: Communication is described as a __________ process in which the sender and the receiver of messages participate simultaneously.
qs.e: Reciprocal means both people act as sender and receiver at the same time rather than in a one-way sequence.

qs.q: The AACN standard stating "Nurses must be as proficient in communication skills as they are in clinical skills" is called __________ communication.
qs.e: AACN's skilled communication standard holds nurses to the same proficiency in communication as in clinical skills. Clinical expertise alone does not meet the standard.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who states, 'I feel all right' when asked how he is feeling. However, the nurse notes the client does not maintain eye contact and his facial expression is tense. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Document that the client is feeling all right
Investigate further because of incongruence between verbal and nonverbal communication
Confront the client about the discrepancy between his words and his nonverbal behavior
Assume the client does not want to discuss his feelings
qs.e: When verbal and nonverbal messages are incongruent, the nurse should investigate further because nonverbal communication often conveys the speaker's actual meaning (Taylor p. 176). Documenting 'all right' ignores the tense nonverbal cues, and confronting the client is not a therapeutic response; the appropriate action is to explore the incongruence further.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client from an Asian cultural background who avoids making eye contact during conversation. Which interpretation is most accurate?
c: The client is experiencing anxiety or defensiveness
The client is being confrontational with the nurse
The client may view eye contact as an invasion of privacy or confrontational
The client is daydreaming or inattentive
qs.e: Some Native American and Asian cultures view eye contact as an invasion of a person's privacy or as confrontational. While absence of eye contact may indicate anxiety in some contexts, cultural variations must be considered to avoid misinterpretation.

qs.q: The nurse observes a client recovering from recent abdominal surgery walking down the hall. Which gait does the nurse expect?
c: A bouncy, purposeful walk
Walking slightly bent over and slowly, possibly needing assistance
A shuffling gait suggesting sadness or discouragement
A rigid, stiff appearance with no movement
qs.e: Clients recovering from recent abdominal surgery usually walk slightly bent over and slowly and might need the assistance of handrails or a helping person. A bouncy, purposeful walk signals well-being, which is not expected immediately post-surgery.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client with insufficient intake of fluids. Which general physical appearance findings does the nurse expect?
c: Radiant healthy status with good muscle tone
Dry skin that wrinkles easily, sunken dull eyes, and poor muscle tone
Flush, moist skin with bright eyes
Normal skin turgor with excellent muscle tone
qs.e: A person with insufficient fluid intake has dry skin that wrinkles easily, eyes that might be sunken and dull in appearance, and poor muscle tone. A person in good health tends to radiate a healthy status through general appearance, which is the opposite of fluid deficit.

qs.q: When a client's verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, what does the listener most likely believe?
c: The verbal message
The nonverbal message
The written message
Neither; the listener will ask for clarification
qs.e: If verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, behaviors can negate a verbal message and the listener will believe the nonverbal message. Nonverbal communication often conveys the speaker's actual meaning, making it more trustworthy than words alone.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who flinches when the nurse attempts to provide comfort with a touch on the shoulder. Which statement best explains this reaction?
c: The client is experiencing pain at the touch site
Touch is a very personal behavior shaped by familial, regional, class, and cultural influences
Touch is universally understood as comforting across all individuals
The client has a neurological deficit
qs.e: Touch is a very personal behavior and means different things to different people, largely shaped by familial, regional, class, and cultural influences. Assuming touch is universally comforting ignores the individuality of tactile experiences.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client diagnosed with depression. Which postural finding does the nurse most likely expect?
c: Good body alignment with positive attitude
A rigid, stiff appearance indicating tension and pain
Slouching
A bouncy, purposeful stance
qs.e: Depressed or tired people are more likely to slouch. People in good health and with a positive attitude usually hold their bodies in good alignment, so slouching indicates the opposite of well-being.

qs.q: The nurse observes a client glaring with a fixed stare while clenching fists. Which interpretation of the eye message is most appropriate?
c: The client is daydreaming
The client is experiencing anger
The client is feeling disgust
The client is experiencing fear
qs.e: The eyes fix in a stare during anger, and clenching fists reinforces this interpretation. A blank stare indicates daydreaming or inattentiveness, and the eyes narrow in disgust or open wide in fear, neither of which matches a fixed stare.

qs.q: The nurse is changing burn dressings for a 3-year-old child who is watching the nurse's reaction closely. Which nursing behavior is most important during this interaction?
c: Explain the procedure in detail to the child
Control facial expressions to avoid showing repulsion or disgust
Encourage the child to look away
Smile broadly to reassure the child
qs.e: Nurses need to learn to control their own facial expressions; any sign of repulsion or disgust could greatly impact the child's self-image and recovery. Explaining the procedure is secondary to managing nonverbal cues the curious preschooler is observing.

qs.q: A nurse enters a client's room, touches the client's shoulder while asking about the client's pain, and prepares to administer IV pain medication. The client feels the nurse cares about them as a person. This interaction illustrates which mode of kinesthetic communication?
c: Procedural touch
Caring touch
Empathic listening
Perceptual observation
qs.e: Caring touch conveys emotional support, and the client feeling cared for as a person when the nurse touches their shoulder is the defining example from Box 8-1. Procedural touch involves performing nursing procedures and techniques, such as the actual IV injection, not the emotional connection.

qs.q: According to Box 8-1, what is the outcome of 'listening' in the auditory communication channel?
c: Receiving an auditory stimulus
Interpreting visual stimulation by making note of nonverbal enhancement
Gaining awareness of underlying messages and feelings accompanying auditory events
Assigning meaning to a visual event
qs.e: Listening involves gaining awareness of underlying messages and feelings accompanying auditory events, which goes beyond simple hearing (receiving an auditory stimulus). Options B and D describe visual channel outcomes (observation and perception).

qs.q: According to Box 8-1, a patient concludes that the nurse is willing and able to help and feels comforted. This outcome belongs to which mode of the visual channel?
c: Sight
Observation
Perception
Hearing
qs.e: Perception is the act of assigning meaning to a visual event, which is why the patient concludes the nurse is willing and able to help. Sight is simply receiving the visual stimulus, and observation is interpreting the nonverbal enhancement (e.g., noting competence and confidence).

qs.q: Which of the following are included in nonverbal communication? Select all that apply.
c: Facial expressions
Written words
Boundaries
Spoken words
Eye contact
Body movements
qs.e: Nonverbal communication includes facial expressions, eye contact, boundaries, and body movements (among other elements like space and time). Written words and spoken words are forms of verbal communication, which exchanges information using words.

qs.q: According to Box 8-1, which modes of transmission are part of the visual communication channel? Select all that apply.
c: Sight
Observation
Perception
Hearing
Listening
Procedural touch
qs.e: The visual channel includes sight (receiving a visual stimulus), observation (interpreting visual stimulation), and perception (assigning meaning to a visual event). Hearing and listening belong to the auditory channel; procedural touch belongs to the kinesthetic channel.

qs.q: Which factors shape the meanings associated with touch? Select all that apply.
c: Age
Sex
Familial influences
Blood type
Cultural influences
Number of siblings
qs.e: Touch meanings are largely shaped by familial, regional, class, and cultural influences, with age and sex also playing a key role. Blood type and number of siblings are not mentioned as factors influencing tactile experiences.

qs.q: Which eye movements are correctly matched with their associated messages? Select all that apply.
c: Fixed stare — anger
Eyes narrowing — disgust
Eyes opening wide — happiness
Blank stare — daydreaming or inattentiveness
Avoiding eye contact — always indicates deception
Glancing — closing conversation
qs.e: The eyes fix in a stare during anger, narrow in disgust, and a blank stare indicates daydreaming or inattentiveness. Eyes open wide in fear (not happiness), avoiding eye contact has multiple meanings including cultural preference and anxiety (not just deception), and a glance opens rather than closes conversation.

qs.q: Which gestures are correctly matched with their meanings? Select all that apply.
c: Thumbs up — victory
Kicking an object — love
Wringing hands or tapping foot — anxiety or anger
Waving hand — beckoning someone to come or signaling someone to leave
Crossing arms — comfort and openness
Nodding head — universally means agreement in all cultures
qs.e: Thumbs up means victory, wringing hands or tapping a foot usually indicates anxiety or anger, and a waving hand can beckon or signal someone to leave. Kicking an object expresses anger (not love), and gestures may have different meanings in different cultures so they are not universal.

qs.q: Which factors might influence messages on either end of the communication process? Select all that apply.
c: Previous knowledge
Past experiences
Feelings
Time of day
Sociocultural level
Eye color
qs.e: Messages might be influenced on either end by the person's previous knowledge, past experiences, feelings, or sociocultural level. Time of day and eye color are not listed as factors influencing messages in the communication process.

qs.q: The ______ is the most expressive part of the body.
qs.e: The face is the most expressive part of the body, conveying anger, joy, suspicion, sadness, fear, and contempt. Nurses need to learn to control their own facial expressions to avoid sending unintended messages.

qs.q: Communication is a ______ process in which both the sender and receiver participate simultaneously.
qs.e: Communication is described as a reciprocal process, meaning both parties are engaged simultaneously rather than one passively receiving. This highlights that nurses and patients are both active participants in the exchange.

qs.q: When verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, the listener will most likely believe the ______ message.
qs.e: If verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, behaviors can negate a verbal message and the listener will believe the nonverbal message. This is why nonverbal communication is considered as important as verbal communication, if not more so.

qs.q: According to Box 8-1, the type of kinesthetic touch that conveys emotional support is called ______ touch.
qs.e: Caring touch conveys emotional support, such as when a nurse touches a client's shoulder to show concern. Procedural touch, by contrast, involves performing nursing procedures and techniques.

qs.q: According to Box 8-1, the three channels of communication are visual, auditory, and ______.
qs.e: Box 8-1 identifies three channels: visual (sight/observation/perception), auditory (hearing/listening), and kinesthetic (procedural touch/caring touch). These channels describe how information is transmitted and received during nurse–patient interactions.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who is blind and must perform a procedure that requires touch. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
c: Explain the reason for touching the client before doing so
Touch the client without warning so the client is not startled
Speak in a loud voice so the client understands the plan
Use hand gestures to signal what the nurse is about to do
qs.e: A client who is visually impaired cannot pick up nonverbal cues such as a hand approaching, so explaining the reason for touch prevents startle and builds trust. Touching without warning is unsafe, and a loud voice is not indicated because the client's hearing is intact.

qs.q: The nurse is communicating with a client who is deaf and able to lip read. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
c: Talk directly to the client while facing them and use simple sentences
Cover the mouth so the client focuses on the words being spoken
Chew gum to exaggerate lip movements
Turn away from the client to test the client's lip-reading ability
qs.e: Talk directly to the client while facing them; if the client lip reads, use simple sentences spoken in a quiet, natural manner and pace. Covering the mouth or chewing gum blocks the lip movements the client depends on.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who has an endotracheal tube and cannot speak. Which nursing action is the priority?
c: Ensure the client has an effective means of signaling need for assistance, such as a call bell or alarm
Ask family members to interpret the client's needs
Encourage the client to speak slowly and quietly
Leave the client to rest without any signaling device
qs.e: A client with a physical barrier such as an endotracheal tube must have an effective way to signal for help, such as a call bell or alarm, to ensure safety. Relying on family or leaving the client without a signal device places the client at risk.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who is visually impaired. Which action by the nurse requires follow-up?
c: Leaving the room without telling the client the conversation has ended
Speaking in a normal tone of voice
Placing the call light within easy reach
Orienting the client to the sounds in the environment
qs.e: The nurse must indicate when the conversation has ended and when leaving the room because the client cannot see the nurse's departure. Normal tone, an accessible call light, and orientation to sounds are all correct interventions.

qs.q: A client who is hard of hearing is talking with the nurse. Which nursing action requires follow-up?
c: Chewing gum while talking with the client
Facing the client while speaking
Moving so that the client can see the nurse before speaking
Writing ideas that cannot be conveyed in another manner
qs.e: Do not chew gum or cover your mouth when talking with a client who is deaf or hard of hearing, because it distorts the visible mouth movements the client relies on. Facing the client, orienting to your presence, and writing what cannot be conveyed are all correct.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a laryngectomy who is using a communication board. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
c: Demonstrate patience with the time needed to communicate and reinforce the client's efforts
Finish the client's messages to save time
Limit all communication to yes-or-no questions
Speak for the client during interactions with family
qs.e: Communicating with a device takes time; patience and reinforcement encourage the client's efforts. Finishing messages or speaking for the client discourages independence, and although yes/no responses are one option, the client is not limited to them.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who is visually impaired and wears eyeglasses. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Be sure the eyeglasses are clean and intact or that contacts are in place
Remove the eyeglasses and store them in a drawer to prevent loss
Ask the client to clean the eyeglasses without assistance
Leave the eyeglasses wherever the client last set them down
