qs.e: Maximizing the client's remaining vision begins with clean, intact eyeglasses or properly placed contacts. Removing or misplacing them further reduces the client's ability to function safely.

qs.q: The nurse approaches a client who is deaf to discuss the plan of care. Which action should the nurse take first?
c: Orient the client to the nurse's presence before initiating the conversation
Begin talking from the doorway so the client can hear better
Start talking immediately so the client does not miss any information
Speak in a loud voice to overcome the hearing loss
qs.e: Orient the client to your presence first, using a gentle touch or by moving so you can be seen; this prevents startle and secures the client's visual attention. Beginning to speak without warning or from out of view means the client misses the message.

qs.q: The nurse is orienting a client who is blind to a new room. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?
c: I will describe the sounds you will hear and the arrangement of the room and its furnishings.
There is nothing in the room that you need to worry about.
Just follow the wall and you will find everything you need.
I will leave now so you can explore the room on your own.
qs.e: Orient the patient to the sounds in the environment and to the arrangement of the room and its furnishings so the client can move safely. Vague reassurance or leaving the client unoriented does not provide the information the client cannot see.

qs.q: A client with an endotracheal tube is using a magic slate to communicate. The nurse notes that the client's family members cannot use the device. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
c: Be sure that everyone who communicates with the client understands and can use the selected device
Ask the family to wait outside until the client can speak again
Replace the device with one only the nurse can operate
Tell the client to communicate only with the nurse
qs.e: All communicators-family, friends, and caregivers-must understand and be able to use the selected device so the client's needs are consistently met. Restricting communication isolates the client and risks missed needs.

qs.q: Which nursing actions are appropriate when caring for a client who is visually impaired? (Select all that apply.)
c: Speak in a normal tone of voice
Explain the reason before touching the client
Indicate when the conversation has ended and when the nurse is leaving the room
Keep a call light or bell within easy reach of the client
Speak in a loud voice to ensure the client hears
Avoid touching the client during care
qs.e: All four are listed interventions for the visually impaired client, who cannot see nonverbal cues. A loud voice is unnecessary because the client's hearing is intact, and touch cannot be avoided-but it must be explained first.

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate when communicating with a client who is deaf or hard of hearing? (Select all that apply.)
c: Orient the client to your presence before initiating conversation
Talk directly to the client while facing them
Avoid chewing gum or covering your mouth when talking
Use simple sentences and a quiet, natural manner and pace if the client lip reads
Speak in a loud voice to overcome the hearing loss
Face away from the client so the client listens more carefully
qs.e: The client needs visual access to the nurse's face, so orientation, direct facing, unobstructed lip movements, and simple sentences at a natural pace are correct. A loud voice or turning away defeats lip reading and does not appear in the recommended interventions.

qs.q: The nurse is selecting a communication method for a client with a laryngectomy who cannot speak. Which options are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
c: Eye blinks or hand squeezes to communicate yes or no
Communication boards with words, letters, or pictures
Writing pads or magic slates
Flash cards or sign language
Asking the client to speak in a whisper
Relying on nonverbal cues alone with no signal device
qs.e: Select one or more simple means the client is physically able to use, including blinks/squeezes, writing pads or magic slates, communication boards, flash cards, and sign language. Whispering is not possible with this barrier, and the client also needs a way to signal for assistance.

qs.q: Which nursing actions support effective communication and safety for a client with a physical barrier such as an endotracheal tube? (Select all that apply.)
c: Be sure everyone who communicates with the client understands and can use the selected devices
Demonstrate patience with the time needed to communicate and reinforce the client's efforts
Ensure the client has an effective means of signaling need for assistance, such as a call bell or alarm
Select one or more simple means of communication the client is physically able to use
Complete the client's messages to speed up the interaction
Remove the call bell to reduce alarms
qs.e: These four actions cover device selection, consistent use by all communicators, patience/reinforcement, and a reliable way to summon help. Finishing the client's messages or removing the call bell undermines communication and safety.

qs.q: Which situations require follow-up when caring for clients with communication barriers? (Select all that apply.)
c: Leaving the room without telling a client who is blind that the conversation has ended
Touching a client who is blind without explaining the reason first
Chewing gum while talking with a client who is hard of hearing
Family members who are unable to use the client's communication board
Speaking in a normal tone of voice to a client who is blind
Facing a client who is deaf while talking
qs.e: Each of these four departs from the recommended practice: announce endings and departures, explain touch, keep the mouth visible, and make sure every communicator can use the device. Normal tone and facing the client are correct actions.

qs.q: The nurse should speak in a ________ tone of voice when communicating with a client who is visually impaired.
qs.e: The client's limitation is visual, not auditory, so a normal tone is used. Speaking loudly is unnecessary and can sound abrupt.

qs.q: Eye blinks or hand squeezes may be used by a client with a physical barrier such as a laryngectomy to communicate ________.
qs.e: These simple responses let the client answer questions reliably. More complex messages require a writing pad, slate, board, flash cards, or sign language.

qs.q: A client with an endotracheal tube must have an effective means of signaling need for assistance, such as a ________ or alarm.
qs.e: An accessible call bell or alarm is required so the nonverbal client can summon help. Without it, the client's safety is compromised.

qs.q: When a client who is deaf lip reads, the nurse should use ________ sentences spoken in a quiet, natural manner and pace.
qs.e: Simple sentences are easier to lip read than complex phrasing. A quiet, natural manner and pace support accurate reading of lip movements.

qs.q: Before initiating conversation with a client who is deaf or hard of hearing, the nurse should first orient the client to the nurse's ________.
qs.e: Orienting the client by gently touching or moving so you can be seen prevents startle and secures the client's attention before information is given. Beginning to speak first means the client may miss the message.

qs.q: The nurse is assessing a client who has a fluid deficit. Which finding is consistent with this condition?
c: Dry skin that wrinkles easily with sunken, dull eyes
Skin that appears moist and warm to touch
Bright, alert eyes with strong muscle tone
Radiant general appearance indicating good health
qs.e: A person with a fluid deficit presents with dry skin that wrinkles easily, sunken/dull eyes, and poor muscle tone. A radiant, healthy appearance with good muscle tone is characteristic of someone in good health, making that distractor incorrect.

qs.q: The nurse hears a client gasp loudly during a procedure. This sound most likely indicates:
c: Reluctant agreement or relief
Complete understanding of the situation
Fear, pain, or surprise
Sadness or joy
qs.e: Gasping often indicates fear, pain, or surprise. A sigh is associated with reluctant agreement or relief, making it a tempting but incorrect distractor here.

qs.q: After the nurse explains a treatment plan, the client sighs heavily. The nurse should interpret this sigh as a possible sign of:
c: Anger toward the nurse
Fear or surprise
Reluctant agreement or relief
Sadness or crying
qs.e: A sigh may indicate reluctant agreement to do something or relief. Gasping indicates fear, pain, or surprise — a commonly confused nonverbal sound.

qs.q: A nurse posts on social media about a patient in room 302 diagnosed with pneumonia but does not use the patient's name. Which statement is correct?
c: This is acceptable because no name was used
This is still considered a breach of confidentiality and violation of patient privacy
This is only a violation if the patient files a complaint
This is acceptable if the nurse's privacy settings are on high
qs.e: Describing a patient by room number or diagnosis rather than a name is still a breach of confidentiality and a violation of privacy. Privacy settings do not excuse the disclosure — information posted can still be shared with multiple recipients.

qs.q: A nurse sends an e-mail to a client with discharge instructions. What must the nurse also do?
c: Delete the e-mail immediately after sending
Duplicate the e-mail and make it part of the client's health record
Send a printed copy only to the physician
Nothing further is required if the client signs an authorization
qs.e: Any e-mails sent to a patient must be duplicated and become part of the health record. Deleting the message would compromise documentation integrity.

qs.q: During a telehealth encounter, which nursing action best communicates interest, empathy, and engagement with the patient?
c: Leaning in, nodding, and making eye contact
Speaking rapidly to cover more topics in less time
Allowing environmental noise to remain as background
Avoiding verbal responses to minimize distractions
qs.e: Key nonverbal cues during telehealth include leaning in, nodding, and making eye contact to communicate interest, empathy, and engagement. Increasing noise and clutter are distractors the nurse should decrease, not allow.

qs.q: A nursing student is nervous before her first clinical experience and tells herself, 'You can do this.' This is an example of which level of communication?
c: Interpersonal communication
Intrapersonal communication
Small-group communication
Organizational communication
qs.e: Intrapersonal communication, or self-talk, is communication within a person and affects the nurse's behavior and interactions. Interpersonal occurs between two or more people exchanging messages.

qs.q: Nurses on a practice council work together to review unit policies. This is an example of which level of communication?
c: Intrapersonal communication
Interpersonal communication
Small-group communication
Organizational communication
qs.e: Organizational communication occurs when people and groups within an organization communicate to achieve established goals. Small-group involves nurses interacting with two or more people for a shared goal but not necessarily within an organizational structure like a practice council.

qs.q: A nurse is reported to the state board of nursing for inappropriately disclosing patient information on social media. Which is a possible disciplinary outcome?
c: Only a verbal warning from the employer
Temporary or permanent loss of licensure
No formal consequences if the disclosure was unintentional
Automatic referral to patient advocacy services
qs.e: Disciplinary action by the board of nursing can include a reprimand or sanction, monetary fine, or temporary or permanent loss of licensure. Even unintentional disclosures have serious consequences.

qs.q: A client becomes silent for several moments during a conversation with the nurse. The nurse should recognize that this silence may indicate:
c: Only that the client is angry with the nurse
The client is not interested in communicating
Complete understanding, thinking, or being angry
The nurse should immediately interrupt with a new question
qs.e: Silence between two people might indicate complete understanding, that both are thinking, or that they are angry with each other. It is not always one single meaning, so the nurse should not assume anger or rush to fill the silence.

qs.q: Which of the following are American Nurses Association (ANA) principles for social networking? Select all that apply.
c: Nurses must not transmit or place online individually identifiable patient information
Nurses must observe ethically prescribed professional patient–nurse boundaries
Nurses may post patient information using only a room number for identification
Nurses should take advantage of privacy settings and separate personal and professional information
Nurses should participate in developing institutional policies governing online conduct
Nurses may delete posted information and assume it is permanently removed
qs.e: ANA's principles emphasize protecting patient information, maintaining professional boundaries, using privacy settings, and helping develop policy. Using a room number instead of a name is still a breach, and deleted information may still be available — both are incorrect statements.

qs.q: Which of the following are the four levels of communication nurses engage in during practice? Select all that apply.
c: Intrapersonal communication
Interpersonal communication
Small-group communication
Organizational communication
Transactional communication
Therapeutic communication
qs.e: Nurses engage in four levels: intrapersonal, interpersonal, small-group, and organizational. Transactional and therapeutic communication are not identified as one of the four levels of communication in this chapter.

qs.q: A nurse is preparing for a telehealth encounter with a patient. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
c: Dress professionally
Decrease environmental noise and clutter
Ensure privacy and lack of interruptions
Use nonverbal cues such as leaning in, nodding, and making eye contact
Use text abbreviations to save time during the encounter
Be a good listener
qs.e: For telehealth, nurses should dress professionally, decrease distractors, ensure privacy, use key nonverbal cues, and be good listeners. Text abbreviations should be avoided in e-mail and text messages and are not appropriate for professional telehealth communication.

qs.q: Which of the following are examples of small-group communication? Select all that apply.
c: Staff meetings
Patient care conferences
Teaching sessions
Support groups
Self-talk before entering a patient's room
Strategic planning with interdisciplinary groups
qs.e: Small-group communication includes staff meetings, patient care conferences, teaching sessions, and support groups. Self-talk is intrapersonal, and strategic planning with interdisciplinary groups is organizational communication.

qs.q: Which of the following are potential consequences for a nurse who inappropriately uses social media to disclose patient information? Select all that apply.
c: Reprimand or sanction by the board of nursing
Monetary fine
Temporary or permanent loss of licensure
Civil or criminal penalties, including possible incarceration
Employment consequences including loss of employment
Automatic reassignment to non-patient care duties only
qs.e: Consequences include board of nursing disciplinary action (reprimand, fine, loss of licensure), civil/criminal penalties, and employment consequences. Automatic reassignment is not listed as a consequence in the text.

qs.q: Which of the following are oral but nonverbal forms of communication? Select all that apply.
c: Crying
Moaning
Gasping
Sighing
Speaking in a calm tone
Whispering instructions
qs.e: Crying, moaning, gasping, and sighing are oral but nonverbal forms of communication. Speaking and whispering are verbal forms of communication involving words.

qs.q: Intrapersonal communication, or __________, is communication within a person that affects the nurse's behavior.
qs.e: Intrapersonal communication is also called self-talk. It is crucial because it can enhance or detract from positive interactions with the patient and family.

qs.q: Gasping often indicates fear, pain, or __________.
qs.e: Gasping is a nonverbal sound that often indicates fear, pain, or surprise. A sigh, by contrast, indicates reluctant agreement or relief.

qs.q: Nurses engage in how many levels of communication during practice? Enter a number.
qs.e: Nurses engage in four levels: intrapersonal, interpersonal, small-group, and organizational communication. Remembering the number helps organize all four categories for exams.

qs.q: E-mail and text messages should be concise and avoid text __________.
qs.e: Text abbreviations should be avoided to maintain professional, clear communication and prevent misinterpretation by colleagues or patients.

qs.q: The nurse is explaining an infection to a 10-year-old client. Which approach is most appropriate?
c: Give a detailed explanation using medical terminology.
Explain the infection in simple terms that support cooperation without causing fear.
Avoid explaining the infection until the child develops abstract thinking.
Use the same explanation that would be given to an adult.
qs.e: A 10-year-old has limited understanding of infection, so simple explanations can promote cooperation without frightening the child. More detailed explanations are appropriate for adolescents as abstract thinking develops.

qs.q: The nurse is admitting a client who is a health care professional. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Omit teaching because the client already understands health care.
Provide assistance only if the client specifically requests it.
Respect the client's professional role while assessing teaching and care needs.
Assume the client can independently manage the condition.
qs.e: A professional role may offer insight into identity, but it does not eliminate the need for nursing care, teaching, or counseling. Assuming that health care professionals know everything about their condition is hazardous stereotyping.

qs.q: A client never complains or asks the nurse for anything. Which response is most appropriate?
c: Offer the client an opportunity to express needs.
Assume the client has no unmet needs.
Wait for the client to initiate every conversation.
Limit interactions because the client appears self-sufficient.
qs.e: Power differences in the health care professional–patient relationship may make communication intimidating. Being uncomplaining does not establish that the client has no needs.

qs.q: The nurse is discussing a gallbladder operation with a client who is unfamiliar with medical language. Which action best supports communication?
c: Use abbreviations to keep the explanation brief.
Use 'cholecystectomy' throughout to improve precision.
Avoid discussing the procedure because the client lacks medical knowledge.
Use 'gallbladder operation' when explaining the procedure.
qs.e: Lay terminology helps clients understand health information. Medical terminology and abbreviations can alienate clients and inhibit further communication.

qs.q: A nurse wants to develop greater cultural competence in communication. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Use the nurse's own beliefs as the standard for interpreting every client's behavior.
Identify personal cultural beliefs and prejudices that could affect interactions.
Assume that nonverbal communication has the same meaning for all clients.
Focus on the client's diagnosis rather than cultural preferences.
qs.e: Cultural competence requires awareness of personal cultural beliefs and attitudes that may create communication barriers. Understanding the client's culture also helps the nurse interpret nonverbal communication.

qs.q: A practice council identifies a recurring problem, chooses an appropriate decision-making method, and agrees on a solution. Which action best demonstrates effective group decision making?
c: Move to another issue without assigning importance to the decision.
Leave implementation entirely to members who disagree.
Implement the decision and follow through with strong group commitment.
Delay action until the problem becomes more serious.
qs.e: Effective groups implement decisions, follow through, and demonstrate high commitment. Agreement alone is insufficient if members take little responsibility for resolving the problem.

qs.q: Which observation during a nursing committee meeting requires follow-up because it reflects ineffective group interaction?
c: Members honestly critique one another's suggestions.
Communication flows freely in both directions.
Members support and praise one another.
A member repeatedly blocks discussion without being challenged.
qs.e: Unchecked self-serving roles, including the blocker role, characterize ineffective group interaction. Honest critique is not inherently ineffective; it is part of effective two-way communication.

qs.q: A nurse is evaluating how a committee uses power. Which finding best indicates an effective group?
c: Members consider the needs and interests of those with little power.
Members use power primarily to fix immediate problems regardless of others' needs.
Members give little attention to people without authority.
Members rely on misuse of power when problems persist.
qs.e: Effective groups recognize sources of power, use them appropriately, and consider those with little power. Using or abusing power merely to fix immediate problems characterizes ineffective groups.

qs.q: During a therapeutic encounter, the nurse recognizes personal needs that compete with the client's concerns. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Ask the client to help meet the nurse's needs first.
Give equal attention to the nurse's and client's needs.
Temporarily set aside personal needs and focus on the client's needs.
Continue the original interventions even if the client's goals change.
qs.e: The therapeutic relationship focuses on the client's needs, with the nurse's needs temporarily set aside. Interventions also change as the client's needs and goals change rather than remaining fixed.

qs.q: A student describes the phases of the therapeutic relationship. Which statement indicates understanding?
c: Each phase must end completely before another can begin.
The phases may overlap and interlock in clinical practice.
One nurse must conduct every phase for the relationship to be therapeutic.
A therapeutic encounter must last several days.
qs.e: Therapeutic relationship phases are not clear-cut and may overlap. Different nurses may implement different phases, and a therapeutic encounter may last only a few minutes.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to communicate with an older adult client. Which problems should the nurse assess for because they can affect the interaction? Select all that apply.
c: Hearing problems
Sight problems
Confusion
Depression
A presumed lack of care needs based on professional status
qs.e: Hearing, sight, confusion, and depression can affect communication with older adults. Professional status should not be used to presume that a client has few care needs.

qs.q: Which client characteristics should be evaluated upon contact with health care services and admission to facilitate communication? Select all that apply.
c: Language proficiency
Support system
Cultural preferences
Socioeconomic circumstances
Willingness to abandon cultural preferences
qs.e: The source identifies language proficiency, support system, cultural preferences, and socioeconomic circumstances as admission communication considerations. Care should adapt sensitively to client needs rather than require abandonment of cultural preferences.

qs.q: Which observations indicate an effective nursing group? Select all that apply.
c: Members value and own clearly articulated group aims.
Members trust one another and cooperate.
Members feel responsible for group outcomes.
Participation and leadership are distributed among members.
Members accept imposed goals that have little importance to them.
Members generally work better alone because they feel alienated.
qs.e: Effective groups demonstrate shared identity, cohesion, responsibility, and distributed participation and leadership. Low ownership of goals and alienation characterize ineffective groups.

qs.q: Which committee findings suggest ineffective group functioning? Select all that apply.
c: Communication is mostly one-way.
Problems build without resolution.
Commitment to group decisions is low.
Members use an appropriate method for making decisions.
Members consider the interests of those with little power.
qs.e: One-way communication, unresolved problems, and low commitment to decisions characterize ineffective groups. Appropriate decision-making methods and consideration of less powerful members indicate effectiveness.

qs.q: The nurse is planning communication with clients of different ages. Which statements are supported by the reading? Select all that apply.
c: Adolescents can receive more detailed explanations as abstract thinking develops.
Familiarity with commonly used slang usually helps communication with adolescents.
Adults' past health-related experiences can affect communication.
Inaccurate information can affect communication with adults.
A 10-year-old typically understands infection as fully as an adult.
Older adults' sensory problems need not be considered during communication.
qs.e: Communication should reflect developmental abilities, prior experiences, and existing information. Children may need simple explanations, and older adults should be assessed for hearing or sight problems.

qs.q: Which statements accurately describe therapeutic nurse–client relationships? Select all that apply.
c: Communication follows the sequence of the nursing process.
Communication and the nursing process are continuous and reciprocal.
Different nurses may implement different relationship phases.
The nurse's needs take precedence over the client's goals.
Relationship phases never overlap.
qs.e: Therapeutic communication follows the nursing process, and both processes are continuous and reciprocal. The phases can overlap, and the relationship remains focused on the client's needs rather than the nurse's.

qs.q: What term describes the urge to maintain an exclusive right to a certain space?
qs.e: Territoriality is the urge to maintain an exclusive right to a space. It concerns a person's sense of ownership of an area rather than a professional role.

qs.q: In the commonly described three-phase therapeutic relationship, which phase comes first?
qs.e: The orientation phase precedes the identification and exploration phase and the resolution phase. This is the described sequence, although phases may overlap in practice.

qs.q: The identification and exploration phase of the therapeutic relationship is also called the _____ phase.
qs.e: Identification and exploration is also called the working phase. Resolution or termination refers to a different phase.

qs.q: The resolution phase of the therapeutic relationship is also called the _____ phase.
qs.e: Resolution is also called termination, the third phase in the commonly described sequence. It should not be confused with orientation, which is the first phase.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a newly admitted client during the orientation phase of the therapeutic relationship. Which action is MOST important to prevent the client from becoming confused and mistrustful?
c: Review the client's complete medical history in detail
Introduce themselves by name and offer to write their name for the client
Immediately begin discussing long-term health-promotion goals
Provide the client with a written contract to sign before care begins
qs.e: It is especially important to introduce yourself to the patient and it can be helpful to write your name for them; failure to do so might result in the patient becoming confused and mistrustful because of the number of caregivers most patients encounter. A written contract is occasional (the agreement is usually a simple verbal exchange), and long-term health-promotion goals belong to the working phase. Detailed history review does not prevent confusion or mistrust (in fact, data gathering occurs at the start of the relationship, during the orientation phase).

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who has been receiving care for several weeks and states, 'I feel like we're really working on my problems together.' Interaction is described as the 'essence' of which phase of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship?
c: Pre-interaction phase
Orientation phase
Working phase
Termination phase
qs.e: The working phase is usually the longest phase, and interaction is its essence—nurse and patient work together to meet needs and achieve mutually agreed-upon goals. The orientation phase focuses on establishing roles and guidelines, not ongoing interaction toward goals.

qs.q: The nurse says to a grieving client, 'I know exactly how you feel; I lost my own father last year and it was devastating.' This statement BEST illustrates:
c: Empathy
Sympathy
Therapeutic communication
Rapport
qs.e: Sympathy is the expression of sorrow for someone's situation and shifts the emphasis from the patient to the nurse as the nurse shares personal feelings. Empathy is an objective understanding of the patient's situation without projecting the nurse's own experience onto the patient.

qs.q: The nurse is at change-of-shift time, which marks the conclusion of the initial agreement with a client. What is the priority nursing action during the termination phase?
c: Avoid discussing the relationship to prevent the client from feeling sad
Examine with the client the goals of the relationship for attainment or progress
Hand over all responsibilities to the next nurse without discussing the relationship
Focus exclusively on physical assessment findings for the next nurse
qs.e: During termination, the nurse and patient examine goals for attainment or evidence of progress toward them, and acknowledgment produces satisfaction. Avoiding discussion deprives the client of closure; termination can occur at change-of-shift, so it must be addressed even during routine shift changes.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who speaks a different language and appears frightened. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
c: Speak loudly and slowly to ensure the client understands every word
Use complex medical terminology to maintain professional accuracy
Speak slowly and distinctly but NOT loudly, keeping messages simple and using gestures
Rely solely on a family member to translate all information
qs.e: The nurse should speak slowly and distinctly but not loudly, use simple repeated messages, gestures, and facial expressions to alleviate fear. Speaking loudly can increase anxiety; medical terms create confusion; a family member is not an appropriate substitute for a trained interpreter.

qs.q: During the health history interview, a client becomes evasive and provides minimal responses. Which nursing behavior is MOST likely contributing to this problem?
c: Demonstrating warmth and friendliness
Using active listening techniques
Appearing judgmental toward the client
Showing empathy and honesty
qs.e: Patients who feel that a nurse is judgmental might withhold significant information. Warmth, active listening, and empathy all promote openness and would encourage the client to share more, not less.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client from a culture where sexual matters are not discussed freely with members of the opposite sex. Which action is MOST appropriate?
c: Ask detailed sexual health questions regardless of the client's comfort level
Be aware of this cultural norm and adjust the interview approach accordingly
Delegate all sexual health assessment to a same-gender colleague without explanation
Skip sexual health assessment entirely to avoid offending the client
qs.e: The nurse should be aware that in some cultures sexual matters are not discussed freely with members of the opposite sex and modify the approach respectfully. Skipping the assessment entirely omits important data; forcing questions violates cultural sensitivity.

qs.q: The nurse is using an interpreter to communicate with a client who speaks a different language. Which instruction to the interpreter is MOST appropriate?
c: Translate only the individual words so the client understands each term in isolation
Translate the message—not just individual words—and obtain feedback to confirm understanding
Summarize the message in as few words as possible to save time
Speak as loudly as possible so the client can hear clearly
qs.e: The nurse should ask the interpreter to translate the message (not just individual words), obtain feedback to confirm understanding, and use a culturally sensitive interpreter. Word-for-word translation can distort meaning; summarizing risks omitting critical content.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client at the conclusion of the therapeutic relationship where goals were NOT fully met. Which client response is EXPECTED?
c: A feeling of satisfaction and accomplishment
Anxiety and fear about the future
Indifference toward the end of care
Relief that the relationship is ending
qs.e: If goals have not been achieved, the patient might experience anxiety and fear about the future. Satisfaction and accomplishment are associated with goals that have been met, which is the opposite scenario.

qs.q: A nurse consistently demonstrates warmth, friendliness, empathy, honesty, authenticity, trust, caring, and competence in interactions with clients. These characteristics are BEST described as:
c: Therapeutic communication techniques
Dispositional traits
Nursing diagnoses
Communication barriers
qs.e: A dispositional trait is a characteristic or customary way of behaving, and nurses who consistently demonstrate these qualities are well disposed to communicate effectively. They are not techniques (skills) or barriers—they are inherent personal qualities.

qs.q: The nurse is in the orientation phase of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship. Which patient goals should be established? Select all that apply.
c: The patient will call the nurse by name
The patient will accurately describe the roles of the participants in the relationship
The patient will actively participate in the relationship
The patient and nurse will establish an agreement about goals, location, frequency, length, and duration of contacts
The patient will verbalize feelings about the termination of the relationship
The patient will express feelings and concerns to the nurse
qs.e: Box 8-3 lists orientation-phase goals as calling the nurse by name, accurately describing roles, and establishing an agreement. Active participation and expressing feelings are working-phase goals; verbalizing feelings about termination belongs to the termination phase.

qs.q: The nurse is in the working phase of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship. Which patient goals are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: The patient will actively participate in the relationship
The patient will cooperate in activities that work toward achieving mutually acceptable goals
The patient will express feelings and concerns to the nurse
The patient will call the nurse by name
The patient will participate in identifying goals accomplished
The patient will verbalize feelings about termination
qs.e: Box 8-3 specifies three working-phase goals: active participation, cooperation toward goals, and expressing feelings and concerns. Calling the nurse by name is an orientation-phase goal; identifying accomplished goals and verbalizing feelings about termination are termination-phase goals.

qs.q: During the termination phase of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship, which patient goals are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: The patient will participate in identifying the goals accomplished or the progress made toward goals
The patient will verbalize feelings about the termination of the relationship
The patient will accurately describe the roles of the participants in the relationship
The patient will actively participate in the relationship
The patient will cooperate in activities that work toward mutually acceptable goals
The patient will express feelings and concerns to the nurse
qs.e: Box 8-3 lists only two termination-phase goals: identifying goals accomplished/progress made and verbalizing feelings about termination. The other options are orientation- and working-phase goals.

qs.q: The nurse is planning care for a client from a different culture. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: Set aside judgmental values, biases, and attitudes that may negatively affect care
Determine the ethnic identity of the patient
Assume the patient's cultural beliefs are the same as the nurse's
Encourage the patient to reveal cultural interpretations of health and illness
Communicate at the patient's personal level of functioning
qs.e: Box 8-4 directs nurses to set aside biases, determine ethnic identity, encourage cultural interpretations, and communicate at the patient's level. Assuming the patient shares the nurse's cultural beliefs leads to miscommunication and inadequate care.

qs.q: Which dispositional traits promote effective communication within the therapeutic relationship? Select all that apply.
c: Warmth and friendliness
Openness and rapport
Sympathy and pity
Empathy and honesty
Competence and caring
Authoritarian control
qs.e: The text identifies warmth and friendliness, openness and rapport, empathy, honesty, authenticity, trust, caring, and competence as dispositional traits promoting effective communication. Sympathy shifts focus to the nurse and limits objectivity; authoritarian control creates distrust.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who speaks a different language. Which communication approaches should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
c: Speak slowly and distinctly but not loudly
Keep messages simple and repeat them frequently
Use medical terminology to maintain accuracy and professionalism
Use gestures, pictures, and play acting to help the patient understand
Avoid using medical terms and abbreviations the patient may not understand
Speak as loudly as possible to ensure comprehension
qs.e: Box 8-4 recommends speaking slowly and distinctly but not loudly, keeping messages simple, using gestures/pictures, and avoiding medical terms. Medical terminology creates confusion, and speaking loudly can increase the patient's fear and anxiety.

qs.q: The ________ phase is usually the longest phase of the nurse–patient relationship, during which the roles of teacher and counselor are performed primarily.
qs.e: The working phase is usually the longest phase and is where teacher and counselor roles are performed and interaction toward goals takes place. The orientation phase establishes guidelines; termination concludes the relationship.

qs.q: Sympathy shifts the emphasis from the patient to the ________.
qs.e: Sympathy involves the nurse sharing personal feelings and projecting them onto the patient, shifting focus away from the patient's needs. Empathy, by contrast, remains objective and focused on the patient's perspective.

qs.q: During the ________ phase of the therapeutic relationship, the tone and guidelines for the relationship are established and both people's roles are clarified.
qs.e: The orientation phase is when the nurse and patient meet, learn to identify each other by name, clarify roles, and establish an agreement or contract. This phase typically begins during data gathering in the nursing process.

qs.q: The ________ phase occurs when the conclusion of the initial agreement is acknowledged—for example, at change-of-shift time, discharge, or when a nurse takes vacation.
qs.e: The termination phase occurs at the conclusion of the initial agreement and can happen at change-of-shift, discharge, or other endings. During this phase the nurse and patient review goal attainment and the patient is encouraged to express feelings about the end.

qs.q: A nurse is supporting a client whose family member is critically ill. The family appears frightened and helpless. Which response best demonstrates empathy?
c: I feel so bad for you; I would be a wreck if this were my mother.
This must be a hard time for you; how are you coping?
Don't worry, everything will work out fine in the end.
I understand exactly how you feel because I lost a relative too.
qs.e: An empathic response acknowledges the client's experience while keeping the focus on the client and inviting them to explore feelings. "I feel so bad" shifts focus to the nurse's feelings (sympathy), which limits objective focus on the patient's needs.

qs.q: A newly assigned nurse enters a client's room, checks the IV, changes the drainage bag, and leaves without making eye contact or speaking to the client. The client later states, 'I feel like just a task.' Which concept does this illustrate?
c: Relation-centered caring
Task-centered caring
Therapeutic communication
Optimal pacing
qs.e: Patients quickly sense whether they are merely a 'task to be performed' (task-centered caring) rather than a person of worth who is cared about and cared for (relation-centered caring). The nurse's actions conveyed only task completion without relational engagement.

qs.q: A client tells the nurse, 'I don't know why these injections scare me, but they do.' Which nurse response is most therapeutic?
c: I give hundreds of injections. Don't be so immature.
You are afraid of these injections?
Everyone is afraid of injections sometimes.
Why would you be afraid of something so simple?
qs.e: The reflection response focuses on the client and the client's needs, validating feelings. The first option focuses on the nursing activity and dismisses the client—communication should focus on the patient and patient needs, not the nurse or an activity.

qs.q: The nurse is conducting a client interview in a shared hospital room. Which action best addresses the need for privacy during the interaction?
c: Speak louder so the client can hear over the roommate's TV.
Draw the curtains around the bed and lower the voice.
Move the conversation to the nurses' station where no one can overhear.
Postpone the interview until the roommate is discharged.
qs.e: Every effort should be made to provide privacy and prevent conversations from being overheard; drawing the curtains around the bed can provide the needed sense of privacy. Moving to the nurses' station fails to provide privacy from staff and other patients.

qs.q: A client confides in the nurse about a sensitive family matter and asks, 'Who else will know about this?' Which response is most appropriate?
c: Whatever you tell me stays strictly between us; no one else will ever know.
I'll share it with the entire care team so we can all help you.
I will indicate with whom the information will be shared, and you have the right to specify who can access it.
Anything you say in a hospital is part of the medical record and everyone can see it.
qs.e: Confidentiality should be established with the patient; the nurse should indicate with whom information will be shared, and the patient has the right to specify who might have access. Promising absolute secrecy is inaccurate because some information must be shared with the care team.

qs.q: A nurse has multiple clients and only 20 minutes to complete a detailed nursing history with one client. What is the priority action before beginning the interview?
c: Rush through the list of questions as efficiently as possible.
Let the client know at the beginning that time is limited.
Skip the history and ask another nurse to do it later.
Tell the client to answer as quickly as possible.
qs.e: If time is limited, let the patient know at the beginning of the interaction so the patient does not feel rushed due to lack of concern. Rushing through questions without notice impairs communication.

qs.q: In the Box 8-5 scenario, Mr. Commens says his doctor told him the cancer has spread. Which nurse response from the nontherapeutic example blocks communication?
c: Mr. Commens, how would you describe and rate your pain on a scale of 1 to 10?
Mr. Commens, you seem concerned and a little preoccupied. Is there something bothering you?
Now, who told you that? Maybe the test was wrong, or you misunderstood the health care provider.
Would it help if I spoke to your health care provider to obtain specific details about your treatment plan?
qs.e: This response gives the patient the impression the nurse does not believe the information he relayed and focuses on the nurse's doubt rather than the patient's concerns. The other options are therapeutic techniques shown in Box 8-5.

qs.q: A nurse suspects a client is anxious about pending blood test results, but the client states, 'Those results aren't important.' The nurse then observes the client pacing in the corridor, wringing hands and deep in thought. This nursing observation serves primarily to:
c: Replace the need for verbal communication with the client
Validate the nurse's suspicion that the client is fearful despite verbal denial
Document the client's behavior for the medical record
Determine that the client is being intentionally untruthful
qs.e: Observations involve both effective noticing and interpreting and are especially useful for validating information. The behavior supports the nurse's suspicion of fear, showing the verbal denial may be a cover-up; it does not replace verbal communication or imply deceit.

qs.q: A nurse is caring for a client who states, 'I don't want to talk right now; I just want to be left alone.' Which action best reflects a comfortable, therapeutic environment for future interaction?
c: Dim the lights, close the door, and return later to try again.
Explain the importance of communicating and sit down to begin the interview.
Bring another staff member in to help encourage the client to talk.
Leave the door open so the client can see activity in the hallway.
qs.e: A comfortable environment in which both patient and nurse are at ease promotes interaction; the atmosphere should be relaxed and unhurried, and the nurse should follow the patient's cues. Pressuring the client impairs communication.

qs.q: A nurse is unfamiliar with community resources available for family caregivers of clients with special needs, and the family asks about them. Which response is best?
c: Make up an answer so the family does not feel anxious.
Admit the topic is unfamiliar and direct them to other resources who can help.
Tell the family to look it up on the internet.
Promise to find out and get back to them next week without any timeline.
qs.e: If the topic is unfamiliar, the nurse should admit that to the patient and family and direct them to other resources, conveying confidence and honesty. Guessing or fabricating information undermines trust and competence.

qs.q: A nurse enters a room to care for a 3-year-old child with burns. Which action sets the stage for a caring, therapeutic interaction?
c: Scold the child for crying so the assessment can be completed quickly.
Enter the room and approach the child's bed, touching the shoulder or hand gently and softly.
Avoid touching the child because burns make contact painful and inappropriate.
Ask the child's parent to stop the child's crying before proceeding.
qs.e: Expert nurses communicate genuine caring by how they look at and touch the patient and what they say; the gentle touch approach conveys much more caring than scolding. Scolding focuses on the nurse's task needs, not the child's.

qs.q: Which are purposes of nursing observations in the nurse–patient relationship? Select all that apply.
c: Help increase awareness of the patient's nonverbal messages
Serve as the primary source of information when a patient is unwilling or unable to communicate verbally
Demonstrate caring and interest in the patient
Replace all need for verbal communication in the assessment
Serve as an important component of clinical reasoning and clinical judgment
Allow the nurse to document behavioral deviations in the chart
qs.e: Observation increases awareness of nonverbal messages, is primary when verbal communication is not possible, demonstrates caring, and supports clinical reasoning/judgment. It does not replace verbal communication entirely or serve merely as documentation.

qs.q: Which skills comprise nurse competence as described in the textbook? Select all that apply.
c: Technical skills
Cognitive skills
Interpersonal skills
Ethical/legal skills
Spiritual counseling skills
Financial management skills
qs.e: Competent nurses meet health care needs through their technical, cognitive, interpersonal, and ethical/legal skills. Spiritual counseling and financial management are not listed in this definition of nursing competence.

qs.q: Which variables help build rapport between the nurse and the patient? Select all that apply.
c: Having specific objectives for the interaction
Providing a comfortable environment
Ensuring privacy during conversations
Establishing confidentiality
Maintaining strict time limits during every visit
Focusing conversations on the nurse's experiences
qs.e: Rapport builders include specific objectives, a comfortable environment, privacy, and confidentiality. Strict time limits and nurse-focused conversations impair rather than build rapport.

qs.q: According to the 'Through the Eyes of a Patient' box, which actions do patients value in their nurses? Select all that apply.
c: Really listen to me
Don't treat me like a disease, treat me like a person
Talk to me, not at me
Respect my privacy
Keep me informed
Give me instructions without explaining the steps
qs.e: Patients value listening, person-centered care, respectful dialogue, privacy, and being kept informed. They specifically request that nurses not tell them what to do without also telling them how to do it.

qs.q: Which statements about empathy in nursing communication are correct? Select all that apply.
c: An empathic nurse is sensitive to the patient's feelings and problems
An empathic nurse remains objective enough to help the patient work toward positive outcomes
Empathy is one approach nurses use to communicate emotional support
Being empathic means agreeing with everything the patient says
Sympathy rather than empathy limits the nurse's ability to focus objectively on the patient's needs
Empathy requires the nurse to share their own similar personal experiences with the patient
qs.e: Empathy balances sensitivity with objectivity and is a method of emotional support. Sympathy—becoming emotionally involved—limits objective focus; empathy does not require agreement or self-disclosure of personal experiences.

qs.q: Which techniques can improve conversation with patients? Select all that apply.
c: Control the tone of voice to convey exactly what you mean
Let the tone indicate interest rather than boredom and patience rather than anger
Be knowledgeable about the topic and have accurate information
Admit when a topic is unfamiliar and direct the patient to other resources
Always speak as quickly as possible to cover all content efficiently
Convey confidence and honesty to the patient
qs.e: Effective conversation skills include voice tone control, showing interest and patience, being knowledgeable, admitting unfamiliarity honestly, and conveying confidence. Speaking quickly without regard to pacing is nontherapeutic.

qs.q: Rapport is defined as a feeling of mutual ______ experienced by people in a satisfactory relationship.
qs.e: Rapport facilitates open communication and is a necessary first step in planning care; it is built on mutual trust between nurse and patient or family.

qs.q: Caring that focuses on the patient as a person of worth who is both cared about and cared for is called ______-centered caring.
qs.e: Relation-centered caring contrasts with task-centered caring, where the patient feels like merely a 'task to be performed.' Patients who feel cared for will feel accepted.

qs.q: Failure to protect patient information can be considered a breach of the patient's right to ______.
qs.e: Confidentiality and privacy are linked; failure to consider confidentiality can be considered a breach of the patient's right to privacy. The nurse should establish confidentiality with the patient and indicate with whom information will be shared.

qs.q: The nurse should let the patient set the ______ of the conversation rather than rushing through a list of questions.
qs.e: Optimal pacing means the nurse considers the pace of any conversation and lets the patient set it; if time is limited, the nurse should communicate that at the start so the patient does not feel uncared for.

qs.q: A home health nurse is planning a visit to a client who has expressed concern about family members overhearing conversations. Which intervention best ensures privacy during the visit?
c: Schedule the visit at a time that ensures the privacy the patient desires and needs.
Ask the family to leave the house during the visit.
Conduct the conversation in the client's car outside the home.
Postpone the visit until the client can come to the clinic instead.
qs.e: Home visits might need to be timed to ensure the privacy the patient desires and needs. Asking family to leave or conducting the visit in a car are not listed as appropriate strategies and may not respect the patient's wishes.

qs.q: A client who was recently diagnosed with diabetes is overwhelmed and asks, 'What am I going to do about this?' Which objective should guide the nurse's interaction at this time?
c: Discuss the client's feelings about being newly diagnosed with diabetes.
Perform a head-to-toe physical assessment immediately.
Teach the client about insulin injection technique.
Review the client's medication schedule in detail.
qs.e: Having a specific objective guides a meaningful encounter; one example given is discussing a patient's feelings about a new diabetes diagnosis. Teaching injections or reviewing medications would not address the client's expressed emotional need.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who begins discussing diet concerns during a medication pass. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Redirect the client to the reason for the nurse's visit and discuss diet later
Take time to discuss the client's interest before proceeding, as long as time allows
Tell the client the nurse will return after all medications are given to discuss diet
Document the client's diet concerns and defer discussion to the next shift
qs.e: Following the client's lead is recommended; it is better to talk about the client's interest than to insist on only the procedure at hand, as long as there is enough time. Redirecting the client ignores their concerns and blocks therapeutic communication.

qs.q: A client tells the nurse that she is unsure about a medication side effect and the nurse is not certain of the answer. What is the nurse's best response?
c: Provide an educated guess to avoid appearing uninformed
Tell the client that the provider will address this at discharge
Admit the nurse does not know and seek an accurate answer
Change the subject to avoid an uncomfortable pause
qs.e: Being truthful builds trust; if unsure, admit you do not know and seek an answer rather than making a comment that may be an error. Providing false information leads to client distrust.

qs.q: The nurse is communicating with a client and notices the client keeps crossing his arms and legs while the nurse talks. What is the most likely interpretation of this body language?
c: The client is comfortable and content in the interaction
The client is being stoic and can cope without help
The body language conveys being closed to comments and blocks communication
The client's culture requires longer pauses between verbal exchanges
qs.e: The source states that crossing arms or legs conveys a message of being closed to the patient's comments. This body language disrupts open communication rather than indicating comfort.

qs.q: The student nurse is sitting at a client's bedside conducting an interview. Which action best demonstrates effective listening?
c: Maintain a neutral facial expression and avoid all gestures to stay professional
Maintain eye contact without staring and use appropriate facial expressions to show attention
Cross arms to show attentiveness and prevent fidgeting
Speak frequently to fill any gaps and keep the conversation moving
qs.e: Effective listening includes eye contact without staring and appropriate facial expressions and gestures to indicate attention. Crossing arms signals being closed to the client, and excessive talking shifts focus to the nurse.

qs.q: A client becomes silent during a nursing interview. The client's culture is known for using longer pauses between verbal communication. What is the most likely meaning of this silence?
c: The client is angry and using silence to display this emotion
The client is fearful and using silence as an escape
The client's culture may require longer pauses between verbal communication
The client is demonstrating stoicism and the ability to cope without help
qs.e: One meaning of silence is that the patient's culture may require longer pauses between verbal communication. Fear and anger are other possible meanings, but the scenario specifically points to a cultural factor.

qs.q: A hospitalized older adult has no living family to provide caring touch. Which nursing action is most appropriate to promote a sense of well-being?
c: Avoid touch because the client is unable to give consent
Hold the client's hand to provide caring touch
Offer a referral for therapeutic touch therapy sessions
Ask family friends to visit and provide touch
qs.e: Many older people long for touch, especially when isolated from loved ones; the nurse can provide special care by holding the patient's hand. Therapeutic touch is a separate modality requiring specialized training.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to give an older adult client an injection. Prior to touching the client, which action is most important?
c: Ensure the medication is within expiration date
Observe the client for cues indicating touch is desired and ask about touching
Explain the procedure in detail to build rapport
Position the client in a side-lying position for comfort
qs.e: The source emphasizes weighing the benefit of touch against its detrimental use and states the nurse should observe the client for cues and ask about touching prior to implementation. Not all clients tolerate touch well.

qs.q: During a nursing history, the nurse asks, "What did your health care provider tell you about your need for this hospitalization?" This question is an example of which interviewing technique?
c: Closed question or comment
Leading question
Open-ended question or comment
Focused question or comment
qs.e: An open-ended question allows the client a wide range of responses and encourages free verbalization and more descriptive information. A closed question limits responses to one or two words or yes/no.

qs.q: A client is experiencing a long period of silence and appears to be inwardly focused. Which meaning of silence does this most likely represent?
c: The client is comfortable and content in the nurse–client relationship
The client is trying to demonstrate stoicism
The client is exploring inner thoughts or feelings and needs time to think
The client is angry and using silence to display emotion
qs.e: Silence may mean the patient is exploring inner thoughts or feelings; in effect, saying "I need some time to think." Comfort/contentment and stoicism are other possible meanings, but inward focus points to self-exploration.

qs.q: The nurse is using humor with a client during a stressful hospitalization. Which statement indicates the nurse is using humor appropriately?
c: Making a joke about the client's diagnosis to lighten the mood
Using humor without considering the client's cultural background
Laughing at the client's attempts to cope with illness
Maintaining a balanced perspective and considering how the client's culture perceives humor in illness
qs.e: Humor is a learned skill that can be healing when used appropriately, but the nurse must be aware of how cultures perceive humor in the presence of illness. Inappropriate humor can be destructive.

qs.q: A nursing student is conducting an assessment interview. Before beginning to collect data, what should the student do first?
c: Ask the client to describe the chief complaint
Explain the purpose of the interview
Obtain the client's full name and date of birth
Review the client's medical record
qs.e: All interviews should begin with an explanation of the purpose of the interview. This sets expectations and establishes the therapeutic interaction as part of the orientation phase.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who repeatedly changes the subject whenever the topic of discharge planning arises. Which listening skill should the nurse employ?
c: Ignore the behavior and continue discussing discharge
Listen for themes and note which topics the client avoids
Ask closed questions to keep the client focused
Tell the client that avoidance will delay discharge
qs.e: Effective listening includes listening for themes and noting what topics the client tends to avoid. This helps the nurse understand the client's true meaning and concerns.

qs.q: A nurse is implementing therapeutic touch with a client. Which outcomes are associated with this technique? Select all that apply.
c: Promote comfort and relaxation
Promote healing and a sense of well-being
Serve as a substitute for pain medication
Replace the need for verbal communication
Increase the nurse's therapeutic authority
qs.e: Therapeutic touch may be used to promote comfort, relaxation, healing, and a sense of well-being. It is not a substitute for medication, does not replace verbal communication, and does not increase nurse authority.

qs.q: Which are recommended techniques to improve listening skills? Select all that apply.
c: Sit when communicating with a client when possible
Do not cross arms or legs during conversation
Pretend to listen politely if the topic is uninteresting
Think before responding rather than responding impulsively
Maintain eye contact without staring if culturally appropriate
Speak rapidly to keep the conversation productive
qs.e: Sitting, uncrossed limbs, thoughtful responses, and culturally appropriate eye contact all facilitate listening. Pretending to listen is detected by clients and disrupts trust; speaking rapidly is not a listed technique.

qs.q: Which are possible meanings of silence during a nurse–client interaction? Select all that apply.
c: The client may be comfortable and content in the relationship
The client may be fearful and using silence as an escape from a threat
The client is always bored with the conversation
The client may be angry and using silence to display the emotion
The client's culture may require longer pauses between verbal communication
The client is avoiding responsibility for health decisions
qs.e: Silence can mean comfort/contentment, fear, anger, cultural pause patterns, stoicism, or inner exploration. Silence is not always boredom and does not necessarily indicate avoidance of responsibility.

qs.q: Which actions demonstrate effective, client-centered communication? Select all that apply.
c: Stay on one subject at a time to prevent confusion
Use words like 'love' and 'freedom' freely since all clients understand them the same way
Be truthful and admit when the nurse does not know an answer
Keep an open mind and acknowledge that clients can contribute to their own care
Take advantage of caregiving opportunities to facilitate conversation
Always steer the conversation to the nurse's planned topic
qs.e: Client-centered communication includes staying on one subject, being truthful, keeping an open mind, and using caregiving time to converse. Words like love and freedom have different meanings (semantics), and steering away from the client's concerns is nurse-centered.

qs.q: A student nurse is preparing to interview a client. Which techniques are appropriate for gathering information during an interview? Select all that apply.
c: Begin the interview by explaining its purpose
Use open-ended questions to encourage free verbalization
Use closed questions to gather specific information and focus on a particular area
Remain flexible in approach during the interview
Avoid asking any questions until the client volunteers information
Make plans for further interactions at the end of the interview
qs.e: Effective interviewing includes explaining the purpose, using both open-ended and closed questions appropriately, remaining flexible, and planning future interactions. Waiting for the client to volunteer all information would be passive and unreliable.

qs.q: Which statements about the use of touch in nursing care are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Touch is the most highly developed sense at birth
Touch can communicate reassurance, warmth, and emotional support
Touch should be used routinely with all clients regardless of preference
The nurse should weigh the benefit of touch against its detrimental use for each client
Touch can also communicate aggression and invade personal space
Tactile experiences in infants are unnecessary for normal development
qs.e: Touch is powerful and highly developed at birth; it can be supportive or invasive. It must be individualized (benefit vs. detriment), and tactile experiences in infants are essential for normal development of self-awareness.

qs.q: The study of the meaning of words, in which words such as 'love' and 'health' may have different meanings to different people, is called ______.
qs.e: Semantics is the study of word meanings. Even when two people speak the same language, abstract words can carry different interpretations, which can block clear communication.

qs.q: An interviewing technique that allows the client a wide range of responses and prevents simple yes-or-no answers is the ______-______ question.
qs.e: Open-ended questions encourage free verbalization and more descriptive information. Closed (focused) questions, by contrast, limit responses to specific information or one- to two-word answers.

qs.q: The type of touch used by a trained nurse to promote comfort, relaxation, healing, and a sense of well-being is called ______ touch.
qs.e: Therapeutic touch is a specific modality studied by nurses to promote comfort and healing. It is distinct from routine caring touch used during daily care.

qs.q: When the nurse asks a question with limited possible responses that can be answered in one or two words or 'yes/no,' this is a ______ question.
qs.e: Closed (focused) questions gather specific information and keep the interaction focused on a particular area. Open-ended questions do the opposite by allowing a wide range of responses.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client newly prescribed antihypertensive medication. The client states, "I've been really upset about my blood pressure and have to take these pills." Which response by the nurse uses the reflective technique?
c: You've been upset ...
At home, you have been taking both a water pill and a blood pressure pill every day. Did you take them today?
Is this the first health problem you have had?
Your tiredness began after you started taking your medicine?
qs.e: The reflective technique repeats what the person has said or describes the person's feelings, encouraging the client to elaborate on thoughts and feelings. Option B validates what the nurse heard and option D is sequencing, not reflection.

qs.q: A client tells the nurse, "I don't feel like myself anymore since I've been taking my blood pressure medicine. I'm tired and don't have any energy." Which response by the nurse uses sequencing to investigate a possible cause-and-effect relationship?
c: Your tiredness began after you started taking your medicine?
You've been upset ...
What sort of complications?
At home, you have been taking both a water pill and a blood pressure pill every day. Did you take them today?
qs.e: Sequencing places events in chronologic order and investigates possible cause-and-effect relationships, which facilitates nursing assessment. The other options reflect, direct, or validate rather than establish sequence.

qs.q: A client reports taking a water pill and a blood pressure pill daily at home. The nurse responds, "At home, you have been taking both a water pill and a blood pressure pill every day. Did you take them today?" The client later seems irritated when the nurse repeatedly confirms information. Which understanding should the nurse apply?
c: Clarifying questions are used to confirm what the nurse believes was heard or observed
Validating questions may lead the client to think the nurse is not listening when overused
Reflective comments may cause the client to stop sharing feelings
Sequencing questions may confuse the client about chronology of events
qs.e: The nurse's response validates what the nurse believes was heard or observed; overusing validating questions and comments may lead the patient to think the nurse is not listening. Clarifying questions are used when the patient's meaning is unclear, not to confirm what was heard; reflective comments encourage the patient to elaborate on thoughts and feelings; and sequencing places events in a chronologic order and investigates possible cause-and-effect relationships.

qs.q: A client makes a statement that is unclear to the nurse. After the nurse asks a clarifying question, the client becomes visibly annoyed. Which understanding should the nurse apply?
c: Overuse of clarifying questions may lead the client to believe the nurse is not listening or lacks appropriate knowledge
Clarifying questions should only be used with clients who have cognitive impairment
The nurse should assume understanding whenever the client appears calm
Clarifying questions are a form of aggressive communication
qs.e: Clarifying prevents misconceptions that could lead to an inappropriate diagnosis or patient problem, but overuse can suggest inattention or lack of knowledge. The nurse should never assume understanding of the client's meaning when there is doubt.

qs.q: A nurse consistently returns 30 minutes late from lunch, leaving another nurse to cover both assignments. Which statement by the affected nurse is assertive?
c: I know we all lose track of time occasionally, but I'm finding it harder and harder to cover for you when you take extra time for lunch. I don't think it's fair for your patient and me to have to wait an extra 30 minutes every day. Can we talk about this?
Huh? No, I didn't really mind. Luckily I wasn't too busy today.
I'm sick and tired of covering for you. You are lazy and unreliable and I'm going to talk to the unit leader about you.
What kind of nurse are you! I hope you lose your job!
qs.e: Assertive communication stands up for self and others using open, honest, direct statements focused on the issue, not the person. Option B is nonassertive/acquiescent, and options C and D are aggressive, blaming, and threatening.

qs.q: A nurse believes a client's pain remains uncontrolled after a dosage change. Which statement demonstrates assertive communication with the health care provider?
c: I know we talked about Mr. Esposito's pain medication before, but I've collected some new data. Even with the change in dosage, he is only getting 1-1½ hours of relief. I believe a different analgesic agent may work better for him.

Um ... yes I know you already changed the dosage. It's just that I thought it still wasn't working. Maybe I didn't give it enough time. Thanks for listening to me anyway. I'm sorry to bother you with this.
What is it going to take to convince you that Mr. Esposito is not exaggerating his pain level so he can get more meds?
This whole attempt to talk to you is a disaster. You give doctors a bad name.
qs.e: The assertive nurse uses "I" statements, presents objective data, and proposes a solution without judgment or blame. Option B is nonassertive and self-diminishing, while options C and D are aggressive and attacking.

qs.q: During a disagreement, a colleague raises their voice, invades the nurse's personal space, uses threatening gestures, and says, "Do it my way." The nurse correctly identifies this behavior as:
c: Aggressive, because it asserts one's rights in a negative manner that violates the rights of others
Assertive, because the colleague is standing up for their own beliefs
Nonassertive, because the colleague is avoiding the real issue
Therapeutic, because the focus is on the issue rather than the person
qs.e: Aggression may be verbal or physical and is marked by tension and anger, including an angry tone, condescending or threatening statements, loud speech, and invasion of personal space. Assertive behavior focuses on the issue and respects others' rights.

qs.q: The nurse is admitting a client who has not stated a preference for how to be addressed. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Ask the client how they prefer to be addressed and use formal titles such as Mr., Mrs., Ms., or Mx. until told otherwise
Call the client by their first name to build rapport quickly
Use terms of endearment such as "honey" or "sweetie" to convey warmth
Address the client by room number to protect privacy
qs.e: Nurses should ask patients how they prefer to be addressed and err on the side of formality, using neutral and inclusive language. Slang terms such as "honey" or "sweetie" are not acceptable.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who answers only in brief replies and appears hesitant. Which action addresses the communication barrier of failure to listen?
c: Focus attention on the client and watch for subtle signals that indicate readiness to talk
Approach the interview with a closed mind so the conversation stays on schedule
Focus on the nurse's own needs to complete assessments efficiently
Ask only closed questions so the client can answer yes or no
qs.e: Failure to listen stems from lack of concentration and absence of active listening skills; clients' readiness to talk is often signaled subtly. Approaching with a closed mind or focusing on the nurse's own needs blocks communication, and closed questions may limit the client's response.

qs.q: The nurse recognizes that closed (focused) questions are often a barrier to effective communication. When is a closed question most appropriate?
c: To gather specific information and allow the nurse and client to focus on a particular area
To encourage the client to elaborate on their thoughts and feelings
To describe the client's feelings back to the client
To place events in chronologic order
qs.e: Closed questions limit the choices of possible responses (often one or two words or "yes/no") and are used to gather specific information or focus on one area. Options B through D describe reflective or sequencing techniques.

qs.q: A preceptor is evaluating a student nurse's communication with staff. Which statement by the student requires follow-up because it is nonassertive?
c: Uh ... I'm sorry to be such a pain again. I have to do this catheterization and don't know where to begin. I know you must be busy, but, uh, is there any way you might have time for me?
Miss Cheng has a new order to be straight catheterized. I reviewed the procedure, but I'd sure appreciate your talking me through this because I've never done it before and I'm terrified.
I know we all lose track of time occasionally, but I'm finding it harder and harder to cover for you. Can we talk about this?
I have collected some new data about this client's pain and I believe a different analgesic agent may work better for him.
qs.e: The apologetic, hesitant statement is nonassertive; assertive communication uses open, honest, direct "I" statements without belittling oneself. Options B, C, and D are assertive examples of asking for help or raising a concern directly.

qs.q: A nurse prepares to interact assertively with the health care team. Which characteristics are associated with the assertive nurse's self-presentation? (Select all that apply.)
c: Confident, open body posture
Eye contact
Use of clear, concise "I" statements
Ability to effectively share thoughts, feelings, and emotions
Invasion of another's personal space
Condescending tone of voice
qs.e: Assertive self-presentation includes confident open posture, eye contact, clear "I" statements, and the ability to share thoughts and feelings. Invading personal space and a condescending tone are characteristics of aggressive behavior.

qs.q: Which behaviors reflect the assertive nurse's attitude toward work? (Select all that apply.)
c: Working to capacity with or without supervision
Freedom to ask for help when necessary
Honesty in admitting mistakes and taking responsibility for them
Focus on "winning at all costs"
Enhancing self-esteem through destructive comments directed at others
Ability to give and accept compliments
qs.e: Assertive work attitudes include working to capacity, remaining calm, asking for help, giving and accepting compliments, and honestly admitting mistakes. "Winning at all costs" and destructive comments describe aggressive behavior.

qs.q: Which are characteristics of aggressive behavior? (Select all that apply.)
c: Angry tone of voice
Condescending communication
Threatening statements
Rude and intimidating behavior
Focus on the issue and not the person
Expressing feelings and beliefs in a nondefensive manner
qs.e: Characteristics of aggressive verbal behavior include using an angry tone of voice and being condescending and threatening, and aggressive behavior is rude and intimidating. Focusing on the issue and not the person and expressing feelings and beliefs in a nondefensive manner are assertive traits.

qs.q: Which nursing actions reflect the communication barrier of failure to perceive the patient as a human being? (Select all that apply.)
c: Focusing on the client's diagnosis rather than the whole client
Using terms of endearment such as "honey" or "sweetie"
Treating the client as merely an object of care
Asking the client how they prefer to be addressed
Using neutral and inclusive language with all patients
qs.e: Treating the client as an object, focusing only on the illness or diagnosis, and using slang terms of endearment all fail to recognize the whole person. Asking the client's preference and using neutral, inclusive language are correct actions.

qs.q: The nurse is using a clarifying question or comment. Which statements apply? (Select all that apply.)
c: The nurse should never assume understanding of the client's meaning
It is used when the client's thoughts or communication are unclear
It can prevent misconceptions that could lead to an inappropriate diagnosis or patient problem
Overuse may lead the client to believe the nurse is not listening or lacks appropriate knowledge
It involves repeating what the client has said to encourage elaboration
qs.e: Clarifying addresses unclear meaning and prevents misidentification of a problem, but overuse may suggest inattention or lack of knowledge. Repeating the client's words to encourage elaboration describes the reflective technique.

qs.q: A nurse is planning assessment techniques for a client interview. Which statements about sequencing and directing questions are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: Sequencing places events in a chronologic order
