Sequencing investigates a possible cause-and-effect relationship between events
Directing allows the nurse to obtain more information about a topic brought up earlier or introduce a new aspect of the current topic
Directing is used to confirm what the nurse believes has been heard or observed
Sequencing facilitates nursing assessment when events leading to a problem are placed in sequence
qs.e: Sequencing orders events and explores cause and effect, which facilitates assessment; directing returns to an earlier topic or introduces a new aspect of the current topic. Confirming what was heard describes validating.

qs.q: The question type that provides the receiver with limited choices of possible responses and is often answered by one or two words or "yes" or "no" is the ______ question.
qs.e: Closed (focused) questions limit responses and gather specific information to focus on one area, though the text notes they are often a barrier to effective communication.

qs.q: Assertive communication includes clear, concise ______ statements such as "I feel ..." and "I think ..."
qs.e: "I" statements express feelings and beliefs in a nondefensive manner and are central to assertive communication.

qs.q: The technique that involves repeating what the person has said or describing the person's feelings in order to encourage the patient to elaborate is called the ______ question or comment.
qs.e: Reflective comments mirror the client's words or feelings and encourage elaboration on thoughts and feelings.

qs.q: The acronym used as a method for health care team members to assertively speak up about patient safety concerns is ______.
qs.e: CUS is cited as an example of an assertive method for team members to raise patient safety concerns (referenced on pages 185-187).

qs.q: The technique used to place events in a chronologic order or to investigate a possible cause-and-effect relationship between events is called ______.
qs.e: Sequencing orders events and explores cause and effect, which facilitates nursing assessment of events leading to a problem.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a postoperative client who is expected to begin getting out of bed today. Which question by the nurse is least therapeutic in this situation?
c: “Did you take your insulin before breakfast this morning?”
“Do you have pain when I move your arm this way?”
“Are you ready to get out of bed?”
“Tell me about your sessions in therapy. How did you feel they went today?”
qs.e: Offering the client the chance to say “no” to getting out of bed can create difficulty when the client should be getting up; this is a pitfall of yes-or-no questions. The insulin and pain questions are appropriate uses of yes-or-no questions for specific factual or assessment detail, and the therapy question is open-ended.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a young woman who suddenly begins crying. Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
c: “You aren't acting very grown up. How do you think your husband would feel if he saw you crying like this?”
“I would like to help. Tell me, what is making you cry?”
“Everything will be all right.”
“Why are you crying? Everybody has problems.”
qs.e: This comment offers help and invites the client to express feelings without judging her. The first response is judgmental and hostile and could end effective communication, while “Everything will be all right” is a cliché that gives false assurance.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for Susie Musashi, a 3-year-old child with burns who is crying. Which response is most appropriate?
c: “You're acting like a baby. You're a big girl now.”
“Can you tell me what is making you cry or feel so sad?”
“Don't worry. You will be just fine in another day or two.”
“Cheer up. Tomorrow is another day.”
qs.e: This response lets the child verbalize concerns without feeling intimidated or scolded and helps establish a trusting nurse–patient relationship. “You're acting like a baby” is intimidating to a young child striving for acceptance, and the other choices are clichés that give false assurance.

qs.q: The nurse asks a client, “Why were you not tired enough to sleep?” Which revision of this question is best?
c: “What were you doing while you were unable to sleep?”
“How did you ever decide to stay awake?”
“Why do you think you couldn't sleep?”
“You weren't tired enough to sleep, were you?”
qs.e: The text states that questions containing “why” and “how” may be intimidating to patients and are better stated as “what” questions; the recommended revision is “What were you doing while you were unable to sleep?” The choice “How did you ever decide to stay awake?” still uses the intimidating “how,” “Why do you think you couldn't sleep?” still uses the intimidating “why,” and “You weren't tired enough to sleep, were you?” is a leading question that suggests the answer the nurse wishes to hear.

qs.q: A nursing student is practicing therapeutic communication. Which question is an example of a leading question?
c: “Tell me about your sessions in therapy. How did you feel they went today?”
“What things prompted you to decide to go on a crash diet?”
“You aren't going to smoke that cigarette, are you?”
“What were you doing while you were unable to sleep?”
qs.e: A leading question suggests the response the speaker wishes to hear and pressures the patient to give an answer that pleases the nurse. The other choices are open-ended questions that encourage honest expression without intimidation.

qs.q: A client who is about to have surgery says, “I think I have a right to be afraid of this operation.” Which response is most therapeutic?
c: “Tell me what makes you feel afraid.”
“There is nothing to be afraid of. Your doctor knows best.”
“Everybody is afraid of surgery. Why should you be any different?”
“Let's talk about something else so you don't upset yourself.”
qs.e: Allowing the client to express feelings without being judged helps the client feel safe. Option 2 is a cliché/false assurance, option 3 is a sweeping generalization and an intimidating “why” question, and option 4 changes the subject, which rejects the topic and may make the client feel personally rejected.

qs.q: A client asks, “When can I expect to be told about my insulin?” The nurse replies, “Let's discuss your diet now so that you will know what to eat when you get home. We can discuss your insulin some other time.” Which outcome is most likely?
c: The client feels heard and is motivated to ask more questions.
The client may feel frustrated or personally rejected.
The client becomes more independent in decision making.
The client gains a clearer understanding of the insulin regimen.
qs.e: Changing the subject is a quick way to stop conversation; rejection of a topic closes it off from exploration and can leave the patient feeling frustrated or personally rejected. The client may be at a point of readiness to discuss the topic, so the other outcomes are unlikely.

qs.q: The nurse realizes that a comment just made to a client provided false assurance. Which action should the nurse take next?
c: Explain with an apology and implement effective communication techniques.
Document the client's response and end the conversation for now.
Repeat the reassurance so the client will feel more comfortable.
Ask a question requiring only a yes or no answer to confirm understanding.
qs.e: If false assurance is used inadvertently, the nurse should explain with an apology and implement effective communication techniques. Repeating the reassurance continues the false assurance, and a yes-or-no question tends to cut off discussion.

qs.q: Which requirement does The Joint Commission leadership standard establish for hospitals and other accredited institutions?
c: Establish a code of conduct defining acceptable, disruptive, and unacceptable behavior.
Immediately terminate any employee reported for incivility.
Allow each nursing unit to determine its own informal norms of behavior.
Require a mediator to be present at every staff disagreement.
qs.e: The standard requires institutions to establish a code of conduct defining acceptable, disruptive, and unacceptable behavior and to create and implement a process for managing unprofessional and inappropriate behaviors. The other options go beyond what the standard mandates.

qs.q: Which statement best reflects the NIOSH definition of workplace violence?
c: Violent acts, including physical assaults and threats of assault, directed toward persons at work on duty.
Only physical assaults that result in documented injury to staff members.
Any disagreement between a nurse and a client or family member.
Verbal harassing and yelling by clients' family members only.
qs.e: NIOSH (2014) defines workplace violence as violent acts, including physical assaults and threats of assault, directed toward persons at work on duty. Threats count as workplace violence even without injury, and the definition is broader than family verbal behavior alone.

qs.q: A nursing instructor is reviewing comments that impede communication. Which statements are clichés or sweeping generalizations? (Select all that apply.)
c: “Everything will be all right.”
“Tell me about your sessions in therapy. How did you feel they went today?”
“Your doctor knows best.”
“Everybody is afraid of surgery. Why should you be any different?”
“What were you doing while you were unable to sleep?”
“You teenagers are all alike. You aren't cooperative because you deny authority.”
qs.e: Clichés are stereotyped, trite, or pat answers that suggest there is no cause for anxiety or offer false assurance; sweeping generalizations cut off communication and make people feel insignificant. The therapy and sleep questions are open-ended and encourage the patient to talk.

qs.q: Which questions represent appropriate uses of a question that can be answered with yes or no? (Select all that apply.)
c: “Did you take your insulin before breakfast this morning?”
“Are you ready to get out of bed?”
“Do you have pain when I move your arm this way?”
“Did you have a good day?”
“You have been well cared for by your nurses, haven't you?”
qs.e: Yes-or-no questions are appropriate when seeking specific factual or assessment detail, such as taking insulin or pain with a movement. “Are you ready to get out of bed?” offers a chance to say no when the client should be getting up, “Did you have a good day?” begs for a noncommittal answer, and the last question is leading.

qs.q: Which behaviors are examples of covert bullying? (Select all that apply.)
c: Withholding information from a colleague
Gossiping and spreading rumors
Using nonverbal communication such as eye-rolling and other body language
Social isolation
Accusing a nurse of errors made by someone else (scapegoating)
Humiliating a person in the presence of others
qs.e: Covert bullying includes withholding information, gossiping and spreading rumors, nonverbal communication such as eye-rolling, and social isolation. Scapegoating and humiliating a person in front of others are overt bullying behaviors.

qs.q: A nurse working in a toxic work environment reports health problems. Which findings are commonly reported physical consequences? (Select all that apply.)
c: Frequent headaches
Sleep disturbances
Gastrointestinal symptoms
Decreased energy
Loss of self-esteem
Suicidal ideation or attempt
qs.e: Frequent headaches, sleep disturbances, gastrointestinal symptoms, and decreased energy are the commonly reported physical consequences. Loss of self-esteem and suicidal ideation are psychological manifestations, not physical ones.

qs.q: Which actions does The Joint Commission advise hospitals to take regarding unacceptable behavior? (Select all that apply.)
c: Educate all staff about the code of conduct
Develop reporting systems
Use mediators when necessary
Document all efforts to address unacceptable behavior
Allow disruptive behavior to continue if patient outcomes are unaffected
Require staff to resolve all conflicts without any written process
qs.e: The Joint Commission advises educating all staff about the code of conduct, developing reporting systems, using mediators when necessary, and documenting all efforts to address unacceptable behavior. The last two options contradict the standard, which requires a process for managing inappropriate behaviors.

qs.q: Which findings are psychological manifestations reported by nurses in a toxic work environment? (Select all that apply.)
c: Increased level of stress
Anxiety and fear
Frustration and loss of self-esteem
Gastrointestinal symptoms
Burnout, emotional exhaustion, and depression
Frequent headaches
qs.e: Increased stress, anxiety, fear, frustration, and loss of self-esteem can result in burnout, emotional exhaustion, depression, and suicidal ideation or attempt. Gastrointestinal symptoms and headaches are physical consequences of the toxic environment.

qs.q: Which behaviors are examples of incivility as described in the text? (Select all that apply.)
c: Refusing to assist a coworker when help is needed
Refusing to share important information about a patient's care
Remaining silent while others are treated with disrespect
Failing to act when action is warranted
Using an open-ended question to explore a client's concerns
Asking a coworker to clarify an unfamiliar order
qs.e: Incivility includes failing to act when action is warranted, such as refusing to assist a coworker or share important information about a patient's care, or remaining silent while others are treated with disrespect. Open-ended questioning and seeking clarification are appropriate professional behaviors.

qs.q: Anger and aggressive behavior between nurses, or nurse-to-nurse hostility, has been labeled __________.
qs.e: Nurse-to-nurse hostility is labeled horizontal violence and is also referred to as bullying, lateral violence, and professional incivility—all breaches in the workplace norms of respect and courtesy.

qs.q: Gossip and rumor in health care settings are sometimes referred to as __________.
qs.e: “The grapevine” is a common form of communication in health care settings; gossip and rumor can damage reputations and block team building, even though they can also be used to inform or entertain.

qs.q: The U.S. Department of Labor agency that has established guidelines for preventing workplace violence for health care and social service workers is __________.
a: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration
qs.e: OSHA (2016) established guidelines for preventing workplace violence for health care and social service workers. The Joint Commission standard addresses codes of conduct and management of disruptive behavior, not the prevention guidelines.

qs.q: Bullying that includes withholding information, gossiping, eye-rolling, and social isolation is called __________ bullying.
qs.e: Covert bullying is indirect (withholding information, rumors, eye-rolling, social isolation), whereas overt bullying includes scapegoating and humiliating a person in the presence of others.

qs.q: In a 12-month period, what percentage of registered nurses and nursing students reported being verbally abused according to OSHA surveys?
qs.e: 50% of RNs and nursing students reported verbal abuse in a 12-month period. The 21% figure refers to physical assault, while 59% applies to emergency department nurses over only a 7-day period.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who makes disrespectful remarks during a routine interaction. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Ignore the remarks to avoid further escalation
Respond assertively and address the issue directly with those involved
Immediately leave the room and contact security
Tell the client that visitation will be restricted
qs.e: When disruptive behavior occurs, the nurse should maintain a professional demeanor and respond assertively, addressing the issue directly. Ignoring remarks would not promote a healthy work environment and could allow the behavior to continue.

qs.q: A nursing student uses diminutive words, exaggerated voice intonation, and high pitch when speaking to an older adult client. The instructor notes this is a form of ageism. This communication style is known as:
c: Therapeutic communication
Active listening
Elderspeak
Reflective response
qs.e: Elderspeak involves diminutive words, exaggerated voice intonation, high pitch, and exaggerated punctuation that imply the older adult is not competent. Therapeutic communication and active listening are respectful, appropriate approaches.

qs.q: A nurse is caring for a client who is becoming increasingly agitated and aggressive. The nurse knows that the most important initial approach to prevent violence is to use:
c: Security personnel stationed at the unit
Effective therapeutic communication techniques
Restraint and seclusion protocols
Psychotropic medication
qs.e: Communication is the first line of defense against patient violence. Therapeutic communication builds trust, establishes rapport, and validates feelings before other measures are needed.

qs.q: A client recovering from a traumatic brain injury has difficulty producing words and speaking. The nurse identifies this as:
c: A language barrier
Impaired verbal communication
Autism spectrum disorder
A normal recovery finding
qs.e: Impaired verbal communication is defined as a decreased, delayed, or absent ability to use speech. A language barrier refers to a difference in languages, not an impairment in the ability to produce speech.

qs.q: The nurse enters the room of a newly admitted visually impaired client. Which action should the nurse take first?
c: Touch the client's hand to announce presence
Speak in a louder voice to ensure the client hears
Acknowledge presence in the room and identify yourself by name
Begin explaining the care plan immediately
qs.e: According to Box 8-6, the nurse should acknowledge presence in the room and identify by name. Touching before explaining why is inappropriate, and a normal tone of voice—not a louder one—is recommended.

qs.q: A client begins making verbal threats toward the nurse. Before interacting with the aggressor, the nurse should first:
c: Confront the client firmly to establish boundaries
Remain calm and ensure a calm attitude
Remove all other clients from the area immediately
Document the incident and leave without interaction
qs.e: Threats or violent behavior require a calm attitude before interacting with the aggressor; being upset will escalate the situation. While documentation is important, the text specifically emphasizes calming oneself first.

qs.q: According to the text, the cost to help a worker who has suffered workplace violence or to hire a new nurse can be as much as:
qs.e: The cost can be as much as $103,000, highlighting the significant financial impact of workplace violence on health care organizations in addition to the human toll.

qs.q: OSHA reports that between 2002 and 2013, incidents of serious workplace violence (requiring days off) were how many times more common in health care than in private industry?
c: 2 times
4 times
6 times
8 times
qs.e: Serious workplace violence incidents requiring days off were four times more common in health care than in private industry on average. This underscores the heightened risk of violence in health care settings.

qs.q: The nurse needs to perform a procedure requiring touching a visually impaired client. Before touching the client, the nurse should:
c: Speak in a high-pitched voice to announce the action
Explain the reason for touching the patient
Ask a family member to inform the patient
Obtain written consent
qs.e: Box 8-6 states the nurse should explain the reason for touching the patient before doing so. High-pitched voice is characteristic of elderspeak and should be avoided; a normal tone is recommended.

qs.q: According to The Joint Commission, which is a key recommendation to prevent disruptive behaviors in health care facilities?
c: Discreetly handling complaints without documentation
Providing education to all staff regarding respectful, professional behavior
Allowing staff to self-regulate without institutional oversight
Limiting reporting to only physical violence
qs.e: The Joint Commission emphasizes education for all staff on respectful, professional behavior and communication. Documentation and reporting systems are also key, not handling complaints discreetly.

qs.q: Which strategies are recommended when communicating with patients who have impaired verbal communication? Select all that apply.
c: Use a calm and reassuring approach
Use nonverbal gestures to aid understanding
Seek clarification and validation of messages
Speak using diminutive words and high pitch
Maintain adjustments that are respectful, positive, and individualized
Use exaggerated voice intonation to emphasize key points
qs.e: Strategies include a calm/reassuring approach, nonverbal gestures, and seeking clarification/validation. Adjustments must be respectful, positive, and individualized. Diminutive words and exaggerated intonation are characteristics of elderspeak and should be avoided.

qs.q: Which actions should the nurse take when caring for a visually impaired patient? Select all that apply.
c: Acknowledge your presence in the patient's room
Identify yourself by name
Keep a call light or bell within easy reach
Speak in a louder than normal voice
Explain the reason for touching before doing so
Avoid telling the patient when leaving to reduce anxiety
qs.e: Box 8-6 recommends acknowledging presence, identifying by name, keeping a call light/bell accessible, and explaining the reason for touching. A normal tone of voice should be used, and the nurse should indicate when leaving.

qs.q: Which of the following are characteristics of elderspeak? Select all that apply.
c: Diminutive words
Exaggerated voice intonation
High pitch
Exaggerated punctuation
Normal tone of voice
Calm and reassuring approach
qs.e: Elderspeak involves diminutive words, exaggerated voice intonation, high pitch, and exaggerated punctuation. These imply the older adult is not competent and are a form of ageism. A normal tone and calm approach are appropriate alternatives.

qs.q: Which of the following are proactive responses to disruptive behavior and workplace violence? Select all that apply.
c: Learning to react professionally and protectively in the moment
Documenting and reporting the incident
Tolerating the behavior to maintain workplace harmony
Using conflict-management strategies when responding to aggressive behavior
Insisting that disruptive behavior and communication are addressed
Asking the aggressor to leave the unit immediately
qs.e: Proactive responses include reacting professionally in the moment, documenting/reporting, using conflict-management strategies, and insisting disruptive behavior is addressed. Tolerating behavior contradicts zero-tolerance policies, and the text does not direct nurses to ask aggressors to leave immediately.

qs.q: When disruptive behavior occurs in the workplace, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
c: Maintain a professional demeanor
Respond assertively and address the issue directly with those involved
Ignore the behavior to prevent escalation
Factually document the occurrence of any bullying behaviors
Seek guidance and support through nurse-managers or appropriate institutional channels
Handle the situation entirely alone without involving the institution
qs.e: The nurse should maintain professionalism, respond assertively, document factually, and seek institutional support. Ignoring behavior allows it to continue, and handling it alone ignores institutional resources and policies.

qs.q: According to the text, what should health care institutions do to prevent workplace violence? Select all that apply.
c: Develop workplace violence prevention programs
Document reports of violence
Ignore verbal abuse since it is an expected part of nursing
Provide training on workplace violence for all workers
Have clearly developed policies including zero tolerance
Investigate reported events at the end of the fiscal year
qs.e: Institutions should develop prevention programs, document reports, provide training, and have zero-tolerance policies. Violence cannot be considered an expected part of nursing, and events should be investigated in a timely manner, not deferred.

qs.q: Which of the following are key recommendations from The Joint Commission to prevent disruptive behaviors? Select all that apply.
c: All staff members must be held accountable for their behavior and use of communication techniques
Zero-tolerance policies must be implemented regarding disruptive behaviors
Bullying behaviors can be handled informally without documentation
Those in leadership positions must function as positive role models
Surveillance and reporting systems must be available to identify unprofessional behaviors
Protection must be provided only for managers who report behaviors
qs.e: The Joint Commission recommends accountability, zero-tolerance policies, leadership role modeling, and surveillance/reporting systems. Bullying must be documented, and protection for reporters extends to all who report, not just managers.

qs.q: In a 12-month period, what percentage of registered nurses and nursing students reported being physically assaulted?
qs.e: 21% of RNs and nursing students reported being physically assaulted in a 12-month period, while 50% reported verbal abuse. These statistics highlight the prevalence of violence against nurses.

qs.q: What percentage of emergency department nurses experienced verbal abuse during a 7-day period?
qs.e: 59% of ED nurses experienced verbal abuse during only a 7-day period, and 12% experienced physical violence in that same time frame. The short time window makes these figures especially striking.

qs.q: The use of diminutive words, exaggerated voice intonation, high pitch, and exaggerated punctuation when communicating with older adults is called:
qs.e: Elderspeak is a form of non-person-centered communication and ageism that implies older adults are not competent. Nurses should communicate with older adults in a normal, respectful tone instead.

qs.q: Communication is considered the ______ line of defense against patient violence.
qs.e: Therapeutic communication is the first line of defense against patient violence, as it helps build trust, establish rapport, and validate feelings. Security and restraints are later measures when de-escalation fails.

qs.q: What term describes a disease state resulting from pathogens in or on the body?
qs.e: Infection is a disease state caused by the presence of pathogens in or on the body. A reservoir is only one component of the infection cycle.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly lists the six components of the infection cycle?
c: Infectious agent → reservoir → portal of exit → means of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host
Reservoir → infectious agent → portal of entry → means of transmission → portal of exit → susceptible host
Infectious agent → susceptible host → portal of exit → reservoir → portal of entry → means of transmission
Portal of entry → reservoir → infectious agent → portal of exit → susceptible host → means of transmission
qs.e: The slide lists these six components in the order shown in the first option. Portal of exit precedes transmission and portal of entry, not the reverse.

qs.q: Which organisms are listed as examples of bacteria? Select all that apply.
c: E. coli
Staphylococcus
Streptococcus
HIV
Influenza
Yeast
qs.e: The bacterial examples are E. coli, staphylococcus, and streptococcus. HIV and influenza are listed under viruses, while yeast infections are listed under fungi.

qs.q: Which groups of examples are listed under viruses? Select all that apply.
c: HIV and the common cold
Influenza and COVID-19
Hepatitis A, B, and C
Athlete's foot and ringworm
E. coli and staphylococcus
qs.e: The viral examples include HIV, the common cold, influenza, COVID-19, and hepatitis A, B, and C. Athlete's foot and ringworm are fungal examples, not viral examples.

qs.q: Which conditions are listed as fungal examples? Select all that apply.
c: Athlete's foot
Ringworm
Yeast infections
Malaria
Hepatitis B
qs.e: Athlete's foot, ringworm, and yeast infections are listed under fungi. Malaria is associated with a parasite, and hepatitis B is listed under viruses.

qs.q: A student discusses malaria during an infection-control review. Which statement matches the slides?
c: Malaria occurs from mosquitoes infected with a parasite.
Malaria is a bacterial infection associated with E. coli.
Malaria is listed as a fungal infection.
Malaria is listed with hepatitis as a viral infection.
qs.e: The slide uses malaria from mosquitoes infected with a parasite as its parasitic example. It does not classify malaria as bacterial, fungal, or viral.

qs.q: Which groups contain only potential reservoirs listed in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: People and animals
Soil and objects
Food and water
Milk
Fatigue and stress
Age and heredity
qs.e: People, animals, soil, objects, food, water, and milk are listed as reservoirs. Fatigue, stress, age, and heredity are host-susceptibility considerations instead.

qs.q: Which are listed human portals of entry that nurses should protect? Select all that apply.
c: Respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts
Genitourinary tract
Skin breakdown
Blood and tissues
Milk and food
Soil and objects
qs.e: The listed portals of entry are the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts; skin breakdown; and blood and tissues. Milk, food, soil, and objects are listed as reservoirs rather than human portals.

qs.q: Which exposure is an example of direct contact transmission in the slides?
c: Touching, kissing, or sexual intercourse
Contact with an inanimate object harboring a pathogen
Transmission by a living vector
Particles remaining suspended in the air
qs.e: Direct contact involves close proximity, with touching, kissing, and sexual intercourse as examples. Contact with a pathogen-harboring object is classified as indirect contact.

qs.q: A living creature that transmits a pathogen to humans is called a what?
qs.e: A vector is a living creature that transmits a pathogen. A fomite is inanimate rather than living.

qs.q: An inanimate object that harbors a pathogen is called a what?
qs.e: A fomite is an inanimate object that harbors a pathogen. The slide places contact involving fomites under indirect contact transmission.

qs.q: Which comparison of droplet and airborne transmission matches the slides?
c: Droplet organisms are greater than 5 micrometers and droplets land on surfaces; airborne organisms are less than 5 micrometers and particles remain in the air.
Droplet organisms are less than 5 micrometers and remain in the air; airborne organisms are greater than 5 micrometers and land on surfaces.
Both involve organisms greater than 5 micrometers that remain in the air.
Both involve organisms less than 5 micrometers that land on surfaces.
qs.e: The slides describe both categories as attaching to dust particles, but distinguish them by size and behavior. Droplets are heavy enough to land on surfaces, whereas airborne particles remain in the air.

qs.q: Which are listed human portals of exit? Select all that apply.
c: Respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts
Genitourinary tract
Skin breakdown
Blood and drainage
Food and milk
Soil and water
qs.e: The exit list includes the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts; skin breakdown; and blood and drainage. Food, milk, soil, and water are reservoirs, not the listed human portals of exit.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with several wounds and poor skin integrity. Why does this increase susceptibility to infection?
c: It creates multiple portals of entry.
It eliminates the need for an infectious agent.
It makes every exposure airborne.
It prevents organisms from leaving the body.
qs.e: Multiple wounds and poor skin integrity provide multiple portals of entry. They do not change all transmission into airborne transmission or remove the need for other infection-cycle components.

qs.q: Which student statement about host defenses indicates understanding?
c: The pH of the gastrointestinal tract, genitourinary tract, and skin helps protect against microbial invasion.
Only the pH of blood is identified as protective in these slides.
Skin breakdown protects against microbial invasion.
The pH of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts has no protective role.
qs.e: The slides identify pH in the GI tract, GU tract, and skin as protective against microbial invasion. Skin breakdown creates entry sites rather than providing protection.

qs.q: Which host characteristics are specifically listed as considerations in infection susceptibility? Select all that apply.
c: White blood cell count
Age, sex, and heredity
Natural, acquired, and passive immunity
Droplet particle size
Whether a reservoir is milk or water
qs.e: White blood cell count, age, sex, heredity, and immunity are listed host considerations. Particle size describes transmission rather than a host characteristic.

qs.q: Which findings belong in an assessment of host susceptibility based on the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Fatigue and stress levels
Nutritional status and general health
Pre-existing illness and certain medications
Use of invasive or indwelling medical devices
Whether an object is a fomite
Whether particles are greater than 5 micrometers
qs.e: The slides list fatigue, stress, nutrition, general health, pre-existing illness, certain medications, and invasive or indwelling devices as susceptibility factors. Fomite classification and particle size concern other parts of the infection cycle.

qs.q: Jimin has a left-leg laceration, continues school and performances, is hospitalized with COVID-19 and dehydration, and has a left-arm IV. Which findings connect directly to the susceptibility factors in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: The laceration provides a portal of entry.
The IV is an invasive medical device.
COVID-19 and dehydration relate to illness and general health.
His activity demands warrant assessment of fatigue and stress.
His childhood vaccinations establish that he received a COVID-19 vaccine.
His age alone establishes that he is in the most susceptible age group.
qs.e: The case connects wounds, invasive devices, illness, general health, and possible fatigue or stress with susceptibility assessment. It explicitly states that Jimin is unvaccinated for COVID, and the slides do not identify the most susceptible age groups.

qs.q: Which factors are listed as influencing whether an organism thrives? Select all that apply.
c: Quantity of the organism and its virulence
The patient's immune system
Length of contact between the organism and patient
Type of contact between the organism and patient
The infection's abbreviation
Whether the precaution name contains the word standard
qs.e: The slide lists organism quantity, virulence, the patient's immune system, contact duration, and contact type. An abbreviation or precaution label is not one of the listed factors.

qs.q: A client with a wound infection is in isolation. Which nursing action specifically targets the mode of transmission in the infection chain?
c: Administering prescribed antibiotics
Wearing gloves during wound care
Ensuring proper nutrition
Monitoring temperature regularly
qs.e: Wearing gloves during wound care targets transmission. Nutrition addresses the host rather than directly interrupting the mode of transmission.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly orders the stages of infection?
c: Incubation → prodromal → full illness → convalescence
Prodromal → incubation → convalescence → full illness
Incubation → full illness → prodromal → convalescence
Full illness → incubation → prodromal → convalescence
qs.e: The slides list incubation first, followed by the prodromal stage, full stage of illness, and convalescence. The prodromal stage comes before full illness, not after it.

qs.q: According to the slides, the common cold incubation period is how many days?
qs.e: The listed common cold incubation period is 1–2 days. The longer 2–21-day range is listed for tetanus.

qs.q: According to the slides, the tetanus incubation period is how many days?
qs.e: Tetanus has a listed incubation period of 2–21 days. Do not substitute the common cold's 1–2-day range.

qs.q: The prodromal stage lasts from hours to what unit of time?
qs.e: The slides describe the prodromal stage as lasting hours to days. The numbered day ranges for the common cold and tetanus describe incubation instead.

qs.q: A school nurse assesses a student who says, 'I'm too tired to keep my head up in class,' and has a low-grade fever. Which infection stage do these findings suggest?
c: Incubation period
Prodromal stage
Full stage of illness
Convalescent period
qs.e: Slide 18 presents this scenario as a knowledge-check question (it does not print the answer). Fatigue and low-grade fever are nonspecific findings consistent with the prodromal stage, which follows incubation (no symptoms) and precedes the full stage of illness (pronounced symptoms); convalescence is the recovery period after illness resolves.

qs.q: A client's illness has resolved and recovery is underway. Which statement best describes this stage according to the slides?
c: This is convalescence; recovery may include return to baseline or a temporary or permanent change in previous health.
This is incubation because all recovery occurs before symptoms.
This is the prodromal stage because illness has resolved.
This is full illness, and previous health must always return unchanged.
qs.e: Convalescence is described as resolution and recovery, with return toward baseline health. The slide also allows temporary or permanent changes, so an unchanged return is not guaranteed.

qs.q: Which abbreviation names the example given for repeatedly cycling through the same infectious process?
qs.e: The slide gives HSV as the example of cycling through the same infectious process. The common cold and tetanus are used on that slide for incubation-period examples.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes medical from surgical asepsis?
c: Medical asepsis reduces pathogens using clean technique; surgical asepsis eliminates pathogens using sterile technique.
Medical asepsis eliminates pathogens using sterile technique; surgical asepsis only reduces them.
Both mean clean technique and only reduce pathogens.
Both mean sterile technique and eliminate pathogens.
qs.e: Medical asepsis is clean technique intended to reduce the number of pathogens. Surgical asepsis is sterile technique intended to eliminate pathogens and maintain a pathogen-free environment.

qs.q: Which actions match the slide's medical asepsis practices? Select all that apply.
c: Perform hand hygiene and wear gloves.
Avoid raising dust.
Work from clean to dirty.
Place soiled linens directly into a hamper, not on the floor.
Work from dirty to clean.
Shake soiled linens to raise dust before disposal.
qs.e: Medical asepsis includes hand hygiene, gloves, avoiding dust, clean-to-dirty technique, and direct hamper disposal of dirty linen. Reversing the direction or raising dust contradicts the slide.

qs.q: The nurse needs to dispose of contaminated liquid. Which action follows the slide's guidance?
c: Pour it directly into the drain or hopper while preventing splashing.
Pour it in a way that creates splashes.
Pour it onto soiled linen on the floor.
Delay disposal until it can be shared with another work area.
qs.e: Contaminated liquids should be poured directly into the drain or hopper to prevent splashing. Splash-producing disposal does not follow the stated clean-technique practice.

qs.q: Which procedures are specifically listed as requiring surgical asepsis? Select all that apply.
c: Foley catheter placement
Central-line placement
Central-line dressing changes
Routine disposal of dirty linen
Routine touching of patient surroundings
qs.e: The slides name Foley catheters and central-line placement and dressing changes as requiring sterile technique. Dirty-linen disposal is addressed under medical asepsis.

qs.q: A nurse prepares for a procedure requiring surgical asepsis. Which plan matches the slides?
c: Create and maintain a pathogen-free environment using sterile-technique supplies such as sterile gloves, a mask, a hair net, and gowns.
Aim only to reduce pathogen numbers using clean technique.
Treat hand hygiene alone as equivalent to maintaining a sterile environment.
Use the same approach described solely for placing dirty linens in a hamper.
qs.e: Surgical asepsis requires creating and maintaining a pathogen-free environment, with sterile gloves, masks, hair nets, and gowns among the listed supplies. Merely reducing pathogens describes medical asepsis.

qs.q: Which are among the WHO Five Moments for Hand Hygiene listed in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Before touching a patient
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
After body-fluid exposure risk
After touching a patient
Only when a patient's diagnosis confirms infection
Only before touching patient surroundings
qs.e: These four moments are explicitly listed. Hand hygiene is not limited to confirmed infection, and the surroundings-related moment is after touching patient surroundings.

qs.q: The nurse touches a client's surroundings without touching the client. Which action matches the fifth WHO hand hygiene moment?
c: Perform hand hygiene after touching the surroundings.
Skip hand hygiene because the client was not touched.
Wait until after the next patient encounter.
Perform hand hygiene only if the client has a confirmed infection.
qs.e: The fifth moment is after touching patient surroundings. Direct contact with the patient is not required for this moment to apply.

qs.q: Besides hospital-acquired, what one-word term do the slides use for healthcare-associated infections?
qs.e: The slides also call healthcare-associated infections hospital-acquired or nosocomial infections. These are alternate labels, not separate transmission categories.

qs.q: Which abbreviation–condition pairs match the listed healthcare-associated infections? Select all that apply.
c: CAUTI — catheter-associated urinary tract infection
SSI — surgical site infection
CLABSI — central-line-associated bloodstream infection
VAP — ventilator-associated pneumonia
CAUTI — central-line-associated bloodstream infection
SSI — ventilator-associated pneumonia
qs.e: All four correct pairs appear on the HAI slide. CAUTI refers to a urinary tract infection, not the bloodstream infection identified as CLABSI.

qs.q: Which expansion of VRE and associated materials matches the slides?
c: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci; feces, urine, and blood
Vancomycin-resistant enterococci; nares only
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; feces, urine, and blood
Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae; nares only
qs.e: VRE is vancomycin-resistant enterococci, and the slide lists feces, urine, and blood beneath it. MRSA is a different organism with different listed locations.

qs.q: The nurse reviews methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Which locations are listed in the slides?
c: Nares, skin, and gastrointestinal tract
Only feces
Only urine and blood
Only soil, water, and milk
qs.e: MRSA is listed as being found in the nares, on the skin, or in the GI tract. Feces alone is the material listed beneath C. difficile.

qs.q: What abbreviation is used for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae?
qs.e: CRE stands for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae. VRE instead refers to vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

qs.q: What material is listed beneath Clostridium difficile on the multidrug-resistant organisms slide?
qs.e: The slide lists feces beneath C. difficile. The nares, skin, and GI tract are the locations listed beneath MRSA.

qs.q: Which items are explicitly listed as personal protective equipment? Select all that apply.
c: Gloves
Gown
Masks
Protective eyewear
Linen hamper
Hopper
qs.e: The PPE slide lists gloves, a gown, masks, and protective eyewear. Hampers and hoppers are mentioned for disposal practices, not as wearable PPE.

qs.q: A hospitalized client has no known infection. Which precaution approach is appropriate?
c: Use standard precautions regardless of diagnosis or possible infection status.
Use no precautions until an infection is confirmed.
Use standard precautions only if blood is visible.
Replace standard precautions with reverse precautions for every client.
qs.e: Standard precautions apply to all hospitalized patients regardless of diagnosis or possible infection status. They are not reserved for confirmed infections or visible blood.

qs.q: Which statement accurately describes the scope of standard precautions in the slides?
c: They apply to blood, body fluids, secretions, and excretions except sweat, as well as non-intact skin and mucous membranes.
They apply only to body fluids with visible blood.
They apply to sweat but exclude non-intact skin.
They apply only to blood and exclude mucous membranes.
qs.e: The slide includes these materials and sites whether blood is present or visible, with sweat as the stated exception. Restricting precautions to visibly bloody fluids is incorrect.

qs.q: Which teaching statement includes all three additions to standard precautions listed in the slides?
c: Include respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practices, and a mask for high-risk prolonged procedures involving spinal canal punctures.
Include cough etiquette, shared equipment without cleaning, and masks only for visible blood.
Include safe injections, open doors for airborne precautions, and no mask for spinal canal punctures.
Include respiratory hygiene only; injection practices and spinal procedure masks are excluded.
qs.e: The listed additions are respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practices, and mask use for the specified spinal canal procedures. Leaving out injection safety or the mask direction makes the teaching incomplete.

qs.q: A hospitalized client has a suspected infection that can spread through contact. How should the nurse apply precautions?
c: Add transmission-based precautions to standard precautions.
Replace standard precautions with transmission-based precautions.
Wait for confirmation before using transmission-based precautions.
Use only standard precautions because the infection is suspected.
qs.e: Transmission-based precautions are used in addition to standard precautions for suspected infections spread by airborne, droplet, or contact routes. They do not replace standard precautions or require confirmation in the slide's wording.

qs.q: Which statement about transmission-based precautions indicates understanding?
c: A disease may have multiple transmission routes, including airborne, droplet, and contact.
Every disease has exactly one transmission route.
Contact precautions rule out all other transmission routes.
Droplet and airborne are interchangeable names for the same category.
qs.e: The slides explicitly recognize that a disease may have multiple routes of transmission. Choosing one category does not establish that no other route exists.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to enter and leave the room of a client on contact or droplet precautions. Which plan follows the slides?
c: Properly don PPE when entering and properly doff it when leaving.
Doff PPE when entering and don it when leaving.
Use PPE only after leaving the room.
Omit PPE if standard precautions are already in use.
qs.e: The slides direct proper donning on entry and proper doffing on leaving. Transmission-based precautions supplement standard precautions, so standard precautions do not justify omitting PPE.

qs.q: A client needs droplet precautions. Which room and PPE plan matches the slides?
c: Private room, door may remain open, surgical mask and gloves
Private room, negative pressure, respirator mask required by the droplet slide
Shared room, no mask, gloves only
Private room, gown only, no gloves
qs.e: The droplet slide describes large-particle spread and specifies a private room, an optionally open door, and a surgical mask with gloves. Negative pressure and a respirator appear under airborne precautions.

qs.q: A client is colonized with a multidrug-resistant organism but is not described as infected. Which plan matches the contact-precaution slide?
c: Use contact precautions with a private room, gown, and gloves.
Withhold contact precautions because colonization does not qualify.
Use a surgical mask alone instead of gown and gloves.
Require negative pressure because all MDRO colonization is airborne.
qs.e: The contact slide includes clients infected or colonized with an MDRO and lists a private room, gown, and gloves. Colonization is not a reason to omit these precautions.

qs.q: During care of a client on contact precautions, the nurse touches infective material. Which action is appropriate?
c: Change gloves after that contact.
Continue care with the same gloves regardless of the material touched.
Remove the gown and omit gloves for the remaining care.
Switch to a respirator instead of changing gloves.
qs.e: The contact-precaution slide directs changing gloves after contacting infective material. Other PPE does not replace the stated glove-change practice.

qs.q: Which equipment-handling action for a client on contact precautions requires follow-up?
c: Sharing equipment with another client
Cleaning all equipment
Keeping equipment from being shared
Following the instruction to clean equipment and not share it
qs.e: The slide says to clean all equipment and not share it. Sharing is therefore inconsistent with the stated contact-precaution guidance.

qs.q: Which room arrangement matches airborne precautions?
c: Private room with negative air pressure, closed door, and the patient remaining in the room
Private room with the door open and no negative-pressure requirement
Shared room with an open door
Private room with the patient routinely outside the room
qs.e: Airborne precautions specify a private room, negative air pressure, a closed door, and the patient remaining in the room. Permission to leave the door open appears under droplet precautions instead.

qs.q: A client on airborne precautions must be transported. Which mask plan matches the slides?
c: The nurse uses a respirator mask for airborne care; the patient wears a surgical mask for transport.
The nurse uses only gloves; the patient wears no mask for transport.
The nurse and patient both omit masks if the door was closed.
The nurse uses a surgical mask instead of a respirator, and the patient uses no mask.
qs.e: The airborne slide lists a respirator mask and specifies a surgical mask on the patient for transport. The patient's transport mask does not replace the caregiver's listed respirator.

qs.q: For which clients are reverse/neutropenic precautions recommended in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: A severely immunocompromised or immunosuppressed client
A resident receiving any cancer treatment
A resident receiving a transplant
A resident with a WBC count below 500 cells/mm³
Every hospitalized client regardless of immune status
A client solely because the client's door can remain open
qs.e: The slide recommends these precautions for severe immune compromise or suppression, cancer treatment, transplants, and WBC counts below 500 cells/mm³. Standard precautions, not reverse precautions, are described as universal for hospitalized patients.

qs.q: The reverse/neutropenic precaution slide lists a WBC count below what number of cells/mm³ (µL)?
qs.e: The listed threshold is below 500 cells/mm³ (µL). The wording is below 500, not simply a count equal to 500.

qs.q: A gram-positive bacterium is stained violet because of which characteristic?
c: It has a thick cell wall that resists decolorization
It has chemically complex cell walls that can be decolorized by alcohol
It requires oxygen to live and grow
It is the smallest of all microorganisms
qs.e: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick cell wall that resists decolorization (loss of color) and are stained violet. Gram-negative bacteria, with complex walls, decolorize with alcohol and do not stain—so the second option describes gram-negative, not gram-positive.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with viral influenza who requests an antibiotic to recover faster. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
c: Antibiotics are effective against all microorganisms, including viruses
Antibiotics have no effect on viruses, but antiviral medications can decrease the severity and duration of your infection
Antibiotics and antivirals are the same medication class and treat all infections
You should not need any treatment for a viral infection
qs.e: Antibiotics have no effect on viruses; antivirals can decrease the severity and duration of certain viral infections such as influenza. Antibiotics are specifically effective against bacteria, not viruses.

qs.q: The nurse is educating a client with recurrent herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) cold sores. Antiviral medications are most effective when given during which stage?
c: Prodromal stage, when infection has begun but symptoms are just beginning and may be vague
The incubation period, after the pathogen has entered the body but before symptoms appear
The convalescent stage, after symptoms have fully resolved
Peak illness, when symptoms are at their most severe
qs.e: Antivirals given in the prodromal stage (infection/disease has begun, but symptoms are just beginning and may be vague) can shorten the course of the illness with certain viruses such as HSV-1 (cold sores). The incubation period is before symptoms appear and the convalescent stage is after symptoms resolve; the source identifies the prodromal—not the peak or convalescent—stage as the effective treatment window.

qs.q: A client was recently diagnosed with HIV. Which statement indicates that the client understands teaching about antiretroviral therapy (ART)?
c: ART should be delayed until my immune system weakens further
ART is initiated as soon as possible after diagnosis to block HIV replication and ultimately render the virus undetectable
ART completely eliminates the virus from my body
ART replaces the need for annual immunizations such as the flu shot
qs.e: ART regimens are initiated as soon as possible after diagnosis because they disrupt the life cycle of the virus, block replication, and render it undetectable. Delaying ART endangers the client, and ART does not eliminate the virus entirely.

qs.q: Which type of microorganism is the most significant and most commonly observed infection-causing agent in health care institutions?
c: Viruses
Fungi
Bacteria
Parasites
qs.e: Bacteria are the most significant and most commonly observed infection-causing agents in health care institutions. Although viruses are the smallest microorganisms, bacteria are identified as the most prevalent in healthcare settings.

qs.q: According to the CDC, which statement best distinguishes antimicrobials from antibiotics?
c: Antimicrobials and antibiotics are identical terms and always interchangeable
Antimicrobials technically include antifungals and drugs that treat parasites and viruses, while antibiotics specifically treat bacterial infections
Antibiotics are the broader category that encompasses all antimicrobial drugs
Antimicrobials are effective only against gram-positive organisms
qs.e: Although the terms are occasionally used interchangeably, antimicrobials technically include antifungals and drugs for parasites and viruses, while antibiotics treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics are a subset of antimicrobials—not the broader category.

qs.q: The nurse is inserting a sterile indwelling urinary catheter and realizes the catheter has been contaminated. Which action should the nurse take?
c: Continue the procedure because the client is receiving postoperative antibiotics
Discard the contaminated equipment and obtain a new sterile catheter kit before proceeding
Wipe the catheter with antiseptic and continue insertion
Complete the procedure and simply document the contamination
qs.e: A contaminated sterile item must be discarded and replaced with a new sterile kit to prevent health care–associated infections (HAIs). Continuing despite contamination violates the standards of surgical asepsis and risks serious patient harm.

qs.q: A client asks the nurse which of the following is an infection caused by a fungus. Which answer is correct?
c: Common cold
Hepatitis B
Ringworm
Malaria
qs.e: Fungal infections include athlete's foot, ringworm, and yeast infections. The common cold and hepatitis B are caused by viruses, and malaria is caused by a parasite transmitted through a mosquito.

qs.q: According to the chapter, what is the first critical step in breaking the cycle of infection?
c: Administering prescribed antimicrobial therapy
Applying infection prevention and control principles
Placing every client with a fever on isolation precautions
Performing hand hygiene before every client interaction
qs.e: Applying infection prevention and control principles is identified as the first critical step in breaking the cycle of infection. Hand hygiene and isolation are important components but fall under the broader framework of infection prevention and control.

qs.q: The nurse reviews a culture report noting gram-negative bacteria. The nurse understands that these bacteria are characterized by which feature?
c: A thick cell wall that resists decolorization and stains violet
Chemically more complex cell walls that can be decolorized by alcohol and do not stain
Being the smallest of all microorganisms, visible only with an electron microscope
A mandatory requirement for oxygen to survive
qs.e: Gram-negative bacteria have chemically more complex cell walls and can be decolorized by alcohol, so they do not stain. The thick cell wall that resists decolorization and stains violet describes gram-positive bacteria.

qs.q: Select all that are components of the infection cycle (chain of infection):
c: Infectious agent
Reservoir
Susceptible host
Immune response
Convalescent period
Portal of exit
qs.e: The six components of the infection cycle are: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, means of transmission, portals of entry, and susceptible host. Immune response and convalescent period are not components of the chain.

qs.q: Select all factors that determine whether an organism a person is exposed to will cause disease:
c: Number of organisms
Virulence of the organism
Competence of the person's immune system
Length and intimacy of contact
Time of day the exposure occurs
Color of the organism under a microscope
qs.e: Disease production depends on the number of organisms, virulence, immune competence, and length/intimacy of contact. Time of day and microscopic color are not listed factors in the source.

qs.q: Select all statements that are true regarding bacteria:
c: Bacteria are categorized by shape: spherical (cocci), rod shaped (bacilli), or corkscrew shaped (spirochetes)
Bacteria are categorized as gram-positive or gram-negative based on reaction to the Gram stain
Bacteria that require oxygen to live and grow are termed anaerobic
Bacteria are the most commonly observed infection-causing agents in health care institutions
Antibiotics have no effect on bacteria
Bacteria are the smallest of all microorganisms
qs.e: Bacteria are categorized by shape and Gram stain and are the most common healthcare infection-causing agents. Aerobic (not anaerobic) bacteria require oxygen; antibiotics DO affect bacteria; viruses are the smallest microorganisms.

qs.q: Select all statements that are true regarding viruses:
c: Viruses are the smallest of all microorganisms
Viruses can be seen with a standard light microscope
Antibiotics have no effect on viruses
Antiviral medications can decrease the severity and duration of viral infections
Hepatitis A, B, and C are caused by viruses
All viral infections are treated with antibiotics
qs.e: Viruses are the smallest microorganisms, visible only with an electron microscope—not a standard light microscope. Antibiotics do not affect viruses; antivirals can help, and hepatitis A/B/C are viral infections.

qs.q: Select all statements that are true regarding parasites and fungi:
c: Parasites are organisms that live on or in a host and rely on it for nourishment
Malaria occurs when a parasite infects a certain type of mosquito that then feeds on humans
Fungi include molds and yeasts
Many infections due to fungi are resistant to treatment
Fungal infections are treated with antibiotics
Parasites are visible only with an electron microscope
qs.e: Parasites live on/in hosts, malaria is parasite-transmitted via mosquito, fungi include molds and yeasts, and many fungal infections resist treatment. Fungal infections are treated with antifungals, not antibiotics.

qs.q: Select all true statements about bacterial classification:
c: Bacteria are categorized by shape as spherical, rod, or corkscrew
Bacteria are categorized as gram-positive or gram-negative based on Gram stain reaction
All bacteria require oxygen to live and grow
Most bacteria require oxygen to live and grow and are termed aerobic
Gram-positive bacteria can be decolorized by alcohol
Bacteria are visible only with an electron microscope
qs.e: Bacteria are categorized by shape and Gram stain; most require oxygen (aerobic). Not all bacteria require oxygen (some are anaerobic); gram-positive resists decolorization (gram-negative is decolorized); bacteria do not need electron microscopy (viruses do).

qs.q: The three shapes by which bacteria are categorized are cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod shaped), and ___.
qs.e: Bacteria are categorized by shape as spherical (cocci), rod shaped (bacilli), or corkscrew shaped (spirochetes).

qs.q: How many components make up the infection cycle (chain of infection)?
qs.e: The infection cycle consists of six components: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, means of transmission, portals of entry, and susceptible host.

qs.q: What is the smallest of all microorganisms, visible only with an electron microscope?
qs.e: A virus is the smallest of all microorganisms and can be seen only with an electron microscope. Bacteria are larger and do not require electron microscopy to visualize.

qs.q: Bacteria that require oxygen to live and grow are referred to as ___ bacteria.
qs.e: Most bacteria require oxygen to live and grow and are referred to as aerobic. Those that can live without oxygen are termed anaerobic.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client whose stool specimen is positive for C. difficile organisms, but the client has no clinical signs of disease. The nurse documents this finding as:
c: Infection
Colonization
Opportunistic infection
Normal flora
qs.e: When C. diff organisms are present without clinical manifestations, this is colonization; an infection is only present once the person exhibits specific disease manifestations. 'Normal flora' refers to organisms that are part of the body's natural defense system and does not describe a C. diff finding.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching about factors that affect a person's risk of developing an infection after exposure to a microorganism. Which of the following is NOT identified in the text as a factor?
c: Number of organisms
Virulence of the organism
Client's age
Competence of the person's immune system
qs.e: The text identifies number of organisms, virulence, immune competence, and length/intimacy of contact as factors. Although age might seem relevant, the text specifically identifies immune system competence rather than age as the factor.

qs.q: A client is admitted with a urinary tract infection (UTI) caused by E. coli. The nurse knows that E. coli normally resides harmlessly in the intestinal tract. This situation best illustrates which concept?
c: Endemic disease
Normal flora
Opportunistic infection
Pandemic
qs.e: When a typically harmless organism (E. coli from the intestinal tract) migrates to another body site and causes disease (UTI), it is an opportunistic infection. 'Normal flora' describes the organism's harmless state in its usual habitat, not when it causes disease elsewhere.

qs.q: A community health nurse is tracking malaria cases that occur with predictability in sub-Saharan Africa. The nurse identifies this disease pattern as:
c: Pandemic
Endemic
Opportunistic
Arboviral
qs.e: Endemic diseases occur with predictability in one specific region or population, such as malaria in Africa. A pandemic is a global outbreak of a novel virus, which does not describe malaria's regional pattern.

qs.q: The nurse is assessing a client who was bitten by a raccoon. The nurse is most concerned about the risk of which infection?
c: West Nile virus
Tetanus
Rabies
Zika virus
qs.e: Rabies is transmitted when a person is bitten by an infected animal, and raccoons are identified as a reservoir for the rabies virus. West Nile and Zika are mosquito-borne, and tetanus is associated with soil, not animal bites.

qs.q: The nurse places a stethoscope on a client's bedside table after use. Without proper cleaning, the stethoscope is best described as:
c: A vector
A portal of exit
A fomite
A reservoir
qs.e: A fomite is an inanimate object that can harbor and transfer organisms, and stethoscopes are specifically identified as potential fomites. A vector is a living creature (usually an insect), not an object.

qs.q: The nurse is providing food-safety education to a client. According to the CDC recommendation cited in the text, ground beef should be:
c: Served medium-rare for best flavor
Cooked until well done
Washed with soap before cooking
Stored frozen and never cooked
qs.e: The CDC recommends that all ground beef be cooked until well done to prevent E. coli infection. Serving it medium-rare leaves the meat undercooked and increases infection risk, as undercooked ground beef has been linked to outbreaks.

qs.q: A pregnant client asks the nurse about the risks of Zika virus. The nurse explains that preconception counseling is recommended because Zika virus can cause:
c: Endocarditis
Microcephaly
Listeria
Gas gangrene
qs.e: Zika virus can cause poor pregnancy outcomes and microcephaly (a brain defect), which is why preconception counseling is recommended. Listeria is associated with unpasteurized milk and gas gangrene with soil—neither is caused by Zika.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an asymptomatic client who tested positive for HIV. The client asks how they could transmit the virus to others. The nurse explains that an asymptomatic person may transmit HIV through:
c: Touching the client's skin
Sharing a contaminated needle and syringe
Breathing the same air in a room
Drinking from a shared water supply
qs.e: Even an asymptomatic person can transmit HIV through condomless sexual contact or sharing a contaminated needle and syringe. Skin contact, shared air, and shared water are not identified routes of HIV transmission in the text.

qs.q: The nurse notices a coworker wearing artificial nails while providing direct client care. The nurse is most concerned because artificial nails:
c: Damage sterile gloves during procedures
Harbor a large number and variety of microbes
Are strictly prohibited by all infection control standards
Only increase fomite transmission risk
qs.e: Artificial nails may harbor a large number and variety of microbes under the nails, increasing infection risk for patients. The text highlights this as a concern for transferring organisms but does not state they are prohibited by all standards.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing factors that influence whether a person develops an infection after exposure to a microorganism. Select all that apply:
c: Number of organisms
Virulence of the organism
Client's blood type
Competence of the person's immune system
Length and intimacy of contact
Time of day the exposure occurred
qs.e: The text identifies number of organisms, virulence, immune competence, and length/intimacy of contact as key factors. Blood type and time of day are not mentioned as factors influencing infection development.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching about reservoirs that can harbor pathogenic organisms. Select all that apply:
c: People
Soil
Noise levels
Water
Inanimate objects
Clothing color
qs.e: Reservoirs include people, animals, soil, food, water, milk, and inanimate objects. Noise levels and clothing color are not biological or environmental reservoirs of microorganisms.

qs.q: The nurse is identifying common portals of exit for microorganisms in humans. Select all that apply:
c: Respiratory tract
GI tract
GU tract
Breaks in the skin
Intact skin
Unbroken mucous membranes
qs.e: Common portals of exit include the respiratory, GI, and GU tracts as well as breaks in the skin. Intact skin and unbroken mucous membranes cannot serve as portals because organisms cannot escape through unbroken barriers.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing examples of direct contact transmission. Select all that apply:
c: Touching
Kissing
Sexual intercourse
Contact with a contaminated countertop
Exposure to a mosquito bite
Touching a contaminated stethoscope
qs.e: Direct contact requires close proximity and includes touching, kissing, and sexual intercourse. Contaminated countertops and stethoscopes are fomites (indirect contact), and mosquito bites involve a vector (indirect contact).

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing food items and food conditions that have been identified as reservoirs for infection outbreaks. Select all that apply:
c: Undercooked ground beef
Fresh leafy vegetables
Pasteurized milk
Unpasteurized milk
Well-done steak
Canned goods
qs.e: Undercooked ground beef and fresh leafy vegetables have been linked to E. coli outbreaks, and unpasteurized milk can contain Listeria. Pasteurized milk is safe because pasteurization eliminates Listeria, and the other items are not identified as risks in the text.

qs.q: The nurse is matching organisms to their associated reservoirs. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply:
c: Soil – gas gangrene
Water – rabies
Soil – tetanus
Water – Giardia
Pasteurized milk – Listeria
Inanimate objects – influenza virus
qs.e: Soil harbors organisms causing gas gangrene and tetanus; water can contain Giardia; and inanimate objects can harbor the influenza virus. Rabies is transmitted by animal bites, not water, and it is unpasteurized—not pasteurized—milk that can contain Listeria.

qs.q: A disease that occurs with predictability in one specific region or population is referred to as __________.
qs.e: Endemic diseases are predictable within a defined geographic region or population, such as malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. This is different from a pandemic, which is a global outbreak of a novel virus.

qs.q: An asymptomatic person who carries an infectious agent and can transmit the disease to others is called a __________.
qs.e: A carrier harbors the infectious agent without showing signs or symptoms of disease but can still transmit it to others. This is distinct from a reservoir, which is the habitat where organisms grow and multiply.

qs.q: The natural habitat where microorganisms grow and multiply is called the __________.
qs.e: The reservoir is the natural habitat supporting growth and multiplication of microorganisms and can include people, animals, soil, food, water, milk, and inanimate objects. The portal of exit is where the organism escapes the reservoir, not where it grows.

qs.q: A living creature, usually an insect, that transmits an infectious agent to a human is called a __________.
qs.e: A vector is a living creature (usually an insect) that transmits an infectious agent as part of indirect contact transmission. A fomite is an inanimate object, not a living creature.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing transmission-based precautions for several clients. Which statement correctly distinguishes airborne from droplet transmission?
c: Airborne particles are greater than 5 μm
Droplet particles are smaller than 5 μm
Airborne particles are smaller than 5 μm
Both airborne and droplet particles are the same size
qs.e: Airborne particles are smaller than 5 μm, while droplet particles are greater than 5 μm; this distinction matters when designing prevention strategies. Options A and B reverse the sizes, and D is incorrect because the size difference is precisely what distinguishes the two routes.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a community health class about the stages of infection. During which stage is a person most infectious to others?
c: Incubation period
Prodromal stage
Full stage of illness
Convalescent period
qs.e: The prodromal stage is when a person is most infectious; early nonspecific symptoms (fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever) appear but the person is often unaware of being contagious. A tempting distractor is the full stage (C) when symptoms are obvious, but the text specifically identifies prodromal as the most infectious.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client's surgical wound and notes redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function at the site. The nurse documents this as:
c: Infection-specific signs of the full stage of illness
Hallmark signs of acute infection
Systemic symptoms of infection
Convalescent period manifestations
qs.e: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function are the hallmark signs of acute infection, usually appearing at the site of injury or invasion. These are localized symptoms, not systemic (C), and convalescent period (D) involves disappearance of signs and symptoms.

qs.q: The nurse notes that a client's wound is producing an exudate that contains pus. The nurse correctly identifies this type of exudate as:
c: Serous
Sanguineous
Purulent
Fibrous
qs.e: Exudate containing pus is purulent. Serous exudate is clear (A), and sanguineous exudate contains red blood cells (B). Fibrous (D) is not a type of exudate described in the text.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing information about Escherichia coli infections with students. The nurse states that the most common manifestation of E. coli infection is:
c: Pneumonia
Diarrhea
Skin infection
Endocarditis
qs.e: According to Table 25-1, the most common manifestation of E. coli infection is diarrhea, as E. coli is transmitted through contact (direct/indirect) with feces or contaminated food and water. Respiratory infection (A) and endocarditis (D) are associated with Staphylococcus aureus per Table 25-1.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an older adult client at risk for pulmonary infections due to decreased cough reflex and abnormal swallowing. Which nursing strategy is most appropriate to reduce aspiration risk during meals?
c: Encourage the client to eat while lying flat
Place the client in a sitting position to eat and drink
Restrict fluid intake to prevent excess secretions
Keep the client in a supine position after meals
qs.e: Per the Focus on the Older Adult box, the client should be placed in a sitting position to eat and drink because of age-related changes including decreased cough reflex and abnormal swallowing. Lying flat (A) increases aspiration risk, and fluids should be encouraged rather than restricted (C).

qs.q: The nurse explains to a client that redness and heat at a wound site occur during the vascular phase of inflammation because:
c: White blood cells migrate to the area
Vasodilation of arterioles and venules increases blood flow to the area
Histamine decreases vessel permeability
Scar tissue replaces damaged cells
qs.e: During the vascular phase, vasoconstriction is followed by vasodilation of arterioles and venules, increasing blood flow and causing redness and heat. Histamine increases permeability (not decreases, ruling out C), and white blood cell migration (A) occurs during the cellular phase.

qs.q: A client was exposed to a pathogen 12 hours ago and has no symptoms yet. The nurse correctly identifies that the client is in which stage of infection?
c: Prodromal stage
Incubation period
Full stage of illness
Convalescent period
qs.e: The incubation period is the interval between pathogen invasion and the appearance of symptoms; organisms are growing and multiplying during this stage. The prodromal stage (A) involves early vague symptoms such as fatigue and malaise, which are absent here.

qs.q: The nurse is explaining immune responses to a student. Which statement correctly describes humoral immunity?
c: It involves an increase in lymphocytes that destroy harmful cells
It is also known as cell-mediated immunity
It involves the body producing antibodies in response to an antigen
It is the primary defense mechanism of the skin
qs.e: Humoral immunity is the antigen-antibody reaction in which the body produces antibodies in response to foreign material (antigens). Cell-mediated immunity (A, B) involves increased lymphocytes that destroy recognized harmful cells; skin (D) is a first-line defense, not part of the immune response.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a Staphylococcus aureus infection. Per Table 25-1, the reservoirs for S. aureus include:
c: Blood and semen
Feces and contaminated food
Skin surface, mouth, nose, and throat
Ticks and mice
qs.e: Per Table 25-1, the reservoirs for S. aureus are the skin surface, mouth, nose, and throat. Blood and semen (A) are reservoirs for HIV; feces (B) is the reservoir for E. coli; ticks (D) are vectors for Lyme disease.

qs.q: The nurse is identifying factors that increase a hospitalized client's risk for infection. Select all that apply.
c: Intact skin and mucous membranes
Increased stress level
Use of invasive or indwelling medical devices
Adequate rest and nutrition
Neonate or older adult age
Normal pH of GI and GU tracts
qs.e: Increased stress (B), invasive or indwelling devices (C), and extremes of age such as neonates and older adults (E) all increase susceptibility to infection. Intact skin (A), adequate rest/nutrition (D), and normal pH (F) are protective factors that reduce infection risk.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching about the body's first-line defense mechanisms against infection. Select all that apply.
c: Skin
Mucous membranes
Inflammatory response
Normal flora, especially GI tract flora
Immune response
Antibody production
qs.e: The skin, mucous membranes, and normal flora (particularly GI tract flora) are considered first-line defenses. The inflammatory response (C) and immune response (E, F) help combat infection only if pathogens breach first-line defenses.

qs.q: The nurse is assessing a client for signs of acute infection at the site of injury. Select all that are hallmark signs of acute infection.
c: Redness
Heat
Nausea
Swelling
Pain
Loss of function
qs.e: The hallmark signs of acute infection are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function, usually appearing at the site of injury or invasion. Nausea (C) is not listed as a hallmark sign in this text.

qs.q: The nurse is documenting wound drainage. Which types of exudate are described in the text? Select all that apply.
c: Serous
Sanguineous
Purulent
Serosanguineous
Mucoid
Fibrinous
qs.e: The text describes three types of exudate: serous (clear), sanguineous (contains red blood cells), and purulent (contains pus). Serosanguineous (D), mucoid (E), and fibrinous (F) are not described in this text.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a community group about health behaviors that increase the risk of infection. Select all that apply.
c: Sensible nutrition
Sharing intravenous (IV) needles
Adequate rest and exercise
Condomless anal or vaginal sex with an unsuppressed HIV viral load
Good personal hygiene
Stress-reduction techniques
