qs.e: Sharing IV needles (B) and condomless sex with an unsuppressed HIV viral load (D) are dangerous behaviors that provide an opportunity for pathogens to enter the host. Sensible nutrition (A), rest (C), good hygiene (E), and stress reduction (F) all promote wellness and reduce susceptibility.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing common portals of entry and exit for microorganisms. Select all that apply.
c: Skin
Urinary tract
Respiratory tract
Gastrointestinal tract
Musculoskeletal system
Endocrine system
qs.e: The skin and the urinary, respiratory, and gastrointestinal tracts are common portals of entry and exit. The musculoskeletal (E) and endocrine (F) systems are not listed in the text as portals.

qs.q: In microorganism transmission, airborne particles are smaller than ____ μm (micrometer).
qs.e: Airborne particles are smaller than 5 μm, while droplet particles are greater than 5 μm. This size distinction matters when designing prevention strategies.

qs.q: A person is most infectious during the ____ stage of infection.
qs.e: During the prodromal stage, early nonspecific symptoms appear (fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever) and the person is most infectious but often unaware of being contagious, leading to spread to other hosts.

qs.q: Exudate that contains pus is classified as ____ exudate.
qs.e: Exudate may be clear (serous), contain red blood cells (sanguineous), or contain pus (purulent). Identifying the type of exudate aids wound assessment and documentation.

qs.q: An infection progresses through ____ stages or phases.
qs.e: The four stages of infection are incubation period, prodromal stage, full (acute) stage of illness, and convalescent period. Understanding the stages helps the nurse intervene and disrupt the infection cycle.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an older adult client who is at risk for respiratory infection. Which intervention is most appropriate to reduce this risk?
c: Place the client in a supine position for meals.
Place the client in a sitting position.
Withhold oral fluids to reduce the risk of aspiration.
Defer pneumococcal and influenza vaccination until after discharge.
qs.e: Placing the patient in a sitting position is a listed nursing intervention to reduce respiratory infection risk in older adults. Fluids are encouraged unless contraindicated, and pneumococcal vaccination (per guidelines) plus annual influenza vaccination are recommended, so withholding fluids or deferring vaccines is wrong.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an older adult client in long-term care who is newly confused, lethargic, and falling more often, with a delayed fever response. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?
c: These findings are expected changes of aging.
These findings may indicate an infection with an atypical clinical presentation.
These findings indicate a latex allergy.
These findings require no additional nursing assessment.
qs.e: Confusion, disorientation, lethargy, falls, and a delayed fever response are all atypical manifestations of infection in older adults. Dismissing them as normal aging delays detection, because older adults often do not mount a classic fever response.

qs.q: A client asks how to reduce the risk of a urinary tract infection after sexual intercourse. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
c: Drink fewer fluids before intercourse.
Void after sexual intercourse.
Wear an absorbent incontinence pad for 24 hours afterward.
Hold the urine until the bladder feels full.
qs.e: Voiding after sexual intercourse is a specific teaching point for UTI prevention. Restricting fluids or holding urine promotes urinary stasis and bacterial growth, and pads do not prevent UTIs.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching an older adult client who wears an absorbent incontinence pad. Which instruction is most important to include to reduce UTI risk?
c: Change the pad only when it is soiled with stool.
Change the pad frequently and perform good perineal care.
Restrict fluids so the pad stays dry longer.
Apply lotion to the perineum after each pad change.
qs.e: For clients wearing absorbent products, frequent pad changes plus good perineal care limit pathogen exposure and moisture. Fluid restriction is not indicated; fluids are encouraged unless contraindicated.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client recovering from abdominal surgery. Which finding best indicates a localized infection at the surgical site?
c: Enlarged, tender lymph nodes
Redness, swelling, and warmth in the involved area
Lethargy and anorexia
Increased pulse and respiratory rate
qs.e: A localized infection presents as redness, swelling, warmth, pain or tenderness, and loss of function of the affected part. Enlarged tender lymph nodes, lethargy, anorexia, and increased pulse and respiratory rate are systemic manifestations.

qs.q: A client with an infection is febrile with an increased pulse and respiratory rate, lethargy, anorexia, and enlarged tender lymph nodes. The nurse recognizes these findings as manifestations of which type of infection?
c: A localized infection
A systemic infection
A latex allergy
A knowledge deficiency
qs.e: Fever with increased pulse and respiratory rate, lethargy, anorexia, and tender enlarged lymph nodes are classic systemic manifestations. Localized infection produces site-specific findings such as redness, swelling, and warmth.

qs.q: The nurse is inserting an indwelling urinary catheter. Which type of asepsis does this procedure require?
c: Medical asepsis (clean technique)
Surgical asepsis (sterile technique)
No special aseptic technique is required
Standard precautions only
qs.e: Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) keeps objects and areas free of microorganisms and is required for inserting an indwelling urinary catheter or IV catheter. Medical asepsis only reduces the number and transfer of pathogens.

qs.q: The nurse performs hand hygiene and puts on gloves before emptying a client's urinary drainage bag. This action is an example of which category?
c: Surgical asepsis
Medical asepsis
Environmental cleaning
Neither category; gloves are PPE only
qs.e: Medical asepsis (clean technique) includes procedures such as hand hygiene and wearing gloves that reduce the number and transfer of pathogens. Surgical asepsis involves keeping objects and areas free of microorganisms, such as catheter insertion.

qs.q: Which action is the most effective way to help prevent the spread of infectious agents in a health care setting?
c: Performing hand hygiene
Wearing gloves for every client contact instead of performing hand hygiene
Carefully sharing client equipment between rooms
Restricting all visitors
qs.e: Hand hygiene is the most effective way to prevent the spread of infectious agents, since most health care-associated pathogens are transmitted via the contaminated hands of health care workers. Gloves are a barrier that does not replace hand hygiene.

qs.q: A public health nurse is implementing contact tracing for a client with a reportable infectious disease. Which action describes contact tracing?
c: Notifying the client's employer of the diagnosis
Identifying people with an infectious disease and locating individuals and groups with whom they have come into direct contact
Collecting laboratory data to confirm the infection
Developing a teaching plan for the client's family
qs.e: Contact tracing identifies people with an infectious disease and locates those with whom they have had direct contact to interrupt actual or potential transmission. Notification of an employer and teaching plans are separate nursing actions and do not interrupt transmission.

qs.q: The nurse cares for an older adult client with dry, thinning skin and loss of skin elasticity. Which nursing action is most appropriate to reduce the risk of skin infection?
c: Assess frequently for any breaks in skin integrity, rashes, or changes in skin
Massage reddened areas vigorously to increase circulation
Restrict oral fluids to decrease perspiration
Share lotion and towels among clients to conserve supplies
qs.e: Frequent assessment for breaks in skin integrity, rashes, or skin changes allows early detection of infection, and lotion and daily hygiene support the skin. Vigorous massage and fluid restriction damage or dry the skin further, and shared supplies spread pathogens.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching staff about atypical clinical manifestations of infection in older adults. Which manifestations should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
c: Confusion
Delayed fever response
Failure to thrive
Lethargy
Elevated blood pressure
Increased appetite
qs.e: Atypical manifestations in older adults include confusion, disorientation, lethargy, anorexia, delayed fever response, falls, incontinence, and failure to thrive. Elevated blood pressure is not listed, and the text names anorexia rather than increased appetite.

qs.q: Which assessment findings are manifestations of a localized infection? (Select all that apply.)
c: Redness of the involved area
Swelling of the involved area
Warmth in the involved area
Pain or tenderness of the involved area
Enlarged, tender lymph nodes
Lethargy
qs.e: Localized infection produces redness, swelling, warmth, pain or tenderness, and loss of function of the affected part. Enlarged tender lymph nodes and lethargy belong to the systemic infection picture.

qs.q: Which factors place an older adult at risk for a urinary tract infection? (Select all that apply.)
c: Incomplete emptying of the bladder
Decreased sphincter control
Bladder-outlet obstruction due to an enlarged prostate gland
Reduced renal blood flow
Increased estrogen levels
Increased fluid intake
qs.e: UTI risk factors listed are incomplete emptying of the bladder, decreased sphincter control, bladder-outlet obstruction (BPH), pelvic floor relaxation from estrogen depletion, and reduced renal blood flow. Estrogen is depleted, not increased, and fluids are encouraged unless contraindicated.

qs.q: The nurse is writing expected patient outcomes for a client at risk for infection. Which outcomes are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
c: The patient will demonstrate effective hand hygiene and good personal hygiene practices.
The patient will identify the signs of an infection.
The patient will adhere to infection control precautions (isolation, equipment, visitors).
The patient will verbalize an understanding of health risks associated with a latex allergy.
The patient will restrict fluid intake to prevent urinary elimination.
The patient will avoid all physical activity to reduce infection risk.
qs.e: The listed outcomes include hand and personal hygiene, identifying signs of infection, adhering to infection control precautions, and understanding latex allergy risks. Restricting fluids and avoiding all activity are not listed outcomes and would work against infection prevention.

qs.q: The CDC hand hygiene guidelines define hand hygiene to include which practices? (Select all that apply.)
c: Handwashing with plain soap and water
Use of antiseptic handrubs including waterless alcohol-based products
Surgical hand antisepsis
Wearing gloves in place of hand hygiene
Applying lotion to the hands between client contacts
Using shared drinking cups after rinsing
qs.e: Hand hygiene applies to handwashing with plain soap and water, antiseptic handrubs (including waterless alcohol-based products), or surgical hand antisepsis. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and shared drinking cups are considered unsanitary.

qs.q: Which assessment findings are potential signs and symptoms of dehydration listed in the table of actual or potential health problems or needs? (Select all that apply.)
c: Decrease in blood pressure, pulse pressure, and pulse volume
Dry mucous membranes
Increase in body temperature
Sudden weight loss
Increased skin turgor
Decrease in body temperature
qs.e: The table lists decreased blood pressure, pulse pressure, and pulse volume, dry mucous membranes, increased body temperature, sudden weight loss, and weakness or other neurologic symptoms. Skin turgor decreases with dehydration, and the table reports an increase, not a decrease, in temperature.

qs.q: The most effective way to help prevent the spread of infectious agents in a health care setting is ______.
qs.e: Hand hygiene is identified as the most effective way to help prevent the spread of infectious agents because most health care–associated pathogens are transmitted via the contaminated hands of health care workers.

qs.q: According to the CDC survey cited, approximately 1 in ___ hospitalized patients has a health care-associated infection (HAI).
qs.e: The estimate is 1 in 31 hospitalized patients with an HAI, a decrease since the original 2011 survey. This figure highlights why infection prevention vigilance remains essential.

qs.q: Surgical asepsis is also called ______ technique.
qs.e: Surgical asepsis, or sterile technique, renders and keeps objects and areas free from microorganisms, as with urinary or IV catheter insertion. Medical asepsis is the clean technique that only reduces the number and transfer of pathogens.

qs.q: The average baseline compliance rate for handwashing in the 16 studies reviewed was ______%.
qs.e: Baseline handwashing compliance averaged 34.1%, rising to 56.98% after multimodal educational and motivational interventions. Knowing this gap supports why institutions stress ongoing education, role modeling, and readily available supplies.

qs.q: The nurse is cleaning a client's bedside table after dressing a wound. Which action demonstrates correct medical asepsis technique?
c: Clean the most soiled areas first, then the less soiled areas
Clean the least soiled areas first, then the more soiled ones
Shake the used linens to remove loose debris before disposal
Place soiled bed linen on the floor temporarily while finishing the task
qs.e: Box 25-2 states to clean the least soiled areas first and then the more soiled ones to prevent cleaner areas from being soiled by dirtier areas. Shaking linens raises dust that transports organisms, and the floor is grossly contaminated.

qs.q: A nursing student removes gloves after assisting a client to turn in bed. The student then reaches for the client's water pitcher. According to the WHO 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene,' hand hygiene is required at which moment before this action?
c: Moment 1 — Before touching a patient
Moment 2 — Before a clean or aseptic procedure
Moment 4 — After touching a patient
Moment 5 — After touching patient surroundings
qs.e: The student has just completed direct contact with the patient and then removed gloves, so Moment 4 (After touching a patient) is the moment that applies before moving on to the next task. Moment 1 applies before touching a patient, Moment 2 before a clean or aseptic procedure, and Moment 5 only when patient surroundings are touched without touching the patient.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a new staff member about bacterial flora on the hands. Which statement about transient bacteria is accurate?
c: They cling tenaciously to skin and require a brush with friction to remove
They are found in greatest number under the fingernails
They are normally found in skin creases and are stable in number and type
They are less susceptible to antiseptics than resident bacteria
qs.e: Table 25-2 lists transient bacteria as found in greatest number under the fingernails and loosely attached in grease, fats, and dirt. They are relatively easily removed by frequent handwashing; the other options describe resident bacteria.

qs.q: The infection control nurse observes a staff member wearing artificial nails while caring for clients on a medical-surgical unit. Which action by the infection control nurse is most appropriate?
c: Report the violation to The Joint Commission immediately for a citable offense
Remove the artificial nails and instruct the staff member that natural nails should be less than 1/4 inch long
Allow the artificial nails because the restriction applies only in the operating room
Apply additional alcohol-based handrub before each client contact to compensate
qs.e: The CDC guideline states health care personnel involved in patient care should not wear artificial nails because they harbor higher bacterial counts; natural nails should be less than 1/4 inch. Although the OR restriction is citable by The Joint Commission, the general patient-care prohibition is the key teaching point here.

qs.q: The nurse has just completed suctioning a client's oropharynx and hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand hygiene method is recommended?
c: Soap and water for a full 2-minute wash
Alcohol-based handrub
Antimicrobial soap and water only
No hand hygiene is needed because gloves were worn
qs.e: If hands are not visibly soiled, alcohol-based handrubs are recommended because they save time, are accessible, and reduce bacterial counts. Hand hygiene is still required after removing gloves (Moment 3 / after glove removal).

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to remove soiled bed linens from a client's bed. Which action is correct according to basic principles of medical asepsis?
c: Shake the linens to dislodge debris before placing them in the hamper
Place the linens on the floor while gathering other items
Carry soiled linens so that they do not touch the nurse's clothing
Hold linens away from the body and fan them to reduce odor
qs.e: Box 25-2 states to carry soiled linens or used articles so they do not touch your clothing. Shaking linens raises dust that transports organisms, and the floor is grossly contaminated.

qs.q: The nurse is orienting students to unit infection control practices. After a client coughs directly toward the nurse, which action best prevents transmission by airborne droplets?
c: Move equipment closer to the client to create a barrier
Provide the client with disposable tissues and instruct the client to cover the mouth and nose
Ask the client to turn away and hold the breath until the cough subsides
Raise dust near the client to settle airborne particles
qs.e: Box 25-2 directs the nurse to provide disposable tissues and instruct clients to cover the mouth and nose to prevent spread by airborne droplets. Raising dust actually spreads organisms further.

qs.q: A quality improvement committee reports results from The Joint Commission Hand Hygiene Project using the Targeted Solutions Tool. Which outcome reflects the reported findings?
c: 26% reduction in health care-associated infections (HAIs) and $1.4 million saved
45% reduction in HAIs and up to $2.8 million saved in direct medical costs
80% reduction in HAIs and $5 million saved
59.6% reduction in HAIs and $2.8 million saved
qs.e: The Joint Commission Center for Transforming Healthcare reported a 45% reduction in HAIs (up from 26%) and up to $2.8 million saved in direct medical costs. The 59.6% figure relates to mean hand hygiene compliance, not HAI reduction.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing a systematic review on hand hygiene compliance in ICUs. According to the data, which group had the lowest compliance rate?
c: Nurses (43.4%)
Physicians (32.6%)
Other staff such as respiratory therapists and custodial staff (53.8%)
Neonatal ICU staff (67.0%)
qs.e: Compliance rates were nurses 43.4%, physicians 32.6%, and other staff 53.8%; physicians had the lowest rate. Neonatal ICU compliance of 67.0% is a unit type statistic, not a worker category.

qs.q: The nurse has just used a contaminated needle to draw a blood sample. Which action is correct?
c: Recap the needle using the one-handed scoop technique before disposal
Place the uncapped needle directly into a puncture-proof disposable container
Break the needle before placing it in a regular trash bag
Set the needle on the bedside table while documenting the procedure
qs.e: The assessment checklist specifies avoiding recapping used needles and placing them in a puncture-proof disposable container. Recapping, even one-handed, is not endorsed in this source.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to discard materials after a wound care procedure. Which actions are consistent with Box 25-2 principles of medical asepsis? (Select all that apply.)
c: Wrap items moist with body drainage in waterproof containers before discarding
Pour used mouth rinse directly into the drain to avoid splattering
Place soiled dressings on the floor until a trash bag is available
Move equipment away from the body when brushing or scrubbing
Sterilize equipment suspected of containing pathogens
qs.e: Box 25-2 directs wrapping moist items in waterproof containers, pouring liquids into the drain, moving equipment away when scrubbing, and sterilizing suspect equipment. The floor is grossly contaminated and must not be used for temporary storage.

qs.q: The instructor asks a student to identify WHO 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene.' Which are correctly identified? (Select all that apply.)
c: Before touching a patient
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
After a body fluid exposure or risk of exposure
Before entering a patient's room
After touching patient surroundings
qs.e: The five WHO moments are: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings. Entering a room is not one of the five designated moments.

qs.q: The nurse is determining when an alcohol-based handrub can be used to decontaminate hands. Which situations are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
c: Before direct contact with a patient
After removing gloves
When moving from a contaminated body site to a clean body site
When hands are visibly soiled with dried blood
After contact with objects in the patient's environment
qs.e: The source lists all of these as indications for alcohol-based handrub when hands are NOT visibly soiled. Visibly soiled hands require soap and water first; alcohol rubs are less effective over visible soil.

qs.q: The nursing student is describing transient bacteria on the hands. Which characteristics are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: Occur on hands with activities of daily living
Attached loosely in grease, fats, and dirt
Found in greatest number under the fingernails
Cling tenaciously to skin by adhesion and absorption
Can be pathogenic or nonpathogenic
qs.e: Table 25-2 describes transient bacteria as loosely attached in grease/fats/dirt, most numerous under fingernails, and potentially pathogenic or nonpathogenic. Clinging tenaciously by adhesion describes resident bacteria.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching about resident bacteria of the hands. Which statements are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
c: Normally found in skin creases
Usually stable in number and type
Removal requires considerable friction with a brush
Removed relatively easily by frequent handwashing
Less susceptible to antiseptics than transient bacteria
qs.e: Table 25-2 states resident bacteria live in skin creases, remain stable, require friction with a brush for removal, and are less susceptible to antiseptics. Easy removal by frequent handwashing describes transient bacteria.

qs.q: The nurse reviews personal grooming practices that help prevent spreading microorganisms. Which practices are consistent with the source? (Select all that apply.)
c: Keep fingernails short and free of broken cuticles
Wear rings with grooves and stones to maintain compliance with facility dress code
Shampoo hair regularly and keep hair short or pinned up
Avoid wearing artificial nails when involved in patient care
Keep natural nails less than 1/4 inch long
qs.e: Box 25-2 and the CDC guideline support short clean nails, regular hair care, no artificial nails, and natural nails under 1/4 inch. Rings with grooves and stones harbor microorganisms and are to be avoided.

qs.q: Alcohol-based handrubs have an alcohol concentration between ______ and ______ percent.
qs.e: The source states alcohol-based handrubs have a concentration between 60% and 95% and are available as foam, gel, or lotion.

qs.q: Natural nails should be less than ______ inches long.
qs.e: The CDC guideline specifies natural nails should be less than 1/4 inch long; longer nails harbor greater bacterial counts.

qs.q: Mean hand hygiene compliance reported in the ICU systematic review is approximately ______ percent.
qs.e: The systematic review found mean international hand hygiene compliance of 59.6%, which falls below the accepted standard of 80% to 90%.

qs.q: The Joint Commission Center for Transforming Healthcare's project uses a tool abbreviated as ______ to measure and improve hand hygiene performance.
qs.e: The Targeted Solutions Tool (TST) facilitates a step-by-step process to measure actual performance, identify barriers, and direct organizations to proven solutions.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection. The client's hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand hygiene method should the nurse use?
c: Alcohol-based handrub only
Soap and water handwashing
Either method is equally effective
Antimicrobial wipes followed by handrub
qs.e: Alcohol does not kill C. diff bacterial spores—it only kills the vegetative form—so soap and water are the preferred method when C. diff is suspected or diagnosed. Alcohol-based handrub is tempting because it kills many pathogens, but it is specifically less effective against C. diff, norovirus, and Cryptosporidium.

qs.q: The nurse is performing hand hygiene using an alcohol-based handrub. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Stop rubbing when hands appear dry to the eye
Apply approximately 3 mL to one palm and rub until completely dry, at least 20 seconds
Apply the product to wet hands and rinse after 10 seconds
Apply a single pump of product and rub for 5 seconds
qs.e: The recommended amount is usually 3 mL (may require two pumps) and the nurse must rub until hands are completely dry—at least 20 seconds—covering all surfaces including fingertips and under nails. Stopping too soon or using too little product reduces effectiveness.

qs.q: A client has an indwelling urinary catheter that has been in place for 7 days. Each day the catheter remains, the client's risk of acquiring a CAUTI increases by approximately what percentage?
qs.e: Each patient has a 3% to 7% increased risk of acquiring a CAUTI each day the catheter remains in place. The 12% to 16% figure refers to the proportion of hospitalized adults with an indwelling catheter, not the daily risk increase.

qs.q: The nurse is documenting that an infection was caused by a diagnostic procedure performed during the client's hospital stay. This type of infection is classified as:
c: Exogenous
Endogenous
Iatrogenic
Nosocomial
qs.e: An iatrogenic infection results from a treatment or diagnostic procedure. Exogenous infections come from other people, and endogenous infections come from organisms harbored within the person. Nosocomial is a former term that has been replaced by HAI.

qs.q: A ventilated client is being cared for by the nurse. Which action is part of the VAP prevention bundle?
c: Keeping the head of the bed flat for comfort
Changing the ventilator circuit tubing every 24 hours
Elevating the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees and providing regular oral care
Using a heated humidifier set at maximum temperature
qs.e: VAP bundles include elevating the head of the bed 30–45 degrees, providing regular oral care, and changing the ventilator circuit only as needed—not on a routine schedule. Keeping the bed flat increases aspiration risk, and routine circuit changes are not evidence-based.

qs.q: A nurse manager is reviewing CMS regulations. As of 2013, CMS no longer reimburses hospitals for which of the following?
c: Any hospital-acquired infection
Specific preventable hospital-acquired conditions (HACs)
Sentinel events only
All infections not present on admission
qs.e: CMS no longer reimburses for specific preventable HACs—high-cost, high-volume events preventable with evidence-based guidelines. Not every infection is included; only specific categories such as CAUTI, vascular catheter–associated infections, and SSIs among the current 14 categories.

qs.q: Which statement by a student nurse indicates correct understanding of alcohol-based handrub effectiveness?
c: "Alcohol-based handrub is effective against C. diff spores."
"Alcohol-based handrub is effective against MRSA, VRE, HIV, and influenza."
"Alcohol-based handrub should be used when hands are visibly soiled with blood."
"Alcohol-based handrub requires rinsing with water after application."
qs.e: Alcohol-based handrubs are effective against MRSA, VRE, HIV, influenza, and many other organisms but are less effective against C. diff, norovirus, and Cryptosporidium. Visibly soiled hands require soap and water, and the rub is not rinsed off—it is rubbed until dry.

qs.q: The Joint Commission requires that death or serious injury caused by an infection-related event be classified as:
c: An adverse event
A never event
A sentinel event
A reportable HAC
qs.e: The Joint Commission mandates that death or serious injury caused by an infection-related event must be reported as a sentinel event. A HAC is a CMS reimbursement category, not the Joint Commission's classification for serious harm.

qs.q: A nurse is performing hand hygiene after contact with a client's contaminated wound dressing. The client's hands and the nurse's hands are visibly soiled with blood. Which action is required?
c: Alcohol-based handrub for 20 seconds
Antimicrobial soap and warm water with a scrub of at least 20 seconds
Plain soap and cold water for 10 seconds
Antiseptic wipes followed by alcohol-based handrub
qs.e: If hands are visibly soiled or contaminated with blood or body fluids, washing with antimicrobial soap and water is required with at least a 20-second scrub; visibly soiled hands need a longer scrub. Alcohol-based handrub is only for hands that are not visibly soiled.

qs.q: A nurse is reviewing the HAI action plan targets. Which of the following is NOT one of the seven targets tracked by the Federal Steering Committee's action plan?
c: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)
Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)
Central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)
Clostridioides difficile infections (CDIs)
qs.e: The listed action plan targets include CAUTI, SSI, CLABSI, MRSA, and C. diff—VAP is not listed among them. VAP prevention bundles are discussed, but VAP is not one of the named Federal Steering Committee action plan targets in this source.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to use an alcohol-based handrub. Select all that apply to correct technique (Guidelines for Nursing Care 25-1).
c: Apply approximately 3 mL (may require two pumps) to one palm
Cover all surfaces of hands, fingers, and between fingers
Clean fingertips and the area beneath fingernails
Continue rubbing until completely dry, at least 20 seconds
Rinse hands with water after rubbing to remove residue
Apply only to the backs of the hands
qs.e: Guidelines 25-1 specify applying ~3 mL to one palm, covering all surfaces including between fingers, cleaning fingertips and under nails, and rubbing until completely dry (at least 20 seconds). The rub is not rinsed off, and application is not limited to the backs of hands.

qs.q: A client is suspected of having a C. diff infection. Select all nursing actions that are appropriate for preventing transmission.
c: Use soap and water for hand hygiene
Use contact precautions including a private or cohorted room
Wear a gown during care
Continue contact precautions until diarrhea stops
Use alcohol-based handrub as the primary hand hygiene method
Ensure glove use as a cornerstone of prevention
qs.e: Soap and water are preferred for C. diff; contact precautions (private/cohorted room, gown) continue until diarrhea stops, and glove use is the cornerstone for preventing transmission. Alcohol-based handrub is less effective against C. diff and should not be the primary method.

qs.q: The nurse is implementing infection prevention for a client with an invasive device. Select all statements that are true.
c: Bundles are typically three to five evidence-based practices implemented together
ANA's CAUTI prevention includes prevention of inappropriate short-term catheter use
ANA's CAUTI prevention includes timely nurse-driven removal of catheters
ANA's CAUTI prevention includes catheter care during placement
Bundles are individualized for each client rather than standardized
The interprofessional team collaborates to determine and document device necessity
qs.e: Bundles are standardized sets of 3–5 evidence-based practices; ANA's CAUTI focus areas are (1) prevention of inappropriate short-term use, (2) timely nurse-driven removal, and (3) catheter care during placement. The interprofessional team documents device necessity. Bundles are not individualized—they are standardized protocols.

qs.q: Select all organisms against which alcohol-based handrubs are effective.
c: MRSA
VRE
HIV and influenza
Cryptosporidium
Norovirus
HBV and HCV
qs.e: Alcohol-based handrubs are effective against MRSA, VRE, HIV, influenza, HBV, and HCV. They are less effective against Cryptosporidium and norovirus, for which soap and water are recommended.

qs.q: Select all factors that influence the speed with which infection-control initiatives are embraced.
c: Environmental factors: who benefits and whether change is mandatory
The nature of the innovation: ease of understanding and strength of evidence
Whether people can make the change and individualize decision making
Organizational factors: competing priorities and resource issues
The client's insurance coverage type
The season of the year
qs.e: The source identifies four categories of factors: environmental, nature of the innovation, whether people can make the change, and organizational factors. Insurance type and season of the year are not listed.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing CDC core actions to fight antibiotic-resistant strains. Select all that apply.
c: Preventing infections, thereby preventing the spread of resistance
Tracking resistant organisms
Improving antibiotic prescribing/stewardship
Developing new drugs and diagnostic tests
Mandatory isolation of all clients receiving antibiotics
Banning all broad-spectrum antibiotics
qs.e: CDC lists four core actions: prevent infections, track resistance, improve antibiotic prescribing/stewardship, and develop new drugs/diagnostic tests. Mandatory isolation and banning all broad-spectrum antibiotics are not among these core actions.

qs.q: Effective handwashing requires at least a ______-second scrub with plain soap or disinfectant and warm water.
qs.e: The minimum handwashing scrub time is 20 seconds; visibly soiled hands need a longer scrub. This aligns with the same minimum duration for alcohol-based handrub drying time.

qs.q: An infection is referred to as ________ when the causative organism comes from microbial life harbored in the person.
qs.e: Endogenous means the organism originates from within the person's own microbial flora. Exogenous means acquired from other people; iatrogenic results from treatment or diagnostic procedures.

qs.q: The recommended amount of alcohol-based handrub per application is usually ______ mL (may require dispensing two pumps).
qs.e: The manufacturer-recommended amount is usually 3 mL, which may require dispensing two pumps. Using less product reduces coverage and effectiveness.

qs.q: VAP bundles include elevating the head of the bed to ______ to 45 degrees.
qs.e: The head of the bed should be elevated to 30–45 degrees as part of the VAP prevention bundle, along with regular oral care and changing the ventilator circuit only as needed.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a community health class about Staphylococcus aureus. Which statement by a participant indicates correct understanding of colonization?
c: Colonization means the person has a full-blown infection requiring antibiotics.
About one third of people in the United States carry S. aureus, usually in the nose, and may spread it to others without having symptoms.
Colonized individuals cannot pass S. aureus to anyone else.
S. aureus is found only in the respiratory tract of colonized people.
qs.e: Approximately one third of the U.S. population is colonized with S. aureus—typically in the nose—without symptoms but still able to transmit the organism. The distractor claiming colonized people cannot spread it is wrong because asymptomatic carriers can pass the organism to others.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an afebrile, otherwise healthy client with a small, uncomplicated CA-MRSA abscess. According to current guidelines, what is the recommended initial treatment?
c: Begin IV vancomycin immediately.
Perform incision and drainage of the abscess.
Start broad-spectrum oral antibiotics before any procedure.
Apply an alcohol-based antiseptic and reassess in 24 hours.
qs.e: Guidelines recommend incision and drainage for afebrile, healthy patients with mild, uncomplicated abscesses; antimicrobial therapy may not be required. Starting antibiotics immediately is incorrect because I&D is the first-line approach in this scenario.

qs.q: A client with a wound draining purulent material is suspected of CA-MRSA, and the provider plans to order antibiotics. Which nursing action is essential before antibiotic therapy is initiated?
c: Collect a complete blood count.
Send wound drainage for culture and sensitivity testing.
Apply a wet-to-dry dressing to the wound.
Perform a tuberculin skin test.
qs.e: Wound drainage should be sent for culture and sensitivity testing before antibiotic therapy to identify the organism and its drug susceptibilities. A CBC does not identify the causative organism or guide antibiotic choice.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a postoperative client who has been hospitalized for 10 days, has a central venous catheter, and develops a positive blood culture for MRSA. What is the first-line medication for health care–associated MRSA?
c: Oral methicillin
IV vancomycin
IV carbapenem
Oral linezolid
qs.e: IV vancomycin remains one of the first-line medications for treatment of health care–associated MRSA. Methicillin is ineffective because MRSA is, by definition, methicillin-resistant.

qs.q: A client on the medical-surgical unit develops watery diarrhea, fever, and mild abdominal cramping after a prolonged course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which hand hygiene method is required when caring for this client?
c: Alcohol-based handrub only, since it kills all pathogens.
Soap and water, because C. diff is not killed by alcohol-based handrubs.
Either method is acceptable; no special requirements.
Chlorhexidine wipe only.
qs.e: C. diff is not killed by alcohol-based handrubs, so soap and water are required. The belief that handrub kills all pathogens is a dangerous misconception; spores of C. diff survive alcohol-based products.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing the definitions of disinfection and sterilization. Which statement accurately distinguishes the two?
c: Disinfection destroys all microorganisms including spores; sterilization destroys only vegetative bacteria.
Sterilization destroys all microorganisms including spores; disinfection destroys pathogenic organisms but not spores.
Both disinfection and sterilization destroy all microorganisms including spores.
Disinfection and sterilization are interchangeable terms.
qs.e: Disinfection destroys all pathogenic organisms except spores; sterilization destroys all microorganisms, including spores and endospores. Confusing the two is a common error—the key difference is the spores.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing a piece of equipment that will enter a sterile portion of the body during a procedure. Which method of preparation is required?
c: Cleansing with soap and water only
Disinfection only
Sterilization
Wiping with an alcohol swab
qs.e: Sterilization is required for equipment that enters a sterile portion of the body. Disinfection is acceptable for equipment that does not enter a sterile body part, so it is insufficient here.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a confirmed CRE infection. Which precaution does the CDC recommend?
c: Droplet precautions
Airborne precautions
Contact precautions
Standard precautions only
qs.e: The CDC recommends contact precautions for CRE to prevent patient-to-patient spread. Droplet and airborne precautions do not address the direct/indirect contact transmission of CRE.

qs.q: A client develops VRE after a recent surgery involving invasive devices and prolonged vancomycin use. How is VRE most commonly spread?
c: Through airborne droplets during coughing
Through contact with feces, urine, or blood of an infected or colonized person
Through contaminated food and water only
Through insect vectors such as mosquitoes
qs.e: VRE is spread via contact with the feces, urine, or blood of an infected or colonized person. Airborne or droplet transmission is not the primary route, so those precautions would be inappropriate.

qs.q: The infection control nurse is reviewing factors that influence the selection of a sterilization or disinfection method. Which statement regarding the time factor is accurate?
c: Time is a minor consideration; slight deviations are acceptable.
Failure to follow recommended time periods is grossly negligent.
Time only matters when using chemical methods, not physical methods.
Longer times are only needed when disinfecting, not sterilizing.
qs.e: Time is a key factor, and failure to follow the recommended time periods is grossly negligent regardless of method. Treating time as minor endangers patients by leaving viable microorganisms on equipment.

qs.q: The nurse is identifying individuals most at risk for community-associated MRSA (CA-MRSA). Which groups should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
c: Young children
Older adults
Athletes in close physical contact
Daycare attendees
People living alone in isolated settings
Military personnel
qs.e: Those most at risk for CA-MRSA include young children, older adults, and people in close physical proximity to others—athletes, military personnel, inmates, and daycare attendees. People living in isolation are at lower risk because CA-MRSA requires close contact to spread.

qs.q: A nurse is assessing a client's risk for VISA or VRSA. Which factors place this client at higher risk? Select all that apply.
c: History of kidney disease
History of diabetes
Previous MRSA infection
Presence of an invasive catheter
Recent exposure to vancomycin
History of seasonal allergies
qs.e: Patients most at risk for VISA and VRSA have kidney disease, diabetes, a previous MRSA infection, an invasive catheter, or recent vancomycin exposure. Seasonal allergies are not a listed risk factor.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing risk factors for VRE infection in hospitalized clients. Which factors should be included? Select all that apply.
c: Compromised immune system
Recent surgery
Invasive devices
Prolonged antibiotic use, especially vancomycin
Prolonged hospitalization
Routine use of an electric toothbrush
qs.e: Risk factors for VRE include compromised immune systems, recent surgery, invasive devices, prolonged antibiotic use (especially vancomycin), and prolonged hospitalization. An electric toothbrush is not a recognized risk factor for VRE.

qs.q: The nurse is educating staff about clients at risk for CRE infection. Which clients are at higher risk? Select all that apply.
c: Client with a bladder catheter
Client on prolonged antibiotic therapy
Client requiring ventilator assistance
Client with an open surgical wound
Client with frequent ICU or long-term care stays
Client who is a healthy young adult athlete
qs.e: Clients with bladder or venous catheters, ventilator support, open surgical wounds, lengthy antibiotic courses, or frequent hospitalizations (especially ICU or long-term care) are at risk for CRE. CRE rarely impacts healthy people, making the young adult athlete a lower-risk distractor.

qs.q: A nurse is implementing strategies to reduce transmission of C. diff. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: Use soap and water for hand hygiene instead of alcohol-based handrub
Place the client in a private room or cohort with the same strain
Use full-barrier contact precautions (gown and gloves)
Disinfect dedicated patient-care items such as stethoscopes between patients
Use terminal cleaning with sporicidal agents on discharge
Use alcohol-based handrub as the primary method of hand hygiene
qs.e: C. diff prevention includes soap-and-water hand hygiene, private room or cohorting, gown and gloves, disinfecting dedicated equipment, and terminal cleaning with sporicidal agents. Alcohol-based handrub is ineffective against C. diff spores and must not be used as the primary method.

qs.q: A nurse is selecting a sterilization or disinfection method for contaminated equipment. Which factors must be considered? Select all that apply.
c: Nature of organisms present
Number of organisms present
Type of equipment (lumens, crevices, joints)
Intended use of the equipment
Available means for sterilization and disinfection
Patient's blood type
qs.e: Method selection depends on the nature and number of organisms, type of equipment, intended use, available means, and time. The patient's blood type is irrelevant to choosing a disinfection or sterilization method.

qs.q: Disinfection destroys all pathogenic organisms EXCEPT ______.
qs.e: The key distinction between disinfection and sterilization is that disinfection does not destroy spores; only sterilization eliminates spores and endospores.

qs.q: The CDC recommends which type of precautions to control transmission of both MRSA and VRE?
qs.e: Contact precautions, combined with meticulous hand hygiene, reducing invasive devices, environmental cleaning, and decolonization of high-risk patients, form the bundle for MRSA and VRE control.

qs.q: Before initiating antibiotic therapy for CA-MRSA, wound drainage should be sent for ______ and sensitivity testing.
qs.e: Culture and sensitivity testing identifies the organism and its susceptibilities so antibiotics can be targeted appropriately. Skipping this step risks ineffective treatment and promotes resistance.

qs.q: For a mild, uncomplicated abscess in an afebrile, healthy CA-MRSA client, the recommended treatment is ______ and drainage.
qs.e: Guidelines recommend incision and drainage as first-line treatment for mild, uncomplicated abscesses; antimicrobial therapy may not be required unless I&D is not effective.

qs.q: The nurse is performing morning care for a client on standard precautions. For which activity can the nurse appropriately omit gloves?
c: Turning the client in bed
Emptying a urinary drainage bag
Changing a soiled dressing
Performing oral care with visible blood-tinged secretions
qs.e: Gloves are only needed when there is a possibility of soiling the hands with body fluids; turning, feeding, vital signs, and changing IV fluid bags do not require them. The other options all involve potential body-fluid contact.

qs.q: The nurse completes wound care and, while still wearing the same gloves, moves to the nurses' station. Which action requires follow-up?
c: Writing in the client's paper chart
Removing the gloves in the client's room
Performing hand hygiene after glove removal
Discarding the gloves according to facility policy
qs.e: While wearing gloves the nurse never writes in the chart, never uses the computer keyboard or telephone, and never touches pagers or cell phones. Gloves are removed and hands decontaminated before leaving the room.

qs.q: Studies confirm microbial growth in what percentage range of the mobile phones tested?
qs.e: 82% to 88% of tested phones carried microbes because warm pockets and dirty hands seed the device; hand hygiene breaks this cycle.

qs.q: Which statements about glove use are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Gloves should be changed before moving from a contaminated task to a clean task
Gloves are a substitute for good hand hygiene
Double gloving reduces glove perforations when exposure to blood or body fluids is expected
Glove-barrier failure is always immediately detected by the wearer
Warmth and moisture inside gloves create an environment where bacteria multiply
One pair of gloves may be worn for all of a nurse's client interactions
qs.e: Gloves are a barrier, not a substitute for hand hygiene, and each patient interaction requires a clean pair. Undetected barrier failure is common, which is why double gloving is recommended for expected fluid exposure (perforations reduced by 71% in the OR).

qs.q: In the OR setting, double gloving reduced glove perforations by what percentage?
qs.e: Evidence cited in the chapter (AORN, 2020) shows a 71% reduction in perforations, supporting double gloving when blood/body fluid exposure is expected.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing use of radiation sterilization for heat-sensitive plastics and pharmaceuticals. Which caution applies to this method?
c: The object must be directly exposed to the radiation on all surfaces
Plastic and rubber devices are damaged by the process
Spores and some viruses are not destroyed
The method is not used in health care facilities
qs.e: Radiation requires direct exposure of every surface and poses a risk to personnel. Damaging plastic/rubber is the caution for steam autoclaving, and surviving spores is the caution for boiling water.

qs.q: The home care nurse teaches a client about disinfecting items by boiling water. Which statement is accurate?
c: The item should boil for at least 10 minutes, but spores and some viruses may survive
Boiling for 2 minutes sterilizes items contaminated with spores
Boiling water destroys all endospores and viruses
Boiling water is the sterilization method used in health care facilities
qs.e: Boiling water is simple and inexpensive for home use and requires at least 10 minutes, but it does not destroy spores and some viruses—so it is disinfection, not reliable sterilization.

qs.q: Which statements about methods of sterilization and disinfection are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Ethylene oxide gas destroys spores and endospores and is toxic to humans
Autoclaving is the method of choice for most plastic and rubber devices
Dry heat uses an oven at 350°F for 2 or more hours for metal items
Chemical solutions destroy all spores on instruments
A 1:100 dilution of sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) inactivates HIV
Ethylene oxide gas is released while items such as oxygen and suction gauges and blood pressure equipment are contained in an autoclave
qs.e: Steam autoclaving damages most plastic and rubber devices, and chemical solutions do not destroy all spores (and may corrode metal). Ethylene oxide is effective against spores but toxic to humans, requiring precautions.

qs.q: What dilution of sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) effectively inactivates HIV?
qs.e: A 1:100 bleach dilution inactivates HIV and is useful for water and housekeeping disinfection; chlorines do not destroy all spores.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client who developed dry, crusty bumps, erythema, and pruritus on the palms 48 hours after wearing latex gloves. The nurse identifies this reaction as:
c: Irritant contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV delayed hypersensitivity)
True latex allergy (type I immediate hypersensitivity)
A normal response to glove powder
qs.e: Type IV reactions appear 24 to 96 hours after contact as localized pruritus, erythema, and lesions including on the palms. Type I allergy is immediate and systemic; irritant dermatitis is dry, irritated skin and is not an allergy.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a known latex allergy who develops angioedema and bronchospasm during a procedure. Which action is the priority?
c: Remove all latex-containing articles from the room and begin emergency treatment (e.g., epinephrine subcutaneously) per protocol
Apply hydrocortisone 1% cream to the affected area
Apply cool compresses and give oral diphenhydramine
Document the reaction and notify the provider at the end of the shift
qs.e: Angioedema and bronchospasm signal a systemic type I reaction (possible anaphylaxis), treated with epinephrine subcutaneously, systemic steroids/antihistamines, removal of all latex items, and transport to the ED. Cool compresses and hydrocortisone treat only localized reactions.

qs.q: Which clients are at increased risk for latex sensitivity? Select all that apply.
c: A client with spina bifida
A client with allergies to banana, avocado, and kiwi
A client with hypertension
A client with asthma
A client with a history of multiple surgical procedures or latex exposures
A client with osteoarthritis
qs.e: Box 25-3 lists these risk factors: occupational exposure to latex, people with allergic tendencies, people with food allergies (specifically banana, papaya, avocado, potatoes, kiwi fruit, chestnuts, and pineapples), and people with asthma, spina bifida, or a history of multiple surgical procedures or exposures to latex. Hypertension and osteoarthritis are not listed risk factors.

qs.q: Which items are frequently used products that contain latex? Select all that apply.
c: Stethoscopes
IV tubing
Alcohol swabs
Urinary catheters
Tourniquets
Powder-free nitrile gloves
qs.e: Box 25-3 lists gloves, BP cuffs, electrode pads, stethoscopes, IV tubing, urinary catheters, tourniquets, syringes, surgical masks, and baby bottle nipples/pacifiers. Nonlatex gloves (such as nitrile) are the alternative recommended for sensitive workers.

qs.q: Approximately what percentage of health care workers are sensitized to traditional latex?
qs.e: About 10% of health care workers and 1% to 2% of the general population are sensitized, which is why latex-safe environments and alternative gloves are required.

qs.q: The nurse teaches a client newly diagnosed with a latex allergy. Which statement indicates the client understands the teaching?
c: I will wear a medical alert bracelet and tell all of my health care providers about the allergy
I will wear latex gloves with cornstarch powder at home to prevent irritation
I will take diphenhydramine every day to prevent reactions
My allergy will resolve after I avoid latex for one month
qs.e: There is no cure for latex allergy, so avoidance, a medical alert bracelet, and notifying providers (including before injections/immunizations) are essential. Powder is a causative factor in allergy development, and diphenhydramine treats localized reactions rather than preventing them.

qs.q: Which interventions are appropriate for a localized latex contact reaction? Select all that apply.
c: Oral diphenhydramine
Cool compresses
Hydrocortisone 1% cream
Epinephrine subcutaneously
Systemic corticosteroids
Removal of all latex-containing articles from the room
qs.e: Localized reactions are treated with oral diphenhydramine, cool compresses, and hydrocortisone 1% cream. Epinephrine, systemic steroids, and removing latex articles are interventions for a systemic reaction.

qs.q: Which diagnostic test detects IgE antibodies to latex in the client's blood?
c: Radioallergosorbent test (RAST)
Skin prick test
Complete blood count
Serum electrolyte panel
qs.e: The RAST is the blood test for IgE antibodies to latex. The skin prick test uses latex-derived serum placed on a small prick in the skin rather than measuring blood antibodies.

qs.q: The nurse's gown becomes heavily soiled with the client's blood during care. Which action is correct?
c: Remove the gown, perform thorough hand hygiene, and don a clean gown
Continue care and change the gown after leaving the client's room
Don a second gown over the soiled gown
Turn the gown inside out and continue providing care
qs.e: A gown that is heavily soiled or moistened with blood/body fluids must be removed immediately, followed by hand hygiene and a clean gown, because the barrier is compromised. Gowns use individual gown technique—one wearing only, then appropriate discard.

qs.q: With individual gown technique, a barrier gown is worn _____ time(s) before being discarded.
qs.e: Individual gown technique means the gown is used once and then discarded according to facility policy; waterproof/impervious gowns are used when contact with blood or body fluids is likely.

qs.q: Respiratory droplets generated by coughing, sneezing, or talking typically travel less than 3 ft but may reach ____ ft.
qs.e: Large particle pathogens (>5 μm) travel usually <3 ft but may reach 6 ft; particulate respirators target the much smaller (≤5 μm) droplet nuclei that travel longer distances.

qs.q: Which statement about masks and particulate respirators is correct?
c: A particulate respirator filters inspired air, whereas a surgical mask filters only expired air
A surgical mask filters inspired air better than an N95 respirator
The N95 respirator is not approved for tuberculosis exposure control
The N95 respirator is designed for use only outside health care settings
qs.e: Surgical/procedure masks filter expired air and protect against large particles (>5 μm) and splashes; the NIOSH-approved N95 respirator filters inspired air and meets CDC guidelines for tuberculosis exposure control in health care settings.

qs.q: Which practices regarding masks in the clinical setting are correct? Select all that apply.
c: A mask is typically worn only once and is not lowered around the neck for reuse
A mask must be changed before it becomes damp from the wearer's exhalations
A surgical mask filters inspired air
Masks protect the wearer from large particle pathogens greater than 5 μm
Particulate respirators filter airborne droplet nuclei and small particle aerosols 5 μm or smaller
Droplet nuclei remain suspended and travel only 3 feet
qs.e: Surgical masks filter only expired air and cover droplet-size particles (>5 μm); respirators handle the ≤5 μm nuclei that stay suspended and travel longer distances. A mask is single-use and must be changed before it becomes damp.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing glove use with a new graduate. Which statement is correct?
c: Hand hygiene before and after gloving is essential because warmth and moisture inside gloves promote bacterial growth
Hand hygiene after glove removal is unnecessary if the gloves appear intact
Gloves eliminate the need for hand hygiene between clients
One pair of gloves may be safely reused for the same client throughout the shift
qs.e: The warm, moist glove interior is an ideal bacterial growth environment, so meticulous hand hygiene is performed before and after gloving; barrier failure often goes undetected, so intact-appearing gloves cannot justify skipping hand hygiene.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing the specifications of the N95 respirator before caring for a client with suspected tuberculosis. Which statement about the N95 respirizer is accurate?
c: It filters airborne particles as small as 1 μm with 95% efficiency
It filters expired air only to protect the client from the nurse
It can be worn in any size because the elastic straps adjust to fit
It eliminates the need for an airborne infection isolation room
qs.e: The N95 is a particulate respirator that filters inspired air, trapping particles as small as 1 μm at 95% efficiency. A surgical mask filters only expired air, and proper fit-testing (not just adjustable straps) is required for respirators.

qs.q: A nurse has completed a fit test to determine the appropriate respirator size. Which action should the nurse perform EVERY time the respirator is subsequently worn?
c: Repeat the full fit test before each shift
Perform a seal check to ensure an adequate seal
Wear a surgical mask underneath the respirator for added protection
Reapply double-sided tape to the respirator edges
qs.e: Fit-testing is done once to select the correct size; a seal check is performed each time the respirator is donned to confirm an adequate facial seal. Adding a mask underneath or tape interferes with the seal rather than improving it.

qs.q: A client is admitted to an airborne infection isolation (AII) room with known multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Which respirator must the nurse wear when entering the room?
c: Any standard surgical mask
A NIOSH-certified N95 respirator or higher-level respirator
A HEPA filter attached to the room exhaust system
A cloth mask with a face shield only
qs.e: CDC guidelines require a NIOSH-certified N95 or higher-level respirator for entry into an AII room of a client with known or suspected TB. Surgical and cloth masks filter only expired air and do not protect the nurse from airborne particles.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to suction a client's tracheostomy. Which eyewear is acceptable for this procedure?
c: The nurse's regular prescription glasses
A pair of plain sunglasses
Goggles or a face shield
No eye protection is necessary because gloves are worn
qs.e: Goggles or a face shield protect the mucous membranes of the eyes from splattering secretions. Plain glasses are unacceptable because side shields are required.

qs.q: After cleaning a large spill of bloody drainage on the floor, the nurse disposes of the saturated paper towels. Which container is most appropriate?
c: A red bag marked BIOHAZARD
A standard white trash bag on the client's unit
A yellow linen bag for laundry
A puncture-resistant sharps container
qs.e: A red BIOHAZARD bag is used for trash containing liquid or semiliquid blood/OPIM, trash that would release these substances if compressed, or trash caked with dried blood/OPIM. Sharps containers are only for needles and sharp devices.

qs.q: A nursing student tells the instructor, 'We should use paper trays and plastic utensils for clients in isolation to stop germ spread.' Which response by the instructor is correct?
c: Correct; disposable items are required for all isolation clients
Incorrect; paper trays and plastic utensils do not prevent transmission and are no longer recommended
Correct; but they are only needed for airborne precautions
Incorrect; only metal utensils are permitted in isolation
qs.e: Paper trays and plastic eating utensils do not prevent transmission; commercial dishwashers using hot water and detergent sufficiently decontaminate dishes, glasses, and utensils. This is a common misconception among students.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a highly communicable respiratory virus requiring droplet precautions. The nurse dons PPE prior to entering the room. When should the nurse remove the PPE?
c: Immediately after performing hand hygiene inside the room
When leaving the client's room
After completing all client care and documenting at the desk
Only after the client's visitor has exited
qs.e: The 2007 CDC guidelines direct staff to don PPE upon entering the room and remove it only when leaving. Keeping contaminated PPE on outside the room risks contaminating the environment.

qs.q: The nurse must recap a used needle because a sharps container is not immediately available. Which technique is acceptable?
c: Using two hands to replace the cap quickly
Asking the client to hold the cap while the nurse inserts the needle
The one-handed scoop technique or a needle-recapping device
Laying the uncapped needle on the overbed table until disposal
qs.e: Recapping should be avoided; when unavoidable, never use two hands. Use a recapping device or the one-handed scoop technique, then place the needle in a puncture-resistant container. Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injury.

qs.q: A client on standard precautions has spilled urine on the bed linens. Which item does standard precautions apply to?
c: Sweat only
Urine and other excretions
Intact skin only
Hair and nails
qs.e: Standard precautions apply to blood, all body fluids, secretions, excretions (EXCEPT sweat), nonintact skin, and mucous membranes. Sweat is the notable exception and often appears as a distractor.

qs.q: The nurse is assisting with an endotracheal intubation of a client with COVID-19. Which PPE combination is required for this aerosol-generating procedure?
c: Gloves and gown only
Surgical mask and gloves
Particulate respirator, goggles or face shield, gloves, and gown
Face shield and gown without a respirator
qs.e: Aerosol-generating procedures (intubation, bronchoscopy, suctioning) require a particulate respirator for nose/mouth, goggles or face shield for eyes, and gloves and gown for the body. A surgical mask does not filter fine aerosols.

qs.q: A client is being admitted with suspected tuberculosis. The nurse verifies the environmental controls of the assigned room. Which finding requires follow-up?
c: Negative pressure in the room
Air flow rate of 6 to 12 air changes per hour
Exhaust vented directly to the outside
Positive pressure with a HEPA filter on the intake
qs.e: AII rooms require NEGATIVE pressure, 6-12 air changes per hour, and direct exhaust to the outside or HEPA filtration. Positive pressure would push contaminated air out to other areas and is incorrect for TB.

qs.q: While collecting a wound culture, the nurse accidentally contaminates the outside of the specimen container with drainage. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Send the specimen as collected since the contents are unaffected
Wipe the outside with a paper towel and send it
Recollect the specimen in a new container, preventing contamination of the outside
Place the container in a red BIOHAZARD bag
qs.e: The nurse must prevent the outside of the container from becoming contaminated; if it is contaminated, the specimen should be recollected and the container replaced. All specimens are placed in sealed plastic bags for transport.

qs.q: The infection control nurse is presenting on the newer elements added to standard precautions. Which of the following are included? (Select all that apply.)
c: Respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette
Safe injection practices
Use of a mask for high-risk prolonged spinal canal punctures
Routine contact precautions for all clients with MRSA
Routine use of disposable dishes for all isolation clients
N95 respirator use for every client encounter
qs.e: New standard-precaution elements include respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practices, and a mask for spinal canal punctures. Routine MRSA contact precautions and disposable dishes are not recommended; an N95 is only for specific airborne risks.

qs.q: Which environmental controls are required in an airborne infection isolation (AII) room? (Select all that apply.)
c: Negative pressure
Air flow rate of 6 to 12 air changes per hour
Direct venting of exhaust to the outside
Use of a HEPA filter as an alternative exhaust method
Positive pressure to push clean air in
Sealed windows that cannot be opened, with no exhaust
qs.e: AII rooms combine negative pressure, 6-12 air changes per hour, and exhaust either vented outside or passed through a HEPA filter. Positive pressure is the opposite of what is needed for airborne isolation.

qs.q: Standard precautions apply to which of the following? (Select all that apply.)
c: Blood
All body fluids
Secretions and excretions (except sweat)
Nonintact skin
Mucous membranes
Sweat
qs.e: Standard precautions cover blood, all body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), nonintact skin, and mucous membranes. Sweat is the single exception and is a classic test distractor.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing procedures considered aerosol-generating that require a particulate respirator. Which procedures qualify? (Select all that apply.)
c: Endotracheal intubation
Bronchoscopy
Suctioning
Administering an oral medication
Routine blood pressure measurement
Changing a dry dressing without drainage
qs.e: Intubation, bronchoscopy, and suctioning are the aerosol-generating procedures named in the text; they generate fine particle aerosols over greater than 3 ft. Routine tasks do not create aerosols and do not require a respirator.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a group of unlicensed assistive personnel about Box 25-4 standard precautions. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: Wear clean nonsterile gloves when touching blood, mucous membranes, or nonintact skin
Change gloves between tasks on the same patient as necessary
Wear a fluid-repellent gown when splashes or sprays are likely
Offer a surgical mask to coughing patients during periods of increased respiratory infections
Encourage coughing patients to maintain more than a 3-ft separation from others
Two-handed recapping is acceptable if done quickly
qs.e: All listed items are Box 25-4 standard precautions. Two-handed recapping is never acceptable — use the one-handed scoop technique or a recapping device.

qs.q: Which statements about transmission-based precautions are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: They are used in addition to standard precautions
They include airborne, droplet, and contact categories
A disease may have multiple routes of transmission
They replace standard precautions when a specific diagnosis is known
They may be used alone or in combination with each other
They are applied only in acute care hospitals
qs.e: Transmission-based precautions add to (never replace) standard precautions and can be combined; a disease can spread by more than one route. The 2007 guideline applies to all health care settings, not only acute care.

qs.q: The N95 respirator filters airborne particles as small as ____ micrometer(s), with what efficiency percentage? (Answer: size, then percentage.)
qs.e: The N95 filters particles as small as 1 μm with 95% efficiency — the source of the 'N95' name.

qs.q: The air flow rate for an airborne infection isolation (AII) room is ____ to ____ air changes per hour.
qs.e: AII rooms maintain 6-12 air changes per hour along with negative pressure and external venting/HEPA filtration. Students often confuse this with '3 ft' (cough separation) or '6 ft' (COVID social distancing).

qs.q: What is the foundation of all infection control practices?
qs.e: Hand hygiene is named as the foundation of all infection control practices, decreasing fomite and mucous membrane transfer.

qs.q: During respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, a coughing client in the health care facility should maintain more than a ____-foot separation from others. (Enter the number.)
qs.e: Cough etiquette inside the health care facility calls for more than 3 ft of separation; the 6-ft figure was COVID-era public social distancing guidance and is a common distractor.

qs.q: Which colored bag marked BIOHAZARD is used to dispose of trash containing liquid or semiliquid blood or OPIM?
qs.e: Red bags marked BIOHAZARD are designated for liquid/semiliquid blood or OPIM, trash that would release these if compressed, or trash caked with dried blood/OPIM.

qs.q: A nurse finishes caring for a client on contact precautions and removes gloves. The nurse then prepares to perform a blood glucose check on the same client using the glucometer. Which instruction is correct?
c: Reuse the same gloves since it is the same client
Change gloves between tasks on the same client as necessary and remove gloves promptly after use
Wear two pairs of gloves to save time
Wipe the gloves with alcohol instead of changing them
qs.e: Box 25-4 requires changing gloves between tasks on the same client as necessary and removing them promptly after use to prevent cross-contamination between tasks. Reusing gloves transfers organisms between sites.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to place a lumbar epidural catheter. Which standard-precaution actions apply? (Select all that apply.)
c: Wear a face mask for the procedure
Wear a gown to protect skin and clothing
Wear gloves for the procedure
Use eye protection if a splash of blood or body fluid is possible
The procedure does not require any special precautions
Use only a surgical gown with no gloves to maintain tactile sensitivity
qs.e: A face mask is worn when placing a catheter or injecting material into the spinal/epidural space; gloves, gown, and eye protection (if splash is possible) complete standard precautions. Omitting gloves or PPE violates standard precautions.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with known tuberculosis who must be transported to radiology. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Place a surgical mask on the client if possible
Place a respirator on the client before leaving the room
Leave the room door open during transport so air can circulate
Assign the client to a semi-private room until the test is completed
qs.e: Transport the client out of the room only when necessary and place a surgical mask on the client if possible. The respirator is required for the health care worker entering the room, not the client.

qs.q: A nurse who is not immune to rubeola is assigned to care for a client with measles (airborne precautions). Which personal protective equipment must the nurse wear before entering the room?
c: A face mask only
Respiratory protection (a respirator)
Gloves and a gown only
A face shield only
qs.e: Respiratory protection should be worn for rubeola or varicella unless the person entering the room is immune to the disease. A surgical face mask is not the protection required for airborne transmission.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to inject medication into a client's epidural space. Which additional item of personal protective equipment is required?
c: A face mask
A respirator
Sterile goggles
A shoe cover
qs.e: A face mask is worn if placing a catheter or injecting material into the spinal or epidural space. A respirator is used for airborne precautions, not for this procedure.

qs.q: The nurse is admitting a child with mumps to the unit. Which room assignment is most appropriate for droplet precautions?
c: A private room, if available, with the door remaining open
A private room with monitored negative air pressure and the door kept closed
A semi-private room with the beds placed 3 ft apart
A private room with monitored positive air pressure
qs.e: Droplet precautions use a private room if available, and the door may remain open. Negative pressure with a closed door is required for airborne, not droplet, transmission.

qs.q: The nurse has finished caring for a client colonized with a multidrug-resistant organism (contact precautions). Which action is correct?
c: Remove PPE before leaving the patient environment and wash hands with an antimicrobial or waterless antiseptic agent
Remove PPE in the hallway after closing the door
Keep the same gloves on while charting at the bedside computer
Wash hands with water only, since gloves were worn
qs.e: PPE is removed before leaving the patient environment and hands are washed with an antimicrobial or waterless antiseptic agent. Removing PPE in the hallway contaminates the environment outside the room.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing room assignments and notes a client who is incontinent. Where should this client be placed?
c: In a private room, because the client may contaminate the environment
In a semi-private room with another incontinent client
In a semi-private room nearest the nurses' station
In any available bed, since incontinence requires no special placement
qs.e: Review room assignments carefully and place patients who may contaminate the environment (such as a patient who is incontinent) in private rooms. Pairing two incontinent clients still spreads contamination to another patient.

qs.q: The nurse's unit is implementing the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act. Which action is required by this act?
c: Involve health care workers in the selection process of safer devices
Require that all injections be given by two licensed nurses
Prohibit the use of needles in all patient care
Report every needlestick to the state board of nursing within 24 hours
qs.e: The act requires health care providers to involve health care workers in the selection process of safer devices. The other options are not requirements listed in the source.

qs.q: A nursing student is reviewing national sharps injury data. Which statement is accurate?
c: Close to 40% of sharps injuries occurred in surgery, and teaching hospitals had higher rates than nonteaching hospitals
Sharps injuries have declined every year since 2001
Most sharps injuries occur in outpatient clinics
Teaching hospitals have lower rates of sharps injuries than nonteaching hospitals
qs.e: Close to 40% of these injuries occurred in surgery, and teaching hospitals had higher rates than nonteaching hospitals. The decline after 2001 has not continued; rates have risen for the last 3 years.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client colonized with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (contact precautions). Which action requires follow-up?
c: The nurse uses a stethoscope for another client without cleaning or reprocessing it
The nurse changes gloves after contact with infective material
The nurse washes hands with a waterless antiseptic agent after removing PPE
The nurse limits the client's movement out of the room
qs.e: Sharing patient-care equipment is to be avoided under contact precautions, and items used for another patient must be cleaned and reprocessed appropriately. The other actions are correct interventions.

qs.q: The nurse is verifying the room set up for a client with varicella (airborne precautions). Which finding requires follow-up?
c: The client is in a semi-private room with another client
There are 10 air changes per hour
The air is discharged outside the building
The door is kept closed and the client remains in the room
qs.e: Airborne precautions require a private room with monitored negative air pressure. A shared room allows airborne contamination of the roommate.

qs.q: The nurse is planning care for several clients. Which infections require airborne precautions? (Select all that apply.)
c: Tuberculosis
Varicella (chicken pox)
Rubeola (measles)
Rubella
Mumps
Diphtheria
qs.e: Airborne precautions are used for infections that spread through the air: tuberculosis, varicella, and rubeola. Rubella, mumps, and diphtheria are spread by large-particle droplets.

qs.q: Which requirements are included in the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act? (Select all that apply.)
c: Identify and provide safer medical devices that reduce or eliminate injuries from sharps
Involve health care workers in the selection process of these safer devices
Develop a sharps injury surveillance log
Educate employees regarding how to safely use these devices
Require that all sharps procedures be performed by two licensed nurses
Prohibit the use of all needles in patient care
qs.e: The act requires safer devices, worker involvement in selecting them, education on their use, and a sharps injury surveillance log. Two-nurse sharps procedures and banning needles are not requirements in the source.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client infected with a multidrug-resistant organism. Which interventions are included in contact precautions? (Select all that apply.)
c: Place the patient in a private room, if available
Wear PPE whenever you enter the room for all interactions involving contact with the patient or contaminated areas
Change gloves after having contact with infective material
Avoid sharing patient-care equipment
Keep the door closed and the patient in the room at all times
Keep visitors 3 ft from the infected person
qs.e: Contact precautions include a private room if available, PPE on entry, glove changes after infective material, and no sharing of equipment. A closed door with the patient confined and a 3-ft visitor distance belong to airborne and droplet precautions.

qs.q: Which interventions are included in droplet precautions? (Select all that apply.)
c: Use a private room, if available; the door may remain open
Wear PPE upon entry into the room for all interactions that may involve contact with the patient and contaminated areas
Keep visitors 3 ft from the infected person
Transport the patient out of room only when necessary and place a surgical mask on the patient if possible
