qs.e: The usual stopping point is 1 degree above the desired temperature, according to facility policy. Temperature monitoring continues until it stabilizes rather than stopping when the blanket is turned off.

qs.q: When using a skin probe with a hypothermia blanket, tuck the probe deep into which site and tape it in place?
qs.e: The procedure directs the nurse to tuck the skin probe deep into the axilla and tape it in place. The esophageal probe is specified for comatose or anesthetized clients.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a postoperative client whose tympanic membrane temperature is needed. On assessment, the nurse notes drainage from the client's left ear. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Measure the tympanic temperature in the left ear using a slightly larger probe
Measure the tympanic temperature in the right (opposite) ear
Substitute an oral temperature measurement in place of tympanic
Apply a temperature-sensitive patch to the forehead instead
qs.e: If a patient has drainage from the ear, ear pain, ear infection, or scarring on the tympanic membrane on one side, the opposite ear may be used. Oral temp may be contraindicated for other reasons, and temperature patches are inaccurate and require thermometer reassessment.

qs.q: A client who smokes has just finished a cigarette. The nurse needs to obtain an oral temperature. How long should the nurse wait before measuring?
c: 5 to 10 minutes
15 to 30 minutes
30 to 45 minutes
60 minutes
qs.e: After smoking or chewing gum (or hot/cold food/fluids), wait 15 to 30 minutes for oral tissues to return to normal temperature. Shorter waits can yield inaccurate readings.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing normal temperature ranges by site. Which of the following readings would be considered within the normal range? (Select all that apply.)
c: Tympanic: 99.0°F (37.2°C)
Axillary: 98.8°F (37.1°C)
Temporal artery: 99.5°F (37.5°C)
qs.e: Normal ranges: oral 96.6–99.5°F, tympanic 98.2–100.9°F, rectal 97.4–100.5°F, temporal artery 98.7–100.5°F. Axillary normal range is 95.6–98.5°F, so 98.8°F exceeds the upper limit for that site.

qs.q: A client with thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) needs a temperature measurement. The nurse selects the rectal route. Which response is required?
c: Proceed, as the rectal route is the most accurate
Follow-up is required; rectal thermometry is contraindicated
Use a rectal thermometer with extra lubrication only
Take the rectal temperature only after checking the INR
qs.e: Rectal thermometry is contraindicated in patients with low platelet counts because the rectum is very vascular and insertion could cause rectal bleeding. The accuracy of the route does not override safety contraindications.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to use a noncontact infrared (IFR) thermometer. Which action should the nurse perform first?
c: Place the device in the testing room 10 to 30 minutes prior to use
Take the device directly from the cart and use it immediately
Apply a disposable probe cover to the device
Wipe the client's forehead with alcohol before measuring
qs.e: The noncontact IFR thermometer should be placed in the testing environment for 10 to 30 minutes before use to allow the device to adjust. No probe covers are needed because there is no body-surface contact.

qs.q: A nurse is assessing a client's peripheral pulse. Which characteristics should be documented? (Select all that apply.)
c: Rate
Rhythm
Strength (amplitude)
Elasticity
Skin color
Body temperature
qs.e: Characteristics of the peripheral pulse are rate, rhythm, strength (amplitude), and elasticity. Skin color and temperature are not listed among pulse characteristics in this text.

qs.q: A client is receiving oxygen by mask and the nurse selects the oral route for a temperature measurement. Which statement best explains why this action needs to be corrected?
c: Oral temperature should not be assessed in patients receiving oxygen by mask because the time it takes to obtain the reading is likely to result in a serious drop in the patient's blood oxygen level
Oral temperature is the preferred route whenever possible
The probe should remain in the sublingual pocket for the full measurement time
The site of the temperature measurement must be documented
qs.e: Per the text, oral temperatures should not be assessed in patients receiving oxygen by mask, because the time it takes to assess a reading is likely to result in a serious drop in the patient's blood oxygen level. The other statements are correct and do not indicate a need for correction.

qs.q: If no site is listed with the temperature documentation, it is generally assumed to be what route?
qs.e: Documenting the site is essential; if no site is listed, the oral route is assumed. This can lead to incorrect data comparison if the actual site was different.

qs.q: The nurse is measuring a client's temporal artery temperature. The client is wearing a thick headband across the forehead. Which effect will this have on the reading?
c: Falsely low reading due to insulating the area
Falsely high reading due to insulating the area
No effect on the reading
The reading will be accurate after waiting 30 minutes
qs.e: Anything covering the area (hats, hair, wigs, bandages) insulates the skin and results in falsely high readings. The nurse must remove coverings before measuring.

qs.q: Which factors should the nurse consider when selecting a temperature measurement site? (Select all that apply.)
c: Patient's age
State of consciousness
Amount of pain
Care or treatments being provided (e.g., oxygen administration)
Facility policy and procedures
The client's insurance provider
qs.e: Site selection depends on age, consciousness, pain, other care/treatments, and facility policy. Insurance type does not influence clinical site selection.

qs.q: The nurse is considering the rectal route for a temperature measurement in a client who recently had spinal cord surgery. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Proceed with rectal measurement since it is the most accurate route
Select an alternative site; rectal thermometry is contraindicated in patients with certain neurologic disorders such as spinal cord injuries
Take the rectal temperature and have another nurse supervise
Take the rectal temperature using a smaller probe
qs.e: Rectal thermometry is contraindicated in patients with certain neurologic disorders including spinal cord injuries. Accuracy of the route does not override contraindications.

qs.q: A client requires a rectal temperature measurement. In which situations should the nurse avoid the rectal route? (Select all that apply.)
c: Newborn
Child with diarrhea
Neutropenic patient (low WBC)
Patient with a low platelet count
Patient who is embarrassed by the procedure
Patient with recent rectal surgery
qs.e: Rectal thermometry is contraindicated in newborns, children with diarrhea, neutropenic patients (low WBC), thrombocytopenia (low platelets), and patients with recent rectal/anal/vaginal/prostate surgery. Embarrassment alone is not a medical contraindication, though it is a reason to consider comfort and dignity.

qs.q: The apical pulse is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves ('lub') and which valves ('dub')?
qs.e: Heart sounds are 'lub-dub'; 'lub' is closure of mitral and tricuspid valves, 'dub' is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. The two sounds together are counted as one beat.

qs.q: A nurse is using a noncontact infrared thermometer. Which environmental condition will most likely interfere with an accurate reading?
c: Measuring in a warm, enclosed room away from drafts
Measuring in a draft-free space out of direct sun
Measuring near a radiant heat source such as a heater
Allowing the device to adjust to the room temperature for 20 minutes first
qs.e: Temperature measurement should be performed in a draft-free space, out of direct sun, and away from radiant heat sources. Measuring near a radiant heat source can distort the reading.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a confused, elderly client who cannot follow directions. Which temperature measurement site should be avoided?
c: Axillary
Tympanic
Oral (sublingual)
Rectal
qs.e: The oral site is not suitable for confused or comatose patients because they cannot reliably close their mouth around the probe. Tympanic, axillary, or rectal routes may be alternatives.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about noncontact infrared (IFR) thermometers. Which statements are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
c: They are suggested for screening for fever, not ongoing monitoring
Risk of cross-infection is negligible because no body surface contact is needed
They are effective as the sole means of detecting infection such as COVID-19
No disposable probe covers are needed
The device should be placed in the room 10 to 30 minutes before use
They require an invasive sensor placed in the patient's body
qs.e: Noncontact IFR thermometers are for fever screening (not ongoing monitoring), have negligible cross-infection risk, need no probe covers, and require 10–30 min of environmental adjustment. They are NOT effective as the only means of detecting infection (e.g., COVID-19) and do not use invasive sensors.

qs.q: A neonate needs a temperature measurement. Which site is most commonly used for temperature measurement in a neonate?
c: Oral
Rectal
Axillary
Temporal artery
qs.e: The axilla remains the most common place for temperature measurement in the neonate. Rectal thermometry is contraindicated in newborns, and oral thermometry is unsuitable for children under 6 years.

qs.q: Temperature-sensitive patches or tape that change color at different temperatures are considered __________ for measuring temperature accurately.
qs.e: These devices are described as inaccurate; if the patch or tape indicates an out-of-range temperature, a thermometer should be used to reassess.

qs.q: A client has scar tissue over the right temporal artery area. The nurse is measuring temporal artery temperature. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Measure over the scar tissue as long as the probe is flat against the skin
Do not measure over scar tissue; select an alternative area or route
Measure on the scar and repeat the measurement for accuracy
Cover the scar with a bandage and measure over it
qs.e: Do not measure temporal artery temperature over scar tissue, open lesions, or abrasions. A bandage would further insulate the area and cause falsely high readings.

qs.q: A nurse is selecting a temperature measurement site. Which situations make the oral (sublingual) site unsuitable? (Select all that apply.)
c: Client younger than 6 years old
Client unable to follow directions
Client with changes in or inflammation of the oral mucosa
Client receiving oxygen by mask
Client with a history of smoking 45 minutes ago
Client who is comatose
qs.e: The oral site is unsuitable for children younger than 6 years (and some children with developmental delay), for patients unable to follow directions, for patients with changes in or inflammation of the oral mucosa, for patients receiving oxygen by mask (risk of a serious drop in blood oxygen level), and for confused or comatose patients. After smoking, one only needs to wait 15 to 30 minutes, so smoking 45 minutes ago does not make the oral site unsuitable.

qs.q: Which temperature site is considered reflective of core body temperature and one of the most accurate routes?
qs.e: The rectal temperature is considered reflective of core body temperature and one of the most accurate routes, though multiple contraindications exist.

qs.q: The nurse notes that a client has diaphoresis (sweating) on the forehead. The nurse is measuring temporal artery temperature. What is the most appropriate action?
c: Proceed; sweat does not affect the reading
Dry the area first; diaphoresis can impair the reading
Apply a head covering and measure over it
Use the noncontact IFR thermometer instead without addressing the sweat
qs.e: Diaphoresis or sweat can impair the temporal artery temperature reading. The area should be assessed and addressed before measurement for accuracy.

qs.q: A client's tympanic temperature is affected by cerumen (earwax). The client has significant cerumen in both ears. Which statement is correct?
c: Tympanic temperature is accurate regardless of cerumen
The reading may be impacted by cerumen; an alternate route should be considered
Cerumen causes falsely low readings and can be corrected by subtracting a constant
Both ears must be measured and averaged to correct for cerumen
qs.e: Cerumen (earwax) can impact tympanic temperature readings. The nurse should consider an alternative measurement site when cerumen is present.

qs.q: A nurse is comparing the accuracy of axillary temperature to other routes. Which statement is correct?
c: Axillary readings are the most accurate of all routes
Axillary readings are less accurate than oral or rectal readings and should not be used where accurate measurement is required
Axillary readings are more accurate than temporal artery readings
Axillary readings always match rectal readings
qs.e: Axillary measurement may provide readings less accurate than oral or rectal routes and should not be used where accurate temperature measurement is required. Temporal artery readings are more accurate than axillary.

qs.q: How long (in minutes) should a noncontact infrared thermometer be placed in the testing environment before use?
qs.e: The device must be placed in the testing room 10 to 30 minutes prior to use to adjust to the environmental temperature.

qs.q: A nurse is considering rectal temperature measurement for a client. Which client conditions make rectal thermometry contraindicated or inappropriate? (Select all that apply.)
c: Client who is neutropenic (low WBC, e.g., leukemia)
Client who had cardiac surgery (vagal stimulation can slow the heart rate; some institutions do not allow rectal thermometry in these clients)
Client with a history of recent vaginal surgery
Client with thrombocytopenia (low platelets)
Client who has been on bed rest for 2 days
Client with a disease of the rectum
qs.e: Rectal thermometry is contraindicated in neutropenic patients (low WBC), in patients with a low platelet count (rectum is very vascular; risk of rectal bleeding), and in patients who have had recent rectal, anal, vaginal, or prostate surgery or who have a disease of the rectum. Because rectal insertion can slow the heart rate by stimulating the vagus nerve, rectal temperatures may not be allowed in patients with heart disease or after cardiac surgery in some institutions. Bed rest alone is not a contraindication.

qs.q: The nurse is documenting a client's axillary temperature of 97.8°F (36.6°C). Which documentation entry is most appropriate?
c: Axillary T 97.8°F
Oral T 97.8°F
Temperature 97.8°F (site per chart)
qs.e: If a temperature is obtained from a site other than oral, the site must be documented with the result to ensure accurate comparison. Omitting the site would cause the reader to assume it was oral.

qs.q: A student nurse is learning to auscultate an apical pulse. Which statement best explains how heart sounds are counted as one beat?
c: The "lub" (mitral and tricuspid closure) combined with the "dub" (aortic and pulmonic closure) is counted as one beat
The "lub" is counted as one beat and the "dub" is counted as a second beat
Only the "dub" sound is counted because it represents ventricular contraction
Only the "lub" sound is counted because it represents atrial contraction
qs.e: The "lub-dub" combination produced by closure of all four heart valves constitutes a single cardiac cycle and is counted as one beat. Counting the two sounds separately would overestimate the pulse rate by double.

qs.q: A nursing student is asked to explain how the autonomic nervous system regulates pulse through the sinoatrial (SA) node. Which response is correct?
c: Parasympathetic stimulation via the vagus nerve decreases heart rate, and sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and force of contraction
Parasympathetic stimulation via the vagus nerve increases heart rate, and sympathetic stimulation decreases heart rate
Both sympathetic and parasympathetic stimulation increase heart rate through the SA node
The SA node is stimulated only by the sympathetic nervous system
qs.e: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic impulses that slow the SA node; sympathetic impulses speed the SA node and increase the force of contraction. Reversing these roles is a common misconception.

qs.q: The nurse obtains a radial pulse of 52 beats/min on a resting, asymptomatic college athlete who feels well. Which interpretation is best?
c: The finding may be normal for a well-conditioned athlete and may not require treatment unless the client is symptomatic
The finding indicates bradycardia that must be treated immediately with atropine
The finding indicates the client is hypothermic and should be rewarmed
The finding is inconsistent with the autonomic regulation of the SA node and should be reported as an error
qs.e: Bradycardia can be a normal finding in athletes and during sleep and may not require treatment unless the client is symptomatic. Atropine is not indicated for an asymptomatic, well-conditioned athlete.

qs.q: A client is admitted after a motor vehicle crash with significant blood loss. The nurse expects the pulse rate to change in which way and why?
c: Increase, because decreased stroke volume triggers a compensatory rise in heart rate to maintain cardiac output
Decrease, because the body slows metabolism to conserve oxygen
Remain unchanged, because pulse rate is independent of stroke volume
Become irregular, because vagal tone is increased
qs.e: When stroke volume falls (as with hemorrhage), heart rate increases to maintain cardiac output. A decrease in rate is the opposite of the expected compensatory response.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a pulse of 128 beats/min. Which effect does this tachycardia most likely have on cardiac output?
c: Decreased cardiac filling time reduces stroke volume and can decrease cardiac output and tissue perfusion
Increased filling time increases stroke volume and cardiac output
No effect on stroke volume; only oxygen demand is altered
Increased vagal tone slows filling and increases output
qs.e: Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling time, decreasing stroke volume and potentially lowering cardiac output and tissue perfusion. This is why persistent tachycardia at rest signals an underlying problem.

qs.q: The nurse palpates a peripheral artery and notes a pulse that is forceful and full. How should this pulse strength be documented using the Table 26-5 scale?
c: +3, bounding
+2, normal
+1, diminished
0, absent
qs.e: Pulse strength (amplitude) is assessed by the feel of the blood flow through the vessel. A forceful, full pulse is documented as full and bounding, which is graded +3 on the Table 26-5 scale. +2 is normal/brisk, +1 is diminished/weaker than expected, and 0 is absent.

qs.q: A client with a documented +2 (normal, brisk, expected) peripheral pulse would have which characteristic on palpation?
c: A brisk, expected pulse at the palpated artery
A pulse weaker than expected
A forceful, full, bounding pulse
No palpable pulsation
qs.e: Per Table 26-5, +2 equals normal, brisk, expected. Diminished/weaker than expected is +1, bounding is +3, and absent is 0.

qs.q: The nurse is auscultating respiratory sounds with a stethoscope. Which chest piece should be used and why?
c: The diaphragm, because it is more useful for high-frequency sounds and screens out low-frequency sounds
The bell, because it amplifies high-frequency respiratory sounds
The bell, because it is best for high-frequency sounds such as breath sounds
Either; the diaphragm and bell are interchangeable
qs.e: The diaphragm favors high-frequency sounds such as respiratory sounds by screening out low frequencies. The bell does the opposite and is preferred for low-frequency heart and vessel sounds.

qs.q: The nurse is listening for low-frequency heart sounds. Which stethoscope chest piece is most appropriate?
c: The bell, which screens out high-frequency sounds
The diaphragm, which screens out low-frequency sounds
The diaphragm, because it amplifies low-frequency sounds
Both should be used simultaneously
qs.e: The bell favors low-frequency sounds commonly made by the heart and blood within vessels. The diaphragm is used for high-frequency sounds such as breath sounds.

qs.q: A student is setting up a stethoscope. Which instruction regarding earpiece placement is correct?
c: Direct the earpieces into the ear canal toward the tympanic membrane, not against the ear itself
Place the earpieces against the outer ear to reduce discomfort
Insert the earpieces loosely so sound is not distorted
Angle the earpieces posteriorly toward the mastoid process
qs.e: Earpieces should be directed into the ear canal toward the tympanic membrane for optimal sound transmission. Placement against the ear or loosely in the canal impairs auscultation.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a fever of 39.4°C (103°F). Which change in pulse rate is expected and why?
c: Increased pulse rate, because elevated temperature increases metabolic demands and compensatory mechanisms to increase heat loss
Decreased pulse rate, because fever lowers metabolic rate
No change; temperature does not affect pulse rate
Irregular pulse, because fever affects the vagus nerve
qs.e: Fever raises metabolic demands and stimulates heat-loss mechanisms, increasing pulse. Hypothermia (not fever) decreases pulse as metabolism slows.

qs.q: A client has a weak and thready peripheral pulse. Which condition is most likely to cause this decreased pulse strength?
c: Hypovolemia
Fluid volume excess
Early septic shock
Exercise
qs.e: Heart failure, hypovolemia, shock, hypernatremia, and arrhythmias cause decreased pulse strength. Fluid volume excess, early septic shock, and exercise cause bounding (increased) pulses.

qs.q: The nurse palpates a peripheral artery and describes it as rigid, crooked, and less resilient. Which age-related change does this finding reflect?
c: Decreased arterial elasticity associated with aging
Increased cardiac output
Increased sympathetic tone
Dysrhythmia
qs.e: Arteries normally feel smooth, straight, and springy; with aging they become less elastic, more rigid, and crooked. This describes vessel wall changes, not rhythm or cardiac output.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client's pulse as regular with slight speeding during inhalation and slowing during exhalation. The client is a 24-year-old. Which interpretation is best?
c: Minor variation with respirations is a common and normal finding in children and young adults
This represents a dysrhythmia requiring immediate treatment
This indicates hypoxemia
This is a sign of increasing intracranial pressure
qs.e: Minor rhythm variation with the respiratory cycle (rate increases with inhalation, slows with exhalation) occurs most commonly in children and young adults and is not a dysrhythmia. A dysrhythmia refers to unequal, varied intervals between beats and pauses.

qs.q: A nurse is preparing to assess the pulse of a client whose peripheral pulses are very difficult to palpate. Which equipment is most appropriate?
c: Doppler ultrasound
The diaphragm of the stethoscope
Cardiac monitor only
The bell of the stethoscope applied to the radial artery
qs.e: Doppler ultrasound is used to assess pulses that are difficult to palpate. A stethoscope is typically used for apical auscultation, and cardiac monitoring observes rate and rhythm continuously but does not substitute for Doppler detection of a weak peripheral pulse.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing Table 26-4. Which factors affect a client's pulse rate? (Select all that apply.)
c: Age
Biologic sex
Physical activity
Body temperature
Height
Eye color
qs.e: Table 26-4 lists age, biologic sex, physical activity, body temperature, stress, medications, and disease/health conditions. Height and eye color are not listed as factors affecting pulse rate.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for clients with various conditions. Which factors contribute to tachycardia? (Select all that apply.)
c: Elevated body temperature
Pain
Hyperthyroidism
Hypothyroidism
Anemia causing poor oxygenation of blood
Digitalis
qs.e: Box 26-3 lists elevated temperature, pain, hyperthyroidism, and poor oxygenation (e.g., anemia) under tachycardia. Hypothyroidism and digitalis are listed under bradycardia.

qs.q: Which factors contribute to bradycardia? (Select all that apply.)
c: Increased intracranial pressure
Response to vagal stimulation such as vomiting
Hypothyroidism
Myocardial infarction
Hyperthyroidism
Strong emotions such as fear and anger
qs.e: Box 26-3 lists increased ICP, vagal stimulation, hypothyroidism, and MI/CAD under bradycardia. Hyperthyroidism and strong emotions are listed under tachycardia.

qs.q: A client has a full and bounding peripheral pulse. Which conditions could cause this finding? (Select all that apply.)
c: Early stages of septic shock
Fluid volume excess
Fever
Hypovolemia
Anxiety
Heart failure with decreased cardiac output
qs.e: Bounding pulses may occur with early septic shock, exercise, fever, fluid volume excess, and anxiety. Hypovolemia and heart failure cause decreased (weak, thready) pulse strength.

qs.q: Which conditions can cause decreased pulse strength? (Select all that apply.)
c: Hypovolemia
Shock
Hypernatremia
Arrhythmias
Fluid volume excess
Exercise
qs.e: Heart failure, hypovolemia, shock, hypernatremia, and arrhythmias cause decreased pulse strength. Fluid volume excess and exercise are associated with bounding (increased) pulses.

qs.q: A nursing instructor is demonstrating methods and equipment for assessing the pulse. Which statements accurately reflect the assigned reading? (Select all that apply.)
c: The pulse can be assessed by palpating peripheral arteries
The apical pulse is auscultated with a stethoscope over the apex of the heart
Doppler ultrasound may be used when pulses are difficult to palpate
Electrocardiography is a graphic or digital recording of the electrical activity of the heart and may be used to assess pulse rate and rhythm
The pulse rate is the number of pulsations felt or heard in 30 seconds and then doubled
Cardiac monitoring provides continuous observation of heart rate and rhythm
qs.e: The reading describes assessing the pulse by palpating peripheral arteries, auscultating the apical pulse with a stethoscope over the apex of the heart, and using a portable Doppler ultrasound when pulses are difficult to palpate. Electrocardiography is a graphic or digital recording of the electrical activity of the heart and may be used to assess pulse rate and rhythm, and cardiac monitoring provides continuous observation of heart rate and rhythm. The 30-second-and-double statement is incorrect: the source defines the pulse rate as the number of pulsations in 1 minute.

qs.q: What is the normal pulse rate range for adolescents and adults in beats per minute?
qs.e: The normal adult/adolescent pulse rate is 60 to 100 beats/min. Rates outside this range (with defined cutoffs at 60 and 100) are classified as bradycardia or tachycardia.

qs.q: In an adult, tachycardia is defined as a pulse rate greater than ______ beats/min.
qs.e: An adult has tachycardia when the pulse rate is greater than 100 beats/min. Tachycardia at rest usually indicates an underlying problem.

qs.q: What pulse strength (amplitude) grade corresponds to "normal; brisk, expected"?
qs.e: Table 26-5 grades +2 as normal, brisk, expected. +1 is diminished, +3 is bounding, and 0 is absent.

qs.q: Which structure is the pacemaker of the heart through which the autonomic nervous system regulates pulse?
qs.e: The sinoatrial (SA) node is the heart's pacemaker and is regulated by parasympathetic and sympathetic input.

qs.q: An irregular pattern of heartbeats with unequal, varied intervals between beats and pauses is called a ______.
qs.e: Pulse rhythm is normally regular; an irregular pattern of heartbeats is termed a dysrhythmia and should be distinguished from minor respiratory variation.

qs.q: A nurse is teaching about factors that affect pulse rate. Which statements accurately reflect the assigned reading? (Select all that apply.)
c: Older adults may have a decreased pulse rate as metabolic rate changes with aging
Women on average have slightly higher pulse rates than men
Well-conditioned athletes may have a significantly decreased pulse rate
Hypothermia slows metabolism with a corresponding decrease in pulse rate
Stressors such as pain, fear, and anxiety increase pulse rate
Every medication decreases pulse rate
qs.e: Table 26-4 supports each of the first five statements. Medications can increase or decrease pulse rate — the effect may be intended or an unintended adverse effect — so the last statement is incorrect.

qs.q: A client with sepsis has a full, bounding peripheral pulse. Which grade should the nurse document if the pulse feels forceful?
qs.e: Bounding is graded +3 on the Table 26-5 scale, and bounding pulses may occur in early septic shock. +2 is normal/brisk, +1 is diminished/weaker than expected, and 0 is absent.

qs.q: Which statements about pulse strength (amplitude) are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: Pulse strength describes the fullness of the pulse and indicates the volume of blood flowing through the vessel
Pulse strength reflects the strength of left ventricular contraction
The strength of each pulse beat is normally strong at all palpable arterial sites
A weak and thready pulse is always a normal variant in young adults
Nurses should be familiar with the grading system used at their facility
qs.e: Pulse strength reflects blood volume in the vessel and left ventricular contraction, is normally strong at palpable sites, and nurses must know their facility's scale. A weak and thready pulse is a decreased quality, not a normal variant.

qs.q: The nurse is assessing the carotid pulse of an adult client in hypovolemic shock. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Palpate both carotid arteries simultaneously to compare strength
Lightly palpate only one side at a time
Palpate firmly to ensure an accurate reading in a hypotensive client
Use the brachial artery instead because carotid palpation is contraindicated in shock
qs.e: The carotid pulse is used during emergencies such as shock, but only one side should be lightly palpated at a time to prevent any decrease in cerebrovascular circulation. Palpating both sides simultaneously or pressing firmly could compromise blood flow to the brain; the brachial site is used most often for infants, not adults.

qs.q: When auscultating an apical pulse on an adult client, the nurse places the stethoscope at which anatomical landmark?
c: Second intercostal space, left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
Fourth intercostal space, right midclavicular line
Third intercostal space, midaxillary line
qs.e: The apical pulse is obtained at the fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line. Erb's point (second or third intercostal space, left sternal border) is an alternative site, not the primary location described in the guidelines.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an 18-month-old child whose radial pulse is weak and difficult to palpate. Which method should the nurse use to obtain an accurate pulse rate?
c: Palpate the radial pulse for 1 minute despite the difficulty
Use a Doppler ultrasound device at the radial site
Auscultate the apical pulse for 1 full minute
Count the radial pulse for 30 seconds and multiply by two
qs.e: The radial pulse is difficult to palpate accurately in children younger than 2 years of age; the apical pulse should be auscultated for 1 minute. Counting for 30 seconds and multiplying by two risks missing irregularities and is unreliable in a child with a weak pulse.

qs.q: Two nurses obtain an apical-radial pulse and find the apical rate is 88/min and the radial rate is 76/min. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
c: This is an expected finding and requires no further action
The radial rate is inaccurate and should be retaken
A pulse deficit of 12 beats/min suggests insufficient cardiac force or volume
The client is in sinus tachycardia and needs a 12-lead ECG immediately
qs.e: A difference between the apical and radial pulse rates is called a pulse deficit (here 88 − 76 = 12) and indicates that not all heartbeats are reaching the peripheral arteries, suggesting insufficient cardiac force or volume and decreased tissue perfusion. This is not a normal finding and does not by itself indicate tachycardia.

qs.q: The nurse is assessing a client with peripheral vascular disease whose posterior tibial pulse cannot be palpated. Which device is most appropriate to evaluate the pulse?
c: Pulse oximeter placed on the affected foot
Doppler ultrasound device
A stethoscope diaphragm over the popliteal site
Electrocardiogram monitor
qs.e: A Doppler ultrasound device may be used to assess pulses that are difficult to palpate or auscultate. A pulse oximeter measures oxygen saturation, not a specific pulse site, and an ECG records electrical activity, not peripheral perfusion.

qs.q: A client reports severe postoperative pain. Which change in respirations does the nurse anticipate?
c: Increased rate with decreased depth
Decreased rate with increased depth
Cheyne-Stokes pattern with regular rhythm
No change because pain affects heart rate, not respirations
qs.e: Acute pain increases respiratory rate but may decrease respiratory depth. Cheyne-Stokes is associated with brain lesions or high altitude, and claiming pain does not affect respirations is incorrect.

qs.q: Which physiological factor is the most powerful stimulant of respiration, increasing both respiratory depth and rate?
c: An increase in oxygen levels
An increase in carbon dioxide levels
A decrease in hemoglobin
Stimulation of the cerebral cortex
qs.e: An increase in carbon dioxide is the most powerful respiratory stimulant. Oxygen acts through chemoreceptors but is not described as the most powerful; the cerebral cortex allows voluntary control but is not a chemical stimulant.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client's respiratory pattern and notes 28 breaths/min, shallow, regular. Which term correctly describes this finding?
c: Bradypnea
Tachypnea
Normal respirations
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
qs.e: Tachypnea is defined as a respiratory rate greater than 24 breaths/min that is shallow. Bradypnea is less than 10 breaths/min; normal is 12-20 breaths/min; Cheyne-Stokes is a cyclical pattern not described here.

qs.q: Two nurses are preparing to take an apical-radial pulse. Which piece of equipment is essential for this procedure?
c: Two separate watches, one for each nurse
One watch with a sweep second hand readable by both nurses
A stopwatch with a digital display
A Doppler ultrasound device
qs.e: One watch with a sweep second hand is placed so that both nurses can read it simultaneously and start counting at the same time. Two separate watches or a digital stopwatch could lead to timing discrepancies, and a Doppler is not needed for this procedure.

qs.q: A client has received morphine IV. Which effect on respirations should the nurse monitor for most closely?
c: Increased rate and increased depth
Decreased rate and decreased depth
Sighing respirations with increased depth
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
qs.e: Narcotics and sedatives slow both respiratory rate and depth, placing the client at risk for respiratory depression. Increased rate and sighing respirations are associated with anxiety or stimulants such as amphetamines.

qs.q: The nurse is auscultating heart sounds to obtain an apical pulse. How should the stethoscope diaphragm be prepared before placement on the chest?
c: Cooled under running water
Coated with conducting gel
Held against the palm for a few seconds to warm it
Sterilized in an autoclave before each use
qs.e: The diaphragm should be held against the palm for a few seconds to warm it, improving client comfort and cooperation (Guidelines 26-3). Conducting gel is used with a Doppler transducer probe, not a standard stethoscope diaphragm. The diaphragm is cleaned with an alcohol swab before and after use; cleaning with an alcohol swab is not sterilization, and autoclaving is not part of the routine procedure.

qs.q: A client has a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min. Which term describes this finding?
c: Tachypnea
Bradypnea
Normal respirations
Hyperventilation
qs.e: Bradypnea is a regular respiratory rate of less than 10 breaths/min, often from depression of the respiratory center. Tachypnea is greater than 24 breaths/min; hyperventilation involves increased rate and depth, typically from acidosis.

qs.q: The nurse identifies which factors as increasing respiratory rate? Select all that apply.
c: Exercise
Narcotic medications
Acidosis
Anemia
Acute pain
General anesthetics
qs.e: Exercise, acidosis, anemia, and acute pain all increase respiratory rate. Narcotics and general anesthetics depress both rate and depth, making them the opposite effect—classic distractors on this topic.

qs.q: A nurse determines an apical pulse is indicated in which situations? Select all that apply.
c: The peripheral pulse is irregular
The client is receiving a medication that alters heart rate or rhythm
The client is an infant younger than 2 years
The client is an alert adult with a regular, strong radial pulse
The peripheral pulse is weak or very rapid
The client is in cardiac arrest and the nurse needs a quick check
qs.e: Apical pulse assessment is preferred when the peripheral pulse is irregular, weak, or very rapid, when giving rate- or rhythm-altering medications, and for children under 2. A routine adult with a regular pulse does not require apical assessment; during cardiac arrest the carotid (not apical) site is used.

qs.q: When using a portable Doppler ultrasound device to assess a peripheral pulse, the nurse performs which actions? Select all that apply.
c: Place conducting gel on the Doppler transducer probe
Hold the probe perpendicular to the skin
Count the heartbeat for 1 minute and note rhythm
Wipe excess gel off the client's skin after the assessment
Set the volume at high before applying the probe
Record the fact that the pulse was obtained with a Doppler ultrasound device
qs.e: Gel is applied to the probe, it is held perpendicular to the skin, counted for 1 minute, gel is wiped off, and documentation notes Doppler use. The volume should be set at low, not high, before turning on the device—so the 'high volume' choice is incorrect.

qs.q: The nurse includes which steps when assessing an apical pulse? Select all that apply.
c: Clean the diaphragm of the stethoscope with an alcohol swab
Warm the diaphragm by holding it against the palm
Place the diaphragm at the fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
Count each 'lub-dub' as one beat
Count the rate for 30 seconds and multiply by two
Note the rhythm of the beats
qs.e: These are the key steps from Guidelines 26-3. The apical pulse is counted for a full 1 minute, not 30 seconds doubled—halving the time risks missing irregularities.

qs.q: The nurse correctly identifies which definitions related to respiration? Select all that apply.
c: Ventilation is movement of gases in and out of the lungs
Diffusion is gas exchange between the alveoli and circulating blood
Perfusion is gas exchange between the blood and tissue cells
Ventilation has both autonomic and voluntary control
Diffusion is controlled solely by the autonomic nervous system
Perfusion occurs only in the lungs
qs.e: Ventilation, diffusion, and perfusion are defined exactly as described; ventilation has both autonomic and voluntary control unlike heart rate. Diffusion is not solely autonomic, and perfusion occurs between blood and tissue cells throughout the body, not only in the lungs.

qs.q: The nurse preparing to take an apical-radial pulse notes which correct elements? Select all that apply.
c: Two nurses are needed
Both nurses count for 1 full minute
One watch with a sweep second hand is used
The difference between the two rates is the pulse deficit
Only one nurse is needed if the client is cooperative
The radial pulse is counted by auscultation
qs.e: Guidelines 26-4 specify two nurses, one shared sweep-second-hand watch, a full 1-minute count by both, and the difference is the pulse deficit. One nurse cannot simultaneously auscultate and palpate; the radial pulse is assessed by palpation, not auscultation.

qs.q: The normal adult respiratory rate is ______ breaths/min.
qs.e: Normal adult respirations are 12-20 breaths/min and regular. A rate above 24 is tachypnea and below 10 is bradypnea.

qs.q: A respiratory rate below ______ breaths/min is classified as bradypnea.
qs.e: Bradypnea is defined as fewer than 10 breaths/min, typically from depression of the respiratory center. Tachypnea is greater than 24 breaths/min.

qs.q: Name the intercostal space where the apical pulse is located: the ______ intercostal space, left midclavicular line.
qs.e: The apical pulse is at the fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line. The second or third intercostal space at the left sternal border (Erb's point) is an alternative site, not the standard one.

qs.q: The most powerful respiratory stimulant is an increase in ______.
qs.e: An increase in carbon dioxide is the most powerful respiratory stimulant, causing increased respiratory depth and rate. Oxygen and other factors play a role but are not the most powerful stimulant described.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who receives an opioid analgesic and subsequently breathes at a rate of 8 breaths/min. Which term should the nurse use to document this finding?
c: Tachypnea
Bradypnea
Hyperventilation
Apnea
qs.e: Bradypnea is a respiratory rate of less than 10 breaths/min and is commonly caused by opioid depression of the respiratory rate and depth. Tachypnea is a rate greater than 24 breaths/min, and apnea means there is no breathing at all.

qs.q: Under normal conditions, a healthy adult breathes about how many times each minute? (enter the range)
qs.e: The normal adult respiratory rate is 12 to 20 breaths/min; infants and young children breathe more rapidly.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client whose respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min. Which conditions could contribute to this tachypnea? Select all that apply.
c: Fever
Hypoxia
Pain in the thoracic area
Increased metabolic rate
Opioid overdose
Deep restful sleep
qs.e: Tachypnea (>24 breaths/min) occurs with increased metabolic rate such as fever, with hypoxia, and with thoracic pain. Opioids depress the respiratory center and cause bradypnea/hypoventilation, not tachypnea.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with heart failure who has alternating periods of deep, rapid breathing followed by periods of apnea that occur at regular intervals. Which respiratory pattern should the nurse document?
c: Biot's respirations
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Kussmaul's respirations
Hypoventilation
qs.e: Cheyne-Stokes respirations are alternating periods of deep, rapid breathing and apnea that follow a regular pattern, and are associated with heart failure, drug overdose, increased intracranial pressure, and renal failure. Biot's respirations are irregular with varying depth and rate.

qs.q: Which findings are associated with Cheyne-Stokes respirations? Select all that apply.
c: Alternating periods of deep, rapid breathing followed by apnea
A regular pattern to the cycles
Heart failure
Increased intracranial pressure
Irregular breathing with varying depth and rate
Meningitis
qs.e: Cheyne-Stokes is a regular cycle of deep, rapid breathing and apnea linked to heart failure and increased intracranial pressure. Irregular varying depth/rate with apnea and meningitis describe Biot's respirations.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with meningitis who has respirations of varying depth and rate followed by periods of apnea, with an irregular rhythm. Which pattern does the nurse identify?
c: Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Biot's respirations
Bradypnea
Orthopnea
qs.e: Biot's respirations show varying depth and rate followed by apnea and an irregular rhythm, and are associated with meningitis and severe brain stem injury. Cheyne-Stokes cycles are regular and alternate deep rapid breathing with apnea.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with diabetic ketoacidosis who is breathing at an increased rate and depth. Which term describes this pattern?
c: Hypoventilation
Bradypnea
Hyperventilation (Kussmaul's respirations)
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
qs.e: Hyperventilation is an increase in both rate and depth and may result from metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis (Kussmaul's respirations). Hypoventilation is decreased rate and depth, not increased depth.

qs.q: Which conditions can cause hyperventilation (increased rate and depth)? Select all that apply.
c: Extreme exercise
Fear
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hypoxia
Opioid overdose
Heart failure
qs.e: Hyperventilation may result from extreme exercise, fear/anxiety, hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Opioid overdose depresses respirations and heart failure is associated with Cheyne-Stokes respirations.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client in the postanesthesia care unit who has a decreased respiratory rate and depth with an irregular rhythm after receiving an anesthetic and a narcotic. Which term describes this finding?
c: Hyperventilation
Hypoventilation
Tachypnea
Eupnea
qs.e: Hypoventilation is shallow, slow (decreased rate and depth), irregular breathing and may be related to sedation or overdose of narcotics or anesthetics. Hyperventilation is increased rate and depth, and eupnea is normal unlabored breathing.

qs.q: The nurse documents that a client has normal, unlabored respirations. What term is used for normal respiration?
qs.e: Normal, unlabored respiration is called eupnea. Tachypnea and dyspnea both describe abnormal breathing experiences or rates.

qs.q: Which methods does the nurse use to assess respirations (rate, depth, rhythm, and respiratory effectiveness)? Select all that apply.
c: Inspection (observing and listening)
Listening with a stethoscope
Pulse oximetry
Arterial blood gas monitoring
Measuring chest circumference with a tape measure
Palpating the trachea
qs.e: The nurse assesses respiratory rate, depth, and rhythm by inspection (observing and listening) or by listening with a stethoscope. Other methods of assessing respiratory effectiveness include using a pulse oximeter to determine oxygenation of the blood and monitoring arterial blood gas results. Measuring chest circumference and palpating the trachea are not described as assessment methods for respirations.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with COPD who becomes short of breath when lying flat and can breathe most comfortably while sitting upright. Which term describes this client's condition, and which position is best?
c: Dyspnea; supine with the head of the bed flat
Orthopnea; upright or sitting position
Apnea; prone position
Tachypnea; Trendelenburg position
qs.e: Orthopnea is shortness of breath when lying flat with easier breathing upright; gravity pulls abdominal organs away from the diaphragm, giving the lungs more room to expand. Apnea is absence of breathing, which is not the case here.

qs.q: Which conditions may be associated with orthopnea? Select all that apply.
c: Pulmonary edema
Heart disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Meningitis
Severe brain stem injury
Diabetic ketoacidosis
qs.e: Orthopnea may be associated with pulmonary edema, heart disease, and chronic respiratory diseases such as COPD. Meningitis and brain stem injury relate to Biot's respirations, and ketoacidosis relates to hyperventilation.

qs.q: A client reports shortness of breath, but the nurse measures a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min with regular rhythm. Which statement best guides the nurse's response?
c: The report can be disregarded because the rate is within normal limits
Dyspnea can be perceived only by the person experiencing it
Dyspnea is always accompanied by an irregular rhythm
Orthopnea is the same as dyspnea
qs.e: Dyspnea (difficult or labored breathing) is subjective and can be perceived only by the person experiencing it, so the client's report is meaningful even with a normal rate. A normal rate does not rule out difficult breathing.

qs.q: In healthy people, the relationship of one respiration to about every ______ heartbeats is fairly consistent.
qs.e: The normal relationship is 1 respiration to 4 heartbeats in healthy people. This ratio changes when either rate becomes abnormal, such as with fever or opioid depression.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client whose blood pressure is 156/92 mm Hg. Which explanation of the 92 mm Hg reading is correct?
c: The pressure during ventricular contraction
The pressure in the arteries when the heart rests between beats
The difference between systolic and diastolic pressures
The pressure generated by the aortic valve only
qs.e: Diastolic pressure is the lowest pressure on arterial walls while the heart rests between beats (ventricular diastole). The systolic pressure is created during ventricular contraction, and the difference between the two is the pulse pressure.

qs.q: A client's blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. What is the pulse pressure in mm Hg?
qs.e: Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure; 120 minus 80 equals 40 mm Hg. Confusing pulse pressure with mean arterial pressure is a common error.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing a client's blood pressure readings. Which reading meets the textbook definition of normal blood pressure?
c: 118/76 mm Hg
124/82 mm Hg
130/70 mm Hg
110/85 mm Hg
qs.e: Normal blood pressure is defined as systolic less than 120 mm Hg AND diastolic less than 80 mm Hg, so 118/76 qualifies. In 130/70 the systolic is not below 120, and in 110/85 the diastolic is not below 80.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client who becomes dizzy when rising from a lying to an upright position. Which normal cardiovascular response does the nurse expect?
c: Heart rate and peripheral vascular resistance increase
Heart rate decreases and blood vessels dilate
Baroreceptors send impulses to decrease heart rate
Blood pressure rises and baroreceptor stretch increases
qs.e: Rising to an upright position decreases baroreceptor stretch, so the cardiovascular center increases heart rate and peripheral vascular resistance to raise blood pressure. The opposite response would lower pressure further and worsen dizziness.

qs.q: Which are short-term mechanisms for blood pressure regulation (occurring over minutes or hours)? Select all that apply.
c: Neural mechanisms centered in the cardiovascular center of the brain
Humoral mechanisms involving body fluids and hormones
Release of epinephrine from the adrenal gland to increase heart rate and contractility
Vagus nerve stimulation, which slows the heart rate
Renal regulation of extracellular fluid volume as an ongoing equilibrium mechanism
Increased elasticity of arterioles with aging
qs.e: Short-term regulation is neural and humoral, including the cardiovascular center/vagus nerve and epinephrine release. Long-term regulation works through the kidneys and extracellular fluid volume, and aging arterioles become less elastic rather than more.

qs.q: A client's usual blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg. Today the reading is 138/88 mm Hg and the client feels fine. Which understanding is most important for the nurse?
c: The reading is significant because a rise or fall of 20 to 30 mm Hg is significant even if within the normal range
The reading is insignificant because it is within the generally accepted normal range
A single blood pressure measurement is always significant
Only diastolic changes matter clinically
qs.e: A rise or fall of 20 to 30 mm Hg from a person's baseline is significant even if the number falls within the generally accepted normal range. Individual baseline values matter, but a single elevated reading alone is not necessarily significant.

qs.q: Stroke volume and ______ determine cardiac output.
qs.e: Cardiac output is the product of stroke volume and heart rate. Cardiac output and peripheral resistance together determine systolic and diastolic pressures, so a distractor like 'blood pressure' confuses cause with effect.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for an adult client whose blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. According to Table 26-7, which category does this reading fall into?
c: Normal
Elevated
Hypertension Stage 1
Hypertensive crisis
qs.e: Elevated is systolic 120–129 AND diastolic <80 mm Hg. Normal requires systolic <120 AND diastolic <80, so a systolic of 128 rules out Normal.

qs.q: The nurse documents a blood pressure of 118/82 mm Hg for an adult client during a routine visit. Which classification is correct?
c: Normal
Elevated
Hypertension Stage 1
Hypertension Stage 2
qs.e: Stage 1 is systolic 130–139 OR diastolic 80–89; the diastolic of 82 meets the OR criteria even though the systolic is <120. Normal requires BOTH values to be <120 and <80.

qs.q: An adult client has a blood pressure of 135/78 mm Hg. The nurse classifies this reading as which category?
c: Normal
Elevated
Hypertension Stage 1
Hypertension Stage 2
qs.e: Stage 1 uses OR, so a systolic of 130–139 qualifies even when the diastolic is below 80. Elevated only covers systolic 120–129 with diastolic <80.

qs.q: A client's blood pressure is 186/118 mm Hg. Which category does the nurse assign to this reading?
c: Hypertension Stage 1
Hypertension Stage 2
Elevated
Hypertensive crisis
qs.e: Hypertensive crisis is systolic >180 and/or diastolic >120; the systolic of 186 alone meets the criteria. Stage 2 (≥140 and/or ≥90) does not capture the urgency of a crisis.

qs.q: A client tells the nurse, 'My blood pressure was 150/92 mm Hg today, so I definitely have hypertension.' Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
c: A single elevated measurement is not necessarily significant; diagnosis uses an average of two or more readings on two or more occasions.
You are correct—one reading of 140/90 or higher confirms the diagnosis.
Hypertension is only diagnosed when both the systolic and diastolic pressures are elevated.
Your reading is normal for someone your age, because blood pressure rises with age.
qs.e: A single elevated blood pressure measurement is not necessarily significant; the diagnosis is based on the average of two or more readings obtained on two or more occasions. Diagnosis also does NOT require both numbers to be high—systolic 130 or higher OR diastolic 80 or higher qualifies.

qs.q: The nurse is assisting a client to ambulate for the first time after several days of prolonged bed rest. Which action should the nurse perform FIRST?
c: Raise the head of the bed.
Assist the client directly from lying to standing.
Have the client walk quickly to build tolerance.
Encourage the client to dangle for 30 minutes before any other step.
qs.e: The source specifies the sequence: first raise the head of the bed, then assist the client to a sitting position on the side of the bed ('dangling') for a few minutes to assess for dizziness or faintness. Standing immediately risks orthostatic hypotension.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client with a blood pressure of 84/52 mm Hg. Which finding requires the nurse to communicate the assessment immediately?
c: Mild thirst
Syncope
Mild anxiety about a procedure
Mild hunger
qs.e: Symptoms of hypotension that warrant immediate communication include dizziness, tachycardia, pallor, syncope, increased sweating, blurred vision, nausea, and confusion. Syncope is on this list; the other options are not listed hypotension symptoms.

qs.q: The nurse is performing a clinical evaluation on an older adult client. Which assessment should the nurse include?
c: Orthostatic blood pressure measurements
Blood pressure measured only while the client is supine
Blood pressure monitoring only if the client reports dizziness
A single standing blood pressure at the end of the visit
qs.e: Orthostatic blood pressure measurements should be included in the clinical evaluation of ALL older adults, since aging is a risk factor and orthostatic hypotension increases fall risk. Waiting for symptoms misses asymptomatic cases.

qs.q: A client newly diagnosed with hypertension asks the nurse why the condition is called the 'silent killer.' Which explanation is most accurate?
c: There are often few symptoms beyond increased blood pressure.
It causes dramatic symptoms that clients routinely ignore.
It only affects clients who do not take their medications.
It cannot be controlled with current medications.
qs.e: Hypertension is called a 'silent killer' because there are often few symptoms beyond the increased blood pressure itself. The absence of symptoms does not mean the absence of risk for CVA, MI, or heart failure.

qs.q: A client who takes an oral contraceptive reports a slightly higher blood pressure at today's visit. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
c: Oral contraceptives cause a mild increase in blood pressure in many women.
Oral contraceptives always cause a dangerous increase in blood pressure.
Blood pressure only rises after eating, never because of medications.
Women usually have higher blood pressure than men of the same age.
qs.e: Box 26-5 states oral contraceptives cause a mild increase in BP in many women. The source also notes women usually have LOWER BP than men of the same age until menopause, contradicting the last option.

qs.q: The nurse teaches students about factors that contribute to blood pressure variations in healthy people (Box 26-5). Which factors cause the blood pressure to INCREASE? Select all that apply.
c: Emotional states such as anger, fear, excitement, and pain
Eating food
Exercise and strenuous activity
Prone or supine body position
Obesity
Rising in the morning
qs.e: Box 26-5 lists emotional states, food intake, exercise, and obesity as factors that raise BP. Blood pressure is LOWER in prone or supine position and is usually lowest on arising in the morning.

qs.q: The nurse teaches a client about risk factors for developing hypertension. Which are identified as risk factors in the source? Select all that apply.
c: Family history of hypertension
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sedentary lifestyle
High dietary intake of salt, fats, and calories
Regular physical activity
Increased fruit and vegetable intake
qs.e: Significant risks include family history, race, aging, obstructive sleep apnea, and metabolic disorders; lifestyle risks include sedentary lifestyle, excessive alcohol, and high dietary intake of salt, fats, and calories. Regular physical activity and increased fruits/vegetables are recommended changes, not risk factors.

qs.q: The nurse reviews antihypertensive medication categories with a student. Which pairings of drug class and action are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Diuretics — decrease fluid volume
ACE inhibitors — block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) — bind angiotensin II receptors to block vasoconstriction and aldosterone release
Beta-adrenergic blockers — increase cardiac output
Calcium channel blockers — relax smooth muscle of arterioles and decrease peripheral vascular resistance
Vasodilators — increase peripheral vascular resistance
qs.e: Beta-adrenergic blockers block sympathetic stimulation and DECREASE cardiac output; vasodilators and calcium channel blockers decrease (not increase) peripheral vascular resistance. The other pairings match the source.

qs.q: The nurse assesses a client with hypotension. Which findings must the nurse communicate immediately? Select all that apply.
c: Tachycardia
Syncope
Increased sweating
Confusion
Increased appetite
Warm, dry skin
qs.e: Symptoms of hypotension to communicate immediately include dizziness, tachycardia, pallor, syncope, increased sweating, blurred vision, nausea, and confusion. Increased appetite and warm, dry skin are not on this list.

qs.q: The nurse teaches lifestyle changes for a client with hypertension. Which interventions are recommended in the source? Select all that apply.
c: Weight loss for overweight or obese patients
Reduced sodium; diet low in saturated fat and total fat
Increased intake of fruits, vegetables, and grains
No more than two alcoholic drinks per day for women
Managing and coping with stress
No more than one alcoholic drink per day for men
qs.e: Alcohol limits are no more than two drinks/day for MEN and no more than one for WOMEN, so the male and female limits in the distractors are swapped. The other choices are recommended lifestyle changes.

qs.q: The nurse identifies factors that may cause or contribute to orthostatic hypotension. Select all that apply.
c: Dehydration
Blood loss
Use of certain classes of medications
Aging
Increased dietary sodium
Regular physical activity
qs.e: Orthostatic hypotension is caused by dehydration or blood loss, neurologic/cardiovascular/endocrine problems, and certain medications; aging is also a risk factor. Increased sodium and regular physical activity are not listed as causes.

qs.q: Classical orthostatic hypotension is a sustained decrease in systolic blood pressure of ≥______ mm Hg (or a decrease in diastolic blood pressure of ≥10 mm Hg) within 3 minutes of standing.
qs.e: Classical orthostatic hypotension uses a ≥20 mm Hg systolic drop (or ≥10 mm Hg diastolic) within 3 minutes of standing. Students often confuse this with the ≥40 mm Hg drop used for INITIAL orthostatic hypotension.

qs.q: Hypotension is defined as a blood pressure lower than ______.
qs.e: Hypotension is blood pressure lower than 90/60 mm Hg. It is not defined as 'below 120/80,' which would include normal readings.

qs.q: Screening for hypertension in children is recommended beginning at the age of ______ years.
qs.e: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends screening beginning at age 3 years; diagnosis requires auscultatory-confirmed readings ≥95th percentile on 3 different visits. False elevations can result from anxiety or caffeine.

qs.q: Initial orthostatic hypotension is a transient reduction in systolic blood pressure of ≥______ mm Hg (and/or transient diastolic decrease ≥20 mm Hg) within 15 seconds of standing.
qs.e: Initial orthostatic hypotension uses a transient systolic drop ≥40 mm Hg within 15 seconds of standing; classical orthostatic hypotension instead uses ≥20 mm Hg within 3 minutes. Do not mix the two thresholds.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to assess a client for orthostatic hypotension. After having the client lie supine for 5 minutes and obtaining initial blood pressure and pulse readings, what is the next step in the procedure?
c: Assist the client to a standing position immediately
Assist the client to sit on the side of the bed with legs dangling
Lower the head of the bed further
Repeat the blood pressure while the client remains supine
qs.e: The correct sequence is supine → dangling → standing. After the supine measurement, the client sits on the side of the bed with legs dangling for 1–3 minutes before any standing. Standing immediately skips the critical dangling phase where early symptoms may appear.

qs.q: A client becomes dizzy and lightheaded while dangling on the side of the bed during an orthostatic hypotension assessment. Which action should the nurse take?
c: Have the client stand to see if symptoms improve with activity
Return the client to bed immediately and place in a supine position
Take the blood pressure while the client is dangling and continue
Encourage the client to take deep breaths and remain sitting
qs.e: If symptoms of hypotension appear, the client should be returned to a supine position immediately, which restores blood flow to the brain. The nurse should NOT have the client stand if symptoms occur while sitting, as this could lead to a fall or syncope.

qs.q: The nurse is measuring a blood pressure on an obese client using a standard adult-sized cuff. The nurse understands that a cuff that is too narrow will most likely produce which result?
c: An erroneously low blood pressure reading
An erroneously high blood pressure reading
An accurate reading regardless of cuff size
An inability to detect any blood pressure
qs.e: A cuff that is too narrow does not evenly transmit pressure to the artery, resulting in an erroneously high reading. A too-wide cuff would produce the opposite error—an erroneously low reading—because pressure is dispersed over too large a surface area.

qs.q: A client scheduled for blood pressure measurement reports drinking two cups of coffee 15 minutes ago. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Proceed with the measurement and document the coffee intake
Wait 30 minutes after caffeine consumption before measuring
Have the client lie down for 5 minutes and then measure
Use an oscillometric device to eliminate the effect of caffeine
qs.e: The client should not have consumed caffeine, exercised, or smoked for 30 minutes before BP measurement to avoid inaccurate readings. Proceeding now risks an elevated reading; a change in position or device type does not eliminate caffeine's effect.

qs.q: While measuring a client's blood pressure, the nurse notices the client has crossed legs. What is the potential effect on the reading?
c: Systolic pressure may be decreased by up to 8 mm Hg
Systolic pressure may be increased by up to 8 mm Hg
Diastolic pressure may be decreased by up to 15 mm Hg
The reading will not be affected by leg position
qs.e: Crossing the legs can raise systolic BP by as much as 8 mm Hg and diastolic BP by as much as 5 mm Hg. Leg position does affect the reading; uncrossing the legs is a simple correction that prevents an inaccurately high measurement.

qs.q: During an orthostatic hypotension assessment, a client's supine blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and the standing blood pressure at 2 minutes is 92/62 mm Hg. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
c: The findings are normal and no further assessment is needed
The findings indicate significant orthostatic hypotension
The findings indicate a hypertensive crisis
The readings are within acceptable variability
qs.e: The systolic drop of 26 mm Hg (118→92) meets the ≥20 mm Hg criterion and the diastolic drop of 10 mm Hg (72→62) meets the ≥10 mm Hg criterion for significant orthostatic hypotension. A normal finding would show less than these threshold drops within 3 minutes of standing.

qs.q: A client with a known history of hypertension (supine systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg) is being assessed for orthostatic hypotension. A decrease of which amount in systolic blood pressure is significant in this population?
c: 10 mm Hg
20 mm Hg
30 mm Hg
50 mm Hg
qs.e: In patients with hypertension (supine systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg), a systolic drop of at least 30 mm Hg is the criterion for orthostatic hypotension. The standard ≥20 mm Hg criterion applies to non-hypertensive patients, not this population.

qs.q: The nurse is measuring blood pressure on a client who is sitting in a chair without back support. What is the potential effect on the reading?
c: Systolic pressure may increase by up to 15 mm Hg
Systolic pressure may decrease by up to 15 mm Hg
Diastolic pressure will be the only measurement affected
There is no significant effect on blood pressure
qs.e: Lack of back support can increase systolic readings by up to 15 mm Hg and diastolic readings by up to 6 mm Hg, producing an inaccurately high reading. The nurse must support the client's back to obtain an accurate measurement.

qs.q: During an orthostatic hypotension assessment, the client reports feeling faint while sitting on the edge of the bed with legs dangling. What should the nurse do next?
c: Proceed with standing and monitor closely
Return the client to a supine position and do not proceed to standing
Take another blood pressure reading while the client is sitting
Encourage the client to stand slowly and hold onto the bed
qs.e: If symptoms of hypotension occur when the patient is sitting, the nurse should NOT have the patient stand. Returning to supine restores cerebral blood flow and prevents syncope or falls. Standing with symptoms present is unsafe.

qs.q: After applying a blood pressure cuff to a client's arm, which finding indicates proper cuff tightness?
c: No fingers can fit under the cuff at the edges
One finger fits easily at the top and bottom, and two fingers fit but are very snug
Two fingers fit easily at the top and bottom of the cuff
The cuff is as tight as possible to ensure an accurate reading
qs.e: Proper cuff tightness allows one finger to fit easily at the top and bottom while two fingers fit but are very snug. Too tight or too loose leads to inaccurate readings; 'no fingers' indicates the cuff is excessively tight.

qs.q: The nurse is assessing a client for signs and symptoms of orthostatic hypotension. Which findings should the nurse monitor for? (Select all that apply.)
c: Dizziness
Lightheadedness
Pallor
Diaphoresis
Syncope
Tachycardia
qs.e: Dizziness, lightheadedness, pallor, diaphoresis, and syncope are the signs and symptoms of hypotension listed in the guidelines for monitoring during the procedure. Tachycardia is not listed in the source as a sign to monitor for during orthostatic assessment.

qs.q: A nurse is preparing to measure a client's blood pressure. Which actions are part of proper patient preparation? (Select all that apply.)
c: Ensure the client has not consumed caffeine, exercised, or smoked for 30 minutes
Have the client talk throughout the procedure for comfort
Support the client's feet and back
Position the arm at heart level
Allow the client to cross legs for comfort
Measure in a quiet environment
qs.e: Proper preparation includes avoiding caffeine/exercise/smoking for 30 minutes, supporting feet and back, positioning the arm at heart level, and using a quiet environment. The client should NOT talk during the procedure and legs should NOT be crossed, as both actions increase BP readings.

qs.q: Which methods of blood pressure measurement are described in the chapter? (Select all that apply.)
c: Auscultatory method using stethoscope and sphygmomanometer
Oscillometric (automated electronic) devices
Doppler ultrasound
Palpation
Direct arterial measurement
Infrared thermography
qs.e: The chapter describes auscultatory, oscillometric, Doppler, palpation, and direct arterial methods for blood pressure measurement. Infrared thermography is not mentioned as a BP measurement method; it relates to temperature assessment, not blood pressure.

qs.q: The nurse is educating a client about preventing orthostatic hypotension. Which interventions should be included? (Select all that apply.)
c: Rise and move about slowly, especially after bed rest
Dangle on the side of the bed before standing
Ensure adequate hydration
Use compression stockings or abdominal compression garments if prescribed
Take antihypertensive medications in the morning to control blood pressure
Stand up quickly to train the body to adjust
qs.e: Prevention includes rising slowly, dangling before standing, adequate hydration, and compression garments. Contributing medications such as antihypertensives should be administered at bedtime if possible, not in the morning. Standing up quickly is the opposite of safe practice and increases fall risk.

qs.q: Which statements about blood pressure cuff selection are correct? (Select all that apply.)
c: The cuff bladder length should be 75% to 100% of the arm circumference
The cuff width should be 37% to 50% of the arm circumference
A cuff that is too wide may produce an erroneously high reading
A cone-shaped cuff may be necessary for obese patients
The wrist should be used if a cuff cannot be fitted correctly
A length-to-width ratio of 1:2 is recommended
qs.e: Bladder length 75–100% and width 37–50% of arm circumference are correct. A too-WIDE cuff produces a falsely LOW reading (not high), and the recommended ratio is 2:1 (not 1:2). Cone-shaped cuffs and wrist cuffs are appropriate when arm cuffs do not fit.

qs.q: Which actions or conditions can cause an inaccurately high blood pressure reading? (Select all that apply.)
c: Crossing the legs during measurement
Not supporting the client's back
Using a cuff that is too narrow
Having the client talk during the procedure
Using a cuff that is too wide
Not supporting the arm at heart level
qs.e: Crossed legs, lack of back support, a too-narrow cuff, talking, and unsupported arm positioning all produce falsely HIGH readings. A too-WIDE cuff produces a falsely LOW reading, making it the incorrect choice here.

qs.q: The blood pressure cuff bladder length should be ___% to ___% of the patient's arm circumference.
qs.e: The cuff bladder length should encircle 75% to 100% of the arm circumference to ensure accurate pressure transmission to the artery. Deviating from this range leads to erroneous readings.

qs.q: During an orthostatic hypotension assessment, the patient should lie in a supine position for ___ to ___ minutes before the initial blood pressure and pulse measurements are taken.
qs.e: The guidelines specify 3 to 10 minutes of supine rest before obtaining the baseline measurement. This allows hemodynamics to stabilize before testing for positional changes.

qs.q: After the patient stands during an orthostatic hypotension assessment, the first blood pressure and pulse measurements are taken at ___ seconds.
qs.e: The first standing measurement is taken at 30 seconds, with additional measurements at 60 seconds, 2 minutes, and 3 minutes. The 30-second reading captures the immediate hemodynamic response to standing.

qs.q: The patient should not have consumed caffeine, exercised, or smoked for ___ minutes before blood pressure measurement.
qs.e: A 30-minute abstinence period from caffeine, exercise, and smoking is required before BP measurement to prevent artificially elevated readings. These activities stimulate the cardiovascular system and skew results.

qs.q: The nurse is measuring a client's blood pressure using the auscultatory method. Which technique during cuff deflation is correct?
c: Deflate the cuff at a rate of 2 to 3 mm Hg per second
Deflate the cuff as rapidly as possible to minimize client discomfort
Deflate the cuff at a rate of 10 to 15 mm Hg per second
Keep the cuff fully inflated for 2 minutes before releasing any air
qs.e: Deflation faster than 2 to 3 mm Hg per second is a listed source of error because sounds can be skipped and pressures misidentified. Rapid deflation feels faster for the nurse, but it produces inaccurate readings.

qs.q: The nurse obtains a blood pressure by auscultation. How should the measurement be documented?
c: To the nearest even number (nearest 2 mm Hg)
To the nearest odd number (nearest 1 mm Hg)
Rounded to the nearest 10 mm Hg
Exactly as the needle appears on the aneroid gauge, with no rounding
qs.e: Readings are read to the nearest even number (nearest 2 mm Hg) so documentation is consistent and reproducible. Rounding to 10 mm Hg discards clinically meaningful detail.

qs.q: While measuring the blood pressure of a client with hypertension, the nurse hears tapping sounds that become muffled, disappear briefly, and then reappear before all sounds finally cease. Which action is most important?
c: Recognize the auscultatory gap so that systolic pressure is not underestimated
Document the very first sound heard as systolic and move on to the next client
Record a low systolic and a high diastolic pressure as read and notify no one
Deflate the cuff more rapidly so the sounds cannot disappear
qs.e: The auscultatory gap (Phase II) may cover up to 40 mm Hg; failing to recognize it causes underestimation of systolic or overestimation of diastolic pressure. Rapid deflation is itself a listed source of error and would worsen the problem.

qs.q: A client's blood pressure sounds are indistinct with a stethoscope, so the nurse uses a Doppler ultrasound device. Which statement about this measurement is accurate?
c: Only an estimate of the systolic blood pressure is obtained
Both systolic and diastolic pressures are obtained and documented
An arterial catheter must be inserted before the device can be used
Korotkoff sounds are identified to determine the diastolic pressure
qs.e: The Doppler amplifies sound and is useful when sounds are indistinct, but it provides only an estimate of systolic pressure. An arterial catheter is direct (invasive) measurement, not Doppler.

qs.q: A client is scheduled for 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?
c: 'I can take a bath while wearing the monitor as long as I dry the cuff afterward.'
'I should keep the monitor on while I sleep, but avoid bathing and swimming.'
'The monitor records my pressure only while I am awake.'
'I should remove the monitor before going to bed each night.'
qs.e: ABPM is fully automated and records while the client is awake or asleep (readings every 20-30 minutes by day, every hour at night), but the client must avoid bathing and swimming. The device is not limited to waking hours.

qs.q: The nurse is observing a nursing student measure a client's blood pressure. Which action by the student requires follow-up?
c: The client is talking with the student during the measurement
The cuff bladder is centered over the artery with the artery marker aligned
The client rested in a chair before the measurement began
The gauge needle was checked to be at the zero mark before inflation
qs.e: Patient talking during measurement is an identified source of blood pressure error (Box 26-6). The other three actions reflect correct, error-reducing technique.

qs.q: A client has just walked briskly into the clinic exam room. Which action should the nurse take before measuring blood pressure?
c: Allow the client a rest period before taking the measurement
Measure immediately to capture the highest possible reading
Have the client walk a few more minutes to 'warm up' the arm
Measure the pressure with the client standing to save time
qs.e: Failure to allow a rest period prior to measurement is a listed source of error. Measuring right after activity or in a hurried position distorts the reading.

qs.q: A client in the intensive care unit has a thin catheter inserted into the radial artery connected to a monitor displaying a pressure waveform. The nurse identifies this as:
c: Direct (invasive) electronic blood pressure measurement (arterial line)
An oscillometric blood pressure monitor
An ambulatory blood pressure monitor
A Doppler ultrasound device
qs.e: An arterial line senses pressure directly at the catheter tip (most commonly radial or femoral artery) and displays systolic and diastolic values as a waveform; it is used primarily in intensive care. Oscillometric, ambulatory, and Doppler devices are all indirect methods.

qs.q: A student makes a statement about Korotkoff sounds. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?
c: 'Korotkoff sounds are heard only when a stethoscope is used to assess blood pressure.'
'The sounds occur as blood flow is reestablished while the cuff is gradually deflated.'
'The first sound heard represents the systolic pressure.'
'Korotkoff sounds are identified using an oscillometric monitor without a stethoscope.'
qs.e: Korotkoff sounds are audible only through a stethoscope with the auscultatory method; oscillometric devices analyze blood flow oscillations and do not require or produce Korotkoff sounds. The other statements match the text.
