qs.q: While measuring the blood pressure of a pregnant client, the nurse hears sounds all the way down to zero. Sounds begin at 112 mm Hg and muffle at 62 mm Hg. How should the nurse record the reading?
qs.e: When sounds persist to zero (e.g., pregnant clients, clients with arteriovenous fistulas), the recording includes Phase IV as 112/62/0. Recording 112/62 omits the documented convention for these clients.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing potential sources of error in blood pressure measurement. Select all that apply.
c: Use of a cuff of incorrect size
The client talking during the measurement
Deflation of the cuff faster than 2 to 3 mm Hg per second
Deflation of the cuff at 2 to 3 mm Hg per second
Use of a validated, calibrated device
Failure to allow for a rest period prior to measurement
qs.e: Box 26-6 lists incorrect cuff size, patient talking, deflation faster than 2-3 mm Hg/sec, and no rest period as error sources. Deflating at 2-3 mm Hg/sec and using a validated calibrated device are correct technique, not errors.

qs.q: Which statements about Korotkoff sounds (Table 26-9) are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Phase I is the first appearance of faint but clear tapping sounds; the first tapping sound is the systolic pressure
Phase II is characterized by muffled or swishing sounds that may temporarily disappear
Phase III is characterized by a distinct, abrupt muffling sound with a soft, blowing quality
Phase IV is characterized by a distinct, abrupt muffling sound with a soft, blowing quality
Phase V is characterized by distinct, loud sounds as blood flows relatively freely through the artery
The auscultatory gap may cover a range of as much as 40 mm Hg
qs.e: Phase III is the distinct, loud sounds; the abrupt muffling with a soft blowing quality is Phase IV. The gap occurs in Phase II and may span up to 40 mm Hg, so missing it produces serious measurement errors.

qs.q: Which findings are associated with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM)? Select all that apply.
c: A noninvasive, fully automated method of blood pressure measurement
Readings usually taken every 20 to 30 minutes during the day and every hour at night
Useful in confirming a diagnosis of hypertension and monitoring antihypertensive drug therapy
The client must avoid bathing and swimming while wearing the device
Provides only an estimate of systolic blood pressure
Requires insertion of a catheter into the radial or femoral artery
qs.e: ABPM is noninvasive and automated, records timed readings over ~24 hours, supports hypertension diagnosis and therapy monitoring, and requires water precautions. A systolic-only estimate describes the Doppler, and an arterial catheter describes direct measurement.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to assess blood pressure with a Doppler ultrasound device. Which actions are part of the procedure? Select all that apply.
c: Place a small amount of conducting gel on the Doppler transducer probe
After the pulse disappears, pump the cuff another 20 to 30 mm Hg
Wait at least 1 minute between repeat readings to allow normal circulation to return
Hold the device in the nondominant hand and move the probe so it is perpendicular to the skin
Allow clothing to remain between the cuff and the limb
Deflate the cuff as rapidly as possible once the pulse disappears
qs.e: Guidelines 26-6 include gel on the probe, inflating 20-30 mm Hg past pulse disappearance, waiting 1 minute between readings, and holding the probe perpendicular in the nondominant hand. Clothing under the cuff and rapid deflation are both listed error sources.

qs.q: Which statements about sites for assessing blood pressure are correct? Select all that apply.
c: The brachial artery and the popliteal artery are the most commonly used sites
The radial (forearm) site may be used with individuals who have very large upper arms or who are obese
Blood pressure may be obtained at the ankle in patients who cannot have it measured in their upper arms
The femoral artery is the most commonly used site for routine blood pressure measurement
The ankle site is used only when a Doppler device is available
The cuff should be wrapped loosely with clothing underneath to protect the skin
qs.e: Brachial and popliteal sites are most common, with radial/forearm and ankle alternatives for specific clients. The femoral artery is named as a site for direct A-line measurement, and clothing under the cuff is a listed error source.

qs.q: Which statements about the oscillometric method of blood pressure measurement are accurate? Select all that apply.
c: Devices can be set to take and record blood pressure readings at preset intervals
Calibration of devices at regular intervals, based on manufacturer guidelines, is recommended
Health care providers must ensure use of validated and calibrated devices
Many of these devices have integrated equipment such as a thermometer and pulse oximetry
A stethoscope is required to identify Korotkoff sounds with this method
This method reports only the diastolic pressure
qs.e: Oscillometric monitors analyze blood flow sounds or oscillations, can run on preset intervals, require validated/calibrated devices, and often include other vital sign equipment. Korotkoff sounds require the auscultatory method with a stethoscope.

qs.q: Korotkoff sounds are audible only when a ______ is used to assess blood pressure.
qs.e: These sounds accompany reestablished blood flow during cuff deflation and can only be heard through a stethoscope with the auscultatory method, not with an oscillometric monitor.

qs.q: Auscultatory blood pressure readings are recorded to the nearest ______ mm Hg (nearest even number).
qs.e: Reading to the nearest even number (2 mm Hg) keeps documentation consistent and reproducible. Rounding to a single odd digit or to 10 mm Hg is not the standard described.

qs.q: The Korotkoff sound phase characterized by the first appearance of faint but clear tapping sounds is Phase ______.
qs.e: Phase I's first tapping sound marks the systolic pressure; Phase V marks diastolic, so confusing the phases misassigns the blood pressure numbers.

qs.q: Retraining of health care professionals in accurate blood pressure measurement is recommended every ______.
qs.e: Periodic retraining (every 6 months to 1 year) supports measurement accuracy because inaccurate technique is common. Longer intervals allow technique drift and error.

cards.def: The study of how the body moves and aligns during activity; applies ergonomic principles to prevent musculoskeletal injury during everyday activities.
Optimal musculoskeletal balance and operation so that no undue strain is placed on the joints, muscles, tendons, or ligaments.

A state in which the center of gravity is close to its base of support and the object has a wide base of support. Body balance increases when people spread the feet apart and flex the hips and knees, decreasing musculoskeletal strain.
The point of the body or an object where mass is concentrated; keeping it close to the base of support maintains balance and reduces strain.
The area beneath an object or person (formed by the feet) that determines stability; widening it increases balance.
Muscles working together for purposeful movement, using major and stronger muscle groups.
Reflexes that maintain body position and equilibrium during rest or movement; include sensory organs in the inner ear, vision, and autonomic contractions.
Self-care activities that maintain quality of life, such as eating, bathing, dressing, and toileting.
Movement and alignment change from infant through older adult; nurses promote neuromuscular development and facilitate each patient's use of the body to perform self-care activities.

Postural abnormalities (hip dysplasia, torticollis, scoliosis), bone/muscle disorders (dwarfism, osteoporosis, muscular dystrophy), joint/bone mobility issues (arthritis, trauma), and CNS disorders (stroke, spinal cord injury) affect movement.
Depression affects activity level, posture, and energy for ADLs; lifestyle factors include diet, sedentary vs active habits, smoking, and cultural values regarding movement and exercise.
The practice of designing equipment and work tasks to conform to the capability of the worker; provides a means for adjusting the work environment and work practices to prevent injuries.

Applying ergonomics to patient care; proper body movement during all everyday activities (moving a medication cart, pushing a bed, reaching to silence an alarm) helps develop good musculoskeletal habits.
Develop a habit of erect posture with correct alignment; listed first among the applications of ergonomics to prevent injury.
Use the longest and strongest muscles of arms and legs for maximum power; back muscles are weaker and prone to injury when used improperly.
Engage core muscles to stabilize the pelvis and protect the abdomen; contract the gluteal muscles downward and the abdominal muscles upward.
Work as closely to an object as possible to keep the body's center of gravity close to the object being moved, permitting most of the burden to be borne by the legs and arms rather than the back.
Face the direction of your movement; do not twist your body.
Push rather than pull when possible; keep arms close and push with your whole body.
Spread feet shoulder width apart and flex the knees to broaden the base of support.

Assess the patient's ability to assist with planned movement: ability to understand instruction and cooperate, medical diagnosis and health issues, movement capabilities, apply braces/devices, and encourage the patient to assist within capabilities to promote independence.
Ensure enough staff are available to safely move the patient; assess the area for clutter, accessibility, and availability of devices, removing any obstacles or barriers.

cards.term: Safe handling Steps 4–6: Screening, equipment, planning
cards.def: Use a screening or assessment tool; decide which equipment to use; plan carefully and communicate to care team members and the patient.

cards.term: Safe handling Steps 7–9: Pain, bed, wheels
cards.def: Administer prescribed analgesic if the patient is in pain prior to movement; elevate the bed as necessary; lock wheels.
Ensure patient safety during transfer: avoid friction on skin, support the body properly (good alignment, avoid grabbing), and move in a smooth, rhythmic motion.

Causes include uncoordinated lifts, high exertion in awkward positions, manual lifting without assistive devices, repetitive movements, lifting while fatigued, standing for long periods, and transferring/repositioning dependent, cognitively impaired, or obese patients who cannot actively participate.
A device placed under a patient to reduce friction and ease movement during repositioning or transfers.
A belt secured around a patient's waist to assist with standing and ambulation, giving the nurse a safe grasp point.
A device used to help move a patient laterally (side to side) in bed or between surfaces with less effort and risk.
A mechanical lifting device that supports the patient's full body weight to transfer safely between bed, chair, or other surfaces.
A device that helps a patient move from sitting to standing, reducing the effort required by the nurse.
Skills practiced include turning the patient in bed, moving a patient up in bed, moving from bed to gurney, moving from bed to chair, dangling a patient, and ambulating a patient.
Basic self-care activities such as eating, bathing, dressing, and toileting. Health problems can interfere with a patient's ability to move purposefully to perform ADLs.
More complex self-care activities such as housekeeping, meal preparation, management of finances, and transportation. Assessment includes the patient's ability to perform both ADLs and IADLs.

Age and degree of neuromuscular development markedly influence body proportions, posture, body mass, movements, and reflexes. By 5 months head control is usually achieved; 6–9 months: sits steadily, rolls over, creeps, pulls to standing; 9–12 months: progresses toward unassisted walking and picks up small objects.

Gross and fine motor development continues rapidly: by 15 months most walk unassisted; at 18 months most run; at 2 years most jump; at 3 years most stack blocks, work simple puzzles, and dress themselves.

By age 4 the child can negotiate stairs, walk backward, and hop on one foot; by age 5 the child can skip, jump rope, and jump off heights of several steps. The child is also able to manipulate writing materials (listed as a separate Child milestone in the table, not tied to a specific age).

Adolescence brings a growth spurt and appearance of secondary sex characteristics. Nurses assess activity level, safety of recreational choices, muscle mass/tone/strength and joint mobility, and screen for scoliosis (lateral curvature of the spine).

cards.term: Pregnancy: shift in center of gravity
cards.def: During pregnancy the center of gravity shifts because of the developing fetus, affecting body alignment and movement; adults otherwise stand and sit erect with balanced, coordinated purposeful movement.

A good lifting position uses the long and strong muscles of the arms and legs and holds the object so the line of gravity falls within the base of support. Incorrect lifting pulls on the back muscles and leaning causes the line of gravity to fall outside the base.

Begin activities by broadening your base of support; spread the feet to shoulder width. Use the weight of the body to push an object by falling or rocking forward and to pull an object by falling or rocking backward.

Make sure the surface is dry and smooth when moving an object to decrease the effects of friction. Rough, wet, or soiled surfaces increase friction and the amount of effort required to move an object.

cards.term: Lifting technique: flex knees & internal girdle
cards.def: Flex the knees, put on the internal girdle, and come down close to an object that is to be lifted. Break up heavy loads into smaller loads and take breaks from lifting or moving to relax and recover.

cards.term: Guidelines for moving and lifting patients
cards.def: Assess the patient (diagnosis, capabilities, restrictions; apply braces/devices first); assess ability to assist and to understand instructions; ensure enough staff are present; clear the area of clutter and have devices available; use a standardized screening/assessment tool for SPHM decisions.

cards.term: Safe handling of patients with dementia (positive instructions)
cards.def: Face the patient, speak slowly with clear short sentences, call the patient by name, allow time for response, and give simple one-step instructions. Phrase instructions positively (e.g., "Stand up" rather than "Don't sit down"), as the patient may not register "don't" and will try to sit too early.

The semi-sitting position calls for the head of the bed to be elevated 45 to 60 degrees. It is used to promote cardiac and respiratory functioning because abdominal organs drop, providing maximal space in the thoracic cavity; the buttocks bear the main body weight and the heels, sacrum, and scapulae are at risk for skin breakdown.

A variation of Fowler's position in which the head of the bed is elevated 90 degrees. A bedside table with a pillow allows the patient to lean forward with arms resting on the pillow, a posture that allows for maximal lung expansion.

A variation of Fowler's position in which the head of the bed is elevated only 30 degrees. The semi-Fowler's (semi-reclining) position should be avoided in patients at risk for alterations in skin integrity; raising the head of the bed even a few centimeters increases the shearing force over the sacral area.

The patient lies flat on the back with the head and shoulders slightly elevated with a pillow unless contraindicated, such as spinal anesthesia or surgery on the spinal vertebrae. Preventive actions (Table 34-6) include a firm supportive mattress/bed board and pillows under shoulders, neck, and head for correct alignment.

The patient lies on the side and the main weight of the body is borne by the lateral aspect of the lower scapula and the lateral aspect of the lower ilium. It relieves pressure on the scapulae, sacrum, and heels and allows the legs and feet to be flexed, but support pillows are needed for correct positioning.

The patient turns toward the side with the hip of the top leg flexed at a 30-degree angle (instead of 90 degrees) and the knee flexed at 35 degrees, with the calf of the upper leg positioned slightly behind the body's midline. This places significantly less pressure on the trochanter and sacrococcygeal areas.

A variation of the lateral position in which the lower arm is behind the patient and the upper arm is flexed at both the shoulder and the elbow. The main body weight is borne by the anterior aspects of the humerus, clavicle, and ilium, so the major pressure points differ from other bed-lying positions.

The person lies on the abdomen with the head turned to the side and the body straight; periodic use on bed rest helps prevent flexion contractures of the hips and knees. Gravity produces marked lordosis of the lumbar spine, so it is contraindicated for people with spinal problems, and the feet must be positioned carefully to avoid plantar flexion.

Skeletal muscles produce movements by pulling on bones; bones serve as levers, and joints act as fulcrums for the levers. This principle is illustrated by the movement of the forearm lifting a weight.

cards.term: Base of Support and Line of Gravity
cards.def: Balance is determined by whether the line of gravity passes through the base of support; a wider base with the line of gravity passing through it gives the greatest stability. When the line of gravity does not pass through the base of support, the person is unstable.

cards.term: Graduated Compression Stockings & Pneumatic Compression Devices
cards.def: Passive mechanical interventions prescribed to aid in the prevention of venous stasis, thrombophlebitis, and venous thrombosis of immobility. These mechanical methods of prophylaxis may be used alone or with pharmacologic prophylaxis for venous thromboembolism (VTE).

The frequency of repositioning/turning should be evaluated and reevaluated and tailored to the specific needs of the individual patient based on the patient's unique responses to care. When the patient cannot change position independently, use a repositioning schedule to assist with and document the rotation of positions.

A standardized tool used to aid in patient assessment and decision making regarding safe patient handling and mobility; it supports consistency and appropriate use of SPHM equipment to assist patients with the appropriate level of mobility. Obstacles that make moving and lifting inconvenient should be removed.

In Fowler's and supine positions, support the feet in dorsal flexion using a footboard or high-top sneakers to prevent footdrop. Use a trochanter roll alongside the hips and upper thighs to prevent external rotation of the femurs/hips.
The process of exchanging information and generating and transmitting meanings between two or more people.
Initiates information in the communication process.
Actual communication product from the source; can be visual, auditory, or kinesthetic.
How the information is sent (audio, visual, kinesthetic).
Person to whom the message is sent in the communication process.
Response the receiver sends back to the sender in the communication process.
Spoken communication reliant on language.
Body language including touch, eye contact, facial expressions, posture, gait, gestures, physical appearance, dress/grooming, sounds, and silence.
If the verbal and non-verbal messages conflict, the non-verbal message is believed.
Self-talk with oneself; can be very damaging.
Communication with two or more people.
Involves small-group and organizational communication with group dynamics, group identity, cohesiveness, patterns of interaction, decision making, responsibility, leadership, and power.

Developmental level, gender, sociocultural differences, space and territory, roles and relationships, occupations/hobbies (can impact communication preference), physical/mental/emotional state, values, environment, and trust.
Head, mouth, feet, face, neck, front of body, and genitalia are considered private zones in space and territory.
Mutual exchange between two people that occurs spontaneously; needs of both friends are heard and considered with no time limits and equally shared information.
Exists among people who provide and receive assistance in meeting human needs; is goal-directed, has a definitive conclusion, and involves unequal sharing of information.
A helping relationship consists of three phases; it occurs for a specific purpose/goal (goal-directed) and has a definitive conclusion. (The slide text does not name the individual phases.)
Warmth and friendliness, openness, respect, empathy, honesty, authenticity, trustworthiness, caring, and competence are dispositional traits for therapeutic relationships.
Trying to see things from the patient's point of view.
Shifts the perspective away from the patient to the nurse; the nurse shares feelings and personal concerns which are then projected onto the patient.
Tone of voice, flexible with discussion, be clear, avoid confusing words, truthful, open mind, and look for openings.
Sit, be alert, relaxed, natural, and use eye contact if appropriate.
Allow the client to speak freely; when a patient is silent, allow time to think and explore inner thoughts.
Hand on the shoulder or hand is acceptable; anything more requires asking for consent.
Assess the situation and use humor appropriately.
Questions that allow expansive answers, e.g., 'What did you have for lunch today?' 'How are you feeling right now?'
Questions to check understanding or confirm feelings, e.g., 'Are you having pain right now?' 'You seem upset, can we talk about it?'
Questions to confirm or expand on what was said, e.g., 'You mentioned a history of trauma, can you elaborate on that?' 'Did I understand you correctly?'
Focus on feelings; state observed behaviors, reflect/restate/rephrase what the patient said, and provide neutral responses, e.g., 'It sounds like you're frustrated about your health right now.'
Encourage the patient to talk more, e.g., 'Let's talk about it.' 'What is going on in your life that is stressful?'

Techniques to avoid include forgetting they are human, closed-ended questions, failure to listen, leading questions, giving advice, changing the subject, talking about yourself, telling the patient they are wrong, false reassurance, cliches, giving approval, asking why, and defending other health care team members.
An inappropriate technique, e.g., 'I am sure everything will be fine. You have nothing to worry about.'
Non-therapeutic technique that suggests a desired answer, e.g., 'You're not really sad, right?'
Non-therapeutic technique using meaningless comforting phrases, e.g., 'Everything happens for a reason.'
Nursing communication tool standing for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; used to improve effectiveness of communication in hand-off and nurse-to-provider discussions.
Situation → Background → Assessment → Recommendation.
Communication is directly linked to establishing and sustaining a healthy work environment; provides safety and quality care.
Nurse responses that use patient-centered techniques (empathy, respect, assigned therapeutic technique) to support the patient and facilitate understanding.
Nurse responses that demonstrate a communication barrier (e.g., arguing, judgment), which escalate or shut down the interaction.
Four roles are assigned: patient (acts out the situation with cues), therapeutic nurse, nontherapeutic nurse, and narrator (introduces each approach and explains the difference).
Introduces the setting and patient's concern, briefly explains that two different nursing responses will be demonstrated, then explains and wraps up why one response is therapeutic.
Uses the patient statement from the assigned scenario and adds realistic emotions, body language, and follow-up lines.
Uses the assigned therapeutic technique and responds with empathy, respect, and patient-centered language.
Demonstrates the assigned communication barrier realistically (not cruelly or theatrically).
A fifth role added in the single group of 5 when 82 students are divided into 20 groups of 4 plus 1 group of 5.
20 groups of 4 = 80 students, plus 1 group of 5 = 82 students total; roles should be rotated if time allows.
Group preparation: 8–10 minutes; skits: 2–3 minutes each; debrief: 1 minute per skit.
Sequence: (1) narrator sets the scene, (2) patient gives opening and cues, (3) therapeutic nurse responds, (4) nontherapeutic nurse demonstrates the barrier, (5) narrator explains and wraps up.
Include words, tone, facial expression, and body language showing how the patient responds to each nurse.
Confirm: both nurses responded to the same patient concern; assigned techniques are clear; scene is realistic and respectful; narrator explains why responses differ.
Therapeutic technique that acknowledges the patient's frustration and invites the patient to explain the main concern (Scenario 1).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse escalates the interaction with a defensive or confrontational tone (Scenario 1).
Therapeutic technique kept gentle, patient-led, and paired with a real answer to the concern (Scenario 2).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse debates the patient's fear or tells the patient there is no reason to be afraid (Scenario 2).
Therapeutic technique that invites the patient to say more about what a statement (e.g., 'no point') means to them (Scenario 3).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse looks distracted, changes the subject, or responds without attending to the concern (Scenario 3).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse asks 'Why weren't you listening?' or otherwise implies blame (Scenario 4).
Therapeutic technique that acknowledges the fear, explains what the team can do, and offers to find answers to specific questions (Scenario 5).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse guarantees that nothing bad will happen (Scenario 5).
Therapeutic technique: listen without interrupting and reflect the burden the patient describes (Scenario 6).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse makes critical or evaluative remarks toward the patient (Scenario 6).
If the patient reports new or worsening symptoms, the nurse should assess and escalate them rather than treating the issue as only a complaint.
Humor is not appropriate for every patient; if the patient does not respond positively, stop and use another supportive approach.

Hopelessness may signal a safety concern; the nurse should listen directly and assess for thoughts of self-harm or suicide when indicated, following clinical protocol and notifying the appropriate team.

cards.term: Clinical note — scope and plain language
cards.def: Explain within the nurse's role, use plain language, and contact the provider for questions that require medical clarification.

cards.term: Clinical note — do not promise outcomes
cards.def: Do not promise an outcome; refer procedure-specific questions to the appropriate member of the surgical team.
Realistic emotional tone and body language (e.g., 'Speak sharply, glance toward the desk, and interrupt once') that make the scenario believable and indicate the patient's state.
After each skit (about 1 minute), the narrator states the technique demonstrated, what the therapeutic nurse did well, and what the nontherapeutic nurse could do differently.
Clinical note: Explore barriers such as cost, side effects, routines, and food access before discussing options with the care team.
Therapeutic technique used with a grieving family member; ask what support would feel helpful and whether spiritual or cultural practices matter to the family.
Nontherapeutic stock phrases such as 'Everything happens for a reason' that dismiss the person's grief.

cards.term: Do not assume beliefs or rush grief
cards.def: Clinical note: Do not assume the person's beliefs or try to make grief feel better immediately.
Therapeutic technique for a newly confused patient: introduce yourself, calmly state where the patient is and why, and offer a simple next step.
Nontherapeutic response telling the confused patient they are being silly or have nothing to worry about.
Clinical note: New confusion after a procedure requires assessment and prompt reporting; do not assume it is a normal part of aging. Protect the patient from falls.
Therapeutic technique of reflecting the central feeling or meaning back to the patient and allowing them to respond; used with an isolated adolescent.
Nontherapeutic behavior: sighing, checking a phone, looking at the clock, or appearing uninterested during conversation.
Clinical note: Maintain privacy and speak respectfully with adolescents; do not dismiss concerns as 'teen drama.'
Therapeutic technique to clarify what the patient means by 'not worth it' and what matters most to them; used when a patient is considering refusing treatment.
Nontherapeutic response in which the nurse scolds, shames, or implies the patient is giving up by refusing treatment.
Clinical note: Do not pressure the patient; communicate concerns and questions to the oncology team when a patient considers refusing treatment.
Therapeutic technique that recognizes the difficulty of a transition and validates the feeling without judging the person's ability; used with an overwhelmed new parent.
Nontherapeutic response of immediately telling the person what they should do without first listening.

cards.term: Respond to safety concerns and escalate
cards.def: Clinical note: If a parent describes feeling unsafe, unable to care for themselves or the baby, or having thoughts of harm, respond seriously and follow the appropriate assessment and escalation process.
Therapeutic technique: ask a neutral question about pain—its location, severity, timing, or effect on movement.
Nontherapeutic question that suggests the expected answer, such as 'It's not that bad, is it?'

cards.term: Assess pain; do not assume expected complication
cards.def: Clinical note: Assess pain and associated symptoms, follow the care plan, and report concerning changes. Do not assume pain is an expected complication.
Therapeutic technique that acknowledges the hurt and embarrassment without judging appearance; used with a teenager with body image concerns.
Nontherapeutic rapid questioning of personal topics that feels prying before establishing trust.

cards.term: Eating changes and body dissatisfaction warrant follow-up
cards.def: Clinical note: Eating changes and intense body dissatisfaction warrant sensitive follow-up and appropriate assessment; do not reinforce weight stigma or offer appearance-based reassurance.
Therapeutic technique: ask before offering a hand or other appropriate touch, respect the patient's response, and stay present; used with a seriously ill patient afraid of dying.
Nontherapeutic response in which the nurse shifts attention away from the patient by sharing a story about their own experience.
Clinical note: Respect consent, culture, trauma history, and the patient's cues regarding touch; presence and listening are alternatives.
Therapeutic technique: describe the specific behavior (e.g., grimacing, guarding an incision) without accusing the patient of dishonesty, then invite them to explain.
Nontherapeutic behavior of accepting a pain number without further assessment or ignoring behavior that contradicts the self-report.

cards.term: Do not infer pain solely from appearance
cards.def: Clinical note: Do not infer pain solely from appearance or stereotype how a person should express it. Respect self-report and assess further using an open, culturally responsive approach.
Therapeutic technique: ask what name and pronouns the patient uses, use them consistently, and acknowledge the concern; used with a transgender patient.
Nontherapeutic response that dismisses the patient's identity request, argues, or treats identity as irrelevant to respectful care.
Clinical note: Protect privacy and follow applicable documentation and care policies. Do not make the patient responsible for educating the entire team.
Each scenario pairs one therapeutic technique to demonstrate with one nontherapeutic technique to avoid, illustrating the contrast in nurse responses.

Scenarios cover a patient struggling with chronic illness adherence, grieving families, confused elderly patients, isolated adolescents, treatment refusal, new parents, postoperative pain (including a mismatch between the pain rating and the patient's behavior), body image concerns, dying patients, transgender patients, and parents of chronically ill children—each requiring adapted communication.

cards.term: Parent of a chronically ill child
cards.def: Scenario 17 (clinic visit after another hospitalization): a parent expresses distress—"It's not fair that my child has to go through all this." The provided source excerpt ends mid-statement, so the therapeutic and nontherapeutic techniques for this scenario are not specified and should not be assumed from the source.
Allow a brief, attentive silence without rushing to fill it; then follow the parent's lead.
Silence should communicate presence, not withdrawal. Stay attentive and offer support when the parent is ready.
After the pause, the nurse follows the parent's lead rather than steering the conversation away from the emotion.
Relying only on a yes-or-no question cuts off the emotion with a closed question that limits expression.
Work together to identify the immediate concern and realistic next steps, rather than taking over or blaming.
Nontherapeutic problem-solving takes over for the student or assigns blame instead of identifying realistic next steps together.
Discussing the student's situation with others unnecessarily or spreading assumptions is a nontherapeutic response.
Respect confidentiality and clarify when information must be shared for safety or academic support.
Offer time to practice, review the steps together, and identify what the parent wants to work on first.
The nontherapeutic nurse appears rushed, distracted, dismissive, or unprepared.
Use teach-back and supervised return demonstration as appropriate to confirm understanding of instructions.
Use supervised return demonstration as appropriate; the parent practices the skill with the nurse observing.
Never imply that the parent should administer medication without adequate instruction and demonstrated understanding.
Discharge teaching after a child's new diabetes diagnosis addresses the parent's fear of making a mistake with insulin and the volume of steps to remember.
Arrange a qualified medical interpreter for the patient with limited English proficiency when explaining medication and discharge instructions.
Speak directly to the patient in short segments, and pause for interpretation.
The patient speaks limited English, nods politely, but cannot explain when or how to take the medication.
The nontherapeutic nurse raises their voice, relies on gestures alone for complex information, or treats nodding as proof of understanding.
Treating polite nodding as proof of understanding is nontherapeutic; the patient must be able to explain when and how to take the medication.
Do not rely on a child or unqualified bystander to interpret important clinical information when qualified interpretation is available.
Follow organizational policy for interpretation and for applicable documentation and care policies.
Follow applicable documentation and care policies. Do not make the patient responsible for educating the entire team.
After each skit: (1) What did the therapeutic nurse do or say? (2) How did the patient respond? (3) What made the nontherapeutic response ineffective? (4) What could the nurse try next?
Respect the patient's dignity and choices in all communication.
Use plain language and listen before advising.
Notice verbal and nonverbal cues without making assumptions.
Escalate clinical or safety concerns appropriately.

A communication practice exercise in which a scenario, patient acting cues, therapeutic technique, and nontherapeutic counterpart are demonstrated and compared; it is not a substitute for formal support.
Involves a source (encoder), message, channel, and receiver (decoder). The process is initiated based on a stimulus, such as a patient need that must be addressed.
A person or group who initiates or begins the communication process. The source encodes the message to be transmitted.
A communication channel using spoken words and cues. Nurses use this channel to communicate with patients and other health care providers.
A communication channel using sight, observations, and perception. Nurses use this channel to communicate with patients and other health care providers.
A communication channel using touch. Nurses use this channel to communicate with patients and other health care providers.

Factors that distort the quality of a message; can interfere with communication at any point in the process. These distractors might be from the television, or from pain or discomfort experienced by the patient.

Nurses must be as proficient in communication skills as they are in clinical skills. Effective communication supports collaborative relationships and continuous improvement in patient safety and quality of care.

A reciprocal process in which both the sender and the receiver of messages participate simultaneously; messages may be influenced by previous knowledge, past experiences, feelings, or sociocultural level.

When verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, behaviors can negate a verbal message and the listener will believe the nonverbal message; nonverbal communication often conveys the speaker's actual meaning.

Visual (sight) receives and interprets visual stimuli through observation and perception; Auditory (hearing) receives and interprets auditory stimuli through listening; Kinesthetic (touch) includes procedural touch (performing nursing procedures and techniques) and caring touch (conveying emotional support).

A very personal behavior and one of the most effective nonverbal ways to express feelings of comfort, love, affection, security, anger, frustration, aggression, and excitement; shaped by familial, regional, class, and cultural influences.

Communication often begins with eye contact; in many cultures it suggests respect and a willingness to keep communication open. Its absence often indicates anxiety, defenselessness, or avoidance of communication.
The face is the most expressive part of the body, conveying anger, joy, suspicion, sadness, fear, and contempt; nurses need to learn to control their own facial expressions.
The way a person holds the body carries nonverbal messages; good alignment usually reflects health and a positive attitude, while a rigid, stiff appearance might indicate tension and pain.
Movements using various parts of the body that carry numerous messages (e.g., thumbs up = victory, wringing hands = anxiety); gestures may have different meanings in different cultures.
A bouncy, purposeful walk usually carries a message of well-being, whereas a less purposeful, shuffling gait often means the person is sad or discouraged; certain gaits are associated with illness.
Speak in a normal tone of voice; explain the reason for touching the patient before doing so; indicate when the conversation has ended and when you are leaving the room.
Keep a call light or bell within easy reach. Orient the patient to the sounds in the environment and to the arrangement of the room and its furnishings.
A visually impaired patient will be unable to pick up most nonverbal cues during communication. Be sure the patient's eyeglasses are clean and intact or that contacts are in place.

cards.term: Deaf/Hard of Hearing – Orient Before Speaking
cards.def: Orient the patient to your presence before initiating conversation. This may be done by gently touching the patient or moving so that you can be seen.

cards.term: Deaf/Hard of Hearing – Facing the Patient
cards.def: Talk directly to the patient while facing them. If the patient can lip read, use simple sentences and speak in a quiet, natural manner and pace.
Do not chew gum or cover your mouth when talking with the patient. Demonstrate or pantomime ideas as appropriate; use sign language or finger spelling as appropriate.

cards.term: Deaf/Hard of Hearing – Writing & Hearing Aids
cards.def: Write any ideas that you cannot convey to the patient in another manner. Be sure that hearing aids are clean, functioning, and inserted properly.
Select one or more simple means of communication the patient can physically use: eye blinks or hand squeezes (yes/no); writing pads or magic slates; communication boards; flash cards; sign language.
Be sure that everyone communicating with the patient—family, friends, and caregivers—understands and is able to use the communication devices selected.

Demonstrate patience with the time needed to communicate effectively and reinforce the patient's efforts. Ensure the patient has an effective means of signaling need for assistance, such as a call bell or alarm.

Crying, moaning, gasping, and sighing are oral but nonverbal forms of communication that can be interpreted in numerous ways. Gasping often indicates fear, pain, or surprise; a sigh might signal reluctant agreement or relief.
Periods of silence during a conversation often carry important nonverbal messages, indicating complete understanding, that both parties are thinking, or that they are angry with each other.

Web-based technologies that allow users to create, share, and participate in dialogue in virtual communities and networks. Nurses must adhere to HIPAA regulations and employers' policies; describing a patient by room number or diagnosis is still a breach of confidentiality.

Six principles for nurses: (1) do not transmit or place online individually identifiable patient information, (2) observe ethically prescribed professional patient–nurse boundaries, (3) understand that patients, colleagues, institutions, and employers may view postings, (4) take advantage of privacy settings and seek to separate personal and professional information online, (5) bring content that could harm a patient's privacy, rights, or welfare to the attention of appropriate authorities, (6) participate in developing institutional policies governing online conduct.

Efficient means to communicate with staff and patients; risk for violating privacy exists any time a message is sent electronically. Messages should be concise, avoid text abbreviations, and any e-mails to a patient must become part of the health record.

Use of telecommunications and virtual technology to deliver health care services and health-related information outside traditional facilities. Nurses should dress professionally, decrease distractors, ensure privacy, and use nonverbal cues (leaning in, nodding, eye contact) to communicate interest and empathy.
Nurses engage in four levels during practice: intrapersonal, interpersonal, small-group, and organizational communication.

Communication occurring when nurses interact with two or more people (e.g., staff meetings, patient care conferences, teaching sessions, support groups). The more people involved, the more complex the process becomes.

Communication occurring when people and groups within an organization communicate to achieve established goals, such as a practice council reviewing unit policies or interdisciplinary groups working on strategic planning.
How individual group members relate to one another during interaction; studied to determine the effectiveness or ineffectiveness of a group.

Effective groups show clear group identity, high cohesiveness, honest two-way communication, resolved problems, shared leadership, and appropriate use of power. Ineffective groups lack commitment, have one-way or sparing communication, allow problems to build, and use authority-based leadership.

The common lifestyles, languages, behavior patterns, traditions, and beliefs that are learned and passed from one generation to the next. Understanding a patient's culture helps you understand nonverbal communication and deliver appropriate care.

Requires becoming aware of your own personal cultural beliefs and identifying prejudices or attitudes that could affect interactions with persons different from you or be a barrier to good communication.

Low health literacy and difficulty understanding and using health information compound problems for patients with limited English proficiency. Use lay terminology rather than medical jargon (e.g., say 'heart attack' not 'myocardial infarction,' 'stroke/brain attack' not 'cerebrovascular accident'), unless you know the patient is a health care professional.

Patients function through various roles (family, occupation, activities) that influence identity and preferred manner of communicating. Stereotyping a person according to roles can be misleading and should be avoided.

The urge to maintain an exclusive right to certain space. Patients behave differently when interviewed in their homes versus institutional settings because they feel comfortable in areas they consider their own.
The nurse–patient relationship in which the focus is on the patient's needs and goals; the nurse's own needs are temporarily set aside. It varies in depth, length, and focus.

Three phases: (1) orientation phase, (2) identification and exploration (working) phase, and (3) resolution (termination) phase (Peplau, 1952). The communication process follows the sequence of the nursing process; both are continuous and reciprocal.

Assuming that patients who are health care professionals know everything about their condition and need little teaching can be hazardous. Always provide an opening for the patient to verbalize needs regardless of role.

A professional relationship between nurse and patient organized into three phases—orientation, working, and termination—each with specific patient goals. In modern brief-hospitalization settings, phases may function as different emphases rather than a strict sequence.

The initial phase in which the tone and guidelines for the relationship are established; the nurse and patient identify each other by name, clarify roles, and establish an agreement (contract) about goals, contacts, and duration.

Usually the longest phase of the nurse–patient relationship where the nurse works with the patient to meet physical and psychosocial needs through purposeful interactions designed to achieve mutually agreed-upon health goals.

The phase occurring when the conclusion of the initial agreement is acknowledged; the nurse and patient examine goal attainment or progress, and the patient is encouraged to express emotions about the ending.

The patient will call the nurse by name, accurately describe roles of the participants, and establish an agreement with the nurse about goals, location/frequency/length of contacts, and duration of the relationship.
The patient will actively participate in the relationship, cooperate in activities toward mutually acceptable goals, and express feelings and concerns to the nurse.
The patient will participate in identifying goals accomplished or progress made toward goals and will verbalize feelings about the termination of the relationship.

An agreement, usually a simple verbal exchange related to goals and the means of achieving them, established between nurse and patient; may occasionally be a written document for long-term relationships.

A characteristic or customary way of behaving; nurses who consistently demonstrate warmth, friendliness, openness, rapport, empathy, honesty, authenticity, trust, caring, and competence are well disposed to communicate effectively.

A dispositional trait in which a pleasant greeting and friendly smile facilitate the orientation phase and place the patient at ease; maintaining these qualities conveys continuous acceptance of the patient.
One key factor to effective communication—being open, accepting, frank, respectful, and without prejudice; patients who feel a nurse is being judgmental might withhold significant information.

cards.term: Relating to Patients from Different Cultures (Box 8-4)
cards.def: Assess personal beliefs and cultural communication variables; plan care based on communicated needs and cultural background; modify communication approaches (slow, distinct speech, gestures, simple messages); use validating techniques and culturally sensitive interpreters.

Patients should be able to trust that nurses are who they say they are (professional caregivers) and can be trusted to do everything within their level of expertise to secure resources and meet patient needs.

Patients sense whether they are merely a 'task to be performed' (task-centered caring) or a person of worth who is both cared about and cared for (relation-centered caring). Patients who feel cared for will feel accepted.

Competent nurses are skilled in all aspects of basic nursing and can meet patients' health care needs through technical, cognitive, interpersonal, and ethical/legal skills. Patients develop trust and respect for competent nurses, facilitating therapeutic relationships.
A feeling of mutual trust experienced by people in a satisfactory relationship. Rapport facilitates open communication and is a necessary first step in planning care.

Having a purpose for an interaction provides guidance toward achieving a meaningful encounter. Even the shortest encounter can have an objective; be flexible and follow the patient's cues to meet all needs.

A comfortable environment in which both patient and nurse are at ease promotes interactions. Suitable furniture, proper lighting, moderate temperature, and a relaxed, unhurried atmosphere are important; communication is impaired if the nurse seems preoccupied.

Every effort should be made to provide privacy and prevent conversations from being overheard by others. Merely drawing curtains around the bed or sitting in a corner can provide the sense of privacy important in most interactions.
Communication in the nurse–patient relationship should focus on the patient and patient needs, not on the nurse or an activity in which the nurse is engaged.

Observations, which involve both effective noticing and interpreting, are especially useful for validating information. Observation serves several important purposes: it helps increase awareness of a patient's nonverbal messages; it is the primary source of information when a patient is unwilling or unable to communicate verbally; it demonstrates caring and interest in the patient; and it is an important component of clinical reasoning and clinical judgment.

Consider the pace of any conversation or encounter; it is more effective to let the patient set the pace. Let the patient know at the beginning if time is limited so they do not feel rushed because of a lack of concern.

Therapeutic communication focuses on the patient's needs and allows the patient to verbalize concerns, while nontherapeutic communication blocks the process by focusing on the nurse's needs, dismissing patient feelings, or conveying disbelief.
The study of the meaning of words. Even when two people speak the same language, some words—such as love, hate, freedom, and health—might have different meanings to different people.

A skill that involves both hearing and interpreting what the other says. It requires attention and concentration to sort out, evaluate, and validate clues to better understand the true meaning of what is being said.

Sit when communicating; do not cross arms or legs; maintain eye contact if culturally appropriate; think before responding; do not pretend to listen; listen for themes, inconsistencies, and gaps in the patient's comments.

Allows the patient to gather their thoughts and proceed at their own pace. Periods of silence can mean contentment, stoicism, exploring inner thoughts, fear, anger, or culturally required pauses; excessive talking by the nurse places focus on the nurse rather than the patient.

A powerful means of communication with multiple meanings. It can connect people, provide affirmation, reassurance, and stimulation; decrease loneliness; increase self-esteem; and share warmth, intimacy, approval, and emotional support. Touch is the most highly developed sense at birth.
A technique in which a trained nurse uses touch to promote comfort, relaxation, healing, and a sense of well-being. It is a widely accepted form of therapy and a subject for nursing research.

Valued as both an interpersonal skill for the nurse and a healing strategy for patients. Laughter releases excess physical and psychological energy and reduces stress, anxiety, worry, and frustration; when used inappropriately, however, it can be destructive.

The purpose is to obtain accurate and thorough information; it is a major tool for collecting data during the assessment step of the nursing process. All interviews should begin with an explanation of the purpose of the interview.

A technique that allows the patient a wide range of possible responses; it encourages free verbalization and more descriptive information and prevents the patient from giving a simple yes or no answer that limits response.

Provides the receiver with limited choices of possible responses and might often be answered by one or two words. Used to gather specific information and allow the nurse and patient to focus on a particular area.

Make statements as simple as possible and stay on one subject at a time to prevent confusion. Avoid words that might have different interpretations, especially since patients are often anxious and may fail to understand complex messages.
A patient who is given false information will soon distrust the nurse. If unsure about something, admit you don't know and seek an answer rather than make a comment that may be an error.
A question or comment that serves to validate what the nurse believes they have heard or observed. Overuse may lead the patient to think the nurse is not listening.

A question that allows the nurse to gain understanding of a patient's unclear comment and prevent misconceptions. The nurse should never assume understanding of the patient's meaning; ask for clarification if there is doubt.
A technique involving repeating what the person has said or describing the person's feelings. It encourages patients to elaborate on their thoughts and feelings.
Used to place events in chronologic order or investigate a cause-and-effect relationship between events. Nursing assessment is facilitated when events leading to a problem are placed in sequence.

Used to obtain more information about a topic brought up earlier or to introduce a new aspect of the current topic, helping the nurse gain additional information for assessing health status and educational or counseling needs.

The ability to stand up for yourself and others using open, honest, and direct communication; the focus is on the issue and not the person. Uses 'I' statements ('I feel…', 'I think…') and expresses views without judgment, belittlement, or blaming.

Factors that block effective communication, including failure to verbalize clearly and compassionately. Recognizing the patient as a human being, listening carefully, and avoiding nontherapeutic statements help overcome these barriers.

cards.term: Failure to Perceive Patient as Human Being
cards.def: Treating the patient as merely an object of care rather than a whole person. Patients should be addressed by their preferred name; err on the side of formality and use neutral, inclusive language—avoid slang like 'honey' or 'sweetie.'
Assertive statements beginning with 'I feel…' or 'I think…' that play an important role in expressing feelings and beliefs in a nondefensive manner. A hallmark of assertive nursing communication.

A stereotyped, trite, or pat answer. Most health care clichés suggest that there is no cause for anxiety or concern, or they offer false assurance; patients tend to interpret them as a lack of real interest in what they have said.

Questions that can be answered by simply saying yes or no tend to cut off discussion, even when the person might wish to continue. The problem arises when seeking more detailed information or when the question might create difficulty (e.g., asking a postop patient 'Are you ready to get out of bed?').
Questions using the words why and how may be intimidating to many patients. They are better rephrased as what-questions (e.g., 'What were you doing while you were unable to sleep?').

Questions that too obviously probe for information might cut off communication. Patients made to feel as though they are receiving the 'third degree' become resentful and stop talking; it is better to follow the patient's lead and let the patient take the initiative.

Giving advice often implies that the nurse knows what is best for patients and denies them the right to make decisions and have feelings. It also tends to increase the patient's dependence on caregivers, though advice has a rightful place when requested and backed by expert knowledge.

A quick way to stop conversation is to change the subject. Rejection of a topic by the nurse closes it off from exploration; the patient might feel frustrated or personally rejected along with the expressed ideas or topic.

Nurses might try to convince the patient that things will turn out well even when the chances are not good. False assurance gives the impression that the nurse is not interested in their problems and impedes communication; if used inadvertently, explain with an apology.

Common forms of communication ('the grapevine') that can produce detrimental effects on relationships and group building. Both might cause blocks to team building and damage the reputations of the people who are the subject of the information.

Rude, disruptive, intimidating, and undesirable verbal and nonverbal communication and behaviors directed at another person. It also includes failing to act when action is warranted, such as refusing to assist a coworker or remaining silent while others are treated with disrespect.

Anger and aggressive behavior between nurses (nurse-to-nurse hostility), also called lateral violence or professional incivility. Bullying occurs when a person is subjected to persistent intimidating behaviors—covert (withholding info, gossiping, eye-rolling, isolation) or overt (scapegoating, public humiliation).

Violent acts, including physical assaults and threats of assault, directed toward persons at work on duty. Patient and/or family violence ranges from verbal harassing, threatening, yelling, and hostile sarcasm to physical slapping, punching, biting, and throwing of objects.

Clearly developed policies and procedures must be in place, including a policy of zero tolerance regarding disruptive behaviors. Protection must be provided for those who report these behaviors and communication.

cards.term: Communication as First Line of Defense
cards.def: Communication is the first line of defense against patient violence. Nurses should use effective therapeutic communication techniques to build trust, establish rapport, meet patient and family expectations, and validate feelings.

When disruptive behavior occurs, maintain a professional demeanor, respond assertively, and address the issue directly with those involved. If not possible, ask to speak to the person in private and address disrespectful remarks; document the occurrence of any bullying behaviors.

Education for all staff on respectful professional behavior; all staff held accountable; zero-tolerance policies with whistleblower protection; leadership training and role modeling; surveillance and reporting systems; emphasis on documenting bullying behaviors.

Threats or violent behavior require a calm attitude before interacting with the aggressor; being upset will escalate the situation. Assertiveness and aggression training are effective in addressing these issues.

Proactive response includes learning how to react professionally and protectively in the moment; documenting and reporting the incident; welcoming new nurses; using conflict-management strategies; and insisting that the disruptive behavior is addressed.
A decreased, delayed, or absent ability to use speech. Impaired communication can affect every aspect of a person's life including learning, working, and social interaction.

Using diminutive words, exaggerated voice intonation, high pitch, and exaggerated punctuation that imply the older adult is not competent. It is non–person-centered communication based on stereotypes of older adults and is a form of ageism.

Use a calm and reassuring approach, nonverbal gestures to aid understanding, and seek clarification and validation to ensure messages are conveyed. Communication adjustments must be respectful, positive, and individualized.

Acknowledge your presence, identify yourself by name, speak in a normal tone, explain the reason for touching before doing so, indicate when conversation ends and when leaving, keep a call light within reach, and orient the patient to sounds.

Health care institutions should develop workplace violence prevention programs, document reports of violence, investigate reported events in a timely manner, and provide training on workplace violence for all workers. OSHA guidelines describe five components of an effective program.
A disease state that results from the presence of pathogens in or on the body. A six-part process must occur in order for an infection to occur.
The six-part process of infection: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, means of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Nursing interventions target breaking this chain.

Microorganisms that cause disease: bacteria (E. coli, staphylococcus, streptococcus), viruses (HIV, common cold, influenza, COVID-19, hepatitis A,B,C), fungi (athlete's foot, ringworm, yeast infections), parasites (malaria from mosquitos infected with a parasite).
Potential sources where pathogens live: people, animals, soil, food, water, milk, objects.
Routes pathogens enter the human body: respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary tracts, skin breakdown, blood & tissues.
Routes pathogens leave the human body: respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary tracts, skin breakdown, blood & drainage.
Direct contact: close proximity, touching, kissing, sexual intercourse. Indirect contact occurs through a vector or a fomite.
A living creature that transmits a pathogen to humans.
An inanimate object that harbors a pathogen. Nurses' equipment and objects in the environment can act as fomites.
Organisms greater than 5um (micrometer) attach to dust particles. Droplets are heavy enough to land on surfaces.
Organisms less than 5um (micrometer) attach to dust particles. Airborne particles remain in the air.

A host at risk for infection: multiple wounds/poor skin integrity (multiple portals of entry), pH levels of GI and GU tracts and skin, WBC count, age, sex, heredity, immunity, fatigue, nutritional status, pre-existing illness, medications, stress, and invasive or indwelling medical devices.
Immunity may be natural, acquired, or passive. It is one factor determining whether a host is susceptible.

cards.term: Factors that make an organism thrive
cards.def: Quantity of organism, virulence, the patient's immune system, how long the organism + patient were in contact, and what type of contact they had.
Four stages: incubation period, prodromal stage, full stage of illness, and convalescent period.
The stage before symptoms appear; examples: common cold 1-2 days, tetanus 2-21 days.
Lasts hours to days; the patient may report nonspecific symptoms such as being too tired to hold up the head with a low-grade fever.
The stage in which the infectious illness is fully manifested, following the prodromal stage and preceding convalescence.
Illness resolved, period of recovery, return to baseline health. There may be a temporary or permanent change in the patient's previous health.
A person can continuously cycle through the same infectious process; HSV is the example given.
Methods to prevent infection, divided into medical asepsis ("clean technique") and surgical asepsis ("sterile technique").

Reduces the number of pathogens: hand hygiene, wearing gloves, not placing dirty/soiled linen on the floor, avoiding raising dust, practicing clean-to-dirty technique, disposing of dirty linens directly into the hamper, and pouring contaminated liquids directly into the drain or "hopper" to prevent splashing.

Eliminates the number of pathogens by creating and maintaining a pathogen-free environment. Required for procedures such as foley catheters and central line placement/dressing changes; uses sterile gloves, mask, hair net, gowns, etc.
Practice moving from clean to dirty areas/objects when providing care to reduce the number of pathogens transferred.
1) Before touching a patient, 2) before a clean or aseptic procedure, 3) after body fluid exposure risk, 4) after touching a patient, 5) after touching patient surroundings.
Also known as hospital acquired/nosocomial infections; infections patients develop during hospitalization.
Catheter Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI), Surgical Site Infection (SSI), Central-Line Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI), and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP).
Vancomycin Resistant Enterococci; a multidrug-resistant organism found in feces, urine, and blood.
Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus; found in the nares, on the skin, or in the GI tract.
Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacteriaceae; a multidrug-resistant organism prevalent in hospitalized patients.
Clostridium Difficile; a multidrug-resistant organism found in feces.
Equipment used to protect the nurse: gloves, gown, masks, and protective eye-wear.

Used in the care of all hospitalized patients regardless of their diagnosis or possible infection status. Apply to blood, all body fluids, secretions, and excretions except sweat (whether blood is present or visible), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes.
Respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practices, and directions to use a mask when performing high-risk prolonged procedures involving spinal canal punctures.
Used in addition to standard precautions for patients with suspected infection with pathogens transmitted by airborne, droplet, or contact routes. A disease may have multiple routes of transmission.
Proper donning of PPE when entering the room of a patient on contact or droplet precautions; proper doffing of PPE when leaving the room.
Infection spreads by large particle droplets. Private room, door can stay open, surgical mask and gloves.
For patients infected or colonized by a multi drug resistant organism (MDRO). Private room, gown and gloves, change gloves after contacting infective material, clean all equipment; do not share.
For infections that spread through the air. Private room, negative air pressure, door closed, patient remains in room, respirator mask; surgical mask on patient for transport.
Recommended for severely immunocompromised & immunosuppressed residents receiving any cancer treatment or transplants. Applies to residents with WBC below 500 cells/mm3 (µL).

The cyclic process by which infection occurs: (1) infectious agent, (2) reservoir, (3) portal of exit, (4) means of transmission, (5) portals of entry, (6) susceptible host. The goal is to break the links of the chain to end the cycle.
Disease-producing microorganisms that cause infection when present in or on the body. Not all organisms to which a person is exposed cause disease.

A living being where an infectious, parasitic, or pathogenic agent resides and receives sustenance. Whether an organism causes disease depends on the type of organism, its location, the host, and the circumstances.

Drugs that treat infections by killing or slowing the growth of microbes causing infection; bacterial infections are treated with drugs called antibiotics. Antimicrobials technically include antifungals and drugs that treat parasites and viruses (CDC, 2019g).

The most significant and commonly observed infection-causing agents in health care institutions. Aerobic bacteria require oxygen to live and grow; anaerobic bacteria can live without oxygen. Categorized by shape (cocci, bacilli, spirochetes) and Gram-stain reaction.

Gram-positive bacteria have a thick cell wall that resists decolorization and stain violet; gram-negative bacteria have chemically more complex walls, are decolorized by alcohol, and do not stain. This is crucial for prescribing appropriate antibiotic therapy.

The smallest of all microorganisms, visible only with an electron microscope. Viruses cause infections including the common cold, hepatitis A/B/C, and HIV; antibiotics have no effect on viruses, but some antiviral medications decrease severity and duration.

Plantlike organisms (molds and yeasts) present in air, soil, and water that can cause infection (e.g., athlete's foot, ringworm, yeast infections). Treated with antifungal medications, though many fungal infections are resistant to treatment.
Organisms that live on or in a host and rely on it for nourishment. Malaria occurs when a parasite infects a mosquito that then feeds on humans.

The ability of an organism to cause disease. An organism's potential to produce disease depends on the number of organisms, its virulence, the competence of the person's immune system, and the length and intimacy of contact.

Not all organisms cause disease; potential depends on: (1) number of organisms, (2) virulence of the organism, (3) competence of the person's immune system, (4) length and intimacy (extent) of contact between person and microorganism.
A disease that occurs with predictability in one specific region or population. Example: malaria endemic in parts of Africa south of the Sahara.
A global outbreak of a novel (new or not previously identified) virus that does not initially have a known immunization or treatment. Example: SARS-CoV-2 / COVID-19 starting in 2019.
Microorganisms that commonly inhabit various body sites and are part of the body's natural defense system. Under normal conditions, some organisms may not produce disease.
A typically harmless organism that may generate an infection, especially in susceptible people. Example: E. coli residing in the intestinal tract migrates to the urinary tract and causes a UTI.
An organism (e.g., C. diff) resides in a person's body but there are no clinical signs of an infection. Microscopic exams reveal the bacteria, yet the person is not infected.

A person who acts as a reservoir for an infectious agent but does not exhibit any manifestations of the disease. Carriers, although asymptomatic, can transmit the disease (e.g., HIV-positive individual).

Requires close proximity between the susceptible host and an infected person or carrier; includes touching, kissing, and sexual intercourse. Health care workers can directly transmit organisms by touching.
Involves personal contact with either a vector (living creature) or a fomite (inanimate object). Proper hand hygiene and glove use can interrupt transmission from nurses to patients.

Airborne particles are smaller than 5 μm (micrometer), and droplet particles are greater than 5 μm. This distinction matters when designing prevention strategies such as masks, social distancing, and PPE.
Susceptibility is the degree of resistance the potential host has to the pathogen. Hospitalized people are often weakened and have less resistance, making them more susceptible to infection.

An infection progresses through four phases in order: (1) Incubation period, (2) Prodromal stage, (3) Full (acute) stage of illness, (4) Convalescent period. Understanding these stages is necessary to intervene and disrupt the infection cycle.
The presence of infection-specific signs and symptoms indicates the full stage. Symptoms limited to one body area are localized; symptoms manifested throughout the entire body are systemic.

Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function, usually appearing at the site of the injury/invasion. These result from the vascular phase (vasodilatation, histamine release) and cellular phase (neutrophil infiltration).

Vascular phase: vessels constrict then dilate, increased blood flow causes redness/heat; histamine increases permeability causing swelling, pain, loss of function. Cellular phase: neutrophils engulf organisms; exudate is released from the wound.
Exudate is composed of fluid, cells, and inflammatory byproducts released from the wound. It may be clear (serous), contain red blood cells (sanguineous), or contain pus (purulent).

Foreign material (antigen) triggers the body to produce an antibody (antigen–antibody reaction = humoral immunity). Cell-mediated immunity involves increased lymphocytes that destroy cells recognized as harmful.

Skin/mucous membrane integrity, GI/GU/skin pH, WBC count, age (neonates & older adults more vulnerable), immunity, fatigue/nutrition/health status, stress, invasive devices, and health habits all influence host susceptibility.
Skin, mucous membranes, and the body's normal flora (especially GI tract) are considered first-line defenses. If pathogens pass these, the inflammatory and immune responses help combat infection.

The most effective way to help prevent the spread of infectious agents. Applies to handwashing with plain soap and water, use of antiseptic handrubs including waterless alcohol-based products, or surgical hand antisepsis.
Identifying people with an infectious disease and locating individuals and groups with whom they have come into direct contact to interrupt actual or potential transmission of the infectious disease.
Redness, swelling, warmth in the involved area, pain or tenderness, and loss of function of the affected part.
Fever often accompanied by an increase in pulse and respiratory rate, lethargy, tenderness and enlargement of lymph nodes, and anorexia.

cards.term: Atypical Infection Signs in Older Adults
cards.def: Confusion, disorientation, lethargy, anorexia, delayed fever response, falls, incontinence, and failure to thrive.
Ways to decrease the spread of pathogens, including hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE), and other barrier techniques. Barriers break the infection cycle.
Estimated 1 in 31 hospitalized patients with an HAI, a decrease since the original 2011 survey. Most healthcare-associated pathogens are transmitted via contaminated hands of healthcare workers.
Average baseline compliance for handwashing was only 34.1%; it increased to 56.98% after multimodal educational and motivational interventions.

cards.term: Expected Patient Outcomes for Infection Control
cards.def: Patient will: demonstrate effective hand hygiene and good personal hygiene practices; identify the signs of an infection; maintain adequate nutritional and fluid intake; demonstrate proper disposal of soiled articles; use appropriate cleansing and disinfecting techniques; verbalize awareness of the necessity of proper immunizations; implement stress-reduction techniques; adhere to infection control precautions (isolation, equipment, visitors); and verbalize an understanding of health risks associated with a latex allergy.

Includes inquiring about immunization status and previous infections, observing for signs of local or systemic infection, and reviewing laboratory data. Extent of interventions depends on susceptibility of host, virulence of organism, and patient signs and symptoms.

WHO (2020c) defined five critical moments: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure or risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings.

Occur on hands with activities of daily living; relatively few in number, attached loosely in grease, fats, and dirt; found in greatest number under fingernails. Can be removed relatively easily by frequent and thorough handwashing.

Normally found in skin creases, usually stable in number and type, and cling tenaciously to skin by adhesion and absorption. Considerable friction with a brush is required to remove them; less susceptible to antiseptics than transient bacteria.
Have an alcohol concentration between 60% and 95% and are available as foam, gel, or lotions. In most situations they more effectively reduce bacterial and viral counts than antimicrobial soap.
Considered adequate for routine mechanical cleansing of the hands and removal of most transient microorganisms. They work by lowering surface tension and acting as emulsifying agents.
Recommended in any setting where the risk for infection is high; when present in certain concentrations these agents can kill bacteria or suppress their growth.

CDC guideline (2002) specifies health care personnel involved in patient care should not wear artificial nails because they are more likely to be associated with higher bacterial counts; wearing them in the OR is a citable Joint Commission offense.
Natural nails should be less than 1/4 inch long to prevent harboring microorganisms.
Mean hand hygiene compliance internationally is 59.6%, which falls below the accepted standard that ranges from 80% to 90%. Nurses are at 43.4%, physicians 32.6%, and other staff 53.8%.

cards.term: Box 25-2 – Basic Principles of Medical Asepsis
cards.def: Complete list of the box: (1) practice good hand hygiene; (2) carry soiled linens or used articles/equipment so they do not touch your clothing; (3) do not place soiled bed linen or other items on the floor; (4) avoid allowing patients to cough, sneeze, or breathe directly on others—provide disposable tissues and instruct them to cover mouth and nose to prevent spread by airborne droplets; (5) move equipment away from you when brushing, dusting, or scrubbing articles; (6) avoid raising dust—use a treated or dampened cloth and do not shake linens; (7) clean the least soiled areas first, then the more soiled ones; (8) dispose of soiled or used items directly into appropriate containers, wrapping items moist with body discharge/drainage in waterproof containers or plastic bags first; (9) pour discarded liquids (e.g., bath water, mouth rinse) directly into the drain to avoid splattering; (10) sterilize equipment suspected of containing pathogens; (11) use personal grooming practices that limit spread of microorganisms (shampoo hair regularly, keep hair short or pinned up, keep fingernails short with intact cuticles and no ragged edges, avoid rings with grooves or stones); (12) conscientiously follow standard and transmission-based precaution guidelines as prescribed by your facility.

Used before direct patient contact, after contact with skin or body fluids (if hands not visibly soiled), after removing gloves, before inserting urinary/vascular catheters, before donning sterile gloves for invasive procedures, when moving from contaminated to clean body site, and after contact with patient environment objects.

cards.term: Hand Hygiene Project / Targeted Solutions Tool (TST)
cards.def: The Joint Commission project using a step-by-step process to measure actual performance, identify barriers, and direct proven solutions. Results included a 45% reduction in HAIs and savings up to $2.8 million in direct medical costs.
