Wear PPE if contact with blood or body fluids is a possibility; use additional protective equipment (gowns, masks, goggles, face shields) as appropriate; dispose of used/contaminated objects in leak-resistant plastic trash bags; never recap used or contaminated needles; place sharps in puncture-proof containers.
Avoid allowing patients to cough, sneeze, or breathe directly on others; provide disposable tissues and instruct them to cover mouth and nose to prevent spread by airborne droplets.

Transient bacteria can adjust to the skin environment when present in large numbers over a long period and become resident bacteria. If pathogenic organisms become resident, the hands become carriers; clean hands promptly when visibly soiled, after contact with contaminated materials, and after removing gloves.

Apply 3 mL (usually two pumps) to palm of one hand. Rub hands together covering all surfaces, fingers, between fingers, fingertips, and under fingernails. Continue rubbing until hands are completely dry—at least 20 seconds.

Less effective with Cryptosporidium, norovirus, and C. diff (alcohol does not kill C. diff spores, only vegetative forms). Soap and water are the preferred hand hygiene method when these infections are suspected or diagnosed.

Required when hands are visibly soiled or contaminated with blood/body fluids, before eating, and after using the restroom. Requires at least a 20-second scrub with plain or antimicrobial soap and warm water; visibly soiled hands need a longer scrub.

A lengthier scrub before assisting with a surgical procedure to reduce resident and transient flora on forearms and hands. Since 2002 CDC recommends antimicrobial soap or alcohol-based surgical scrub; alcohol-based agents significantly reduce scrub time.
An infection that develops as a result of medical care and may occur in hospitals, rehabilitation facilities, outpatient settings, and dialysis centers. The term HAI has replaced 'nosocomial.'
An infection in which the causative organism is acquired from other people or sources outside the patient's body.
An infection that occurs when the causative organism comes from microbial life already harbored in the person's own body.
An infection that results from a treatment or diagnostic procedure performed on the patient.
Typically three to five evidence-based practices that, when implemented together, improve patient outcomes for preventing HAIs.

Approximately 12%–16% of hospitalized adults have an indwelling urinary catheter; each patient has a 3%–7% increased risk of acquiring a CAUTI each day the catheter remains in place. ANA focus areas: prevention of inappropriate short-term use, timely nurse-driven removal, and catheter care during placement.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention includes elevating the head of the bed to 30–45 degrees, providing regular oral care, and changing the ventilator circuit only as needed.

Microorganisms (primarily bacteria) resistant to one or more antibiotic classes. Key resistant organisms include MRSA, VRE, and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE). Indiscriminate broad-spectrum antibiotic use drives resistance.

cards.term: CDC Four Core Actions to Fight Resistance
cards.def: 1) Prevent infections to prevent spread of resistance; 2) Track resistant organisms; 3) Improve antibiotic prescribing/stewardship; 4) Develop new drugs and diagnostic tests.
Seven tracked targets include CAUTI, SSI, CLABSI, invasive MRSA infections, and C. diff infections (CDIs) and CDI hospitalizations.

Approximately one third of people in the United States are colonized with S. aureus, meaning the organism is present (typically in the nose) but the person has no symptoms and remains healthy and uninfected. They can still pass the organism to others.

A strain of S. aureus resistant to methicillin that emerged in the 1960s; vancomycin became the treatment. In health care settings, main mode of transmission is direct contact with contaminated hands of personnel or indirect contact with equipment.

A type of MRSA that appeared in the wider community in the late 1990s; a common cause of skin and soft tissue infections. Those most at risk are young children, older adults, and people in close physical proximity (athletes, military, inmates, daycare attendees).

Once bacteria develop drug resistance, they progress from being sensitive to an antibiotic, to an intermediate resistance, followed by complete resistance to the antibiotic. Prudent use of vancomycin is an important preventive measure.

Enterococci (a species of Streptococcus found in normal GI and GU tracts) that develop resistance to vancomycin; can cause HAIs with a high mortality rate. Spread via contact with feces, urine, or blood of an infected or colonized person.

Very difficult-to-treat organisms (e.g., Klebsiella, E. coli) associated with a 40% to 50% mortality rate; resistance to carbapenems leaves few treatment options. CDC recommends placing the patient on contact precautions with a focus on hand hygiene and prevention education.

A gram-negative bacterium found primarily in hospitals that has developed resistance to many antibiotic regimens, severely limiting treatment options. Because A. baumannii can sustain itself in the environment, the room and all equipment must be cleaned and disinfected to eliminate fomite transmission.

Caused by antibiotic use (particularly broad-spectrum) that destroys helpful bacteria, allowing C. diff to grow out of control. Watery diarrhea, fever, and mild abdominal cramping are common signs; both symptomatic and asymptomatic people and contaminated surfaces serve as reservoirs.

CDI is not killed by alcohol-based handrubs, so soap and water are required for hand hygiene. Full-barrier contact precautions (gown and gloves) and terminal cleaning with sporicidal agents are also essential.

Disinfection destroys all pathogenic organisms except spores; sterilization destroys all microorganisms, including spores/endospores. Disinfection is used for skin prep or non-sterile-body equipment; sterilization is for equipment entering a sterile body part.

Choice of sterilization/disinfection method depends on: nature and number of organisms present, type of equipment (lumens, crevices), intended use of equipment, available means, and time. Failure to follow recommended time periods is grossly negligent.

Per OSHA ruling, health care facilities must provide employees with equipment and supplies necessary to minimize or prevent exposure to infectious material. PPE includes gloves, gowns, masks, and protective eye gear (Skill 25-2, pp. 695-700).

Gloves are not a substitute for good hand hygiene; they are worn only once, discarded per facility policy, then hands are decontaminated with meticulous hand hygiene. Each patient interaction requires a clean pair, and gloves must be changed before moving from a contaminated task to a clean one.
Wearing two gloves on one hand is recommended when exposure to blood or body fluids is expected (e.g., OR setting). Evidence indicates glove perforations were reduced by 71% with double gloving.
Higher temperature caused by higher pressure destroys organisms (e.g., autoclaving). Caution: most plastic and rubber devices are damaged by autoclaving.
Simple and inexpensive method frequently used in the home; boil the item for at least 10 minutes. Caution: spores and some viruses are not destroyed by boiling.
Used for metal items; heat oven to 350°F for 2 or more hours. Insufficient to destroy all microorganisms and not used in health care facilities.

Destroys microorganisms and spores/endospores by interfering with metabolic processes in cells; used for oxygen/suction gauges and blood pressure equipment. Caution: the gas is toxic to humans, so precautions are necessary.

Chemical solutions are used for instrument/equipment and housekeeping disinfection; a 1:100 dilution of sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) effectively inactivates human immunodeficiency virus. Method does not destroy all spores and may corrode metal.

(1) Irritant contact dermatitis – irritated, dry hands from glove contact, not an allergy; (2) allergic contact dermatitis (type IV) – localized pruritus, erythema, urticarial lesions 24 to 96 hours after contact; (3) true latex allergy (type I) – immediate systemic response that may result in anaphylaxis.

Approximately 10% of health care workers and 1% to 2% of the general population are sensitized to traditional latex. There is no cure for a latex allergy; prevention is avoidance of latex-containing products.

Occupational exposure to latex; allergic tendencies; food allergies to banana, papaya, avocado, potatoes, kiwi fruit, chestnuts, and pineapples; asthma, spina bifida, or multiple surgical procedures. Diagnosis: RAST blood test for IgE antibodies or skin prick test.

Gowns prevent soiling of the health care worker's clothing by the patient's blood and body fluids and are donned immediately before entering the room. Individual gown technique involves wearing a gown only one time and then discarding it; a waterproof or impervious gown is used for likely contact with blood or body fluids.

Masks prevent dissemination of biologic particles and protect against large particle pathogens (>5 μm) in respiratory droplets that typically travel less than 3 ft (up to 6 ft); a surgical mask filters only expired air. A particulate respirator (e.g., N95) filters inspired air to prevent inhalation of airborne droplet nuclei or small particle aerosols (≤5 μm) that remain suspended and travel longer distances.

A mask is typically worn only once and is not lowered around the neck and brought back over the mouth and nose for reuse. Regardless of the time worn, a mask must be changed before it becomes damp from the wearer's exhalations.

A particulate respirator that filters airborne particles as small as 1 μm with 95% efficiency and fits comfortably against the face; it is NIOSH approved and meets CDC guidelines for tuberculosis exposure control. Elastic straps give more protection and a better fit than regular surgical mask ties.
A particulate respirator filters inspired air; a surgical mask filters only expired air. Respirators are required for airborne transmission risks, masks are not equivalent protection.

Fit-testing is required to ensure health care workers use the appropriate mask size; once a fit test determines the best respirator size, a seal check is done every time the respirator is worn to ensure an adequate seal.

A single-occupancy patient room designed for airborne transmission with negative pressure, an air flow rate of 6 to 12 air changes per hour, and direct venting of exhaust to the outside or use of a HEPA filter. A NIOSH-certified N95 or higher respirator must be worn when entering for known or suspected tuberculosis.
High efficiency particulate air filter used to treat exhaust air in AII rooms when direct venting to the outside is not used.

Goggles or a face shield must be available whenever there is risk of contaminating the mucous membranes of the eyes (e.g., suctioning a tracheostomy, procedures that may splatter blood or body fluids). Plain glasses are unacceptable because side shields are required.

Used to dispose of trash containing liquid or semiliquid blood or other potentially infective material (OPIM), trash contaminated with blood or OPIM that would release these substances if compressed, and trash caked with dried blood or OPIM.
The broader term (associated with health care delivery in any setting) that replaced the narrower term nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection in the 2007 CDC guideline.

Precautions used in the care of all hospitalized patients regardless of diagnosis or possible infection status; they apply to blood, all body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), nonintact skin, and mucous membranes. New elements include respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practices, and mask use for high-risk prolonged spinal canal punctures.

Precautions used in addition to standard precautions for patients with suspected infection with pathogens transmitted by airborne, droplet, or contact routes. PPE is donned when entering the patient's room and removed only when leaving the room.
Airborne, droplet, and contact precautions may be used alone or in combination, but always in addition to standard precautions; a disease may have multiple routes of transmission.

Elements include education of staff and patients, posted instructions, source control (masks on coughing patients, tissues for sneezes), reinforcement of hand hygiene, and spatial separation. Coughing patients should maintain more than a 3-ft separation from others.

Avoid recapping used needles; if recapping is necessary use the one-handed scoop technique or a recapping device, never two hands. Use safety-engineered needles, single-dose vials when possible, disposable needles and syringes for each injection, and puncture-resistant sharps containers.
Wear a face mask if placing a catheter or injecting material into the spinal or epidural space (high-risk prolonged procedures involving spinal canal punctures).

Public health recommendation of 6 ft separation reflecting the estimated distance of SARS transmission, complemented by handwashing as the foundation of all infection control practices and restrictions on large indoor gatherings.
Wear a face mask when placing a catheter or injecting material into the spinal or epidural space to prevent contamination.

Wear a respirator when entering the room of a patient with known or suspected tuberculosis. For rubeola (measles) or varicella (chicken pox), respiratory protection is worn unless the person entering the room is immune to these diseases.
Transport the patient out of the room only when necessary and place a surgical mask on the patient if possible (applies to airborne and droplet precautions).

OSHA standard developed in 1991 to protect health care workers from exposure or risk of exposure to pathogens such as HIV and HBV. Revised in 2000 by the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act with additional employer specifications and worker involvement requirements.

Requires health care providers to identify and provide safer medical devices to reduce sharps injuries, involve health care workers in device selection, provide engineering controls (sharps disposal containers, self-sheathing needles), educate employees on safe use, and develop a sharps injury surveillance log.

National survey data (170 hospitals in 2016, 224 in 2017) show sharps injury rates have risen every year for the last 3 years and now match rates reported in 2001–2005. Close to 40% of injuries occurred in surgery; teaching hospitals had higher rates than nonteaching hospitals.

cards.def: Indicators of physiologic functioning that reflect the health status of a person. Include temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and pain level.

On admission, per facility policy, any change in patient's condition, loss of consciousness, before/after surgical or invasive procedures, before/after high-risk activity (e.g., ambulation after surgery), before administering cardiovascular/respiratory medications, or whenever the patient reports change in status, pain, or distress.

The hypothalamus controls thermoregulation by conserving body heat or increasing heat loss. It reflects the difference between the amount of heat produced by the body and the amount of heat lost to the environment.
Core body temp locations include intracranial, intrathoracic, and intra-abdominal sites. These are the most accurate sources for core temperature.
The body's tissues and cells function best between 36°C to 37.5°C (98.6°F).
Predictable fluctuations in body temperature—lower in the morning, peak between 1500-1800.

Time of day, biologic sex, age, physical activity, state of health, and environmental temperatures. Older adults' sensitivity to temperature changes is decreased; extreme cold may lead to hypothermia, extreme heat may lead to hyperthermia.
When a patient has an increased temperature they are considered febrile; non-fever is afebrile. Signs/symptoms include loss of appetite, headache, hot dry skin, thirst, muscle aches and fatigue.
Extremely high temperature above 40°C (>104°F) is dangerous; ≥41°C (106°F) is a medical emergency.

Fever is a sign of immune response and an important defense mechanism. Treatment aims to provide comfort and prevent complications: pharmaceutical (antipyretics; treatment of bacterial infection) and non-pharmaceutical (cool bath, cooling blankets, removing excess clothing/blankets, oral fluids to prevent dehydration).

Symptoms include poor coordination, slurred speech, amnesia, hallucinations, stupor; respirations, HR, and B/P decrease. Treatment: raise body temp and promote warmth with warm blankets, warm fluids, and Bair Hugger.

Place thermometer in posterior sublingual pocket under the tongue (close to carotid artery). No hot/cold drinks or smoking 20 min prior; patient must be awake and alert. Not for small children. Leave in place 3 min.

Place bulb in center of axilla with lower arm positioned across chest. Non-invasive and good for children but less accurate (no major vessels nearby). Leave in place 5-10 min. Measures 0.5°C lower than oral temp.

Side lying with upper leg flexed; insert lubricated bulb 1-1½ inch for adults. Used when unsafe or inaccurate by mouth (unconscious, disoriented, or irrational). Leave in place 2-3 min. Measures 0.5°C higher than oral.
Close to hypothalamus and sensitive to core temp changes. For adults, pull pinna up and back. Rapid measurement (2-3 seconds) but cerumen impaction or otitis media can distort reading.

Left ventricle contracts causing a wave of blood to surge through arteries; felt by palpating artery lightly against underlying bone or muscle. Assess rate, rhythm, and amplitude via palpation and auscultation.
Carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.

Place 2nd, 3rd, or 4th fingers lightly on skin where an artery passes over an underlying bone. Do not use your thumb. Count 30 seconds × 2; if irregular, count radial for 1 min and then apically for a full minute.
The beat of the heart at its apex or point of maximal impulse. Auscultate for a full minute, listening for "Lub-Dub." Auscultate for apical; palpate for peripheral pulses.
Normal adult pulse rate is 60-100 bpm with an average of 80 bpm.
An abnormal increase in pulse rate (above 100 bpm).
An abnormal decrease in pulse rate (below 60 bpm).
The pattern of the beats—assessed as regular or irregular.

The volume of blood pushed against the wall of an artery during ventricular contraction. Described as weak/thready (lacks fullness), full/bounding (volume higher than normal), or imperceptible (cannot be felt or heard).
Gas exchange between oxygen and carbon dioxide; both autonomic and voluntary. Inspiration is inhalation (breathing in) and expiration is exhalation (breathing out).
Observe rate, rhythm, and depth after taking pulse while still holding the hand, so the patient is unaware you are counting respirations.
Normal adult respiratory rate is 12-20 breaths/min; 1 cycle = inhale + exhale.
Abnormal increase in respiratory rate (above 20 breaths/min).
Abnormal decrease in respiratory rate (below 12 breaths/min).
Absence of breathing (periods of no breathing).
Difficulty or labored breathing; adventitious digressions from normal effortless breathing. Orthopnea is difficulty breathing laying down.
Force exerted by the blood against vessel walls. Systolic is the highest pressure created during contraction; diastolic is the lowest pressure on artery walls during relaxation.
Normal is less than 120/80 mmHg.
Readings lower than 90 mmHg systolic or 60 mmHg diastolic.
Systolic between 120-129 and diastolic of 80 mmHg.
Systolic 130-139 mmHg, diastolic 80-89 mmHg.
Systolic >140 mmHg, diastolic >90 mmHg.
Blood pressure greater than 180 mmHg systolic. This is a critical emergency situation.

Cuff size is judged by arm circumference, not age. Cuff should cover 40% of arm circumference and bladder should cover 2/3 of the arm. Support arm at heart level, palm upward; above heart causes false low reading. Cuff too wide = false low; too narrow or too loose = false high.
A series of sounds created as blood flows through an artery after it has been occluded with a cuff and cuff pressure is gradually released.
Do not use a limb with a PICC line, arteriovenous (AV) fistula, or on the side of a mastectomy for blood pressure assessment.
Non-invasive measurement of oxygen saturation; calculates SpO2 (pulse oxygen saturation) as a reliable estimate of arterial oxygen saturation. Probes can be placed on finger, ear, nose, or toe.
Remove thick nail polish. Wait until readout reaches constant value and pulse display reaches full strength. During continuous monitoring, inspect skin under the probe routinely and rotate the probe.
A pain assessment tool used for verbal, aware patients to evaluate pain.
Assessment data that may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition in addition to changes that occur progressively over time.
A baseline set of VS are important to identify changes in the patient's condition.
VS may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition; a deviation from baseline signals a status change.
Changes in a client's condition that occur progressively over time and are detected through VS measurement.
A change identified by comparing current VS to the client's baseline; the learner is asked, 'What do you think is the source of his change in health status?'
An assessment finding judged to be within the expected or standard range of values.
The benchmark values used for comparison when judging VS findings.
A client's normal range can be different from our standard values; individual norms must be considered.
Considerations that go 'besides numbers' when assessing VS.
When assessing VS, consider factors other than the numeric values alone.
The data used as the basis to identify and prioritize client problems related to vital signs.
Based upon assessment information, identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs.
Ranking the identified vital sign–related problems, e.g., the top 3 client problems, to guide care.
The highest-priority problems related to vital signs selected from the assessment findings.
A vital sign that may be elevated and require interventions to decrease it prior to medication administration.
Interventions taken to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration.
Actions the nurse can take to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration.
Temperature-lowering interventions are implemented prior to medication administration.
A vital sign that may be increased in the patient; an increased respiratory rate prompts further assessment.
Since the patient has an increased respiratory rate, additional assessment is conducted to determine if he has adequate oxygenation.
Determined by conducting further assessment when the patient has an increased respiratory rate.
Additional assessment conducted to determine if the client with an increased respiratory rate has adequate oxygenation.
A baseline set of VS plus current values are important to identify changes in the patient's condition.
A client's normal range can be different from our standard values, so values are judged in context of the individual client.
Body temperature is the difference between the amount of heat produced by the body and the amount of heat lost to the environment measured in degrees.

Normal body temperature ranges from 96.7° to 100.5°F (35.9° to 38°C), depending on the site and individual. Core body temperature (intracranial, intrathoracic, and intraabdominal) is higher than surface body temperature.
Heat is generated by metabolic processes in the core tissues of the body, transferred to the skin surface by the circulating blood, and then dissipated to the environment.

Assess on admission; per facility policy; any time there is a change in condition or loss of consciousness; before/after surgery or invasive procedures; before/after risky activity (e.g., ambulation after surgery); and before administering medications that affect cardiovascular and respiratory function.

Frequency should be based on the patient's medical diagnosis, comorbidities, treatments and medications, level of acuity and risk for complications, trends in vital signs, prescribed interventions, and facility policies. At minimum, hospitalized patients with abnormal parameters are assessed at 4-hour intervals.

Although vital sign assessment may be delegated to other health care personnel when the patient is stable, it is the nurse's responsibility to ensure the accuracy of the data, interpret vital sign findings, and report abnormal findings. If a patient has abnormal signs or unexpected changes in vital signs, the nurse should validate findings and further assess the patient.

Vital signs, along with oxygen saturation level, have been identified as the best indicators of cardiopulmonary arrest, unplanned ICU admission, and unexpected death. Monitoring and evaluation of trends in intermittently measured vital signs is important for early identification of risk for a serious adverse event.

Normal vital sign ranges vary across the life span; the nurse should know normal variations in vital signs that occur at various ages as listed in Table 26-1 and understand potential variations related to specific health conditions and illnesses.
Core body temperature refers to the temperature of intracranial, intrathoracic, and intraabdominal tissues and is higher than surface body temperature, which is measured at the skin surface.

cards.term: Key terms – temperature & vital sign vocabulary
cards.def: Important terms include: afebrile (without fever), febrile/pyrexia (fever), hypothermia (low body temperature), hyperthermia (high body temperature), tachycardia, bradycardia, tachypnea, bradypnea, apnea, dyspnea, hypertension, hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, Korotkoff sounds, auscultatory gap, pulse deficit, pulse pressure, systolic/diastolic pressure.

cards.term: Appropriate times to measure vital signs
cards.def: Examples include screenings at health fairs and clinics, in the home, upon admission to a health care setting, when medications are given that affect cardiac rate and rhythm, before and after invasive diagnostic and surgical procedures, and in emergency situations.

The core body temperature of a healthy person is maintained within a fairly constant range by the thermoregulatory set point of the thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus. This center receives messages from cold and warm thermal receptors and initiates responses to produce/conservate or increase heat loss.

Body temperature can vary as much as 1.0°F (0.5°C) during a day and is usually lower in the early morning than in the late afternoon and early evening. The peak elevation of a person's temperature occurs between 3 and 6 PM.

The skin is the primary site of heat loss. Heat is transferred to the external environment through radiation, convection, evaporation, and conduction, regulated by arteriovenous shunts under sympathetic nervous system control.

Intermittent: temperature returns to normal at least once every 24 hours. Remittent: does not return to normal, fluctuates a few degrees. Sustained/Continuous: remains above normal with minimal variations. Relapsing/Recurrent: returns to normal for one or more days with one or more episodes of fever.

Hyperthermia differs from fever in that the hypothalamic set point is not changed, but in situations of extreme heat exposure or excessive heat production, the mechanisms that control body temperature are ineffective.

Neurogenic fever is the result of damage to the hypothalamus from pathologies such as intracranial trauma, intracranial bleeding, or increased intracranial pressure. This type of fever does not respond to antipyretic medications.

A fever of 38.3°C (101°F) or higher that lasts for 3 weeks or longer without an identified cause after a minimal diagnostic workup is identified as a FUO. Causes include infections, malignancies, cirrhosis, and noninfectious inflammatory diseases.

Antipyretic (fever-reducing) drugs, such as aspirin, ibuprofen, or acetaminophen, reset the elevated set point regulated by the hypothalamus. Aspirin is not recommended for anyone younger than 19 years of age during fever-causing or flulike illnesses.

When the thermostatic set point is increased by a pyrogen, the hypothalamus initiates shivering, piloerection, vasoconstriction, and increased metabolism. After temperature rises to the new set point, heat-loss mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation, increased respirations) prevent dangerous levels.

Patients with fever may experience loss of appetite, headache, hot dry skin, flushed face, thirst, muscle aches, and fatigue. Respirations and pulse rate increase; infants may have febrile seizures and older adults may experience confusion or delirium.

The purposeful lowering of the core body temperature to improve outcomes after brain injury, during certain surgeries, and after cardiac arrest. Decreased body temperature reduces metabolic rate and oxygen demand to improve survival and neurologic outcomes.

Patients may experience poor coordination, slurred speech, poor judgment, amnesia, hallucinations, and stupor. Respirations decrease and the pulse becomes weak and irregular with lowering blood pressure.

Rewarming can be accomplished by covering with additional clothing and blankets, use of heating blankets and pads, and radiant warmers. Warm fluids are administered orally or IV; additional treatment includes support of vital functions and prevention of complications.

A blanket-sized aquathermia pad that conducts cooled distilled water through coils. Apply lanolin to skin contact areas; cover pad with a sheet; insert rectal/skin/esophageal probe; monitor vitals and neurologic status every 15 min; observe for shivering; turn off when temp reaches 1 degree above desired temperature.
To convert Fahrenheit to Celsius, subtract 32 and multiply by 5/9. To convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9/5 and add 32.

Not used in health care institutions due to federal safety recommendations (EPA). Nurses should encourage patients to use alternative devices such as digital thermometers and include patient teaching in the plan of care.

Measure oral, rectal, or axillary temperature over a few seconds to 60 seconds. Battery-operated with numerical display and disposable probe covers to reduce microorganism transmission. Calibration and charging must be maintained.

Uses infrared sensors to detect heat from the tympanic membrane, reflecting carotid artery blood temperature. Reading takes 1 to 3 seconds. Studies conflict regarding accuracy, especially with temperature elevations; proper technique and calibration are essential.

Measures body temperature by capturing heat emitted by the skin over the temporal artery. Operator technique and cleanliness of the lens can influence the reading; studies conflict regarding accuracy with temperature elevations.

Nonbreakable and register temperature within seconds. Because they are used only once, they eliminate the danger of cross-infection and are sometimes used for patients requiring transmission-based precautions.

Although measurement may be delegated to assistive personnel, the nurse is responsible for assessing findings, assessing effects of changes in body temperature, implementing interventions, and teaching patients/caregivers about measurement methods, normal values, and communicating abnormal findings.

Nondisposable thermometers shared among patients can transfer microorganisms to room surfaces, equipment, providers, and other patients. Cleaning and disinfection of thermometers before and after use are critical interventions.

The probe is placed under the tongue in the sublingual pocket; this site is not suitable for children younger than 6 years old, patients unable to follow directions, or those with oral mucosa changes. Normal oral temperature readings range from 96.6° to 99.5°F (35.9° to 37.5°C).

Infrared sensors in the thermometer sense heat from the tympanic membrane; the thermometer does not touch the membrane. Normal tympanic temperature readings range from 98.2° to 100.9°F (36.8° to 38.3°C).

The thermometer is swiped across the forehead over the temporal artery; do not measure over scar tissue, open lesions, or abrasions. Normal temporal artery temperature readings range from 98.7° to 100.5°F (36.3° to 38.1°C).

Measures body temperature by capturing heat emitted by the skin; suggested for fever screening, not ongoing monitoring. Place the device in the room 10 to 30 minutes prior to use and measure in a draft-free space, out of direct sun, and away from radiant heat sources.

Applied to the abdomen or forehead, these devices change color at different temperature ranges; this method is inaccurate and a thermometer should be used to reassess if the reading is out of the normal average range.

Used to measure body temperature, pulse, respirations, and blood pressure simultaneously; temperature sensors may be part of invasive devices (pulmonary artery catheters, rectal probes, bladder catheters) for continuous core temperature measurement.
If a temperature is obtained from a site other than the oral route, document the site with the result; if no site is listed, it is generally assumed to be the oral route.

Do not assess oral temperature in patients who cannot close their mouth around the probe, those with oral cavity disease or surgery, seizure risk, or patients receiving oxygen by mask (risk of serious drop in blood oxygen). Wait 15 to 30 minutes after hot/cold food, fluids, smoking, or chewing gum.

A throbbing sensation palpated over a peripheral artery resulting from a wave of blood pumped by left ventricular contraction; strength of the pulse reflects the amount of blood ejected with each beat. Pulses may be felt wherever an artery passes over a solid structure such as bone or cartilage.

Characteristics of the peripheral pulse include rate, rhythm, strength (amplitude), and elasticity; these indicate effectiveness of the heart as a pump, stroke volume, and adequacy of peripheral blood flow.

Auscultated over the apex of the heart; heart sounds ('lub-dub') result from closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves ('lub') and aortic and pulmonic valves ('dub'). The combination of the two sounds is counted as one beat.

The pulse rate is the number of pulsations felt over a peripheral artery or heard over the apex of the heart in 1 minute. This rate normally corresponds to the same rate at which the heart is beating.
The normal pulse rate for adolescents and adults ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute (beats/min). Normal pulse rates change across the life span, gradually diminishing from birth to adulthood.

Pulse strength (amplitude) refers to and describes the quality of the pulse in terms of its fullness; it indicates the volume of blood flowing through the vessel and reflects the strength of left ventricular contraction. The peripheral pulse may be documented as full and bounding when it is forceful, or weak and thready when it is decreased in quality. Bounding pulses may occur with the early stages of septic shock, exercise, fever, fluid volume excess, and anxiety. Heart failure, hypovolemia, shock, hypernatremia (elevated plasma sodium level), and arrhythmias can cause decreased pulse strength.
Grade 0 = absent, unable to palpate; +1 = diminished, weaker than expected; +2 = normal, brisk, expected; +3 = bounding. Nurses should be familiar with the grading system used at their facility.

The normal artery feels smooth, straight, and resilient (springy); this is referred to as the elasticity of the artery. Arterial blood vessels become less elastic with increased age, resulting in a more rigid, less-resilient, and crooked vessel.

The pulse is regulated by the autonomic nervous system through the sinoatrial (SA) node, the pacemaker of the heart. Parasympathetic stimulation via the vagus nerve decreases heart rate; sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and force of contraction.

Key factors include age, biologic sex, physical activity, body temperature (fever increases and hypothermia decreases pulse), stress (pain, fear, anxiety increase pulse), medications (may increase or decrease), and the presence of disease/health conditions. Compensatory mechanisms attempt to maintain sufficient blood supply to cells at all times.

The diaphragm is a large flat disk more useful for hearing high-frequency sounds such as respiratory sounds because it screens out low-frequency sounds. The bell is hollowed and curved, screens out high-frequency sounds, and is more useful for low-frequency sounds such as those made by the heart and blood vessels.

The pulse may be assessed by palpating peripheral arteries, by auscultating the apical pulse with a stethoscope, or by using a portable Doppler ultrasound. Electrocardiography and cardiac monitoring may also be used to assess pulse rate and rhythm.
A Doppler ultrasound device may be used to assess pulses that are difficult to palpate or auscultate. The device has an audio unit with an ultrasound transducer.

The radial pulse site is assessed most often in children and adults, but is difficult to palpate in children younger than 2 years; the apical pulse should be auscultated for 1 minute for these patients. The femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis sites assess leg and foot circulation; the carotid is used in emergencies.

When taking a carotid pulse, lightly palpate only one side at a time to prevent any decrease in cerebrovascular circulation. The brachial pulse site is used most often for infants in emergency situations.

Clean the stethoscope diaphragm; warm it on the palm; palpate the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line; place the diaphragm over the apex of the heart; listen for 'lub-dub' sounds (each 'lub-dub' = one beat); count for 1 minute; note rhythm; clean diaphragm; perform hand hygiene.

Counting the pulse at the apex of the heart and at the radial artery simultaneously assesses apical–radial pulse rate. A difference between the two rates is called the pulse deficit and indicates that all heartbeats are not reaching the peripheral arteries, suggesting insufficient cardiac force or volume and decreased tissue perfusion.

Two nurses are needed; one listens over the apex and the other counts at the radial artery. One watch with a sweep second hand is placed so both nurses can read it; both count for 1 full minute starting at the same time. The difference between the two counts is the pulse deficit.

Apply conducting gel to the transducer probe; hold the probe perpendicular to the skin and move slowly until the pulse is heard; count the heartbeat for 1 minute and note rhythm; wipe off gel; record rate, rhythm, site, and that Doppler was used; return the device to the charge base.

Respiration involves ventilation, diffusion, and perfusion. Ventilation (breathing) is movement of gases in and out of the lungs; diffusion is the exchange of O₂ and CO₂ between the alveoli and circulating blood; perfusion is the exchange of O₂ and CO₂ between blood and tissue cells.

Ventilation (breathing) has both autonomic and voluntary control. Inspiration (inhalation) is the act of breathing in, and expiration (exhalation) is the act of breathing out. The component measured as a vital sign is ventilation, more commonly called respirations.

The respiratory rate decreases with age, ranging from a normal range of 30 to 60 breaths/min in a newborn to 12 to 20 breaths/min in an adult. Respiratory rate abnormalities are important predictors of deteriorating patient conditions and serious events, including cardiac arrest.

An increase in carbon dioxide is the most powerful respiratory stimulant, causing an increase in respiratory depth and rate. The cerebral cortex allows voluntary control of breathing, such as when singing or playing a musical instrument.
Normal, unlabored respiration. Healthy adults breathe about 12 to 20 times each minute; infants and young children breathe more rapidly (Table 26-1, p. 718).
An increase in both the rate and depth of respirations. May result from hypoxia, anxiety, exercise, or metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis / Kussmaul's respirations).
Shallow, slow respiration with decreased rate and depth; may be irregular. Related to increased intracranial pressure, sedation, or narcotic/anesthetic overdose.

Alternating periods of deep, rapid breathing followed by periods of apnea; rhythm is regular. Associated with cerebral vascular disease, severe traumatic brain injuries, drug overdose, heart failure, increased intracranial pressure, and renal failure.
Varying depth and rate of breathing followed by periods of apnea; rhythm is irregular. Associated with severe brain stem injury, meningitis, and severe brain damage.

A condition in which a patient can breathe more easily and comfortably in an upright position but experiences shortness of breath when lying flat. Gravity lowers abdominal organs away from the diaphragm, giving lungs more room for expansion. May be associated with pulmonary edema, heart disease, and COPD.
The highest pressure exerted on arterial walls during ventricular contraction (systole), when blood is pushed through the aortic valve into the aorta.
The lowest pressure present on arterial walls when the heart rests between beats during ventricular diastole.
The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures. For example, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, the pulse pressure is 40 mm Hg.

Pressure-sensitive receptors located in the heart and walls of arteries (e.g., aortic arch, carotid). They detect changes in vessel stretch from blood pressure changes and send impulses to the cardiovascular center to adjust heart rate and vascular smooth muscle accordingly.
Systolic 120–129 mm Hg and diastolic less than 80 mm Hg. A single elevated reading is not necessarily significant; factors such as pain, anxiety, and acute conditions can raise BP.

Blood pressure that is above normal for a sustained period. It is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, CVA (stroke), MI, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, and abdominal aortic aneurysm; called a 'silent killer' because there are often few symptoms beyond increased blood pressure.

A sustained decrease in systolic BP of ≥20 mm Hg or a decrease in diastolic BP of ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing or during a head-up tilt test to at least 60 degrees. Older adults at risk are at increased risk for falls.
A sustained reduction in blood pressure that occurs after 3 minutes of standing or upright tilt. It is distinguished from classic orthostatic hypotension by the delayed onset.
A transient reduction in systolic BP of ≥40 mm Hg and/or a transient decrease in diastolic BP of ≥20 mm Hg within 15 seconds of standing. Symptoms are not necessary for diagnosis.

Age (decreased arterial elasticity), circadian rhythm (lowest on arising, rises 5–10 mm Hg by late afternoon), biologic sex (women lower until menopause), food intake (BP rises after eating), exercise (systolic rises), weight (higher in obese), emotional state (anger, fear, pain raise BP), body position (lower when prone/supine), race (more prevalent in African Americans), and drugs/medications (oral contraceptives cause mild increase).

First raise the head of the bed, then assist the patient to a sitting position on the side of the bed ('dangling') for a few minutes to assess for dizziness or faintness, and then assist to standing. Educate patients to arise and move slowly, especially after bed rest.

Diuretics (decrease fluid volume); ACE inhibitors (block conversion of angiotensin I to II, preventing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release); ARBs (block angiotensin II receptors); vasodilators and calcium channel blockers (relax arteriolar smooth muscle, decrease peripheral resistance); beta-adrenergic blockers (block sympathetic stimulation, decrease cardiac output).

A decrease in systolic BP of ≥20 mm Hg or diastolic BP of ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing compared with sitting or supine position. In patients with hypertension (supine systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg), a drop of at least 30 mm Hg systolic is more appropriate.

Have patient lie supine 3–10 min, take initial BP/pulse; assist to sit on the side of the bed with legs dangling 1–3 min, take BP/pulse; assist to stand (unless contraindicated) and take BP/pulse at 30 sec and 60 sec after standing, then again at 2 min and 3 min (four sets of standing measurements). Record the measurements for each position. Return patient to a supine position immediately if symptoms appear during the procedure; do not have the patient stand if symptoms of hypotension occur while sitting.

Educate patients to arise and move slowly after bed rest. First raise head of bed, then assist to sitting (dangling) a few minutes, then stand. Return to supine if dizzy/faint. Administer contributing medications at bedtime if possible; ensure hydration; compression stockings may be used.

The standard clinical method of measuring blood pressure using a stethoscope and sphygmomanometer to detect the appearance and disappearance of the Korotkoff sounds, which represent systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Select a cuff with a bladder length 75%–100% of the arm circumference and a width 37%–50% of the arm circumference, with a length-to-width ratio of 2:1. Incorrect cuff size is the most frequent error in nonacute care settings.

If the cuff is too narrow, the reading is erroneously high because pressure is not evenly transmitted to the artery. If the cuff is too wide, the reading may be erroneously low because pressure is dispersed over a disproportionately large surface area.

Blood pressure is recorded as two numbers written as a fraction (e.g., 120/80 mm Hg). The first number is the systolic pressure; the second number is the diastolic pressure. Measurements should be obtained as two or more readings on two or more occasions and averaged.

Measure in a quiet environment; patient should not have consumed caffeine, exercised, or smoked for 30 min prior; patient should not talk or move. Arm supported at heart level; back and feet supported; legs not crossed to avoid inaccurate readings.

Supine systolic BP may be up to 10 mm Hg higher and diastolic up to 5 mm Hg higher than seated. Lack of back support can raise systolic up to 15 mm Hg and diastolic up to 6 mm Hg. Crossed legs can raise systolic up to 8 mm Hg and diastolic up to 5 mm Hg.

Automated, electronic devices for BP measurement that have been validated for accuracy while reducing human errors associated with the auscultatory approach. Growing evidence supports their use in clinical settings.
The cuff should be pulled taut on the bare limb with comparable tightness at top and bottom. One finger should fit easily at top and bottom; two fingers should fit but be very snug.

Instrument used with a stethoscope to assess blood pressure in the auscultatory method; consists of a cuff (with air compartment), a pump, and the manometer (pressure dial). The cuff is inflated to occlude the underlying artery, then gradually deflated to reestablish flow.

Automated, electronic method that determines BP by analyzing sounds of blood flow or amplitude of oscillations in blood flow during cuff deflation/inflation; reports systolic, diastolic, and mean BP. Devices must be validated, calibrated per manufacturer guidelines, and used with careful technique.
First appearance of faint but clear tapping sounds that gradually increase in intensity; the first tapping sound is the systolic pressure.
Phase II: muffled or swishing sounds that may temporarily disappear; Phase III: distinct, loud sounds as blood flows relatively freely through an increasingly open artery.

Phase IV: distinct, abrupt muffling sound with a soft, blowing quality; Phase V: last sound heard before loss of all sounds, and the pressure at which the last sound is heard is the diastolic pressure. If sounds persist to zero (e.g., pregnancy, AV fistula), record phase IV (e.g., 112/62/0).

Disappearance of sound during the latter part of phase I and during phase II, which may cover a range as much as 40 mm Hg. Failure to recognize this gap may cause serious errors of underestimating systolic or overestimating diastolic pressure.

Systolic is the first number and diastolic the second in the fraction (e.g., 120/80 mm Hg); read measurements to the nearest even number (nearest 2 mm Hg). Follow facility policy and be consistent in taking and documenting readings.

Include noncalibrated/nonvalidated device, incorrect cuff size, patient movement or talking, incorrect cuff placement or patient positioning, incorrect limb positioning, too-rapid cuff inflation, and deflation faster than 2 to 3 mm Hg per second. Also environmental noise, no rest period, incorrect interpretation, and reliance on a single-occasion reading.
Deflate the cuff no faster than 2 to 3 mm Hg per second; too-rapid deflation is a documented source of blood pressure measurement error.

Noninvasive, fully automated method recording BP over an extended period (e.g., 24 hours, awake or asleep), usually every 20–30 minutes during the day and hourly at night. Useful to confirm hypertension, identify BP patterns, and monitor antihypertensive therapy; office readings are often higher than ambulatory/home readings.

Indirect BP measurement using a Doppler device that amplifies sounds, especially useful when sounds are indistinct or inaudible with a regular stethoscope; this method provides only an estimate of systolic blood pressure.

BP measured via a thin catheter inserted into an artery (most commonly radial or femoral — an arterial line/A-line); the catheter tip senses pressure and transmits a waveform displaying systolic and diastolic pressures. Used primarily in intensive care.
The brachial and popliteal arteries are most commonly used; the radial site may be used with very large or obese upper arms, and the ankle may be used when upper-arm measurement is not possible.
